title: Watson Lecture: Katie Bouman Discusses Imaging the Invisible
author: Caltech Media Relations (mr@caltech.edu)
summary: How can we extend the limits of observation to “see” the seemingly invisible? On Wednesday, November 4, 2026, Katie Bouman, professor of computing and mathematical sciences, electrical engineering and astronomy; Rosenberg Scholar; and a Heritage Medical Research Institute Investigator, will share how her lab combines physics and machine learning to see things in the universe that are invisible to traditional sensors.
text:
How can we extend the limits of observation to "see" the seemingly invisible? On Wednesday, November 4, 2026, Katie Bouman, professor of computing and mathematical sciences, electrical engineering and astronomy; Rosenberg Scholar; and a Heritage Medical Research Institute Investigator, will share how her lab combines physics and machine learning to see things in the universe that are invisible to traditional sensors.
In a public talk titled "Illuminating the Hidden Universe with Physics and AI," Bouman will explain how scientific images are increasingly constructed rather than simply captured, not only in extreme astrophysics—such as through black hole imaging—but also in other disciplines.
For centuries, traditional cameras and photography have been modeled on the human eye, Bouman explains. "But if we want to see things that traditional cameras can't, we need to rethink what a camera can be. Instead of simply trying to capture what our eyes would see, we can design sensors that collect information in entirely new ways, then use algorithms and machine learning to fill in missing pieces. The key is doing this responsibly, making sure that what we reconstruct is still grounded in the physics of the measurements we actually collect."
Growing up in West Lafayette, Indiana, Bouman was often encouraged by her father, a professor of electrical engineering, to explore scientific pursuits. One of her earliest memories of doing science was constructing and launching a tissue-paper hot-air balloon with him. Through middle and high school science projects analyzing fingerprint images and investigating whether people all perceive colors in the same way, Bouman developed an early interest in images and visual perception that would eventually lead her to study in the field of computational imaging. Bouman earned her bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the University of Michigan in 2011 and later completed her master's and doctoral studies in electrical engineering and computer science at MIT in 2017. Prior to Caltech, she was a postdoctoral fellow with the Event Horizon Telescope, which published the first picture of a black hole in 2019.
Starting at 6 p.m., members of Katie Bouman's lab will be present to answer questions about their research.
About the series
The Watson Lectures offer new opportunities each month to hear how Caltech researchers are tackling society's most pressing challenges and inventing the technologies of the future. Join a community of curiosity outside Beckman Auditorium to enjoy food, drinks, and music together before each lecture. Interactive displays related to the evening's topic will give audience members additional context and information. The festivities start at 6 p.m. Guests are also encouraged to stay for post-talk coffee and tea as well as the chance to chat with attendees and researchers.
Watson Lectures are free and open to the public.
Advance registration for Bouman's talk is full. Guests who have not registered are still welcome to attend the preshow, which does not require registration, beginning at 6 p.m., featuring food, music, and interactive displays.
After the preshow, non-ticketed guests interested in attending the talk may join our standby line by 6:50 p.m.
A recording will be made available on our YouTube channel.
Learn more about the topic at Katie Bouman's speaker page.

title: Elections Are More Predictable than They Look
author: Katie Neith (katien@caltech.edu)
summary: Social scientist Jonathan N. Katz has helped develop the first generatively accurate statistical model of US congressional elections that can simulate whole elections, reproduce the patterns we see in real election data, and better inform the current political landscape.
text:
As politics in America become more polarized and each voting cycle seems more fraught than the last, a common narrative in the media is that each election is unique and increasingly unpredictable. But new research shows that congressional elections follow strong statistical patterns, even when individual races produce surprises.
"There are a lot of generalities and systematic things happening in elections," says Jonathan N. Katz, Caltech's Kay Sugahara Professor of Social Sciences and Statistics. "It's not to say that there aren't interesting stories, but, overall, elections are very predictable, and I don't think the general public thinks about them that way. Patterns help estimate the odds, but close races—and control of Congress—can remain uncertain."
To help illustrate the effects of different data points on predictions and give people a practical tool with which they can build their own Election Day scenarios, Katz teamed up with former graduate student Danny Ebanks (PhD '24), now a research associate at Harvard's Institute for Quantitative Social Science (IQSS), and political scientist Gary King, the Weatherhead University Professor at Harvard University and director of IQSS, to build a forecasting website called ElectIt. The interactive tool draws on decades of election data that the team assembled—with the help of AI—covering every US House election since 1946 and Senate election since 1954 as well as the current races.
Katz has been modeling election dynamics for more than three decades. The forecaster is one product of a larger project with Ebanks and King: building the first generative statistical model that can simulate whole elections and that accurately describes congressional elections. King, a longtime collaborator of Katz's (he was Katz's postdoctoral advisor at Harvard), had co-developed what became the canonical model for legislative elections in the 1990s with statistician Andrew Gelman. Seven years ago, Katz, Ebanks, and King tried to port that model to a modern programming language and noticed a major flaw.
"The model actually didn't fit very well; results that it treated as less than one-in-10,000 events in individual races showed up in almost every other congressional election cycle," Katz explains. "For example, it badly underestimated how often popular incumbents lose their seats. We tried lots of different models to make one that worked better and finally came up with a framework that fits the data. The forecaster is one application of it."
Unlike many election-prediction models seen in popular media, ElectIt's core model uses no polls at all. Instead, it draws on decades of statistical data—such as past results; which candidates are running and whether one is an incumbent; and the midterm penalty, which is the tendency of the president's party to lose support in midterm elections. That information is used to build three types of forecasts: the "post-nomination forecast," which acts as a baseline, using the candidates and past results but no polls; the "model + generic ballot," which accounts for changes in the national political environment by adding national surveys that ask which party's congressional candidate people plan to vote for; and the "model + all polls," which adds available state- and district-level polls.
"It's a fun tool with lots of bells and whistles that let you adjust and play around with things, like you can call different elections, and it will update the entire map," says Katz, who hopes the public might use it during watch parties on November 3. "On election night, when the Associated Press starts calling races, you can put them into our app, and it will tell you how the probabilities update."
Iterating on the model required rewriting it to run on graphics processing units (GPUs)—a switch made with the help of AI coding tools and substantial GPU computing time. AI tools also helped build the website and construct new measures from historical data, such as statewide election results broken down by congressional district.
"No model is perfect. But one of the key things that we were able to do with AI programming is backfill data on things like gubernatorial elections and presidential elections," Katz says. "Most of this was possible without tools like Claude and Codex, but painfully slow. Without them, we couldn't have iterated on the model the way we did."
The researchers tested their new model by fitting it to earlier elections and checking its forecasts against later results. After the election, Katz says the results will provide another test of the model.
"We can compare the results with our predictions to learn where the model works and where it needs improvement," he explains. "An unexpected result can prompt further investigation, but it is not by itself evidence that anything went wrong with the election." Surprises, he adds, can have ordinary explanations, such as a scandal or an unusually strong challenger.
Katz notes that the team's approach emphasizes transparency: Election data, forecasts, and assessments of historical accuracy are available on the ElectIt forecasting website. A paper that describes their methods, "If a Statistical Model Predicts That Common Events Should Occur Only Once in 10,000 Elections, Maybe it's the Wrong Model," is under review at the journal Political Analysis.
"I'm not in this for forecasting elections," Katz says. "What Gary and Danny and I are interested in is understanding American politics, understanding elections. But in order to make plausible claims about things, we think you have to have a generally accurate model, and ours does forecast really well."
As of October 21, the ElectIt forecasting site was averaging 500,000 Google impressions a day, according to Katz. Build your own forecast at: https://gking.harvard.edu/electit.

title: $7 Million Gift Establishes New HSS Lab in Environmental Economics and Policy Design
author: Katie Neith (katien@caltech.edu)
summary: Funding from the WHH Foundation will bring together multidisciplinary expertise to help find a balance between development and environmental protection.
text:
One of the most effective ways to protect the environment is to make markets work for environmental goals rather than against them, using tools such as tradable permits and payments for ecosystem services. But doing that requires measurements and data: How much of a resource exists, how is it changing, and what is it worth to society? Until recently, that information hasn't been available to the decision-makers developing environmental policy.
A new Caltech lab will soon bridge that gap—combining economics, policy design, and new measurement tools such as satellite imaging and machine learning to inform environmental policy. The lab is being established through a $7 million infusion of funding from the WHH Foundation, a private family philanthropic organization.
"Good environmental policy design requires input from multiple fields," says Prakash Mishra, assistant professor of economics, who will co-lead the lab with Hannah Druckenmiller, assistant professor of economics and a William H. Hurt Scholar. "We need access to remote-sensing data; an understanding of interactions across ecosystems and biomes, which natural scientists supply; and a clear framework for how to trade off the opportunity to develop with the costs of growth on these ecosystems. This lab brings these tools together, with an end goal of proposing policy design."
The new Policy and Environmental Research on Markets, Institutions, and Trade, or PERMIT, Lab will bring together an interdisciplinary team of graduate students, postdocs, and researchers who share the common purpose of exploring environmental policy that strikes a balance between protecting the environment and allowing for development.
"The most exciting thing about the WHH gift is that it will allow us to invest in people over the long term," Druckenmiller says. "We can now support graduate students and postdocs for long enough to build the unique combination of skills in economics, policy, and environmental measurement that make a real impact on environmental policy. That time also helps grow our lab members into leaders in the field."
The WHH Foundation was founded by the late William H. Hurt, a longtime friend of the Institute, member of the Caltech Associates, and former Capital Group Companies executive, who supported research and teaching endeavors at Caltech. For example, he and his wife previously endowed the William H. Hurt Scholars Program to support early-career faculty, like Druckenmiller, and multidisciplinary research. The new grant from their family foundation will provide funding support for 10 years of lab activities.
"We are thrilled to partner with the WHH Foundation on this new HSS initiative," says Tracy Dennison, the Edie and Lew Wasserman Professor of Social Science History and Ronald and Maxine Linde Leadership Chair of the Division of the Humanities and Social Sciences. "Programmatic funding from the foundation will enable the PERMIT Lab to recruit and retain exceptional researchers, helping Hannah and Prakash create the kind of interdisciplinary lab environment that their research requires."
Collaboration is a key focus of the lab; the team plans to work with scientists and engineers at Caltech who have developed or use measurement tools that can help answer policy questions. Druckenmiller and Mishra have active collaborations with faculty and students in the Division of Engineering and Applied Science and the Division of Geological and Planetary Sciences as well as with several groups at NASA's JPL, which Caltech manages for the agency. To build an audience for sustainability policy on campus, they also engage with Caltech's Resnick Sustainability Institute and with the Linde Center for Science, Society, and Policy, which have brought economists and scientists in the sustainability space to campus and funded early-stage research.
"We are also hopeful that, over time, our lab alumni move on to opportunities at universities, policy-facing think tanks, or in government," Mishra says. "The opportunity to keep in touch with this network will open doors to collaborating with organizations outside of Caltech."
Beyond collaboration, Mishra says the long-term investment will allow for researchers—himself and Druckenmiller included—to work on ambitious multiyear projects with large-scale data collection efforts. These efforts may focus on continental land-protection strategies and the US-wide ramifications of regulation or even global forest cover.
"Building expertise at this scale requires long-term thinking and lots of dedicated smart people looking at the same data in order to make informed choices," he says.
Druckenmiller notes that she and Mishra are also committed to ensuring that the lab's work is actually used by decision-makers and not just published in academic journals. Caltech, with its strengths in science and engineering, and its expertise in remote sensing through partnerships with JPL, is the ideal place to do this work, she says.
One example of the work the lab will support is a wetlands project led by Druckenmiller. Wetlands are a valuable resource; they provide water filtration and wildlife habitats, and absorb floodwaters. But, Druckenmiller notes, it is difficult to factor that value into decisions about whether a wetland should be conserved or developed, in large part because it is hard to measure. In collaboration with Caltech's Georgia Gkioxari, assistant professor of computing and mathematical sciences and electrical engineering and a William H. Hurt Scholar, Druckenmiller is developing methods to use AI to estimate the value of ecosystems, location by location, across the entire country, starting with the flood protection value of US wetlands.
"If it works, it will give communities and regulators a clearer picture of what is at stake when an ecosystem is lost," Druckenmiller says.
In another ongoing project, Mishra is trying to understand a deceptively simple question: How much should beef cost? The production of beef involves large environmental costs that include water consumption and the emission of methane, a greenhouse gas. In Brazil, especially, beef production has led to deforestation. But many of these costs don't show up in the price of beef at the meat counter.
"To understand the trade-off, we are working on bringing together global data on cattle stocks, long-run deforestation, and consumers' meat consumption habits both here in the US and around the world," Mishra explains. "This approach allows us to think in the long run about how our meat production system should be designed."
Understanding the incentives to consume meat and how either investments in technology (feedlots or engineered feed) or direct environmental policy (taxing a beef farmer for methane emissions) is a critical sustainability challenge that requires new data and globally consistent measurement, Mishra says.
"As a multigenerational foundation, we recognize how important it is to address climate resilience," says Alyson Sattler, executive director of the WHH Foundation. "Funding the lab is an investment in Hannah and Prakash's leadership and vision, and their ability to propel a new generation of scholars and individuals who will actively pursue solutions by leveraging data and AI to more thoughtfully reframe environmental policy for the future."

title: Judging Faces Without Words
author: Katie Neith (katien@caltech.edu)
summary: New research method shows people perceive personality traits from faces even when they are not overtly rating them.
text:
Imagine sitting on a city bus full of strangers. Look around at the people riding with you. If you needed help, how would you choose whom to trust? By scanning people's faces, your brain is already making interpretations about their personalities by judging certain facial features.
For decades, neuroscientists have been studying how facial bias ultimately influences the way people behave, but the experiments have been limited by the words used to describe people. Studies typically ask participants to rate faces on a fixed set of rating scales that are provided by the experimenter on words like "competent" or "trustworthy." Now, a team of researchers at Caltech has developed a way to study trait judgment of faces without using any word labels.
"We asked people to directly interpret the similarity in personality between faces," explains Yue Xu (PhD '26), who led the study and is first author on a paper about it published online October 19 in Nature Human Behaviour. "It's a more natural way of thinking about people's personalities without being cued to think about specific trait words."
In the past, studies aiming to link our perception of faces with personality traits typically involved study subjects who looked at faces on a computer monitor, then made a quick judgment by answering questions like, "How trustworthy does this person look to you on a scale from 1 to 5?" The results of prior work have linked such snap opinions to decisions people make in real life about politicians, hiring considerations, and more. But they also raise questions about what happens if you speak a different language, if you are only given a particular set of words concocted by the experimenter, or if you're unable to use language at all.
The new study is the latest effort by Ralph Adolphs (PhD '93), Bren Professor of Psychology, Neuroscience, and Biology at Caltech and senior author of the paper, to reduce bias in face perception studies. Instead of rating faces on trait words, Adolphs, Xu, and the team asked more than 3,000 study participants in two different experiments to look at faces on a computer screen without giving them any rating scale. Instead, participants were instructed to arrange the faces based on how similar or different they appeared to be based on personality traits; similar faces were placed close to one another, and different faces were placed further apart.
The first experiment focused on a set of predominantly white faces to allow the researchers to do a direct comparison with a previous study that used those same faces. The second experiment featured Black and Asian faces, in addition to white faces, to examine how the first experiment's findings extend to individuals of different races.
Using computational methods to assess how participants had arranged faces on their screen, the researchers were able to identify five key trait dimensions present across both experiments: approachability, warmth, competence, morality, and youthfulness. As expected by the researchers, the second experiment also showed prominent effects of stereotypes associated with race.
"It's important to note that what we are studying is people's bias and stereotypes, because they actually don't know about these people outside of this task," says Xu, who was a Chen Graduate Fellow during her time at Caltech. "Our findings don't say anything about the true personality of the actual individuals represented by these faces but tell us what people's first impressions are when they look at these faces."
Next, the team compared their five key dimensions with historical data from prior experiments that did use ratings on words such as sociable and caring, and found they matched up well.
"When I took this task myself, it felt extremely difficult to do without language ratings, as is usually done," says Adolphs, who is also an affiliated faculty member of the Tianqiao and Chrissy Chen Institute for Neuroscience. "So, I was amazed that it worked at all. People gave consistent results that they could not have produced if they weren't doing the experiment properly."
Not only does the new method help reduce study bias by removing trait words, but it also makes language unnecessary, opening future experiments to more people from different cultures or backgrounds or those who are nonverbal.
"One obvious application would be that you could do the task with participants who cannot use the English language, perhaps because they are aphasic or do not speak English," Adolphs says. "I could imagine extending it also to infants or nonhuman primates. It opens up a whole new field of research since we now have a model of how we judge people's faces that does not depend on language."
Xu is continuing her research as a postdoctoral fellow at UC Riverside, and the Adolphs lab has plans to look at brain activity to help answer questions such as where these faces are represented in the brain and at what point language enters the judgment process.
In one new project, Adolphs next aims to record single-neuron activity in patients with epilepsy who have electrodes temporarily implanted in their brains to monitor seizures, work that will be performed in collaboration with electrophysiologist and neuroscientist Ueli Rutishauser (PhD '08), who is a faculty associate in biology and biological engineering at Caltech, an affiliated faculty member of the Tianqiao and Chrissy Chen Institute for Neuroscience, and a faculty member at Cedars-Sinai, where he directs the Center for Neural Science and Medicine. Such recordings allow for detailed investigations of these questions as subjects look at faces—with more precise timing than is possible with standard neuroimaging methods like functional magnetic resonance imaging.
The Nature Human Behaviour paper is titled "Trait judgments of faces using a task without word labels." Umit Keles, a computational scientist in the Adolphs lab, and former Adolphs lab member Chujun Lin (PhD '19), now an assistant professor of psychology at Columbia University, are co-authors of the study. The work was supported by funding from the National Institute of Mental Health, the Simons Foundation Collaboration on the Global Brain, and the Japan Science and Technology Agency.

title: NASA's Perseverance Rover Breaks the Distance Record for Driving Off-World
author: Lori Dajose (ldajose@caltech.edu)
summary: Traversing 28.1 miles and counting, the rover has surpassed the record for the furthest distance traveled by any vehicle on another world
text:
On October 11, NASA's Perseverance rover broke the record for the furthest distance traveled by a vehicle on another world. Initially set by NASA's Opportunity rover in 2014, Perseverance has now driven 28.1 miles, navigating—largely autonomously—boulder fields and sandpits on the Red Planet.
We chatted with former Perseverance project scientist Ken Farley, the W. M. Keck Foundation Professor of Geochemistry at Caltech, about the rover's achievements and what the distance record means for Martian exploration.
What has Perseverance been up to lately?
We are at a very interesting place scientifically! The rock types where we are now are different than we've seen before, and they look very much like the kind of rock that one would expect the early Martian crust to have been made out of. These are likely extremely ancient rocks, older than rocks that we've looked at before—probably older than 4 billion years. There are few rocks on Earth older than 4 billion years. So we are in an area that is very deep in the history of the solar system.
Perseverance has self-driving capabilities; what level of input do scientists give to the rover?
First, scientists decide where we want the rover to go for scientific investigation by looking at detailed images of the Martian surface taken by orbiters in space. We can see where it's hilly, where it's rocky, where there are giant fields of sand, or cliffs. Engineers will then give the rover a rough sketch of a route to avoid big hazards, but the rover has to, by itself and based on imaging collected with the cameras and an algorithm, actually figure out how to go around rocks and minor obstacles.
Though it is the most advanced technology that's off of Earth, it still has to take pictures and think about what it sees, where it's safe to go, where it's not safe to go, and how to drive around any hazards that it detects. It's a very slow process; the rover takes five or six hours to go about 100 meters as it's navigating its way through hazards. It's kind of like a self-driving car, except running on a very different and much slower computer.
Perseverance is the size of an SUV, what kind of off-road capabilities does it have to handle the Martian surface?
There's an interesting difference here between what it is possible to do and what it is best to avoid doing. If there's a rock that's bigger than, say, the size of a bowling ball, we go around it. If we have no choice, we can drive over it. The technical limit is much larger than that, but the goal, of course, is to keep the rover going for as long as possible by not overtaxing its capabilities.
The absolute No. 1 rule for the rover is: Don't get yourself into a situation that you can't get out of. The rover has an enormous amount of onboard safety checks. One very common thing that happens is that the rover will drive up to an area where there's a whole bunch of bowling-ball-sized rocks that it is trying to drive across. In some cases, the rover will reach a limit—it will just say, "I don't know what the solution is. I can't get over the hazards that I'm sitting on or are in front of me, so I'm going to stop." A different kind of hazard is sand. As soon as the wheels start slipping significantly because of sand, the rover can tell, "My wheels are spinning, but I'm not going forward. I need to stop." The engineers on Earth can look at these situations and figure out how to get the rover out of it. At least on Perseverance, humans are always smarter than the rover.
What kind of engineering enables a rover to achieve this kind of distance?
One of the motivating scientific justifications for the mission has been to collect samples. If you're going to go to all the trouble to collect samples and then fly them to Earth, you want to get the biggest diversity you can, and that means covering a lot of ground. So, in the development stage of the mission, the rover was designed to be remarkably capable. Right from the get-go, the scientists decided that the mission should land inside Jezero Crater and explore the lake and river system there and then drive up the crater rim and drive around on the external part outside of the crater. Everyone's jaw dropped. People said, "Oh my god, it would be amazing to be able to do that, but no mission has ever driven that far." But the engineers put together an extremely capable vehicle. From a science point of view, it's been really, really successful. JPL has the capability to design things that are remarkably robust.
The samples we've collected are really important, and I'm hoping that in the long run NASA will decide to retrieve them. A sample retrieval mission can teach us a lot about how to get to Mars and, importantly, to come back. If you want humans to be able to safely travel there, sample-return principles will be really useful.
What's your perspective on sending humans to Mars? Will it happen in our lifetimes?
Simply bringing back samples with a robotic mission is complicated, because you have to land something on Mars, then launch it back off and ferry it back to Earth.
What are your hopes for the future of the Perseverance rover?
The rover is currently in excellent health and testing has indicated that it is capable of continuing its mission lifespan. NASA's Curiosity rover has been going for 14 years, and we have every reason to believe that Perseverance will last at least as long as Curiosity. A major goal is collecting diverse samples. The more terrain and different geologic provinces you see, the more interesting things you can put in the sample collection, and the more interesting things that you can discover. My expectation is that we will continue to drive.
Why is Mars important?
There was water on the surface of Mars at the same time that life originated and expanded on Earth. If that happened on Earth, might it have happened on Mars? If not, why not? That's a really profound question. From a purely science perspective, Mars has a very long and rich geologic history in much the same way that Earth does, and we can use a lot of the tools that have been developed to understand Earth.
People say that we need to study extrasolar planets for evidence of life, but the place that will give the richest information is the one you can bring samples from.
Perseverance launched in the pandemic, in the summer of 2020. It was a heroic effort by JPL engineers to get Perseverance to the launchpad. We only have a launch period every two years, and if they hadn't gotten it to the launchpad, it would've cost hundreds of millions of dollars. You do not want to miss the launch period. When we successfully landed, the President made a statement about the importance to the American people of having done something great even in the pandemic. From my personal point of view, this is a purely human endeavor that is not profit-driven but driven by discovery. It allows us to go where we can never go individually, and everyone can feel good about it.

title: How Bacteria Survive a World Full of Killer Bacteriophages
author: Andrew Moseman (amoseman@caltech.edu)
summary: Sujit Datta, professor of chemical engineering, bioengineering, and biophysics, shows that the way bacteria move through the world contains a secret to their escape from predators.
text:
Humans throughout history have invented a variety of ways to fight back against troublesome bacteria. But bacteria live in a dangerous world too. The human body and other bacteria-rich environments abound with bacteriophages, or viruses that prey upon bacteria. Phages can sometimes outnumber bacteria a hundredfold, yet the bacteria endure and even thrive. What gives?
New research from the Caltech lab of Sujit Datta, professor of chemical engineering, bioengineering, and biophysics, helps to explain why.
Among other work, Datta's lab studies bacterial chemotaxis: the movements of microbes in response to chemical stimuli, such as nutrients. To investigate this, the lab has devised experiments in which a dense colony of the gut bacteria Escherichia coli (E. coli), a commonly studied model organism, are deposited in a tube with a kind of "starting line," as in a race. Food—sugar plus an amino acid called L-serine that the bacteria find especially attractive—is placed nearby. As the bacteria begin to move toward the food, they form "these really cool fronts or coherent bands, almost like a peloton, a group of racers moving together in the Tour de France," Datta explains.
The team wondered whether this kind of experiment could help explain how bacteria escape phages in their normal environments, such as biological tissues and soils. But there was a problem. Such environments are complex, porous, and very difficult to see through. So, the team, led by Victoria Muir—then a postdoctoral researcher in Datta's lab and now an assistant professor at the University of Delaware—created the bacterial equivalent of an ant farm.
The transparent setup consists of a glass tube packed with tiny water-filled beads, or hydrogel, each a few times the size of an E. coli bacterium. When compacted, the beads form a solid mass, but one that is riddled with a maze of channels formed by the gaps between the beads. Bacteria added to the system have to navigate that maze, similar to how they swim through their natural soil environment, or, in the body, through materials like mucus. For the experiments, E. coli bacteria are genetically modified to glow green under fluorescent light, allowing their movements to be tracked. "We make environments that are structurally more akin to natural habitats of bacteria but are transparent, so we can actually watch the bacteria swimming through," Datta says.
To that experimental landscape, Muir added a variety of phages, creating a minefield for the bacteria to navigate. At first, the bacteria appeared to do ... nothing. They didn't move, leading the researchers to think, "Oh, okay, the phages won, that's the end of the story," Datta says.
But after a few hours, they kicked into gear. A line of bacteria took off in the direction of a food source, just as they had during experiments without phages. The more phages the researchers peppered into the field of play, the longer bacteria appeared to wait, sometimes as long as 15 hours, before they began to seek out food. But the bacteria managed to stay alive, even at phage concentrations that should have wiped them out.
The bacteria do not delay because they are hesitant of the phages: Bacteria have no way to sense their predators, and they behave the same whether the phages are there or not, Datta says. Rather, the wait is related to population recovery. Early on, bacteria are eating and growing, but the cells killed by phage infection cancel much of the population's growth. As a result, the microorganisms take far longer to reach a density at which they can form the "peloton." Once they do, however, chemotaxis—basically the group's hunt for food—is the key to their escape, allowing them to leave phages in the dust. "The bacteria move in a directed manner because they eat the food around them and so create the very gradient that draws them forward," Datta says. The peloton consumes the food around it, leaving a zone depleted of nutrients behind and an untouched supply ahead. The cells at the leading edge sense more food in front than behind, so the peloton swims in that direction.
Once the peloton is on the move, the phages can never catch up. Phages cannot swim but drift aimlessly, the way a drop of ink spreads in still water. Naturally, some bacterial cells do not win at this game of survival. The scientists spotted the remnants of cells infected by phages at the back of the group. But even though each bursting cell creates about 90 bacteriophages, viruses moving at random could not catch the group of bacteria steadily fleeing. Further testing showed that the bacteria evaded their phage predators without the need to evolve genetic resistance to them, which many biologists thought was necessary.
"The conventional paradigm is that chemotaxis enables the cells to access more nutrients and explore more terrain. Our work also suggests that it also helps them escape predation," Datta says. Indeed, inspired by the experiments, Alejandro Martínez-Calvo—another former postdoctoral researcher working with Datta and theory collaborator Ned S. Wingreen (BS '84) of Princeton University—created a mathematical framework for understanding how bacteria survive and how long it takes for a certain mass of bacteria to escape its phage predators, depending on the phage concentration and environmental conditions. More broadly, this work also illustrates a common axiom in nature (and the human world): There is strength in numbers.
"There's a saying: If you want to go fast, go alone, but if you want to go far, go as a group. To me, this is an interesting manifestation of that," Datta says.
The work is described in a paper in Science Advances titled "Death & Chemotaxis: Bacterial chemotaxis enables collective escape from phage predation." Datta's work was funded by the National Science Foundation, the Camille and Henry Dreyfus Foundation, the Pew Charitable Trusts, and the Princeton Catalysis Initiative.

title: First Light: Celebrate the Inauguration of Caltech's 10th President, Ray Jayawardhana
author: Caltech Media Relations (mr@caltech.edu)
summary: Community invited to celebrate the Inauguration of Caltech's 10th President, Ray Jayawardhana
text:
First light is the threshold moment in astronomy when a telescope makes its first observation and opens a new window to discovery. That same spirit of possibility defines the Caltech community. Through curiosity-driven inquiry, powerful experimentation, and groundbreaking instrumentation, Caltech illuminates new fields of knowledge and accelerates breakthroughs that shape the future of science, technology, and society.
This fall, Caltech celebrates the spirit of first light for the Inauguration of Ray Jayawardhana as the Institute's 10th president. Over two days—Wednesday, October 28, and Thursday, October 29—the campus and broader community are invited to join compelling discussions and experiences that showcase the curiosity and innovation at the heart of Caltech.
The following events are open to the public and free to attend, but registration for each event is required.
Wednesday, October 28: The Brave New Space Age
5:30 p.m. — Science and Discovery Night
7:30 p.m. — Brave New Space Age Panel Conversation
An evening of discovery launches Caltech's inauguration events with an immersive look at the groundbreaking science and engineering shaping our future.
Starting at 5:30 p.m. outside Beckman Auditorium, Caltech researchers will bring their work to life through interactive demonstrations and hands-on experiences. Guests can see meteorites, learn about battery chemistry, examine brain-machine interfaces, engage in an interactive light demonstration, and more.
In the Beckman Institute, just west of the auditorium, visitors can preview Dare Mighty Things: From Rocketry to Space Exploration at Caltech JPL, a special exhibition marking the 90th anniversary of Caltech's founding of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
Guests will receive a Passport to Discovery to collect stamps at interactive stations for a commemorative Caltech pin, and can enjoy live music, photo opportunities, and refreshments along the way.
Brave New Space Age Conversation
At 7:30 p.m. in Beckman Auditorium, the evening's highlight will be a thought-provoking conversation on the new space age.
As innovation and investment expand access to orbit and return our gaze to the Moon and Mars, a new era of ambition, exploration, and discovery also raises profound questions. This public conversation, moderated by Jo Ling Kent, senior business and technology correspondent for CBS News, brings together leading voices in science, industry, government, and media to explore the promise and implications of New Space and what it means to stand on the threshold of a future rapidly coming into view.
The Brave New Space Age panel features:
Lindy Elkins-Tanton, Professor of Earth and Planetary Science and Director of the UC Berkeley Space Sciences Laboratory, UC Berkeley; Principal Investigator of the NASA Psyche Mission
Jared Isaacman, Administrator of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
Eric Schmidt, KBE, Former CEO and Chairman, Google; Chair and CEO, Relativity Space; Co-Founder, Schmidt Sciences
Advance registration for The Brave New Space Age has reached capacity. A standby line will be available.
Thursday, October 29: Inauguration Ceremony and Campus Celebration
10 a.m. — Inauguration Ceremony
12 p.m. — Community Luncheon and Campus Celebration
Celebrate the formal Inauguration of Ray Jayawardhana as Caltech's 10th president.
Ceremony
The ceremony begins at 10 a.m. on Beckman Mall with welcomes from across the Institute—including representatives of the Board of Trustees, faculty, JPL, undergraduate and graduate students, and alumni.
The investiture and inaugural address form the ceremony's centerpiece. The program also features the Caltech Glee Club, performing alongside brass, percussion, and organ.
The ceremony will be livestreamed starting at 9:45 a.m. PDT on Thursday, October 29, on the inauguration website.
Campus Celebration
A community luncheon follows at 12 p.m. Festivities showcasing the breadth and vitality of the Caltech JPL community will take place along the Olive Walk and outside Browne Dining Hall and Red Door Cafe, with live music, giveaways, photo opportunities with Bernoulli the Beaver, student research displays, and other activities.
Register to attend the inauguration ceremony and campus celebration in person, and join in welcoming the next chapter of impact and discovery at Caltech.

title: Forecasting Tipping Points with AI
author: Whitney Clavin (wclavin@caltech.edu)
summary: Caltech-led researchers take key steps in developing deep-learning models that can predict irreversible shifts in climate and other systems
text:
The writer Malcolm Gladwell popularized the term "tipping points" to refer to the moment when a trend or social behavior crosses a threshold and rapidly spreads everywhere. In physics, tipping points occur when systems—say, Earth's climate—reach an unstable point and topple over into a sea of change that is sometimes irreversible. Examples include global warming or the melting of polar ice caps.
While scientists have previously used AI models to predict smaller changes in weather, such as day-to-day variations, forecasting tipping points comes with more uncertainty and has thus proven more challenging. Now, a new Caltech-led paper demonstrates that an AI program—specifically a type of neural network called a recurrent neural operator (RNO)—can be used to predict when tipping points occur in simple models, including models of a climate-change system and simulations of turbulent airflow over a plane's wing.
The paper was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).
"A tipping point is where you don't have that point of return anymore because it's nonstationary," says Anima Anandkumar, Caltech's Bren Professor of Computing and Mathematical Sciences and the principal author of the study. "Parts of a system are changing in a way so that you cannot bring the system back to its original state. That's why it is seen as something that could be catastrophic."
The new research, cited in a recent report from the United Nations on the importance of tipping points in climate science, was performed by Anandkumar and her colleagues at Caltech, the University of Colorado Boulder (CU Boulder), and the tech company NVIDIA. Because tipping points are so universal, the AI tool has potential applications in the fields of climate science, ecology, epidemiology, aeronautical design, and more.
"This work lays the foundations for characterizing tipping points and predicting when they might occur in the future," says Anandkumar, who is also an affiliated faculty member of Tianqiao and Chrissy Chen Institute for Neuroscience. "We demonstrated it on a simplified climate model and a model of air turbulence over a wing—systems that weren't tractable with earlier methods."
In one part of the study, the researchers looked at a specific climate scenario in which low clouds over the oceans rapidly disappear due to rising carbon dioxide levels—a situation that has been predicted to occur in the future but has not yet been observed. This "point-of-no-return" loss of low cloud cover would further add to global warming. The researchers tested their AI program on simulated data to see if it could forecast when the clouds would disappear. The RNO was able to look more than two years ahead of the expected tipping point in the simulated data and predict its timing with an error of about 11 days.
"In the past, we used AI to learn mostly stationary systems that assume the weather from before will be the same as weather in future," Anandkumar says. "Our group has trained such AI-based weather models successfully in the past and can even predict extreme events like hurricanes with good accuracy. On the other hand, if you want to now model how that climate is changing and account for changes such as the carbon dioxide content, the system is no longer stationary, and you can no longer use standard machine learning principles."
The group's latest AI approach, based on an RNO, differs from other machine learning programs because it incorporates a built-in "memory" that tracks how the physics change over time. The RNO detects when the AI's predictions about the physics of a system no longer make sense, indicating a tipping point is imminent. In other words, when the AI's predictions no longer follow the rules of previously defined physics, a significant shift in the model is about to occur.
"The system is drifting away over time, and the laws from physics are no longer holding at the tipping point," Anandkumar says. "We can use the principles of physics on top of recurrent neural operators to make these predictions of when the tipping point is likely to occur."
The PNAS paper also describes testing the RNO on simulations of airflow over a tilting plane wing to see if it could forecast a tipping point that occurs when the wing's lift drops precipitously. The RNO succeeded in predicting the tipping point, suggesting these kinds of AI programs could potentially help with future aeronautical and aerospace designs.
"In aerodynamics, quantities like the angle of attack can change gradually while the flow itself undergoes a much more abrupt transition, such as the onset of stall or a change in the wake," explains study coauthor Jane Bae (BS '12), assistant professor of aerospace at Caltech and a Susan Wu Scholar. "What is exciting about this work is that the model can recognize when the physics it has learned no longer adequately describes what is happening, providing a warning that the system may be approaching a tipping point. Being able to anticipate these qualitative changes before they occur could ultimately be very useful for aerodynamic prediction and design."
The paper is titled "Tipping Point Forecasting in Non-Stationary Dynamics on Function Spaces." In addition to Anandkumar, other Caltech authors are alumni Miguel Liu-Schiaffini (BS '25) and Sze Chai Leung (MS '24); and Jane Bae (BS '12), assistant professor of aerospace and a Susan Wu Scholar. Additional authors are Clare E. Singer (PhD '24) of CU Boulder and Nikola Kovachki (BS '16, PhD '22) and Kamyar Azizzadenesheli of NVIDIA. Funding was provided by the Mellon Mays Undergraduate Fellowship; Eric and Wendy Schmidt, through the AI2050 Senior Fellow Schmidt Sciences program; Caltech trustee Charles Trimble (BS '63, MS '64); the Office of Naval Research; the Carver Mead New Adventures Fund; and Caltech's Center for Autonomous Systems and Technologies (CAST). Computational time for the airfoil simulations was provided by the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center, supported by the National Science Foundation.

title: The Delicate Dance of Dominance: How the Fruit Fly Brain Controls Threat Displays
author: Lori Dajose (ldajose@caltech.edu)
summary: How does the fruit fly brain control its wings and legs to create elaborate social displays?
text:
Limbs evolved as a means of locomotion. From the primitive rotating flagella of bacteria to the wings of flies and even our own legs, animals use these appendages to travel to find food or mates, or escape predators. But in countless species across the animal kingdom, limbs are repurposed to create elaborate social displays: Paradise birds fan out their wings and hop around in courtship dances, while crabs wave their claws to communicate to potential mating partners. As humans, we use our limbs to dance, gesture while talking, wield tools, and conduct a remarkable diversity of behaviors. How does the brain control and coordinate its body parts for such distinct purposes?
A new study from Caltech neuroscientists has discovered how social behaviors—specifically aggressive displays of intimidation—are wired in the brain of the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, a commonly used model organism. The team discovered two brain "modules" that are connected to the wings and to the legs, respectively, that govern the animal's threat displays.
The research was led by Caltech graduate student Shuo Cao and conducted in the laboratory of David Anderson, the Seymour Benzer Professor of Biology, Leadership Chair and director of the Tianqiao and Chrissy Chen Institute for Neuroscience at Caltech, and a Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator. A paper describing the work appears on October 15 in the journal Current Biology.
Male Drosophila exhibit four specific behaviors when trying to intimidate other fruit flies with threat displays. A fly will leap forward in rapid, stuttering bursts of activity; throw up its wings at a 45-degree angle to form a V; repeatedly turn to face the recipient of its aggression; and pump its wings forward in a movement too fast for the human eye to see. Altogether, it's not dissimilar from the actions of an aggressive man who puffs up his chest and throws out his arms in a show of intimidation.
The flies will not conduct these behaviors unless confronted with another male fly.
In 2018, the Anderson lab discovered that a tiny patch of fly brain cells, called AIP neurons, control these threat displays. When AIP neurons are optogenetically activated by researchers in experiments, the study showed, flies will exhibit a threat display even when no other fly is present. If the neurons are silenced, a fly is still physically able to attack another fly it comes into contact with, but it no longer performs the preamble to the fight—the threat display.
Curiously, the fly's brain contains very few AIP neurons—only five to seven are present in each of the insect's two brain hemispheres. How does this tiny group of brain cells coordinate and orchestrate the complex actions of the fly's wings and legs to repurpose them in a choreography of four distinct threat behaviors?
Over the past five years, neuroscientists studying Drosophila have developed an intricate map showing the connections between every cell within the male fruit fly brain. With this map—called a connectome—Cao identified four major neurons that are "downstream" from the AIP. This means that the neurons receive signals that originate in the AIP but do not send signals back to it.
Cao discovered that two of the neurons emanating from the AIP are neurons described as "descending." These descending neurons each have a long fiber that extends from the fly's central brain down to the motor nerve cord, the fly's equivalent of the human spinal cord. Signals originating in the central brain travel down these neurons to control movements of the fly's body. When each of the descending neurons is activated on its own, only weak movements occur in the fly's wings. But activating both simultaneously, Cao found, produces the exact wing movements of the threat display—the V shape and the rapid forward pump.
The other two neurons located downstream from the AIP are "interneurons," which project out and connect to many other downstream descending neurons. When one of these interneurons is activated, Cao found that a fly will walk around continuously. Activating the other causes the fly to stand still. And when the two interneurons are simultaneously activated, Cao discovered, a fly displays the stuttering, charging movements characteristic of a threat display.
Importantly, the descending neurons that control wing movements for threat displays are different cells from the descending neurons that control them in flight: They evolved specifically for that purpose and do not seem to do anything else. However, the neurons involved in turning and charging are part of a larger group of descending neurons used for routine locomotion like walking. The two interneurons activated by the AIP for the charging movements only selectively activate neurons of this larger group and send patterns of signals to produce the short bursts of movement specific to threat displays.
"It's a neurobiological mechanism for what evolutionary biologists call exaptation: Taking parts or processes of an organism that evolved for one function and adapting them to perform a different function—on the fly, so to speak," Anderson says.
In future work, Cao plans to investigate how external sensory cues such as the sight of another fly or the smell of its pheromones shift the animal into a mode where it will exhibit a threat display. Further research could investigate other fruit fly species—there are thousands—to examine their threat displays, if present, and whether they have similar neural circuits.
The paper is titled "Neural coordination of wing and leg movements during a terrestrial threat display." Cao and Anderson are the study's authors. The work was funded by the National Institutes of Health and a Josephine de Karman Trust fellowship, awarded by the Pasadena Community Foundation.

title: Kareem El-Badry Wins Packard Fellowship
author: Whitney Clavin (wclavin@caltech.edu)
summary: The astronomer is known for uncovering hidden populations of black holes
text:
Kareem El-Badry, associate professor of astronomy at Caltech, has been selected as one of 20 Packard Fellows for 2026. The Packard Fellowships for Science and Engineering provide just under $990,000 in unrestricted funds for early career researchers to use over a five-year period.
Much of El-Badry's work involves uncovering hidden populations of black holes. Our Milky Way galaxy is teeming with millions of these extremely dense objects, usually created when massive dead stars explode and then collapse inward under their own gravity. But black holes are hard to find. El-Badry reveals the cosmic objects using data from large-scale surveys, such as the European Space Agency's Gaia mission, along with targeted spectroscopy. One method involves looking for telltale stellar motions, or wobbles, caused by the gravitational tugs of orbiting black holes.
"Massive stars live short but exciting lives," El-Badry says. "They are the primary sources of energy, momentum, and ionizing radiation in the galaxy. Their deaths give rise to spectacular cosmic explosions, and they produce most of the elements from which planets form. Today, the Milky Way contains a few tens of thousands of massive stars. But for every massive star alive today, there are about 1,000 that have already died. These dead massive stars amount to a stellar graveyard of black holes and neutron stars." (Neutron stars are dense remnants that form out of the explosions of massive stars whose cores were not quite dense enough to form black holes.)
In recent work, El-Badry discovered the closest-known black hole to Earth, located about 1,600 light-years away; 21 hidden neutron stars orbiting around stars like our Sun; and the first-known "black hole triple," a system of three stars, one of which is a black hole.
"By measuring the masses, velocities, and companions of these hidden black holes and neutron stars, we can learn about the lives and deaths of the massive stars from which they formed," El-Badry says.
El-Badry learned that he had won a Packard Fellowship after Hirosi Ooguri, the Kent and Joyce Kresa Leadership Chair of Caltech's Division of Physics, Mathematics and Astronomy, invited him to a Zoom call to discuss his research. Unbeknownst to El-Badry, Ooguri had planned for a representative of the Packard Foundation to join the call and deliver the good news.
"I thought this was a routine meeting with Hirosi, so when someone else joined the call, I wondered if I'd done something wrong," El-Badry jokes.
"Kareem has a remarkable ability to turn vast astronomical datasets into discoveries about how stars evolve," Ooguri says. "The Packard Fellowship will give him the freedom to pursue bold ideas. I look forward to the discoveries that he will make, addressing questions about our universe and posing new ones."
El-Badry is looking ahead to analyzing new data from Gaia and from NASA missions including SPHEREx, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, and UVEX, on whose team he serves.
He earned his undergraduate degree from Yale University and his PhD in astrophysics from UC Berkeley, and he was a postdoctoral researcher at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics before joining Caltech. He was named a Sloan Research Fellow and a MacArthur Fellow in 2025.
This year, the Packard Foundation expanded its support for fellows from $875,000 to $985,834 over five years. According to the foundation, "Fellows decide what their research needs, whether that is new equipment, another researcher on the team, travel to a conference, or child care during the demanding early years of running a lab. That flexibility lets Fellows test novel ideas, follow unexpected findings, and lead research that drives real-world impact."
Other Caltech-affiliated winners of 2026 Packard fellowships include alumni Kurtis Carsch (BS/MS '16), an assistant professor of chemistry at the University of Texas at Austin, and three former Caltech postdocs: Soumitra Athavale, an assistant professor of chemistry and biochemistry at UCLA; Liam Connor, an assistant professor of astronomy at Harvard University; and Nathanan Tantivasadakarn, an assistant professor of physics and astronomy at Stony Brook University.
For more information about the Packard Foundation, visit their website.

title: The Magical Mysteries—and Histories—of Physics: A Conversation with Historian Alexander Blum
author: Katie Neith (katien@caltech.edu)
summary: Blum joins the Caltech faculty as a professor of history with a focus on 20th-century physics.
text:
When Alex Blum was growing up in the Black Forest region of Germany, he was consumed by what some might consider an unusual pastime: reading fantasy books and trying to reconstruct the implicit histories of the characters in detail. In the 11th grade, his attention shifted when he was introduced to physics—an interest that would later converge with his passion for history and define his career path.
"I did not know what was going on at all," says Blum, remembering his first physics exam. "Then I had this realization that all they're asking us to do is to put numbers into equations. And that opened up the magical mystery of the mathematical representation of the world to me."
The enigma of physics pushed Blum to study both physics and philosophy at Leipzig University, Michigan State University, and the Technical University of Munich. In 2009, he earned a PhD in theoretical particle physics from the Max Planck Institute for Nuclear Physics in Heidelberg. He then retrained as a historian at the Max Planck Institute for the History of Science in Berlin, where he investigated the search for a final theory of physics. Now, Blum has joined the Caltech faculty as professor of history with a focus on 20th-century physics.
We recently spoke with Blum about his transition from physicist to historian and his focus on modern physics (and a side project focused on listening to all the top albums in the history of popular music).
What inspired your move from theoretical particle physics to the history of the field?
I did my PhD in theoretical particle physics, and I enjoyed the math of it, but I had a hard time believing that what I was doing was going to be confirmed or have some kind of direct connection to the natural world. I took a year off after my PhD and realized that although I still had very many questions, I wanted to think about physics rather than doing it.
I had a long-standing interest in history more generally, not necessarily the history of science, but just history as a process of reconstructing stories from facts. I applied to a project on the history of quantum mechanics at the Max Planck Institute in Berlin, and then I stayed there for 16 years.
How did you decide to focus on the modern history of physics?
That was not necessarily the plan; I was figuring I would branch out and learn interesting stuff about science from the 18th century to today, maybe look at what Isaac Newton was doing. But then I realized that with the skillset that I had acquired as a physicist, I could really engage with the history of 20th-century science in detailed ways that many of my colleagues could not. I had the skills to read the sources in detail and calculate through them to understand what the narrative is and what people are actually doing, and how that contrasts with what they're saying that they're doing; there's always a big gap there.
On the one hand, I saw there was a niche for me to go into. That was the pragmatic aspect. I also felt that I could keep on thinking about the questions that had originally brought me into physics as a youth, especially that question of the mathematical representation of the world and why it's so successful even when it's not perfect. And I had the opportunity to think about these questions from a different, even better vantage point.
What does your research process look like?
When I have a theme I'm interested in, I start with looking at the vast published literature. Because so many papers are published and people cite one another, I try to establish who the relevant people are and how are they related intellectually. Once I've got a map of what's happened on the published record and a list of people who are very relevant, I track down archival sources. Usually, I'm not dealing with super prominent people like Einstein, with source material available in university archives. I have to go treasure-hunting—tracking down relatives to find out whether they still have boxes in the attic or something.
Once that material is assembled, I create a bare-bones chronology. I try to relate the ideas, see when ideas may have circulated before they were published, and how they relate to one another. There's a lot of calculating—a form of translating texts into an argument that you can write about. And then, in the end, the finished product is a story that will also contain detailed mathematical arguments if they're important to understanding what's happening.
Why did you decide to move across the globe to join the Caltech faculty?
I work a lot collaboratively. For example, I've collaborated with a solar physicist on the history of studying the magnetic field of the Sun and with philosophers reflecting on science—maybe in a somewhat different way than historians do. I'm always juggling at least three or four such projects by email. I'm definitely looking forward to that at Caltech; I've heard about the collaboration and communication that the campus and the small size of the faculty enables.
The history of physics that I do engages in detail with the formal mathematics and the conceptual issues of physics. It is not really in the mainstream. Caltech has a small dedicated group for the history of science that is focused on the complicated details of modern and exact natural sciences. And that kind of history is also relevant to the young scientists being trained at Caltech. They don't just hear stories about what the scientists were doing in the olden days. They can talk with the experts about the details of that science and how ideas about nature and its mathematical representation have changed with time. For me, it's the perfect place.
Is there a central focus to your studies?
The overarching research question that I'm interested in pursuing is what do we do once the physics equations that we're trying to solve become too complicated for us to actually solve? People are trying out lots of complicated approximation methods, and there are ideas about somehow transcending this simple equation-solving and moving into a new era of physics where we embrace complexity wholeheartedly. The old cliche of, Oh, I'm a theoretical physicist, I just use pencil and paper, stops working as early as the 1950s.
What will you be teaching this year?
I'm going to be teaching two courses to start. One is a first-year class on the history of the atomic bomb. The most striking thing about that story is that we go from the discovery of nuclear fission in 1939—which was a purely curiosity-driven experiment—to, in just six years, the development of a weapon that changed world history forever. Then, I am teaching an advanced class on how old and traditional ideas are radically changed and uprooted by new experimental discoveries and theoretical developments, tracking how a scientific revolution works in detail.
What do you like to do in your free time?
I like to be outside with my family. I have two sons, and when we came for the recruitment visit in February, Berlin was a frozen-over hellscape; here, we went to the beach and biked and roller skated. Apart from that, I have the very generic pastimes of reading, playing board games with my children, and listening to music. With music, I have an ongoing project, made possible by modern streaming services: I am listening through the entire history of popular music in gory detail. I'm now in the year 1983. I manage about three years per year. I read the Wikipedia article for every album. To me, it's like this sprawling novel of the second half of the 20th century, where all the cultural and societal and political developments intertwine.

title: #SoCaltech: Blake Hawkins
author: Jon Nalick
summary: "What fascinates me most about quantum mechanics is the question of whether uncertainty is really out there in the world or just in our heads. Take something as simple as an electron: In a chemistry class, you're shown this ‘cloud’ of electron distribution probability around the nucleus, denser
text:
"What fascinates me most about quantum mechanics is the question of whether uncertainty is really out there in the world or just in our heads. Take something as simple as an electron: In a chemistry class, you're shown this ‘cloud’ of electron distribution probability around the nucleus, denser in some places, thinner in others. Nobody quite tells you whether the electron is really spread out like that, or whether it's sitting at one location and the cloud just reflects what we don't know yet.
I find beautiful an idea called Newtonian Quantum Mechanics, developed by my mentor, Professor of Philosophy Charles Sebens: Instead of one universe governed by a mysterious, probabilistic wave, picture an enormous number of complete, deterministic universes, all weakly interacting, each containing nothing but classical point particles. What we call quantum uncertainty is just not knowing which universe we're in.
Professor Sebens built that picture for nonrelativistic quantum mechanics, so my SURF project aims to extend it into relativistic quantum field theory, the more accurate framework where particle number can change (the home of Feynman diagrams). I replace the classical particles with classical fields and derive the dynamics from the equations of quantum field theory to test whether the principles that make Sebens’ picture appealing survive the move to a better predictive theory. We are also finding interesting results about how energy conservation is treated in this setting.
It’s a lot of abstract work, but not speculative. I always start from the equations that physicists already trust and ask what the reality is they are telling us.”
Blake Hawkins (BS ’27) is a David C. Elliot SURF Fellow working with Charles Sebens, Caltech professor of philosophy, on the philosophy of physics, extending Sebens’ Newtonian Quantum Mechanics formulation of quantum mechanics into quantum field theory.
#SoCaltech is an occasional series celebrating the diverse individuals who give Caltech its spirit of excellence, ambition, and ingenuity. Know someone we should profile? Send nominations to magazine@caltech.edu.

title: Three Caltech Professors Named Fellows of the American Physical Society
author: Kimm Fesenmaier (kfesenma@caltech.edu)
summary: Marco Bernardi, Sujit Datta, and John Sader are being honored for their outstanding contributions to physics
text:
Caltech professors Marco Bernardi, Sujit Datta, and John Sader have been named fellows of the American Physical Society (APS) for their outstanding contributions to physics.
Marco Bernardi, professor of applied physics, physics, and materials science and the undergraduate and graduate option representative for materials sciences, was nominated by the APS Division of Computational Physics (DCOMP). He studies quantum interactions and dynamics in matter, picking apart the processes that take place on the tiniest of scales—how individual electrons, units of vibration, or spins move and interact in semiconductors and quantum materials, for example. He begins from first principles to build theories and computational methods of making quantitative predictions about these behaviors that will inform the next generation of electronic, optical, magnetic, and quantum technologies.
The APS notes that Bernardi was nominated for "pioneering first-principles calculations of electron interactions, transport, and nonequilibrium dynamics in conventional and quantum materials, especially for electron–phonon interactions and polaron physics; and for the development of novel computational methods and software."
"I am truly honored to be recognized by my peers in DCOMP, and especially grateful to the wonderful students and postdocs whose talent, creativity, and hard work have made this journey possible," Bernardi says. "This milestone is both deeply meaningful and motivating; it inspires us to keep pushing the boundaries of computation to understand quantum interactions and dynamics in matter."
Sujit Datta, professor of chemical engineering, bioengineering, and biophysics, was nominated by the APS Division of Soft Matter Physics (DSOFT) for work that examines how environmental factors change the behavior of "squishy" materials, such as bacteria, mucus, and other polymeric fluids, and how these materials in turn affect their environments. His group uses a combination of experiments, theoretical modeling, and computer simulations to better understand the fundamental principles governing these systems and their potential applications.
According to the APS, Datta was honored for "bridging soft matter physics and biology in realistic settings to advance the quantitative understanding of the dynamics of complex fluids and bacterial suspensions in complex environments."
"APS has been my intellectual home since I was an undergraduate who was given the chance to join a physics lab two decades ago and fell in love with scientific discovery in the process," Datta says. "That joy still drives the work that my group and I do, and this recognition reflects their creativity and hard work. I owe a great deal to my trainees, collaborators, colleagues, and mentors over the years, as well as the broader soft-matter community, for supporting and inspiring me to follow curiosity across disciplines."
Datta subscribes to the credo of one of his intellectual heroes, John Hopfield, Caltech's Roscoe G. Dickinson Professor of Chemistry and Biology, Emeritus, and winner of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics. Datta describes physics as a point of view that the world around us is, with effort, ingenuity, and adequate resources, understandable in a predictive and reasonably quantitative fashion. "I look forward to many more years of exploring the world through that lens with this incredible community," he says.
John Sader, a research professor of aerospace and applied physics, was recognized by the APS Division of Fluid Dynamics (DFD). Over the course of his career, Sader, an applied mathematician with a graduate degree in electrical engineering, has tackled problems such as vortex flows in water and air (the swirling motions seen everywhere from draining bathtubs to aircraft wakes), as well as in more exotic systems, often in close collaboration with experimentalists. These systems include electrons that flow like a viscous fluid through graphene, a sheet of carbon only 1 atom thick, and superfluids that flow with zero viscosity, or no friction at all. His work also underpins precise measurements of the forces between individual atoms. He pioneered the Sader Method, which is widely used to calibrate atomic force microscopes. This method measures the stiffness of the tiny, springlike beam that holds the microscope's nanoscale tip by analyzing how the beam vibrates in air, so the delicate tip is never damaged.
The APS cited Sader for "pioneering contributions to fluid-structure interactions, including the Sader Method for atomic force microscopy, fundamental insights into vortex generation by airfoils, and analyses of Boltzmann transport for gaseous and electronic flows."
"I have been fortunate to work with exceptional students and collaborators from around the world, particularly experimentalists who have helped transform theoretical ideas into practical advances," Sader says. "It is especially gratifying to see the methods we have developed enable others to advance their own research."

title: DOE Funds AI-Driven Catalyst Discovery Project as Part of Genesis Mission
author: Kimm Fesenmaier (kfesenma@caltech.edu)
summary: The effort to better understand how certain catalysts work builds on research started by and crucial to the Liquid Sunlight Alliance and its goal of developing new fuels and valuable chemicals
text:
On October 8, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) announced a second round of funding for its Genesis Mission, a nationwide initiative to use AI to tackle pressing challenges in science and technology. Among the projects that will receive funding is a Caltech effort that will use AI to help identify new and better catalysts, materials that speed up chemical reactions.
The catalysis project is led by the DOE's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in collaboration with Caltech and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. It is one of six newly announced phase I projects that will receive short-term seed funding to explore feasibility. The DOE also announced 12 new phase II funding awards for larger projects that are ready to scale up.
Catalyst Discovery
To produce useful products from chemical reactions, scientists are always searching for the most effective catalysts. The Liquid Sunlight Alliance (LiSA), a DOE-funded Energy Innovation Hub led by Caltech's Harry Atwater, the Otis Booth Leadership Chair of the Division of Engineering and Applied Science, is specifically looking for catalysts that can drive reactions to convert water, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen into liquid fuels and valuable chemicals.
"This Genesis mission project brings together laboratory-based accelerated materials discovery with X-ray beamline measurements to speed the pace of knowledge generation about how catalysts enable pathways for chemical fuel synthesis," says Atwater, who is also the Howard Hughes Professor of Applied Physics and Materials Science.
To fully understand how certain catalysts work and whether they can be improved, scientists with LiSA have used X-ray beamlines at SLAC's Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (SSRL) to measure changes in the physical structures of catalysts as they become active and spur on chemical reactions. That work, though, is extremely time-consuming; although millions of possible catalyst compositions exist—even miniscule changes in the chemical composition can dramatically affect how a catalyst works—only a handful have been tested in this way.
The Genesis-funded project aims to use AI and automated experimentation to speed up the process, enabling the rapid testing and identification of the best catalysts for particular chemical reactions, including the efficient and economically viable creation of liquid fuels.
The catalysis project, "Closed-Loop Autonomous Discovery of Mechanistic Activity-Selectivity-Stability Rules in Catalysis," will build a closed-loop system in which an AI agent will compare competing ideas about how catalysts work, identify what evidence is missing to validate (or disprove) those ideas, and then choose the next experiments that should be conducted.
At SSRL, the system will combine real-time X-ray measurements with electrochemistry, computer models, and published knowledge. Each result will feed back into the system and guide the next measurement. Phase I of the project will test whether this approach can enable scientific understanding with fewer experiments than standard approaches. Faster insight into how catalysts work can help researchers develop more efficient and durable processes for energy and chemical production while advancing the broader vision of autonomous laboratories that can help scientists test ideas on faster timescales.
"The AI weighs the scientific evidence, decides which measurement would tell us the most, and that decision becomes a real experiment at SSRL," said Dimosthenis Sokaras, the project's principal investigator and director of the Chemistry and Catalysis Division at SSRL, in an SLAC press release. "The result comes straight back into the reasoning process. That closed loop is a key step toward autonomous laboratories."
As part of the new project, Caltech researchers will prepare libraries of hundreds to thousands of catalyst compositions to test with SLAC's X-ray beam, says Caltech's Joel Haber, a member of the professional staff and team lead with LiSA. "We can measure how well the material is performing as an electrocatalyst at the same time we're measuring the structure of the catalyst. So, we will be able to see what changes when it turns on and becomes effective as an electrocatalyst and then correlate the structure with that performance."
That data will be combined with electrochemical measurements from labs at Caltech along with information from computational chemists in the collaboration to constantly update the AI model.
Two Caltech-led Genesis Mission projects were announced in the first round of DOE funding for the initiative in July. At the same time, a "programmable cloud laboratory" led by Caltech and funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) was announced as part of a network of AI-enabled automated laboratories that represent a core NSF contribution to the nationwide Genesis Mission.
