title: Shedding Light on the Brain: Neuroscientists Reflect on Optogenetics Nobel
author: Caltech Media Relations (mr@caltech.edu)
summary: Optogenetics, the subject of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, has revolutionized the work of Caltech neuroscientists.
text:
On October 5, three scientists—Peter Hegemann, Georg Nagel, and Karl Deisseroth—were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the development of optogenetics, a revolutionary tool that allows neuroscientists to use light to turn on and off individual brain cells, even those located deep within the brain. Hegemann and Nagel, the Nobel Assembly noted, "discovered a remarkable protein, channelrhodopsin, in a single-celled alga," and Deisseroth "transformed the protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells."
Viviana Gradinaru (BS '05), Caltech's Troendle Professor of Neuroscience and Biological Engineering and a Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator, was one of the first graduate students in Deisseroth's Stanford University laboratory. A Caltech professor since 2012, Gradinaru has spent much of her Caltech career further advancing the optogenetics technique.
In optogenetics, brain cells are genetically modified to carry proteins that enable researchers to excite or inhibit the cells' activity using specific wavelengths of light, even if they are located deep within the brain. Hegemann, from Humboldt University in Berlin, and Nagel, of Germany's University of Würzburg, found in the early 2000s that these proteins enable green algae to swim toward sources of light.
When Gradinaru started doctoral studies at Stanford in 2005 after graduating from Caltech, optogenetics was still a niche specialty. Deisseroth's lab had just begun to develop techniques to insert opsin genes into rodent brain cells in a dish, allowing those cells to be turned on with blue light. Gradinaru's graduate thesis was focused on developing inhibitory opsins and using optogenetics in vivo to understand how deep brain stimulation works for Parkinson's disease.
While excitatory optogenetics had advanced to working smoothly in living animals and was being utilized by more labs worldwide, inhibitory optogenetics—suppressing the activity of cells with light—was more challenging.
"In those early optogenetics days, the inhibitory opsins would aggregate and harm the cells we were trying to study," recalls Gradinaru, who is also director and Allen V. C. Davis and Lenabelle Davis Leadership Chair of the Richard N. Merkin Institute for Translational Research at Caltech. (Deisseroth is a member of the Merkin Institute's advisory board.) "Much of my early PhD was focused on how to evolve inhibitory opsins from bacteria for safe, effective use in mammalian cells. We figured out that we could guide the proteins to where they needed to go within the cell by adding small sequences acting like ZIP codes for delivering mail." This unlocked the path for inhibitory optogenetics with "light-driven chloride pumps like NpHR and its later engineered variants," as the Nobel Assembly noted in its press release.
Gradinaru's other major publication as a graduate student was the first proof-of-concept that optogenetics could be used for preclinical research to modulate behavior in a living animal, specifically a mouse model of Parkinson's disease, to better understand the mechanism underlying deep brain stimulation, a powerful therapeutic option used in clinics.
As a graduate student, Gradinaru taught courses at Stanford and at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory in New York on optogenetics—how to synthesize the opsins, get them into the neurons of lab animals, and use the lasers. When she joined the Caltech faculty, she continued to teach optogenetics as part of a course on experimental techniques in neuroscience. Gradinaru also established the CLOVER Center (CLARITY, Optogenetics, & Vector Engineering) at Caltech's Beckman Institute for dissemination of neurotechnologies and is now also an affiliated faculty member with the Tianqiao and Chrissy Chen Institute for Neuroscience at Caltech.
Over more than a decade at Caltech, Gradinaru has continued to develop optogenetics methods. Early on, she initiated a collaboration with Frances Arnold, the Linus Pauling Professor of Chemical Engineering, Bioengineering and Biochemistry and director of the Donna and Benjamin M. Rosen Bioengineering Center. Arnold pioneered a technique called directed evolution, a lab technique that experimentally mimics the process of natural selection to produce new types of enzymes with specific traits—work that earned her the 2018 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Together, the two labs utilized machine learning–assisted directed evolution to create new opsins that are sensitive to red light; these longer wavelengths of light can penetrate farther into the brain than the blue light, enabling recruitment of larger, deeper brain areas with distant, less damaging light sources. When paired with delivery vectors that could cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB), the team could distribute opsin genes noninvasively across the entire brain, moving one step closer to minimally invasive optogenetics.
"Doing research in Karl's lab was an amazing opportunity for learning, interdisciplinary discovery and lifelong friendships: Feng Zhang, first author on many optogenetics papers and inventor on much of the early patents was my graduate rotation mentor!" Gradinaru says. "I try to bring that same spirit of fluid research and preclinical-relevant work in my own lab."
Optogenetics has continued to mature and is now used widely by neuroscientists. At Caltech, it has been a fundamental tool enabling discoveries about how the brain governs social behaviors, homeostasis (internal balance in the body), sleep, and more.
David Anderson's laboratory, for example, uses optogenetics to study the neurobiology of emotion and social behaviors.
"Optogenetics has revolutionized neuroscientists' ability to move beyond simply observing correlations between brain activity and behavior to establishing cause and effect," says Anderson, the Seymour Benzer Professor of Biology, Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator, and Leadership Chair and director of the Tianqiao and Chrissy Chen Institute for Neuroscience. "With it, we can test whether activating certain neurons is sufficient to evoke a behavior and whether inhibiting them blocks that behavior. For example, it has allowed my lab to discover specific neurons that control basic instinctive behaviors and related emotion states including aggression, mating, and fear in both flies and mice."
In the Nobel award citation, optogenetics is credited with making possible discoveries about the neural circuits underlying thirst—research that was conducted in the Caltech laboratory of Yuki Oka, professor of biology, Heritage Medical Research Institute Investigator, and affiliated faculty member with the Tianqiao and Chrissy Chen Institute for Neuroscience.
"In our work on thirst, we used light to activate a small population of neurons in the brain, and within about a second, a fully hydrated animal began drinking water," Oka explains. "That kind of immediate, direct link between the activity of specific neurons and a motivated behavior was unimaginable before this technology. It allowed us to move beyond describing which neurons respond to thirst and to demonstrate that they drive it. In other words, optogenetics transformed neuroscience from a field of correlation to one of causality. It was a privilege to collaborate with Karl early on, and his work continues to shape how we study the brain."
The tool also can be adapted for use in many different model organisms, such as zebrafish, tiny transparent fish. Researchers in the Caltech laboratory of David Prober, professor of biology and affiliated faculty member with the Tianqiao and Chrissy Chen Institute for Neuroscience, use light to probe the zebrafish brain to answer fundamental questions about the neuroscience underlying circadian sleep rhythms.
"Optogenetics is essential for my lab's research on zebrafish," Prober says. "We routinely use optogenetics to stimulate or inhibit specific neurons while recording the behavior of almost 200 animals at the same time. This has allowed us to discover neurons that regulate sleep and determine how they do so."
When Gradinaru first met Deisseroth early in 2005 during her admissions interview at Stanford, his lab was just getting started, but, she says, there was a clear and exciting vision to use light and genes for neuroscience.
"As a student trained in optics and electronics in Romania and in molecular biology and neuroscience at Caltech, I thought I could really help—at least with some of the empty rooms that needed equipment setup," she says. "I am happy for Karl, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel, and grateful to have played a part as a graduate student at Stanford and assistant professor at Caltech in the development of optogenetics, a method that is now being used beyond academia in industry and health care. Many more exciting discoveries and clinical impacts still lie ahead."

title: Caltech and AIM Build AI Platform with Mathematicians for Mathematicians
author: Kimm Fesenmaier (kfesenma@caltech.edu)
summary: The new tool aims to organize, synthesize, and facilitate mathematical work without losing track of the more human aspects of the mathematical process
text:
In recent weeks, a surprisingly contentious debate has been making headlines around the world: What role should artificial intelligence (AI) play in mathematics? The field, which has centuries-old methods of operating, sharing results, and acknowledging contributions, is grappling with how to incorporate the prodigious power of this new technology.
Some mathematicians are ready to embrace change and argue that the potential advances offered by AI-enabled math solutions outweigh the costs—that AI, with its special capabilities, such as its ability to explore vast search spaces, might be able to attack problems that humans might not otherwise take on. Other mathematicians are publicly denouncing the technology and the ill effects it could have on the field and its practitioners. For example, some are concerned that mathematics will end up being developed by large corporations that, by their nature, are not well suited to sharing results freely.
Into this charged atmosphere, Caltech is introducing a new effort that could bring the two sides together: An AI tool designed with mathematicians for mathematicians. The goal of the platform is to organize, synthesize, and facilitate mathematical work in a way that will allow mathematicians to take advantage of both the piecemeal and collaborative nature of mathematical progress and AI's ability to make connections and synthesize understanding.
The new AI software platform is being developed through a collaboration between the American Institute of Mathematics (AIM), which has been housed on the Caltech campus since 2023, and Caltech's Information Science and Technology initiative (IST).
"I think the community is really craving something that is not just all AI or no AI. This is another path, and, in fact, it has the potential to bring everybody together," says Sergei Gukov, the John D. MacArthur Professor of Theoretical Physics and Mathematics at Caltech, executive director of AIM, and one of the leaders of this new project along with Yisong Yue, professor of computing and mathematical sciences, and Pietro Perona, the Allen E. Puckett Professor of Electrical Engineering and director of IST. Yue and Perona are both affiliated faculty members of the Tianqiao and Chrissy Chen Institute for Neuroscience.
The team hopes the new software platform will be a companion for mathematicians as they explore and develop new ideas. It can help identify connections between problems, suggest conjectures and possible strategies, and pursue many lines of reasoning in parallel. As those lines develop, the system can handle routine technical work while helping mathematicians understand which ideas are actually driving an argument and distill them into a clearer proof or broader principle. The platform will also make the structure of this work visible, showing how conjectures, arguments, references, and competing approaches connect and evolve over time.
This structure is also meant to support collaboration. Different mathematicians or small groups can pursue competing approaches in parallel, while the system helps connect their progress and accelerate insights that emerge from the interaction between different lines of work. Mathematicians can move between these lines of thought, revisit earlier ideas, and build on one another's work without losing the larger picture.
Perona is delighted to see the collaborative effort taking shape. "Clearly AI has a lot to offer in helping researchers become more effective in their work," he says. "Almost every lab at Caltech is now wondering how to best use this technology. We have to be humble and open to change, since it will change how we do business in ways small and large: How we come up with hypotheses and conjectures, how we become aware of other researchers' work, how we develop experiments and proofs, how we collaborate, how we share our findings, and how we get to understand the meaning of our findings. Thanks to our tradition of intellectual courage, curiosity, and collaboration across fields, Caltech researchers can help show the way."
Yue comes to the project from the AI algorithmic side. He talks about the humanness of what he calls "research taste"—the practices and preferences that experts build up through years of experience and perfect with their thoughtfulness and wisdom. This quality, at times elusive in researchers, is something AI currently lacks.
Yue, Perona, and Gukov began working on the new AI platform about nine months ago to find a way to combine mathematicians' curiosity and research taste with AI's encyclopedic knowledge to efficiently reach consensus about which problems are important and how to go about solving them. Beyond that, the researchers want the tool to organize data into useful pieces of information, or knowledge—keeping track of all the progress mathematicians are making along the way.
"Right now, everyone is going after big ideas, but that's actually not how you move a field forward," Yue says. "You move a field forward through the process of understanding what you did to solve the problem."
The researchers say the platform will keep up with needs and advances, providing mathematicians with increasingly capable tools that will augment their ability to formulate conjectures and prove theorems by suggesting relevant theorems from vast databases. It will also streamline the workstream by integrating tools needed by mathematicians that current AI systems treat as outside tools. For example, current LLMs are inefficient when converting human mathematical reasoning or statements into so-called Lean code, a precise language that works with computers. The new system will build the ability to make such conversions right into the system.
The preliminary platform will be up and running in a few months for teams of mathematicians to start testing. Importantly, it will be refined continually over months and years as mathematicians use it. Every year, AIM, one of seven national math institutes funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF), welcomes more than a thousand visiting mathematicians to campus for week-long sessions. Moving forward, these mathematicians will be invited to work with the system and provide feedback in collaboration with Caltech AI engineers to improve the system. "Within a year, we expect to have sufficient data to help us better understand how mathematicians use the platform. That's when we expect to come up with a radical redesign, which will include training a new AI system to better support their work," Gukov says. "We are looking for major sources of support to make that work possible. We are encouraged by initial commitments from Paul Stahura and Rahim Noorani."
Although this new framework is being built specifically with math in mind, the team stresses that it could become a useful approach for other fields. "This can be a template in some ways for how AI impacts many areas of science," Yue says. "It could capture all of this collaborative effort and the pieces of human work that shouldn't be lost."

title: Caltech Biologists Receive High-Risk, High-Reward Grants from the NIH
author: Katie Neith (katien@caltech.edu)
summary: The awards will allow Mitchell Guttman (left) and Markus Meister to build a better platform for developing antibodies and to discover how the brain organizes human behavior, respectively.
text:
Caltech faculty members Mitchell Guttman and Markus Meister (PhD '87) have been selected to receive "high-risk, high-reward" grants from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for cutting-edge work in biomedical science and neuroscience. Guttman's funded work could enable new methods to produce antibodies for any possible protein—a development with implications for both basic laboratory tests and clinical care. Meanwhile, Meister's research aims to explain arguably the core question of neuroscience: how the brain organizes human behavior.
Guttman, a Caltech professor of biology, is a recipient of an NIH Director's Transformative Research Award. These grants support projects that are "inherently risky and untested but have the potential to create or overturn fundamental paradigms," according to the NIH.
Guttman's research seeks to understand fundamental principles of biological regulation within the nuclei of cells. He and his lab have developed numerous genomic methods for mapping the higher-order three-dimensional organization of RNA and DNA in the nucleus. Many of these methods rely on a strategy called split-and-pool barcoding, in which samples are repeatedly divided, tagged with short DNA "barcodes," and pooled again, so that molecules bound together inside a cell end up carrying the same string of barcodes. This allows thousands of molecular interactions to be read out at once by DNA sequencing.
With the new funding, Guttman will apply this approach to developing reliable antibodies, a challenge that touches nearly every area of biomedical research. Scientists use antibodies to detect and measure proteins in everything from basic laboratory experiments to clinical diagnostic tests. However, high-quality antibodies exist for only a small fraction of the roughly 20,000 proteins in the human body. Using split-and-pool barcoding methods, Guttman will develop a platform to create molecules that bind to every human protein. The platform uses nanobodies—miniature antibodies modeled after those made naturally by camels and llamas—which can be produced and screened in enormous numbers in a test tube.
"Nearly every experiment that measures a protein depends on having a good antibody, and, for most human proteins, we simply don't have one," Guttman says. "A complete set would enable experiments that are impossible today, from measuring thousands of proteins within individual cells to mapping how proteins interact with DNA, RNA, and one another, and could ultimately lead to improved diagnostics and new therapies."
Meister, the Anne P. and Benjamin F. Biaggini Professor of Biological Sciences, is the recipient of an NIH Director's Pioneer Award, which "supports scientists with outstanding records of creativity pursuing new research directions to develop pioneering approaches to major challenges in biomedical, social science, and behavioral research."
Meister's research investigates large circuits of neurons to determine how they work. These brain structures consist of many neurons that have some anatomical and functional identity and exchange signals with other brain circuits. While his lab previously focused on circuits involved in visual processing, he is now exploring neural mechanisms responsible for rapid learning and task control.
With the Pioneer Award funding, Meister will investigate "the central question" motivating neuroscience: How does the brain organize the perplexing richness of human behavior? Many of our everyday activities—such as driving to work or making dinner—are composed of hundreds of distinct and brief tasks that are strung together to accomplish an overall goal. Researchers know very little about how the brain implements and coordinates these "microtasks" in a flexible and rapid succession.
"Our goal is to gain an understanding of hierarchical control of human behavior for the first time, all the way from deciding long-term goals to executing individual movements," says Meister, who is also an affiliated faculty member of the Tianqiao and Chrissy Chen Institute for Neuroscience at Caltech. The work, he says, could improve treatments for neuropsychiatric disorders and help build better artificial intelligence systems for controlling the actions of robots, among other applications.
The NIH Common Fund "supports bold scientific programs that catalyze discovery across all biomedical and behavioral research," according to the organization's website.
In 2026, NIH issued seven Pioneer Awards, 42 New Innovator Awards, six Transformative Research Awards, and three Early Independence Awards, including those awarded to Guttman (R01CA325352-01) and Meister (DP1NS155489-01). Funding for the grants comes from the NIH Common Fund, the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders, and the Office of Research Innovation, Validation, and Application.

title: Caltech Faculty Receive NSF CAREER Awards
author: Caltech Media Relations (mr@caltech.edu)
summary: Five receive the National Science Foundation's most prestigious award for junior faculty members
text:
Five Caltech faculty members have been selected to receive the National Science Foundation's (NSF) Faculty Early Career Development (CAREER) Award starting this year.
CAREER awards, the NSF's most prestigious awards for junior faculty members, are designed to enable awardees to develop careers as outstanding teacher-scholars. Awardees are chosen because they "exemplify the role of teacher-scholars through outstanding research, excellent education, and the integration of education and research within the context of the mission of their organizations," according to the NSF.
Jane Bae (BS '11), assistant professor of aerospace and Susan Wu Scholar
Jane Bae (BS '11) studies the physical mechanisms that produce turbulence and develops accurate models that simulate the complex dynamics at play in turbulent flows, such as those near wind farms or around aircraft. The models can then inform simulations capable of improving designs and improving predictions of atmospheric flows. Bae, who is also a Wu Scholar, is particularly interested in applying machine learning, data science, and other novel methods to turbulence modeling.
After earning her undergraduate degree in math at Caltech in 2011, Bae completed graduate work in computational and mathematical engineering at Stanford University. She completed postdoctoral appointments at Caltech and Harvard University before joining the Caltech faculty as an assistant professor of aerospace in 2021.
Kareem El-Badry, associate professor of astronomy
Kareem El-Badry is an astronomer interested in binary stars, black holes, and related stellar phenomena. He has made numerous discoveries involving stars and black holes using datasets from large astronomical surveys. In a recent study, he describes the first-known "black hole triple," a system of three stars, one of which is a black hole. Some of El-Badry's recent findings include the 2024 unveiling of 21 hidden neutron stars orbiting around stars like our Sun. These hidden neutron stars were spotted indirectly through gravitational wobbles induced in their partner stars. And in 2022, El-Badry and his colleagues discovered the closest known black hole to Earth, lying about 1,600 light-years away.
El-Badry attended Yale University as an undergraduate and earned his PhD in astrophysics from UC Berkeley. Before coming to Caltech in 2024, he held a postdoctoral position at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics. In 2025, he was the recipient of a MacArthur Fellowship.
Elias Most, assistant professor of theoretical astrophysics and William H. Hurt Scholar
In a recent study, Elias Most and his team elucidated the radio emission mechanism for long-period radio transients from binary stars. In another set of papers, Most and his colleagues used supercomputer simulations to track what happens when a black hole swallows a neutron star whole. Their calculations demonstrated that in addition to gravitational waves, these systems can potentially produce some of the strongest "monster" shock waves in the universe, leading to the formation of an exotic, previously hypothesized "black hole pulsar."
Most received his bachelor's degree from the University of Göttingen in 2013, and his PhD from Goethe University Frankfurt in 2020, and was a predoctoral fellow at the Flatiron Institute's Center for Computational Astrophysics. Before joining Caltech in 2023, he held joint postdoctoral positions at Princeton University and the Institute for Advanced Study.
Trevor Nolan, assistant professor of biology and biological engineering
Trevor Nolan's research focuses on how the cells that make up a plant's roots send signals to one another and adapt to their environments. In multicellular organisms, the growth and function of organs depend on precise coordination and communication among different types of cells and tissues. How do cell layers align their behaviors to produce coherent organ growth? What signals act across tissues to coordinate development and differentiation, and how are they interpreted by cells precisely through space and over time? These are long-standing questions in developmental biology, from plants to lab animals and humans.
To address these questions, Nolan works with Arabidopsis thaliana, a crucial model organism for understanding plant biology. His lab develops new genetic tools for experiments with A. thaliana and uses the plant to answer open questions in developmental biology.
Nolan completed his undergraduate and doctoral work at Iowa State University and a postdoc at Duke University before joining the Caltech faculty in 2025.
Julia Tejada, assistant professor of geobiology and William H. Hurt Scholar
Julia Tejada is a paleobiologist who studies how the chemistry of organisms records their ecology and physiology, and how those signatures can be used to reconstruct the evolution of life through deep time. Her research combines stable isotope geochemistry, organismal biology, and paleontology to investigate how diet, digestive physiology, and metabolism shape the chemical composition of animal tissues. A major focus of the Tejada lab is expanding what stable isotopes can reveal about animal biology. Beyond their traditional use in reconstructing food webs, her lab investigates how amino acid isotope signatures, particularly threonine, record digestive physiology and dietary adaptations in living and extinct organisms.
Tejada also conducts paleontological fieldwork in the western Amazon, recovering fossil plants and vertebrates from understudied deposits. By integrating the fossil record with geochemical approaches, her lab investigates how organisms and ecosystems have changed through evolutionary time.
Tejada received her undergraduate degree from Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos in Peru, an MSc from the University of Florida, and an MA, MPhil, and PhD from Columbia University. She completed postdoctoral appointments at the University of Montpellier and Cambridge University before joining the Caltech faculty in 2023.

title: NASA's Roman Space Telescope Takes First Coronagraph Instrument Observation
author: Whitney Clavin (wclavin@caltech.edu)
summary: The Coronagraph Instrument, designed to demonstrate technology that can directly image planets, is commanded at Caltech's IPAC astronomy center
text:
On September 22, the Coronagraph Instrument on NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope opened its eyes to cosmic light for the first time. The ultimate purpose of the instrument—which is commanded from Caltech's IPAC, a science and data center for astrophysics and planetary sciences—is to demonstrate technology that can block starlight, providing unprecedented views of the planets and dusty disks around nearby stars.
The coronagraph first woke up on September 1 and stretched its digital, electronic, and mechanical "limbs" mid-month. Once the Roman team confirmed that the fine-guidance system was holding the Coronagraph Instrument steady, scientists adjusted the focus so it could take its first bleary-eyed look at space, which will help scientists fine-tune the instrument's view.
"We're all extremely pleased with how well things are working," says Alexandra Greenbaum, coronagraph data management system lead at IPAC. "There's a lot of collaboration that went into this milestone, so it's wonderful to see all of us working together and to be a part of the team. I'm really looking forward to supporting the rest of commissioning, both on the operations and the data processing."
The coronagraph was designed and built by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which Caltech manages for NASA. It will block out a star's light, making the surrounding area dark enough to image the faint light of orbiting planets. These first tests "build toward digging a dark hole on the sky," Greenbaum says.
In the future, both the Coronagraph Instrument and the observatory's primary Wide Field Instrument, will undergo further calibrations and tests during a three-month commissioning period. NASA anticipates releasing Roman's first images by early 2027.
This first observation "confirms that the instrument can produce a focused image," says Vanessa Bailey, a Roman Coronagraph Instrument scientist at JPL. "It's a very limited test that kicks off a methodical process of increasingly complex tasks that help us prepare for the instrument's future observations."
Read the NASA blog here.

title: Former Caltech Postdoc Commands NASA Mission to the International Space Station
author: Caltech Media Relations (mr@caltech.edu)
summary: Jessica Watkins serves as the commander of NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station.
text:
This morning, NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission successfully launched to the International Space Station, commanded by NASA astronaut and former Caltech postdoc Jessica Watkins. The crew of four astronauts will perform research, technology demonstrations, and maintenance.
This is the second flight to the space station for Watkins, who was selected as a NASA astronaut in 2017. She grew up in Lafayette, Colorado, and earned an undergraduate degree in geological and environmental sciences from Stanford University, then a doctorate in geology from UCLA. A planetary geologist, Watkins studied the Martian surface and was a member of the Curiosity rover science team at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), which Caltech manages for NASA. At Caltech, Watkins worked in the research group of John Grotzinger, the Harold Brown Professor of Geology and former project scientist of the Curiosity Rover.
Watkins first launched to the space station aboard NASA's SpaceX Crew-4 mission in 2022, spending a total of 170 days in orbit across Expeditions 67 and 68. She will be the first NASA astronaut to launch twice aboard a SpaceX Dragon spacecraft.
Read our interview with Watkins from 2017 here: https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/caltech-postdoc-future-astronaut-78560

title: Cambridge and Hogan Lovells Cadwalader build future leaders
author: Cambridge Judge Communications Team
summary: Cambridge Judge Business School and Hogan Lovells Cadwalader launch Leading The Future, a global programme for 60 leaders.
text:
Created following the combination that formed Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, the programme brings together around 60 established and emerging leaders from across the firm’s global network. Developed in collaboration with Cambridge Judge Business School Executive Education’s specialist professional services practice, PSF@Cambridge, it draws on Cambridge academics and practitioners to examine the strategic, organisational and personal dimensions of leadership.
What participants will learn
Starting in-person in Cambridge, and running through October 2027, Leading The Future combines immersive on-campus modules with virtual masterclasses, leadership assessments and individual coaching. Sessions will cover executing strategy at scale, navigating uncertainty, sustaining a high-performance culture, and communicating with impact through storytelling. Participants will also take part in an immersive experience focused on successful collaboration, debate a series of future strategic scenarios, and create a cohort charter to translate their learning into action. Throughout the programme, participants will explore the firm’s vision and strategy alongside wider leadership challenges, with a focus on aligning leaders across practices and regions and translating shared ambitions into institutional action.
Each participant will also address a leadership challenge, applying the programme’s learning to the firm while exchanging perspectives and building relationships across the global partnership.
Commenting on the launch, Professor Stelios Kavadias and Mark Smith of Cambridge Judge Business School, said:
Leadership is rarely about having all the answers; it is about creating the opportunity to step back, question assumptions and learn from the experience of others. Bringing together accomplished leaders with different perspectives creates richer conversations and fresh ways of thinking that benefit not only the individual, but the organisation as a whole. Leading The Future has been designed to create that space, helping participants reflect on the challenges ahead while strengthening the relationships that underpin long-term success.
Leading a global professional firm at the top of the market requires leaders to be at their best. We have built Leading The Future around that reality and are delighted to support partners who will play a significant role in the firm's future.
Miguel Zaldivar, CEO of Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, said:
“The success of our combined firm will depend on our people and the leaders we develop for the future. We are bringing together 60 established and emerging leaders from all over the world, across 2 cohorts, to contribute to our strategy and help translate it into action. Cambridge combines tradition with innovation in a way that strongly resonates with us. It is a place with centuries of academic excellence, but also one focused on new ideas, innovation and the future of business and leadership.

“The focus on our people is also central to our 5-2-1 strategy. We are proud of our low attrition rates and benchmark ourselves against our competitors on that measure of stability. Several of our International Management Committee members have spent their entire careers with us. Leading The Future is another investment in our next generation of leaders, and I look forward to learning alongside them as a member of cohort one in Cambridge.”

Leading The Future forms part of Hogan Lovells Cadwalader’s leadership pathway. Momentum supports high-potential lawyers broadening their leadership impact; Transform supports new partners in their first year as leaders in their practice; and Ignite prepares partners to take on future leadership roles. Together with Leading The Future, these programmes provide a structured framework for developing leaders across the firm and setting them up for success.

title: From Varsity tables to social ventures: my Cambridge MFin year
author: Cambridge Judge Communications Team
summary: Read Shivin Sharma's reflections on his Cambridge MFin experience, from entrepreneurship to social ventures.
text:
Honestly, this year has been a whirlwind, and I mean that in the best way. When I arrived at Cambridge Judge Business School for the Master of Finance (MFin), I expected rigorous coursework and late nights with problem sets. I got all of that, but I also found myself wearing a Cambridge Varsity jersey, pitching a social venture at Trinity Hall and finishing the year with the Lanvern Prize in international finance.
Looking back, the moments that have stayed with me the most are the ones where academic rigour, community and unexpected opportunities came together.
Settling into Cambridge on the MFin
Coming to Cambridge for the MFin was exciting and slightly overwhelming. The programme is intense, and from the first term it was clear that expectations were high. At the same time, College life at St Edmund’s College offered a different rhythm: formal dinners, chance conversations in the bar and friendships that formed quickly.
I decided early on that I didn’t want my year to be only about grades and exams. I started saying yes to more things: College events, cross-programme meet-ups and clubs that had nothing to do with finance. That choice opened doors I didn’t know existed when I arrived with my suitcase and reading list.
From College club to Cambridge Varsity
One of those doors was the pool and snooker table at St Edmund’s. I joined the College club and soon became Vice-President, helping to organise matches and keep things running. It was a welcome counterbalance to the intensity of the Cambridge MFin.
During a match against Homerton College, a member of the Cambridge Varsity pool and snooker team was watching. Afterwards, he invited me to trial. Competition for Varsity places is fierce, so it felt like a long shot, but I went for it.
What followed felt like a wildcard entry into a squad I had only ever hoped to join. I played tournaments at Hatfields, representing the University of Cambridge in the All Southern Universities Tournament, finishing in the top 16 while Cambridge reached the semi-finals. For someone who had come to study finance, representing the University in sport felt surreal.
The highlight was the Varsity match against Oxford. Pulling on the Cambridge jersey and helping the team beat Oxford 86–71 is a story I’ll be telling for years. Yet, when we won, I felt unexpectedly sad. Months of focus and effort had built up to this single moment, and in chasing the result, I realised I had missed parts of the journey, especially the fact that it was my last time playing in Cambridge colours.
I kept thinking I would enjoy it “once we’d won”. Then the win came, and the moment was already gone. That experience taught me something I’ve tried to carry into the rest of the year: you don’t get the time back, so you might as well be present while you’re in it.
Discovering social ventures at King’s E-Lab
Another major thread started just after Michaelmas exams, when I joined the King’s College Entrepreneurship Lab (E-Lab) Social Venture Residential. For 5 days, we lived at King’s College and were thrown into the deep end of entrepreneurship, working in mixed teams to turn rough ideas into social venture concepts.
It was intense, especially straight after exams, but I loved it. Listening to people who had actually built ventures, and testing ideas with peers, made me realise that social ventures interested me far more than I had expected. I began to see how the skills from the MFin could be applied to problems that were about impact as well as returns.
The residential is also where I met Natalie, a fellow with Cambridge Centre for Social Innovation. We clicked early on, and she ended up mentoring me through the rest of the year. In a place as busy as Cambridge, having someone who understood what I cared about and could point me towards the right opportunities made a huge difference.
Natalie was the one who suggested I apply for the Trinity Hall Catalysts programme. At the time, it felt like another learning opportunity. In hindsight, it became one of the defining experiences of my year.
Building a venture with the Trinity Hall Catalysts programme
Trinity Hall Catalysts supports and funds early-stage social ventures. Every other Thursday, we had sessions on the practical side of building something: talking to customers, running focus groups, testing markets and checking whether an idea really holds up.
I started with a vague sense that I wanted to build something with social impact. Through those sessions – and a lot of questioning – I developed a clearer venture I genuinely wanted to pursue. It wasn’t a single lightbulb moment, more a gradual sharpening of what mattered to me and how my finance training could be part of it.
The programme ends with a showcase where you pitch to a panel, and only 6 ventures across the University of Cambridge are selected for further support and a grant. Standing up and pitching felt very different from presenting a case in class. The stakes were personal.
When I found out my venture was one of the 6 selected, it felt slightly surreal. The grant and recognition were encouraging, but what stayed with me most was the sense that if you engage with the Cambridge ecosystem, ideas can turn into real projects. The venture is still with me, and I hope to return to it properly one day.
Academic focus and the Lanvern Prize
Alongside all of this, the core of my year was still the Cambridge MFin. The programme is demanding, particularly in international finance, where the pace is fast and the material is challenging. I spent many hours in the University Library connecting theory with what was happening in markets.
Early in Michaelmas, I started working closely with Marwa Hammam, Executive Director of the Cambridge MFin, who became a key mentor. She has an unusual ability to understand what a student cares about and help them navigate the many options at Cambridge. With her guidance, I was able to focus my efforts and make choices that aligned with where I wanted to grow.
Being awarded the University of Cambridge’s Lanvern Prize on the MFin, for the highest overall performance in international finance in the cohort, was a highlight. It felt like the culmination of a lot of quiet work, supported by excellent teaching and mentoring. More than anything, it reminded me that academic achievement at Cambridge is rarely a solo effort.
Looking back: a year of rigour, community and impact
When I think about what the Cambridge MFin has meant to me, a few themes stand out. It has been academically rigorous, pushing me to deepen my understanding of finance and to approach complex problems with discipline. It has also been unexpectedly diverse in its experiences, from Varsity sport to social ventures.
Most of all, it has been shaped by people: mentors like Natalie and Marwa, friends across the MFin and other programmes and the wider Cambridge community that kept putting opportunities in front of me.
If you’re considering the Cambridge MFin, I’d say: come prepared to work hard, but leave room for the unexpected. Join a club, attend a College event and don’t be afraid to step into something that feels slightly outside your comfort zone. Use the programme not only to deepen your technical expertise, but also to explore where you want that expertise to take you.
And while you’re doing all of that, try to enjoy the journey as you go. The year moves quickly and the moments that feel small now may be the ones you remember most when you look back.
If you’re considering the Cambridge MFin, I’d say: come prepared to work hard, but leave room for the unexpected. Join a club, attend a College event and don’t be afraid to step into something that feels slightly outside your comfort zone.

title: Brazil's presidential elections linked to decades of fluctuating environmental destruction – study
author: Fred Lewsey
summary: A University of Cambridge-led analysis of maps made from satellite imagery covering over three decades and seven presidents shows how the winner of Brazil’s national elections since 1990 directly affected the preservation of its globally vital ecosystems.
text:
A study tracking 35 years of vegetation data from the Amazon to the Cerrado over seven presidencies shows how Brazil’s top political leadership can dramatically slow down or speed up the loss of tropical forests and savannas.
          Brazil has shown the world that deforestation can be dramatically reduced when there is the political will to act. But that progress is fragile...
Vinicius Tonetti
A University of Cambridge-led analysis of maps made from satellite imagery covering over three decades and seven presidents shows how the winner of Brazil’s national elections since 1990 directly affected the preservation of its globally vital ecosystems.
The study reveals a rollercoaster of habitat loss rates across presidencies in the country's three largest biomes – the Amazon, Cerrado, and Atlantic Forest – from a peak of 3.62 million hectares of native vegetation vanishing annually under Itamar Franco in the nineties, to a low of just 1.21 million hectares a year under Temer a decade ago.
Researchers found that the Amazon lost an average of around 994,000 hectares annually during the first three years of Luiz Inácio ‘Lula’ da Silva's current presidency, compared with 1.4 million hectares a year under his predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro.
This represents a reduction of about 29% in the average annual area of Amazon lost under Lula’s return compared with Bolsonaro’s time in office, according to the study, published in Environmental Research Communications.
However, in the Cerrado, the vast tropical savannas of central Brazil, the trend moved in the opposite direction. Annual habitat losses averaged around 1.28 million hectares between 2023 and 2025, an increase of around 50% compared with 854,000 hectares per year under Bolsonaro, during whose presidency savanna loss accelerated.
The Cerrado, a vital source of water that feeds many of Brazil’s rivers, has seen major increases in commercial farming of crops such as soybean, as US-China trade tensions during Trump’s first term saw China pivot to Brazilian soybean.
Weaker legal protections, along with efforts to curb deforestation in the Amazon, may have pushed agricultural expansion into the Cerrado, say researchers. They warn that major soy traders’ withdrawal from a moratorium on growing soy on recently deforested land could have devastating consequences for Brazil’s natural habitats.
The study also reveals how the Atlantic Forest, which stretches along Brazil's eastern coastline but has been “highly fragmented” by centuries of farming and urbanisation, actually experienced periods of recovery rather than simply a slowdown in loss.
During Lula's first two terms, the Atlantic Forest gained an average of around 18,000 hectares of native vegetation a year. Under Rousseff, that figure rose to nearly 30,000 hectares annually. Since Rousseff left office, the Atlantic Forest has returned to net vegetation losses, although at a much smaller scale than in the Amazon or Cerrado.
It is the only one of Brazil's three major biomes to have experienced periods of net vegetation gain in the last thirty-five years.
“Brazilian presidents have dictated the fate of the country’s forests and savannas for over three decades,” said study lead author Dr Vinicius Tonetti, a Brazilian conservation biologist at the University of Cambridge’s Department of Zoology.
“We see that presidential terms characterised by strong environmental laws, satellite monitoring, and zero-deforestation agreements are clearly linked to major reductions in habitat loss,” Tonetti said. “Brazil's recent history shows just how much environmental policy matters and comes from the top.”
"Our findings also show that while deforestation in the Amazon has slowed under Lula, the loss of natural habitats across the Cerrado has remained high. Protecting one ecosystem while losing another is not a sustainable solution."
The study used land-cover maps from the MapBiomas project, derived from decades of satellite data, to track changes in the Amazon, Cerrado and Atlantic Forest between 1990 and 2025.
Across all three biomes combined, the largest average annual net loss of native vegetation occurred during the presidency of Itamar Franco, between 1993 and 1994, when approximately 3.62 million hectares disappeared each year.
Fernando Henrique Cardoso's (FHC) administration, from 1995 to 2002, recorded average annual losses of around 3.30 million hectares.
Lula's first two terms, between 2003 and 2010, marked a major turning point, with loss of natural habitat falling by some 35% to an annual average of around 2.44 million hectares. In the Amazon alone, habitat loss was around 20% lower under Lula than under FHC, with a significant slowdown in the rate of deforestation.
“During Lula's first two terms, agricultural production expanded while stronger monitoring and enforcement resulted in more habitat preservation,” said Tonetti. “Economic development and environmental protection do not have to come at the expense of each other."
Under Lula’s successor Dilma Rousseff, overall habitat loss almost halved again (a further 46% reduction) to about 1.31 million hectares a year, before reaching just 1.21 million hectares a year on average during Michel Temer's time in office.
Under Bolsonaro, however, major cuts to environment agencies, weakened enforcement, reduced environmental fines, and efforts to loosen environmental regulations coincided with a sharp loss of native vegetation across ecosystems, rising to 2.36 million hectares per year on average, almost doubling (95% increase) from the historic low of Temer’s premiership.
While Lula’s return saw deforestation in the Amazon fall significantly, the overall loss of native vegetation across Brazil’s three major biomes has declined by only around 2%, largely because of increasing vegetation loss in the Cerrado.
The collapse of the soy moratorium in the Amazon and new laws restricting Indigenous land claims are part of a worrying trend that may escalate under a new president, according to Tonetti. For example, Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged to overhaul the environmental licensing system if elected.
"Brazil has shown the world that deforestation can be dramatically reduced when there is the political will to act. But that progress is fragile. Recent changes to environmental legislation and the weakening of commitments to deforestation-free soy could undermine years of conservation gains,” said Tonetti.
“As the nation once again elects a president, the voters of Brazil need to understand just how much is at stake for some of the world’s most precious forests and ecosystems.”
The single largest gap in vegetation loss between presidents for any of the biomes was seen in the Amazon, which lost an average of 1.95 million hectares a year under Fernando Henrique Cardoso but just 614,158 hectares a year under Dilma Rousseff – an area of forest the size of Montenegro spared annually.

title: Good growth: Innovate Cambridge Summit 2026
author: Sarah Fell
summary: New analysis from Cambridge Innovation Capital (CIC), published ahead of the Summit, showed the average equity raised per deal across both life sciences and deep tech has increased five-fold in the last decade, with Cambridge-based early-stage companies having raised £9.1 billion in that period.
text:
More than 500 businesses, start-ups, innovators, academics, political and civic leaders attended the fifth Innovate Cambridge Summit. Speakers celebrated an extraordinary year for innovation in Cambridge, including the creation of three Cambridge-born unicorns, while emphasising the need for innovation-led growth to benefit everyone in the City and wider region.
New analysis from Cambridge Innovation Capital (CIC), published ahead of the Summit, showed the average equity raised per deal across both life sciences and deep tech has increased five-fold in the last decade, with Cambridge-based early-stage companies having raised £9.1 billion in that period.
Taking leadership in innovation
Professor Deborah Prentice, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Cambridge reflected on what makes Cambridge such a thriving innovation economy and the importance of taking a proactive and global leadership role in driving innovation that works for everyone: “There are three ways in which Cambridge takes leadership: through research excellence, by acting as one ecosystem and through our partnerships with other places and organisations.”
These themes were echoed by speakers throughout the day, including Mayor Paul Bristow, Peter Freeman (Chair of the Greater Cambridge Development Corporation) and Roland Sinker (Chair of the Inclusive Innovation and Growth Review, University of Cambridge) with a recurring focus on breakthrough research, ambitious partnerships and a shared sense of purpose across the ecosystem.
Strengthening the life sciences ecosystem
Following GSK’s recent announcement that it will be moving its R&D headquarters to Cambridge in 2029, Chief Scientific Officer, Tony Wood spoke about the increasing need for collaboration in the life sciences and that by moving to Cambridge GSK will be able to create more opportunities to achieve breakthroughs in drug discovery and patient care.
Global ambitions for quantum computing
John Aston, Pro-Vice-Chancellor for Research at the University of Cambridge led a discussion considering the UK’s global leadership role in spearheading the development and application of quantum computing. The University’s partnership with IonQ, which next year will bring the UK’s first commercial scale quantum computer to Cambridge, combined with the University’s research strengths in both quantum and its potential applications, underpinned by the ecosystem’s strength in supporting commercialisation, means that Cambridge is uniquely placed to play a national – and global - leadership role.
City partnerships: Manchester and Cambridge
Faye Holland (Director, Cambridge x Manchester Partnership) described the increasing success of the partnership between Cambridge and Manchester in combining the regions’ complementary strengths to increase the UK’s global competitiveness. The pioneering model for this cross-city approach is now being championed by government and adopted by other city partnerships across the UK.
Keeping jobs and know-how in the UK
How to create the right conditions for start-ups to grow, scale and stay in the UK was explored, and the creation of a new task force announced by Pascal Levensohn (Chair of Cambridge Innovation Hub Global Advisory Board) to take forward a new approach (outlined in a white paper published ahead of the Summit) to keeping a company’s footprint in the UK even if it is acquired internationally.
The Summit also heard from some of Cambridge’s most successful start-ups including Nyobolt and T-Therapeutics (both of which spun out of the University with support from Cambridge Enterprise) as well as Pragmatic Semiconductors, Cambridge Aerospace and CuspAI.
Widening opportunities
Ensuring that innovation-led growth benefits everyone who lives and works in Cambridge and the wider region was a central and recurring theme. Included, a new initiative to create more opportunities for young people in Greater Cambridge was announced at the Summit, with organisations present asked to contribute opportunities such as workplace visits, work experience and mentoring.
Accelerating the energy transition
In a parallel session, leaders from across the Cambridge cleantech ecosystem discussed accelerating the UK's clean energy transition. Hosted by DESNZ, Innovate Cambridge and Cambridge Zero, and chaired by Professor Emily Shuckburgh, Chief Scientific Adviser at DESNZ, the session brought together experts from industry, investment, academia and government. Discussions explored the opportunities and barriers to scaling cleantech innovation and commercialisation, alongside the role that innovation clusters such as Cambridge can play in addressing national clean energy challenges.
Kathryn Chapman, CEO of Innovate Cambridge, summed up the day: "Cambridge is ranked second in the world for innovation intensity, the globally leading research and talent at the University of Cambridge underpins this intensity. When academic institutions, business leaders and government come together with a single, compelling vision for innovation - we can turn the research into jobs, investment, innovation and better quality of life for communities in our region and the UK."

title: How early-career success or failure shapes leaders’ mindsets
author: Ioanna Koliou WebEditor
summary: Research from Cambridge Judge Business School reveals how early-career success and failure shape leaders’ mindsets and influence team creativity and performance.
text:
We all learn from our experiences, good and bad. Humans out of self-preservation tend to shy away from situations in which they got burned in the past, and may readily seek a repeat of situations that in the past resulted in success and positive feedback. But the past can be yesterday, last month, a few years ago or even decades ago.
So when it comes to how leader mindsets develop and how this in turn affects team performance, the timing of such previous incidents matters greatly, according to research by 2 academics at Cambridge Judge Business School, Yeun Joon Kim, Associate Professor in Organisational Behaviour, and Andreas Richter, Professor of Organisational Behaviour.
Focusing on key transition periods in a person’s career
Their research, published in the Journal of Applied Psychology, examines project success and failure experiences during 3 periods of a person’s career:
- the transition from education to work, captured by the person’s first project after entering employment
- the non-transition period between career entry and the first formal leadership role
- the transition into that first leadership role
The research defines project success-failure as a ‘continuous project outcome’ related to a given reference point such as a goal set by the organisation, so outcomes falling short of that goal are deemed failures and outcomes that meet or exceed the goal are considered successes.
“We find that in the transition to a first real job, project success fosters a mindset focused on promotion, while project failure during this early period fosters a mindset focused on prevention in order to avoid setbacks,” says Joon. “We also find that these mindsets directly impact team outcomes, with a promotion mindset boosting team creativity and a prevention-focused mindset improving routine performance.”
Adds Andreas: “What’s also interesting here is that the effect to mindset and team outcomes resulting from project success or failure in that first transition period to a job does not apply to the later transition into a first leadership role. Timing really matters here, and the implications are that a mindset formed from project success or failure at the very start of a person’s career carries over for decades as the person advances in their career.”
We find that in the transition to a first real job, project success fosters a mindset focused on promotion, while project failure during this early period fosters a mindset focused on prevention in order to avoid setbacks. We also find that these mindsets directly impact team outcomes, with a promotion mindset boosting team creativity and a prevention-focused mindset improving routine performance.
An outsized effect of experiences at key career moments
The research revolves around Role Transition Theory (RTT), which says that experiences during periods of role transition exert what the authors term “outsized influence on leaders” because people are “especially susceptible to external cues and demands” during such role transitions. While prior research had looked at how incidents affect leader development, those earlier studies had not focused on the timing of such experiences, and the authors also note that relatively little research has focused on mindsets in the leadership literature.
Within the RTT framework, Joon and Andreas also draw on Regulatory Focus Theory (RFT), which suggests that leaders’ regulatory focus mindsets are shaped by experiences of success and failure. As they explained: “RFT suggests that social environments emphasising potential gains (such as project success) induce a promotion focus, whereas environments highlighting potential losses (such as project failure) induce a prevention focus”.
Thus, say the authors: “We argue that these regulatory focus ‘states’, when triggered by project success–failure experiences during career transitions, may crystallise into enduring mindsets”.
Primary and secondary sensitive periods in a person’s career
The transition from education to work at the start of a person’s professional career, a key focus of the research, is characterised by the authors as the ‘primary sensitive period’. During this period, people “are more of a ‘blank slate’ as they are exposed to work-related environmental stimuli for the very first time” and are “more likely to experience cognitive unfreezing, in which their cognitive models are challenged and subsequently replaced with alternatives that are more congruent with the novel environment.”
The later transition into a person’s first formal leadership role is characterised by Joon and Andreas as the ‘“’secondary sensitive period’. By contrast, the period between entering the workforce and assuming the first formal leadership role is considered a ‘non-transition period’, during which individuals “tend to face lower levels of uncertainty and are less susceptible to environmental influences.”
“The transition from education to work is a highly impactful shift, as the organisational context and tasks are entirely new,” says the research. “By contrast, entering a first leadership role, though demanding, occurs within the world of work and often within the same organisation. Novice leaders are less of a ‘blank slate’ as they can draw on prior work experience and cognitive models that reflect organisational realities.”
Tracking careers at an Asian firm
The research is based on a decade-long study of 132 design-team leaders at an East Asian company, whose careers were tracked from their entry into the workforce through and beyond their first formal leadership roles. The researchers collected data from a design department composed of small teams of 3 or 4 members. Designs approved by the company became formal projects, and the success or failure of each completed project was assessed using its return on investment, based primarily on sales and project costs.
To assess whether individuals’ mindsets are promotion-focused or prevention-focused, the study asked participants to answer questions such as whether “I take chances at work to maximise my goals for advancement” (promotion-focus) and “I concentrate on completing tasks correctly to increase my job security” (prevention focus).
Team creativity was based on rating each team based on factors such as the number of new design ideas proposed by each team in certain key periods of the study, while routine performance was assessed based on the percentage of deadlines that each team successfully met for addressing stakeholders’ requests and complaints.
Management implications: a reminder that an employee’s early experiences can have lasting effects
From a practical management and organisational standpoint, the implications of the research are broad.
Based on the findings, employees who experience success on their first project may develop a promotion-focused mindset, which can benefit teams whose work emphasises creativity. However, if their later roles primarily require adherence to rules and routines, “such a mindset may prompt unnecessary risk-taking or a failure to value routine accomplishments.” Given the long-term association between employees’ first project outcomes and their later mindsets, the authors suggest that “managers seeking to promote creativity might assign developmental rather than high-risk projects to avoid unwanted effects on prevention-focused mindsets.”
In addition, as the research goes beyond the usual focus on skills such as decision-making to focus instead on the key role of motivational mindset, the research suggests that firms should think carefully about how they react to a junior employee’s first big project success or failure given its implications for years and decades on that person’s career.
The research advises managers that a junior employee’s first big project isn’t just a performance milestone, but is instead a key experience that can shape their mindset and their teams’ creativity for decades to come. Early wins and losses are not isolated events, the research reminds us, so organisations should recognise them as pivotal points for their employees’ careers as well as the organisation itself.
Featured faculty
Yeun Joon Kim
Associate Professor in Organisational Behaviour
Andreas Richter
Professor of Organisational Behaviour
Featured research
Kim, Y.J. and Richter, A.W. (2026) “Project success-failure experiences and leader development: examining career transitions through role transition theory.” Journal of Applied Psychology (DOI: 10.1037/apl0001404)
Related articles
Emotional intelligence (EI) has been studied intensively since the early 1990s, and a stubborn stereotype has developed that women possess more EI than men. Yet is that really the case? A meta-study of 1,279 academic articles comprising 609,278 participants from 76 countries over 3 decades finds a far more nuanced result.
Prison officers rely on a specific set of de-escalation techniques to shape the atmosphere around them and prevent violence before it starts. This ‘atmospheric work’ goes far beyond managing physical space – it's an active, moment-to-moment skill that officers develop through sensing rising tension, and either amplifying it as a deterrent or dampening it before it boils over. The implications reach well beyond prison walls: as security personnel become a bigger presence in shops, schools and other everyday settings, understanding how they read and control atmosphere matters for anyone who encounters them, according to research by 3 academics associated with Cambridge Judge Business School.
Envy is a natural human emotion, but it can be harmful in the workplace. Research co-authored at Cambridge Judge Business School finds that in evaluating colleagues’ creative ideas, people can have benign envy or malicious envy – so managers need to understand this better to ensure that the most creative ideas are not stifled.

title: Binding commitments needed to keep innovation in the UK
author: Cambridge Judge Communications Team
summary: A new white paper from Cambridge Judge Business School proposes binding commitments to keep UK jobs, labs and R&D after acquisitions.
text:
Such a negotiated commitment, which would be voluntary but binding and enforceable once undertaken, can be implemented without difficult and time-consuming legislation, says the paper, entitled Should I Stay or Should I Go? A Pragmatic Path to Keeping UK Innovation at Home.
The paper, which is the subject of a panel at the Innovate Cambridge Summit is authored by Pascal Levensohn, founder of Levensohn Venture Partners LLC, Executive Chairman of Dolby Family Ventures, Chair of the Cambridge Innovation Hub Global Advisory Board and Fellow of Cambridge Judge Business School.
The paper argues that the debate over world-beating firms leaving the UK has conflated 2 distinct questions – the health of the UK’s capital markets and the robustness of its innovation ecosystem – and has therefore misdiagnosed the problem. The commercial, rather than legislative, solution it proposes is a practical approach that can keep investment and high-quality jobs in the UK while the larger capital-markets debate proceeds.
Migration of productive capability, not foreign ownership, is the real problem
“Foreign acquisition is not the problem – and neither is foreign ownership,” says the paper. “A central problem is the failure to distinguish between three different forms of migration – of ownership and financial returns, of domicile and listing venue, and of productive capability.
“Treated as a single, inevitable sequence, they obscure the opportunities for targeted intervention and invite the assumption that the first or second must lead to the third. It is the third that constitutes the avoidable national loss: a listing or an acquisition followed by the migration or erosion of substantive UK productive capability.”
The solution proposed in the paper: “The UK – government, universities, founders and the investment community together – should far more forcefully seek commitments from international investors and acquirers to create jobs and maintain a meaningful UK footprint for companies born in the UK, nourished by UK taxpayer investment, and first taking root in UK soil. The fruits from the UK’s innovation orchard can be harvested – ownership can change, returns can flow abroad – without pulling up the tree.”
The paper quantifies what is at stake. Between 2015 and 2025, on average 40 UK deep-tech companies were acquired each year. If just 20 of them negotiated a binding commitment resulting in 25 net new UK-based jobs, sustained for the five-year life of the commitment, the programme would generate £312.5 million of additional gross value added a year by the fifth year and would cumulate to £2.5 billion over 10 years.
The decline in London listings, liquidity and institutional support has persisted for 2 decades.
Levensohn adds: “The paper supports the Government’s ongoing capital-markets reform programme while noting that the markets have already spoken: the decline in London listings, liquidity and institutional support has persisted for 2 decades. And while it acknowledges the problems caused by Britain’s exit from the European Union, it argues that the issues examined long predate the 2016 vote and that its proposals can operate entirely within the post-Brexit settlement.”
The paper cites precedents showing the feasibility (though not yet the lasting nature) of the approach, including the binding undertakings Japan’s SoftBank gave when it acquired Cambridge-based chip designer ARM in 2016 – to at least double ARM’s UK headcount within 5 years and keep its global headquarters in Cambridge – which the Takeover Panel’s independent supervisor later verified were honoured. ARM’s subsequent 2023 Nasdaq listing illustrates the paper’s distinction: a change of listing venue is not, in itself, the loss of UK productive capability.
Addressing objections to the proposal upfront
The paper addresses 3 key objections to its approach:
“There is clearly a trade-off here, but it is manageable, often smaller than it appears, and worth making transparent,” the paper says. “Acquirers value a target for its people, its technology, and its pipeline – assets that in deep-technology companies are substantially embodied in a UK team and its tacit knowledge. A commitment to keep that team in place typically protects the very value the buyer is paying for.”
“But the lesson cuts in favour of the mechanism recommended here, not against it. The Cadbury pledge was an informal assurance with no binding force.”
The paper accepts this as the most important objection and says “that gap is the central design question, not a reason to abandon the approach.” The instruments to close it already exist in ordinary commercial practice: contractual covenants in share-purchase and subscription agreements, conditions attached to public grants, procurement and research partnerships, and reputational mechanisms that reward investors who make and honour commitments.
Retention of UK jobs and assets can be made a condition of responsible stewardship
We should welcome global capital and negotiate harder to keep research, skills and high-value jobs at home.
The paper concludes with a call to action for UK leaders to convene a small, authoritative task force – drawing on founders, UK and international investors, strategic acquirers, M&A counsel, universities, public-policy experts and innovation clusters beyond the Oxford-Cambridge-London triangle – with one mandate: to turn footprint retention from an episodic plea into standard market practice.
“The UK can continue to celebrate the companies it creates after their jobs, laboratories, compute, and manufacturing capacity have moved elsewhere. Or it can make retention a condition of serious stewardship: a standard board question, a standard investor expectation, and a standard term of doing business with the country’s most promising technologies. The UK does not need to close itself to global capital to keep more of what it creates. It needs to ask earlier, draft better, measure honestly, and then insist that the roots remain.”
Professor Gishan Dissanaike, Dean of Cambridge Judge Business School commented: “Too many businesses are born in Britain but build their futures elsewhere. We should welcome global capital and negotiate harder to keep research, skills and high-value jobs at home. This timely whitepaper offers a practical way to do both.”
