title: Paying for Bitcoin’s security as the subsidy fades
author: Cambridge Judge Communications Team
summary: Explore how network security will be funded as the programmed block subsidy falls toward zero in Bitcoin's evolving landscape.
text:
Bitcoin relies on economic incentives to maintain its security without central oversight. Every block currently awards a subsidy of newly minted bitcoin to miners who commit computing power to validate transactions and protect the shared ledger. By design, this block subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks – roughly 4 years – and will eventually reach zero. The protocol assumes that transaction fees will seamlessly replace this subsidy, yet the empirical evidence shows that fees have not yet demonstrated the capacity to do so.
A new report published by the Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance (CCAF) at Cambridge Judge Business School, in collaboration with Financial Innovation for Impact (Fii), investigates the long-term viability of this transition. Examining academic literature, on-chain data, and mining industry disclosures, the study evaluates how network security responds when the primary revenue stream funding it recedes.
Shrinking subsidies and fee volatility
The empirical findings highlight a stark imbalance in miner compensation. Over the 90 days to 4 October 2026, transaction fees accounted for just 0.67% of total miner revenue, remaining consistently below 5% for most of Bitcoin’s operational history. Substantial fee revenue materialises almost exclusively during acute mempool congestion, such as the short-lived fee spike accompanying the launch of the Runes token protocol in April 2024.
Furthermore, fee revenue exhibits extreme volatility, swinging 11.7 times more from day to day than the price of bitcoin itself. This dynamic creates a severe dilemma for network participants. Miners face compounded operational uncertainty, while the revenue intended to fund the entire security budget remains negligible outside temporary congestion events.
At the same time, block production has grown increasingly centralised. The three largest mining pools collectively accounted for 60.8% of all blocks mined over a recent one-month sample, whilst the top 6 controlled 83.0%. Widespread proxy pooling arrangements – where nominally independent pools share block templates produced by larger operators – mean that effective control over transaction selection is even more concentrated.
Assessing attack economics and resilience
Academic literature has long cautioned that relying entirely on transaction fees could induce structural instabilities, including selfish mining, block undercutting, and fee sniping. The report finds that none of these theoretical exploits have yet been observed on the Bitcoin mainnet.
This absence of observed instability is largely attributable to the formidable physical barrier required to rewrite the ledger. Executing a 51% attack requires controlling more computing power than the rest of the honest network combined. Model-based estimates evaluate the capital expenditure required to purchase new specialised hardware at tens of billions of dollars, and commercial rental marketplaces offer negligible SHA-256 hashrate.
However, the cost to mount an attack scales directly with miner revenue rather than with the trillions of dollars in value the network secures. As block subsidies fall, miner revenue declines unless fees or asset prices rise proportionally. A lower security budget reduces aggregate hashrate, lowering the capital barrier to attack just as Bitcoin becomes deeply integrated into regulated financial systems through exchange-traded funds and institutional lending facilities.
To move beyond speculative debates, the report introduces the Security Budget Health Indicator (SBHI). The framework tracks 5 distinct dimensions of network vulnerability, including the fee revenue ratio, fee variance, attack costs relative to market capitalisation, security spend, and mining pool concentration.
While continuous monitoring provides a necessary baseline, addressing these structural challenges requires proactive engagement. To that end, the research details practical steps that ecosystem participants can take to strengthen network resilience:
- regulators and financial surveillance bodies can monitor these indicators to assess systemic risks to asset-backed products
- exchange-traded fund issuers can harmonise prospectus disclosures regarding consensus-layer risks
- the community, mining pools and operators can promote and advance protocols that grant individual miners greater agency over block template creation
Wenbin Wu, Principal Researcher at CCAF says: “An issuance schedule has paid for Bitcoin’s security, and it is running down. Fees have not taken over yet. We built the Security Budget Health Indicator so the trajectory can be measured instead of argued about”. Research Lead for Digital Assets Energy and Climate Impact at CCAF, Alexander Neumueller says: “The game-theoretic instabilities identified in academic literature have not appeared on Bitcoin mainnet. However, today’s stability does not guarantee resilience in the 2030s. We have published empirical data on Bitcoin since 2019, and understanding how its security is funded is a critical question we are actively interested in monitoring.”
An issuance schedule has paid for Bitcoin's security, and it is running down. Fees have not taken over yet. We built the Security Budget Health Indicator so the trajectory can be measured instead of argued about.
We have published empirical data on Bitcoin since 2019, and understanding how its security is funded is a critical question we are actively interested in monitoring.

title: When a Cambridge Executive MBA makes sense for Academics
author: Cambridge Judge Communications Team
summary: Read why Umut Gurkan, an already highly successful academic, chose a Cambridge Executive MBA to develop his management skills.
text:
Why would an academic with a doctorate, an endowed chair and successful spin-out companies still need a Cambridge Executive MBA?
When Professor Umut Gurkan (Cambridge EMBA 2026) arrived in Cambridge, he had already built a rare academic career. As the Wilbert J Austin Professor of Engineering at Case Western Reserve University, his laboratory develops micro-engineered point-of-care diagnostics and human disease-on-a-chip models for blood disorders and cancer. His work has led to 2 spin-out companies, BioChip Labs and Hemex Health. Hemex’s Gazelle platform has run more than 5 million diagnostic tests in over 40 countries.
Yet, for all his scientific and entrepreneurial success, Umut recognised a crucial gap in his career: the skills needed to navigate management, finance and leadership at senior level. This led him to Cambridge Judge Business School and the Executive MBA, where he is now reframing how he thinks about research, innovation and leadership in academia. Alongside his studies, he is a Visiting Fellow at Clare Hall and a Visiting Scholar at the Centre for India and Global Business, working with Professor Jaideep Prabhu on frugal innovation.
Closing the leadership gap in academic careers
For Umut, this gap is not an individual oversight but a structural feature of academic training:
“I have a doctorate, an endowed chair at a leading research university, companies, and at no point in 20 years of training did anyone formally teach me management, finance, negotiation, governance, risk or how to lead people through change.”
Academics are typically expected to acquire these capabilities informally, through trial and error, and short workshops rarely build real competence. The Cambridge Executive MBA is his way of addressing that gap through rigorous, assessed education at a top business school, closely connected to the scientific environment that shapes his work.
From discovery to translation
Umut believes universities excel at discovery and invention but are far less equipped for translation: turning research into products, services and policies, particularly in healthcare. He sees much of this global gap as managerial rather than scientific.
In healthcare, he notes, getting the managerial side wrong has serious consequences: a diagnostic that never clears regulation or cannot secure reimbursement remains a paper, not a product. Universities, he argues, need more people inside who can see those issues early enough to act and who are trained to navigate regulation, funding, risk and organisational decision-making.
For Umut, these capabilities are learnable, and the Cambridge Executive MBA develops them explicitly through structured teaching, senior-level presentation workshops and dedicated executive coaching.
He also sees a two-way benefit, with academics bringing deep technical expertise and an understanding of research culture into the Executive MBA classroom and Cambridge Judge Business School’s entrepreneurial ecosystem. Shortly after joining the programme, Umut became an MBA mentor to a Cambridge Judge EnterpriseTECH team commercialising a new point-of-care diagnostic, coaching them to challenge assumptions, use the right market data and learn by doing.
Why Cambridge Judge and the University of Cambridge
Cambridge Judge Business School appealed because it is embedded within the University of Cambridge’s School of Technology, surrounded by engineering, computer science and biotechnology.
“It is not a business school sitting on its own politely beside a university. It is a department of Cambridge’s School of Technology, next door to the Department of Engineering, Computer Science, and Chemical Engineering and Biotechnology. Deep technology is the everyday house subject rather than an occasional guest lecture here.”
The Cambridge Executive MBA curriculum mapped directly onto the skills he felt were missing: corporate finance, management praxis, organisational behaviour, negotiation skills, managing innovation and corporate governance and ethics – “an inventory of my own and almost any academic’s gaps”.
A further draw was the opportunity to link his medical device work to research on frugal innovation at the Centre for India and Global Business, where Professor Prabhu’s work addresses a question Umut cares about deeply: how medical devices reach people in low-resource settings.
It is not a business school sitting on its own politely beside a university. It is a department of Cambridge’s School of Technology, next door to the Department of Engineering, Computer Science, and Chemical Engineering and Biotechnology. Deep technology is the everyday house subject rather than an occasional guest lecture.
Reframing research portfolios and leadership
Even at the start of his Cambridge Executive MBA, Orientation week changed how Umut thinks about his research and innovation portfolio, with corporate finance having the most immediate impact.
He now views translational research as a portfolio of uncertain, long-horizon assets and applies this lens to a new chairside oral cancer test funded by the National Cancer Institute and developed with colleagues in his School of Dental Medicine and Hemex Health. Rather than focusing mainly on scientific novelty and probability of funding, he concentrates on identifying and sequencing dominant uncertainties and investing where the cost of reducing uncertainty is lowest.
Clinical validation remains the critical path, but his view of who pays and how systems shape demand has shifted. He now sees the oral cancer test as part of a wider screening pathway with a clear coverage gap, which helps him articulate its value. Running the test on the existing Gazelle platform lowers costs and risk for new assets while concentrating platform risk across the portfolio.
Management Praxis has also reframed his understanding of leadership in academic settings, underlining that, outside academia, authority is not guaranteed by title and must be earned and maintained through everyday practice.
A Cambridge Executive MBA makes sense for academics
Umut’s experience shapes how he speaks to academics who are questioning the traditional pathway and wondering whether an Executive MBA fits their academic identity. He encourages mid-career academics to begin with an honest assessment of their frustrations. If the problem lies with the science itself, an Executive MBA will not solve it. But if strong work keeps stalling because of money, investment structures, regulation or people, then the Executive MBA directly addresses those issues, and academics are likely to recognise their own challenges within the first week.
He also rejects the idea that an Executive MBA sits beneath academic standards. Academics would never accept “I picked it up as I went along” as a standard for experimental method. Yet, they often rely on exactly that approach for leadership, negotiation, governance and finance – the areas that determine whether their work leaves the bench.
“What surprised me the most is how little of the Executive MBA is about becoming a businessperson, which is what many academics consider an MBA is all about. For me, the Executive MBA is about gaining the missing key leadership skills and being able to hold my ground as an academic in rooms where I previously had to take somebody else’s word for it.”

For me, the Executive MBA is about gaining the missing key leadership skills and being able to hold my ground as an academic in rooms where I previously had to take somebody else’s word for it.
Balancing research, study and family life
Umut and his family have moved from Cleveland, Ohio, for a sabbatical year, bringing 2 research careers, 2 school-age children and an Executive MBA timetable. His wife, a professor of chemical engineering, is spending the year in the Department of Chemistry, and their daughters attend local schools.
Balancing academic work, Cambridge Executive MBA study and family life is demanding, but the programme’s structure helps. Delivered in intensive weekends and week-long blocks rather than daily classes, it allows Umut to stay involved with his lab and companies while preserving most family weekends. The household runs on “2 research calendars and one EMBA timetable”, held together by a shared experience of learning and discovery in Cambridge.
“It is not easy to balance all these responsibilities, but it holds, and it helps that everyone in this house is learning something new at the same time in a fascinating place called Cambridge!”

title: Practical learning on the Cambridge MFin: a competitive edge
author: Cambridge Judge Communications Team
summary: Read how practical learning on the Cambridge MFin programme can give you a competitive edge in academics and the industry.
text:
Practical learning is fundamental to the Cambridge Master of Finance and supports the intellectual rigour of the programme.
Unparalleled networking opportunities, leading industry talks, involvement with the wider University and the chance to work on live consulting projects help make the MFin at Cambridge Judge Business School stand out. It provides a hands-on, practical experience, whilst giving you a competitive edge for future career paths.
We spoke to Marwa Hammam, Executive Director of the Cambridge MFin, and MFin alumni Neha Nagaraj and Queenie Zhao, to find out more about how practical learning is woven into the year and the key skills and experience you can expect to gain by joining.
Neha Nagaraj (MFin 2025) told us “the biggest benefit of the practical side on the MFin for me was the accessibility of people working in the industry. Hearing directly from practitioners gives you a much better understanding of different career paths and what firms are actually looking for.”
For Queenie Zhao (MFin 2025) it was more about how the MFin bridged institutional rigour with practical experience. “What stood out to me most about the MFin was how seamlessly it bridged institutional rigour with real-time market reality. Because the faculty and guest lecturers have spent decades in the market, classroom discussions reflect boardroom debates rather than purely abstract theory.”
The biggest benefit of the practical side on the MFin for me was the accessibility of people working in the industry. Hearing directly from practitioners gives you a much better understanding of different career paths and what firms are actually looking for.
Dining with industry executives
One of the best ways to connect with practitioners while on the Cambridge MFin is through the City Speaker Series. “These events take place regularly and bring in senior professionals to give talks and share their experience,” explains Marwa Hammam.
The executives come from a variety of fields, including investment banking, private equity, fintech, quant hedge funds and venture capital. Previous speakers have come from organisations such as Morgan Stanley, UBS, BNP Paribas and Amadeus Capital Partners.
The City Speaker Series involves an in-class talk followed by an interactive Q&A with the industry expert. After the interactive session, a small group of students join the speaker for dinner at one of the Cambridge Colleges. This offers a unique opportunity to learn more about current market developments and gain invaluable perspectives in an informal setting.
The City Speaker Series is designed to encourage open dialogue between the speaker and students, allowing them to explore how theory translates into practice. This ensures that students gain relevant practical knowledge, rather than sitting in a traditional guest lecture.
This experience not only allows students to develop their network but also provides the opportunity to gain live insights from industry experts who are leaders in their fields.
For Neha, this was about building organic relationships and learning about certain sectors from those who are already operating in them. “The combination of speaker events, alumni interactions, consulting projects and special interest group (SIG) activities also creates opportunities to build relationships organically. Rather than simply learning about a particular sector from a textbook, you can have a conversation with someone who is actually working in it and understand where your own background might fit”, she said.
For Queenie it was about discussions and challenges in live market environments: “Initiatives like the City Speaker series bring senior managing directors, fund managers and policymakers directly into the room to discuss live market turbulence and capital allocation challenges” she said.
Initiatives like the City Speaker Series bring senior managing directors, fund managers and policymakers directly into the room to discuss live market turbulence and capital allocation challenges.
Elective courses by experienced practitioners
It’s not just through speaker events that students can engage with industry experts. Practitioners are at the centre of teaching at Cambridge Judge Business School, with classes led by a mix of world-renowned Cambridge academics and those from the industry.
“Many elective courses are designed and delivered by experienced practitioners,” says Marwa. “This provides exposure to emerging areas such as AI in finance, algorithmic trading, sustainable finance, private credit, digital assets, financial innovation and entrepreneurship, from those directly working in the field.”
“Students select which electives they take, tailoring the programme according to their goals. Our aim is to ensure they graduate not only with strong analytical and technical skills, but with a deep understanding of how finance operates in practice.”
Real-world consulting projects
There’s plenty of opportunity to work on real-world assignments while on the Cambridge MFin too, not least via the Global Consulting Project (GCP). “This is one of the programme’s signature experiential learning experiences,” says Marwa.
“Students work with a client organisation over the space of a few months to address a live business challenge, applying the analytical frameworks and technical skills developed throughout the programme. Organisations they might work with range from global financial institutions and investment firms to start-ups and international multi-lateral organisations,” she explains.
Recent projects have included developing growth strategies for fintech companies, advising private banks on engaging ultra high net worth clients, assessing investment opportunities in emerging technologies, supporting AI-enabled healthcare ventures with fundraising and financial planning, and exploring market entry strategies across a broad range of sectors.
Because each assignment addresses a genuine business need, students gain first-hand, practical experience in client management, consulting, teamwork and problem-solving. The projects involve tackling real commercial challenges, with teams often presenting their recommendations directly to senior decision-makers.
Neha and Queenie agree that GCPs are another great way to gain practical experience.
“There are lots of opportunities to get hands-on experience. For my practical project during the spring term, I had the opportunity to work as a student consultant with CBRE Investment Management in London – an experience that tied together everything we covered in the classroom” Queenie said.
For Neha it meant really strengthening her soft skills alongside her technical skills. “For my GCP, I worked with British International Investment (BII), where our team looked at benchmarking investment returns and risk across regions including Africa and South Asia. This really strengthened my teamwork and communication skills, as well as my ability to connect technical analysis with a practical business question”, she said.
Extra-curricular activities, entrepreneurial ventures and the wider university
Beyond the curriculum itself, there are a myriad of ways to expand your practical experience while at Cambridge Judge Business School, and not just within the finance sector.
“Many students become actively involved in special interest groups (SIGs) within the Business School,” says Marwa. “These provide opportunities to explore areas ranging from private equity and venture capital to entrepreneurship, sustainable finance and AI, via workshops, networking events, company visits and speaker sessions.”
“Students are also encouraged to immerse themselves in the larger Cambridge ecosystem,” she continues. “University and College societies offer the chance to meet students from different subject areas, and many collaborate with peers from engineering, computer science and other fields, sometimes working on startups and other projects together.”
The Entrepreneurship Centre at the Cambridge Judge Business School and Cambridge Enterprise, which both fund startups and support entrepreneurial ventures across the University, are also valuable resources for students interested in launching a business venture.
More broadly, being based at the heart of the Cambridge Cluster (or ‘Silicon Fen’) gives students exposure to one of Europe’s most dynamic innovation ecosystems, with opportunities to connect with entrepreneurs, investors and fast-growing companies well beyond the confines of the programme.
“It’s this combination of academic rigour, practical application and access to one of the world’s most dynamic innovation ecosystems that’s difficult to replicate elsewhere,” Marwa says.
The Cambridge MFin extends beyond teaching finance. It helps students develop into thoughtful, commercially minded professionals who can apply their knowledge in complex workplace situations from day one.
Many students build long-term relationships with speakers, alumni, project sponsors and employers through the programme, leading to internships, consulting opportunities, mentoring relationships and full-time roles. While there is no single pathway to career success, these experiences significantly broaden students’ professional networks and can open doors that help shape their future career paths.
Neha explains that SIGs are a great way to engage with people and activities outside of finance. “I was also involved with several special interest groups (SIGs), including being Co-Chair of the Cambridge Middle East Business Society and the Travel & Tourism groups. Through the Middle East Business Society, I helped organise activities, including virtual consulting panels, that gave me the opportunity to engage with professionals and alumni connected to the region. One of the things I also really appreciated about Cambridge was how interconnected the ecosystem is. You’re surrounded not only by people studying finance, but also by students, academics, entrepreneurs, researchers and professionals from completely different disciplines” she said.
“Cambridge encourages you to look beyond traditional finance and think about how finance interacts with technology, innovation and impact. Being in Cambridge has made me much more curious about these intersections and has broadened the way I think about where a finance career can take me” says Neha.
For Queenie, the cohort itself was a big asset to the practical element of the programme. “Because the projects and speaker sessions are practitioner-led, the interactions are grounded in substantive, technical dialogue. You aren’t just networking at a surface level, you’re presenting models, pitching investment theses and discussing live transactions. Also, the MFin cohort itself is one of the biggest assets. Having peers with backgrounds spanning sovereign wealth funds, private equity, consulting and central banks across dozens of countries creates a global sounding board that extends far beyond the duration of the programme.”
It’s this combination of academic rigour, practical application and access to one of the world’s most dynamic innovation ecosystems that’s difficult to replicate elsewhere.

title: Episode 2: Predicting deep tech success | Predicting Startup Success podcast
author: Ioanna Koliou WebEditor
summary: Isabell Welpe and Ramana Nanda explore why deep tech startups are difficult to predict and how experiments and financing can reduce uncertainty.
text:
Predicting the success of a startup is never easy. Predicting the success of a deep tech startup is harder still.
Built on advances in science and engineering, deep tech ventures often require years of development, substantial capital and specialised expertise before their commercial potential becomes clear. Traditional indicators of startup progress, such as customer traction or revenue growth, may be absent for long periods. Yet investors, universities and policymakers must still make decisions about which ventures to support and which opportunities to pursue.
In conversation with Isabell Welpe in Episode 2 of the Predicting Startup Success podcast, Ramana Nanda, Professor of Entrepreneurial Finance and Associate Dean for Enterprise at Imperial Business School, argues that predicting deep tech success is not about finding a single decisive signal. Instead, it is about understanding uncertainty, how it evolves, and how different actors work to reduce it over time.
Deep tech is not one prediction problem
When evaluating startups, it is tempting to think primarily about market uncertainty.
Will customers want the product? Will the company find a scalable business model? Will growth materialise?
Deep tech ventures face those questions too, but they carry an additional layer of complexity. Before anyone can determine whether a market exists, they often need to establish whether the technology itself can deliver what it promises.
As Nanda explains, technical risk and market risk frequently interact. A technology may have multiple potential applications, each requiring different technical milestones, different customers and different paths to commercialisation. A change in direction is therefore not simply a strategic decision. It can mean revisiting fundamental assumptions about what needs to be proven and how.
This helps explain why the journey can be so difficult to predict. Success depends not on overcoming a single hurdle, but on navigating several uncertainties at once.
When laboratory success is not enough
One of the recurring themes in the conversation is the distinction between scientific achievement and commercial viability.
Academic research is often designed to establish novelty. Investors, by contrast, are trying to understand whether a technology can create value at scale.
As Nanda notes, “the key element that’s being optimised is novelty.”
The challenge is that the conditions that demonstrate an impressive result in a laboratory may not reveal whether a technology will succeed in the real world. A process that works at small scale may prove difficult to manufacture economically. A material that performs well under controlled conditions may behave differently in industrial environments. A proof of concept may answer one question while leaving others unresolved.
For this reason, the most important experiments are not always the most impressive ones.
What matters is whether they provide meaningful evidence about the questions that will determine future success. The goal is not simply to demonstrate that a technology works, but to understand whether it can work under the conditions required for commercial adoption.
Financing is a way of learning
Much of the startup world treats financing as a mechanism for providing resources.
Nanda offers a different perspective.
Rather than viewing venture capital solely as a source of funding, he argues that it should be understood as a process of learning. Each financing round gives founders and investors an opportunity to gather information, reduce uncertainty and reassess what comes next.
“If you think about multi-stage financing as a sequence of experiments,” he explains, “the key question becomes how do you generate more information from these experiments for less money?”
Viewed this way, milestones become more than markers of progress. They are pieces of evidence.
The most effective founders are often not those who simply hit targets, but those who understand what future investors will need to see and design experiments that answer those questions. Likewise, successful investors are not merely allocating capital. They are helping ventures discover which assumptions hold true and which need to change.
Prediction, in this context, becomes a process of reducing uncertainty rather than eliminating it.
Why innovation is a relay race
Towards the end of the discussion, the focus shifts from individual startups to the broader ecosystem that supports them.
Universities, technology transfer offices, seed investors, venture capital firms and later-stage investors all influence a venture’s trajectory. Yet they often operate according to different incentives and priorities.
For Nanda one of the biggest challenges is that organisations frequently concentrate on the stage directly in front of them rather than the stages that follow. A startup may secure early funding, but still struggle later if it has not generated the evidence required by growth-stage investors. Similarly, a university may help develop promising research without fully considering the financing pathway needed to bring it to market.
To explain this, he uses a simple analogy:
“Each of us need to run our relay race where we need to run towards where the next person is standing.”
The image captures a broader point about commercialisation. Progress depends not only on how well an individual contributes, but on how effectively they prepare the venture for the next stage of development.
Rethinking prediction
By the end of the conversation, deep tech prediction looks rather different from the search for a perfect signal.
The question is not simply whether a technology appears promising today. It is whether founders, investors and institutions are generating the evidence needed to understand what that technology might become tomorrow.
For anyone trying to evaluate deep tech ventures, that may be the most important insight of all. Success is rarely revealed in a single breakthrough moment. More often, it emerges through a series of decisions, experiments and commitments that gradually bring an uncertain future into clearer focus.

Predicting Startup Success brings together leading researchers, investors, entrepreneurs and venture builders to explore one of the most challenging questions in entrepreneurship: why do some ventures succeed while others struggle?

title: Episode 1: Looking beyond the hype | Predicting Startup Success podcast
author: Ioanna Koliou WebEditor
summary: Chris Coleridge and Matthew Grimes explore whether investors can see through startup hype and identify the signals that really predict success.
text:
Startup success is notoriously difficult to predict.
Investors, founders and policymakers are constantly searching for signals that might reveal which ventures will thrive and which will struggle. Yet according to Matthew Grimes, Professor of Entrepreneurship and Sustainable Futures at the University of Cambridge, many of the assumptions we make about prediction may be fundamentally flawed.
In conversation with Associate Professor Chris Coleridge on the Predicting Startup Success podcast, Matthew argues that startups are unlike most other organisations because they are built around futures that do not yet exist. Rather than simply uncovering value, investors and other stakeholders often help create it.
Startups are claims about the future
When people think about prediction, they often imagine that a startup’s true value already exists and simply needs to be discovered.
According to Matthew, that assumption breaks down when applied to early-stage ventures. At the point where investors, customers or employees engage with a startup, much of what is being evaluated has not yet been built.
A startup, he argues, is essentially a claim about a future that has not happened yet. Whether that future arrives depends partly on whether enough people believe in the claim and commit resources to it. Value is not merely observed. It is co-created through acts of persuasion and commitment.
This means that observers are rarely neutral participants.
Investors, researchers and ecosystem actors do not simply predict success from the outside. Their decisions help shape the outcome they are attempting to forecast.
That insight also helps explain why conventional signals can sometimes be misleading.
A founder who tells a compelling story may appear more likely to succeed, but what observers have actually witnessed is storytelling ability. Fluency and confidence can be mistaken for substance. As a result, attention often gravitates towards visible, easily performed signals rather than deeper indicators of progress.
What hype really means
One of Matthew’s most significant areas of research concerns hype.
The term is often treated as synonymous with exaggeration or even deception. In some cases, people blur the distinction between hype and fraud. But Matthew offers a different definition.
In his research, hype is understood as a collective vision and promise of a possible future around which attention, excitement and expectations accumulate. It is a social process that unfolds over time. Sometimes those expectations collapse. Sometimes innovations genuinely live up to them.
Viewed this way, hype is not simply noise – it has real effects.
Excitement attracts capital, talent and attention. Those resources improve the odds of success. Success then attracts further excitement, creating a self-reinforcing cycle.
Yet this process has a darker side.
The same forces that bring resources also create expectations. Ventures become accountable not only for what they have achieved but for what they have promised. Expectations begin to accumulate and harden, creating what Matthew describes as a liability as well as a resource.
As expectations solidify, founders may become constrained. They may discover that the most promising opportunity lies in a slightly different direction but find themselves tied to the story they have already told investors, customers and employees.
For this reason, hype may be highly predictive of a startup’s ability to raise money, but much less predictive of its ultimate success. Two ventures can attract similar levels of attention and funding and experience very different outcomes depending on whether they are able to convert expectations into something tangible and sustainable.
Looking for the signals that matter
If stories alone are insufficient, what should investors and other stakeholders focus on instead?
Matthew argues that the most useful signals are often the most costly.
Rather than focusing on impressive pitch decks, media coverage or presentation skills, he suggests paying attention to tangible commitments from others. Customers who have reorganised their workflows around a product, partners who have taken meaningful risks, or talented individuals who have left attractive roles to join a company all provide stronger evidence than a polished presentation.
These are difficult signals to manufacture because somebody has put something valuable on the line.
The same principle applies when evaluating external endorsements. Selective investors and highly competitive programmes can provide meaningful information because the organisations involved have their own credibility at stake. By contrast, awards, publicity and vanity metrics may create visibility without revealing much about underlying quality.
One question in particular emerged as a useful test:
What evidence would convince the founder that they are wrong?
According to Matthew, founders who are genuinely experimenting and learning can usually answer this clearly. Those who are simply defending a narrative often struggle.
Why feedback is harder than it sounds
Entrepreneurship literature often presents adaptation as a straightforward process.
Founders gather information, update their assumptions and improve their ideas. Yet Matthew’s research suggests that the reality is more complicated.
The challenge is that feedback is rarely just feedback about an idea.
For founders, ventures are often deeply connected to identity, values and personal purpose. As a result, criticism of the business can feel like criticism of the individual. What appears from the outside to be an obvious adjustment may feel much more significant to the person receiving it.
This helps explain why intelligent founders sometimes seem resistant to evidence. The problem is not necessarily that they have failed to hear what the market is telling them. Instead, acting on that information may require a change to their sense of self.
The most successful founders, according to his research, appear to develop the unusual ability to be both stubborn and flexible at the same time. They remain committed to the broader problem they want to solve while staying open to changing the specific solution.
Rather than abandoning their identity, they re-author it as they learn.
The limits of pivoting
The startup world frequently celebrates the pivot.
But Matthew’s work on the limits of pivoting suggests there can be costs to continual change.
Repeated pivots create burdens not only for founders but also for employees, investors and partners. Every significant change asks stakeholders to renew their commitment to a different future. Over time, this can erode trust.
The issue is not the number of pivots themselves. Instead, it is whether a coherent story connects them.
As long as stakeholders view change as part of a learning journey, adaptation can strengthen a venture. When changes begin to appear disconnected or contradictory, observers may conclude that the company is simply searching randomly for something that works.
The distinction lies in narrative coherence.
Rethinking what success means
Towards the end of the conversation, the discussion moves beyond prediction to a more fundamental question:
What exactly counts as success?
Much of the startup ecosystem focuses on valuation, funding and growth. While important, Matthew argues that those metrics capture only one dimension of entrepreneurial success.
His recent work on responsible entrepreneurship challenges the assumption that disruption inevitably produces unacceptable social costs. Rather than treating those consequences as unavoidable, he argues that governance, institutions and incentives can be redesigned so that innovation creates value while reducing harmful externalities.
Ultimately, he suggests that prediction depends on definition.
Before deciding which startups are successful, we need to decide what success itself means. The metrics we choose determine what becomes visible, what is rewarded and which ventures are celebrated.
For anyone interested in evaluating startups, that may be the most important question of all.

Professor of Entrepreneurship and Sustainable Futures
About the podcast
Predicting Startup Success brings together leading researchers, investors, entrepreneurs and venture builders to explore one of the most challenging questions in entrepreneurship: why do some ventures succeed while others struggle?

title: Research on foreign exchange honoured at symposium
author: Cambridge Judge Communications Team
summary: Winners of the Pembroke International Finance Prize announced at the Symposium on Foreign Exchange Markets, Cambridge Judge.
text:
This year’s Symposium, organised by the Centre for Endowment Asset Management, brought together leading academics, policymakers and market practitioners to examine how funding markets, derivatives and bond markets jointly shape currency behaviour. Across sessions on dollar funding and markups, FX derivatives, bond-FX interactions, expectations formation and emerging markets, speakers highlighted new evidence on pricing, liquidity, volatility and risk premia, as well as the growing importance of global investors, intervention strategies and hedging beyond dominant currencies in driving the future dynamics of FX markets.
What makes this conference distinctive is the way it connects rigorous academic research with the realities of modern FX markets. By bringing together scholars, central banks and industry practitioners, we are not only documenting how currency markets are changing, but we are also helping to shape the agenda for how they will evolve in the years ahead.
Joint winners due to exceptional paper quality
Owing to the exceptional quality of the papers, this year’s Symposium held 17-18 August decided to share the award among the 2 papers. The winning papers are:
Financial Hedging Beyond Dominant Currency
Co-authored by Laura Alfaro of Harvard Business School, Mauricio Calani of the Central Bank of Chile and Liliana Varela of the London School of Economics
This paper challenges the view the firms are shielded from exchange-rate risk through dominant-currency invoicing, and shows that natural hedging offers limited risk protection. The paper used a unique firm-level dataset linking Chilean companies to international trade transactions, foreign-exchange derivatives and foreign debt over a 20-year period.
When Funding Markets Move Credit Markets: Foreign Investors and Their U.S. CLOs
Co-authored by Amy W Huber of the Wharton School and Shohini Kundu of UCLA Anderson
This paper shows that US leveraged credit and global dollar funding markets are linked through Japanese banks. The paper develops a model that examines the aggregate demand elasticity of Japanese banks, and the results show that exposure of domestic credit markets to external funding shocks depends on the elasticity of foreign demand and not only on foreign participation.
This year’s Symposium also introduced a new Best Discussant Prize, which was awarded to Riccardo Colacito, Professor of Finance at Kenan-Flagler Business School at the University of North Carolina. The award recognises the important role discussants play in facilitating academic discussion and providing constructive feedback on research.
With the support CME Group and Pembroke College, Cambridge and the Cambridge Endowment for Research in Finance (CERF) and the Centre for Endowment Asset Management (CEAM) it has been possible to continue this symposium – recognised globally as one of the leading academic conferences in international finance – as an annual event at the University of Cambridge from 2025.

title: Monetary policy’s hidden conduit: who gets your deposits?
author: Cambridge Judge Communications Team
summary: Trillions of dollars sit in bank deposits. Banks compete for savers' money, but not all banks can put it to equally good use. This article explains why healthy competition steers deposits to the banks that can do the most with it, and how monetary policy can throw sand in the wheels.
text:
A trillion-dollar sorting problem
The banking sector holds trillions of dollars in deposits. In the United States alone, the figure is in the ballpark of US$20 trillion. These funds matter for the real economy as banks lend them out to firms and consumers, financing the investment and spending that drive growth.
Yet banks differ widely in their investment opportunities, and in how willing they are to put this money to work, independent of their size or type. Consider, for example, 3 US banks. JPMorgan – the largest bank in the United States by a wide margin – earns 3.83% on the next dollar it lends, with 34% of its assets in loans and 60% of its deposits lent back out. UMB Financial, a regional bank a fraction of JPMorgan’s size, lends out the very same 60% of its deposits – yet earns 4.3% on the margin. Ally Bank, a smaller, digital-only lender, goes further still: it earns 5.2% on its marginal loan, with 95% of deposits lent out.
The size of the deposit market, and the varying appetite banks show for putting deposits to work, raise an obvious question: how would an efficient market allocate deposits across them? Recent research by CERF Fellow Simone Lenzu (Cambridge Judge and Federal Reserve Bank of New York) and research collaborators Fulvia Fringuellotti (Federal Reserve Bank of New York), Quinn Maingi (USC Marshall), and April Meehl (Villanova University) takes this question to the data.
Allocative efficiency in deposit markets
If deposits were allocated efficiently, banks with better investment opportunities would attract a larger share of them. As in any efficient market, prices (ie the rates paid by banks to depositors) would do the work: banks willing and able to pay more for deposits bid up their rates, and savers respond by banking with them rather than a rival paying less.
Does this happen? Using administrative data on the US banking sector between 2001-2025, the researchers find that savings are, on average, channelled toward the banks that can make the best use of them – but barely so. That is, banks with better investment opportunities do attract more deposits, by offering higher rates, but only a little higher. They also document large fluctuations of allocative efficiency and link these fluctuations to the monetary policy cycle, improving when policy is tight and deteriorating when it is loose.
Measuring banks’ marginal investment opportunities
The authors construct a bank-level measure of marginal investment opportunities (MIO): the measure is proportional to a bank’s investment income – interest income, net of loan-loss provisions, plus securities gains, excluding trading revenue – divided by its assets. The measure is a sufficient statistic for the slope of a bank’s income function at its current scale, capturing how much extra income it earns on one more dollar of assets. This is the number behind the JPMorgan, UMB and Ally figures above.
A bank’s own realised return is the right place to start, because deposits are allocated through the rate a bank chooses to offer, and a bank sets that rate against what it itself expects to earn on the next dollar – not against what society would earn from it. Thus, if deposits are allocated efficiently, they should track exactly this number.
A weak link between investment opportunities and deposit funding
Given MIO, the authors analyse whether banks with better investment opportunities pay more for deposits and get more of them. They find that price and quantity both move the right way – the signature of good competition and allocative efficiency – but the association is weak. On average, a bank with an MIO one percentage point higher than a rival’s (roughly the gap between JPMorgan and Ally Bank) offers a deposit rate that is only about 6 basis points higher and goes on to attract only about 4.5% more deposits.
Monetary policy is the single most important predictor of allocative efficiency. The time series points to what may be the single most important force driving allocative efficiency. Exhibit 1 shows that the average masks wide variation: the degree of allocative efficiency fluctuates widely over the sample, with periods of high efficiency alternating with periods of low or severe inefficiency (blue line). Strikingly, the level of the Fed funds rate – the monetary policy rate in the US – appears to be the single most important predictor of allocative efficiency.
When the Fed funds rate is above 5%, a one-point gap in investment opportunities between 2 banks is associated with about 40 basis points higher deposit rate for the bank with the higher MIO. At the zero lower bound (ZLB) – the point at which the nominal policy rate is pushed down near zero and cannot easily go lower – the two banks, by contrast, offer essentially the same rate; if anything, the bank with the lower investment opportunities pays slightly more.
Why healthy competition stops at the zero lower bound: start from how a bank sets its deposit rate. It uses its market power to pay savers less than what their money is worth to it on the margin – its MIO – keeping the difference as the markdown, once it covers the cost of running the deposit franchise:
deposit rate = MIO – markdown – cost of running the deposit franchise
The Fed funds rate is what banks charge each other on overnight loans, so it is about as close to a risk-free return as exists in the economy. Loan and securities yields are priced off that benchmark plus a spread for credit and duration risk. So when the Fed funds rate moves, those yields move with it – and so does MIO, the return a bank earns on its next dollar. This relation between MIO and the Fed funds rate is why monetary policy – which sets the Fed funds rate – matters for deposit pricing: high policy rates leave banks with room to exercise their market power over their deposit base, allowing them to earn higher markdowns.
What happens as the Fed funds rate approaches the ZLB? To fix ideas, suppose the Fed funds rate is 5%: a bank with good investment opportunities might offer savers 4%, a bank with poor ones just 2% – a gap that tracks the underlying difference in MIO. Now lower the Fed funds rate toward zero. If the banks’ markdowns did not move, we could subtract roughly 5 percentage points from both banks’ rates. Then, the good bank would want to offer -1%, the bad bank -3%. However, depositors will not accept a negative nominal rate when cash is a free alternative. The floor caps the markdown banks can charge, pinning deposit rates near zero no matter how wide a bank’s MIO.
Exhibit 2 shows this in the data. Near the zero lower bound the non-negativity constraint binds and the whole distribution of offered rates collapses towards zero. The gap between banks with the best and the worst investment opportunities narrows with it, from 103 basis points to 31. This constraint, not a change in banks’ market power or investment opportunities, reduces the room for healthy competition and therefore the allocative efficiency of deposit markets.
Risk shifting at the zero lower bound
Shutting down price competition does not just mute the signal healthy competition needs; it invites a pernicious form of competition that runs in reverse. A bank at risk of distress has an incentive to bid aggressively for deposits, paying up for funding it cannot profitably deploy – a gamble for resurrection: fresh funding today, however expensive, buys a chance of surviving tomorrow.
The authors show that the gap between the deposit rate offered by economically healthy banks (those with an MIO in the top quintile) and the rate offered by banks that go on to fail within the next 8 quarters rises monotonically with the Fed funds rate. The spread between the deposit rate of healthy and failing banks is negative at the zero lower bound and strongly positive once the rate is high (Exhibit 3). Monetary policy, in other words, does not just compress deposit rates at the zero lower bound – it flips what a high rate means, from a mark of good investment opportunity to a mark of distress.
At the zero lower bound, the authors also show, a high deposit rate is a strong predictor of a bank’s future failure – and the relationship is strongest among banks with low MIO, precisely those whose high rates cannot be justified by genuine investment opportunities. Away from the zero lower bound, a high deposit rate is, in general, no longer a meaningful predictor of failure.
What this means for bank supervision and monetary policy
If risk shifting takes over precisely when rates hit zero, whatever keeps it in check the rest of the time deserves a closer look. One candidate is banking supervision. Not by chance, in the US and elsewhere, bank examiners watch for this risk-shifting behaviour and lean on banks offering high deposit rates while showing signs of distress. At the zero lower bound, though, deposit rates are compressed and ‘bad competition’ is much harder to detect.
The authors’ analysis also has direct implications for monetary policy and financial stability during extended loose policy cycles, such as 2009-2015 and 2020-2022. The price-based signal that would otherwise sort deposits toward the banks that can use them best goes dark exactly when the central bank has the least conventional room left to stimulate the economy. This is not to say that high rates are safe and low rates are dangerous. Rather, it highlights that a reduction in allocative efficiency in deposit markets works against the stimulus that accommodative monetary policy is meant to provide to the real economy.

title: How kernels of reinvention can help firms thrive
author: Khaled Soufani
summary: Cambridge Judge research shows how firms can reinvent by building on existing strengths. Includes a 5-step playbook and examples.
text:
Business breeds buzzwords: all companies seek innovation, reinvention and growth, and pledge to pivot when old models become obsolete. Yet the pathway to reinvention, despite such a clear goal, is often not obvious. Should a firm totally discard the old ways that are showing signs of obsolescence, or seek to protect core strengths while evolving them for new challenges?
What are kernels of reinvention?
Research at Cambridge Judge Business School finds a pattern among successful corporate reinventions that build on existing capabilities to develop a new strategic purpose – what the research terms ‘kernels of reinvention’.
Kernels of reinvention help firms develop ways to pivot that don't discard the current business model but also don't start from scratch.
“We find that these kernels serve as cornerstones or anchors for building new businesses, and this helps firms develop ways to pivot that don’t discard the current business model but also don’t start from scratch,” says research co-author Khaled Soufani, Management Practice Professor of Financial Economics and Policy, and Director of the Circular Economy Centre at Cambridge Judge.
Adds co-author Samsurin Welch, Fellow at the Circular Economy Centre: “There’s a term for this in evolutionary biology called ‘neofunctionalisation’ in which organisms repurpose genetic material in order to adapt to environmental changes. Companies that pivot successfully often follow this same model: take a core trait or capability and refashion it in order to thrive in an ever-changing business environment.”
The research on how kernels of reinvention can grow into new strategic directions is outlined by Khaled and Samsurin in an article published online alongside the final edition of MIT Sloan Management Review, published by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, Massachusetts, which recently announced that the journal would cease publication after 67 years in favour of a wider digital communications portfolio. The research draws on some well-known articles about innovation, including the 1997 article by the late Clayton Christensen “The Innovator’s Dilemma” that explains how incumbents get trapped by disruptive innovation.
Business reinvention examples: from Fujifilm to Disney
The authors’ observations about pivoting companies include some of the best-known names in areas ranging from photography to automaking to computing.
For example, Chinese automaker BYD had decades of expertise in battery electrochemistry that served as a pivotal kernel in the company’s evolution into a global leader in electric vehicles. Fujifilm used its expertise in precision coating science and chemistry to move into cosmetics, as the science that keeps film stable can keep skin moisturised and protected from UV damage. Disney saw that streaming was disrupting the traditional film business, so the company developed its own direct-to-consumer streaming business Disney+.
The authors focus particularly on Danish energy company Ørsted, which drew on its kernel of expertise in North Sea oil projects to shift aggressively from fossil fuels to renewable energy through offshore wind farms, and Microsoft, which drew on its enterprise business competence and relationships with Fortune 500 chief technology officers to become a leader in enterprise cloud computing.
Why circular economy principles can guide corporate reinvention
Khaled said that he and Samsurin became interested in this topic through their research in economics as well as the principles of the circular economy:
“Economics is fundamentally concerned with the efficient allocation of scarce resources. At the same time, one of the key principles of the circular economy is repurposing, which represents an important form of circularity. We therefore argue that reinvention can benefit from this principle, particularly in times of disruption, when the economic objective of a firm is not only to allocate resources efficiently but also to effectively repurpose existing resources to create new value and opportunities.
We are used to hearing how yesterday's industry leaders become tomorrow's dinosaurs, disrupted by faster, sharper new entrants … But we asked the question, can dinosaurs fly – and why?
Adds Samsurin:
“We are used to hearing how yesterday’s industry leaders become tomorrow’s dinosaurs, disrupted by faster, sharper new entrants. But that is not always what happens. Large companies can reinvent themselves, sometimes proactively and sometimes only after crisis forces the issue. We asked the question, can dinosaurs fly – and why? The answer is rarely to double down on the declining core business, but neither is starting from a blank slate. We were inspired by circular economy and evolutionary biology, where genetic material can acquire new functions under environmental pressure. That became our analogy for corporate reinvention. We still see new examples emerging: BlackBerry, once a poster child for disruption, has rebuilt itself around safety critical software for industries like vehicles, defence and robotics.”
4 traits of a genuine kernel of reinvention
Yet in seeking to repurpose those existing resources, firms need to recognise that not every kernel truly creates new opportunities. So the research identifies 4 characteristics that “distinguishes a genuine kernel from wishful thinking about legacy assets”:
- The kernel lies deep within the firm as a capability, as with Fujifilm, and is not simply what the company sells or is known for.
- Kernels are generative in that they enable new value creation, such as Walmart using its knowledge in grocery retailing and perishable goods to very early develop an e-commerce business.
- Kernels should provide a defensible advantage that rivals cannot easily replicate.
- The kernel should create a coherent and “visible, unbroken narrative thread from the legacy business to the new direction”, which makes the shift more credible to stakeholders including employees and investors.
“There are many different types of kernels,” says Khaled. “Kernels may be technical or scientific as with BYD and Fujifilm, or relational and commercial as with Microsoft, but it’s really important to consider carefully whether a prospective kernel really provides a way to develop a compelling new direction.”
Samsurin adds that it’s important for companies seeking to reinvent themselves to recognise clearly the shifts they face in their business landscapes. “For Fujifilm it was the collapse of traditional film photography, for Ørsted the volatility of fossil fuels and public opposition to coal, and for BYD the electrification of the auto industry.”
The Reinvention Playbook: 5 steps to pivot your business strategy
The authors emphasise the reinvention is not a one-off event, but instead requires a series of decisions as firms adapt over a period of years to their changing industries. So they develop what they term a Reinvention Playbook that outlines 5 steps to reinvention based on their key kernel:
“Start outside the firm” by looking at broader shifts that are changing an industry and thus weakening the current business. There are some more granular rules here as well: avoid misdiagnosing structural shifts as cyclical headwinds, and think about whether industry changes are threatening only the firm’s current performance or its ‘underlying relevance’.
“Excavate” deep inside the firm to look beyond core products or services to uncover latent capabilities and how valuable these will be in new markets. “Kernel identification is not a single act of insight. It is an iterative loop of excavation, validation, market testing, and refinement.”
Build new growth and competitive plans once a promising kernel is identified, as a kernel is “a strong foundation for growth but is not a business on its own”. Such plans may require new partners, hiring new talent or a new scale-oriented operating model.
Give kernels enough space to breathe and develop, but be sure to retain ties to the current business in order to best leverage corporate assets. “Reinvention fails when the new business is suffocated by the old, but it also fails when leaders cut away the old before the new is strong enough to stand,” say the authors.
Bring stakeholders along in the journey by crafting a narrative that shows continuity while also signalling a departure from nonviable elements of the past.
How a credible narrative wins stakeholder support for reinvention
“The best narratives make clear what must change, and how the company is building from an existing advantage to gain a plausible right to win in the new arena,” say Khaled and Samsurin. “Done well, this gives stakeholders a credible reframing of where the company is heading, grounded on past strengths.”

title: Evolving alpha in our volatile era of big data
author: Ioanna Koliou WebEditor
summary: A new test for alpha helps researchers assess asset-pricing models using large financial datasets, including during periods of market stress. Learn more.
text:
In financial markets, everyone wants alpha. Asset managers spend billions trying to find it. Hedge funds promise it. Investors search for it relentlessly. Academics and practitioners build models designed to explain it away.
If alpha exists, it may be due to several reasons – including exceptional skill, a flaw in our understanding of how markets work and inefficiencies in the functioning of financial markets. The latter reason is why policymakers and regulators are also interested in deepening our understanding of how alpha can be identified in the data.
Given this backdrop, one of the central objectives of empirical asset pricing is to determine whether observed returns in financial assets or portfolio strategies are consistent with a proposed model of risk premia. The standard approach is straightforward: estimate the model, compute the resulting pricing errors (‘alphas) and test whether they are jointly equal to zero.
For nearly 4 decades the profession’s benchmark for evaluating alpha-explaining models has been a test introduced in 1989 known as the the Gibbons-Ross-Shanken (GRS) test (named after its 3 authors). This standard is, however, showing its age in an era in which there is now an explosion of financial data that didn’t exist in the late 1980s – as researchers now routinely analyse hundreds or thousands of assets simultaneously. In addition, the rapid growth of factor investing, anomaly testing and machine learning-based asset pricing has significantly expanded the scale at which asset pricing models are evaluated.
A new test for alpha in an era of volatility and crises
A proposed new test for the existence of alpha directly addresses this issue, as it has been designed for high-dimensional asset-pricing applications. The proposed test is labelled ‘MSTV’ after the names of 4 co-authors of a new research paper: Daniele Massacci, Professor of Finance at King’s Business School, Lucio Sarno, Professor of Finance at Cambridge Judge Business School, Lorenzo Trapani, Professor of Econometrics at Universita’ di Pavia and University of Leicester and Pierluigi Vallarino, Postdoctoral Researcher at Universita’ della Svizzera Italiana. Their paper is published in the Journal of the American Statistical Association, a premier journal in statistics.
The research proposes a methodology to test for the ‘null hypothesis’ that the alphas of a panel of asset returns are jointly equal to zero in a linear factor pricing model with observable and tradable factors – referring to the null of ‘zero alpha’. The test does not require estimating any covariance matrix, a task that becomes difficult when the number of assets is large.
New test reflects today’s datasets
The test proposed by MSTV addresses 3 features that increasingly characterise modern financial datasets:
The test works well in simulation experiments
Any new testing procedure must demonstrate that it performs well in realistic environments. To evaluate its statistical properties, the research introducing MSTV conducts an extensive simulation analysis covering a range of processes and structures – and 2 broad findings emerge: the test exhibits satisfactory properties across a wide variety of specifications and it performs well in environments that challenge conventional approaches and are typical of periods of heightened financial uncertainty.
Methodological advances matter most when they help answer substantive economic questions. To illustrate the usefulness of the new framework, the MSTV research applies it to leading asset-pricing models using large cross-sections of S&P 500 stocks observed over rolling windows of length.
During relatively tranquil periods, several models provide a reasonable description of returns. However, their performance deteriorates significantly during episodes of financial turmoil – showing a rejection of traditional model hypotheses during episodes of market stress including the Asian Financial Crisis, the bursting of the Dot-Com bubble, the Global Financial Crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic.
These findings suggest that explaining returns remains particularly difficult during periods when financial markets are under strain. While existing models capture average return patterns reasonably well under normal conditions, they struggle to account satisfactorily for return dynamics during major economic disruptions.
Figure 1 visualises these findings by plotting the time series of the largest estimated absolute alpha for each rolling window. The degree of mispricing varies over time, with the period January 1999-December 2009 (the red shaded area) characterised by particularly large and persistent pricing errors. This is clear evidence that common asset-pricing models appear most vulnerable precisely during periods in which understanding risk is most important.
Implications for empirical finance
The contribution of MSTV is methodological, but its implications are broader. The growth AI-based investing and other new developments have dramatically expanded the dimensionality of empirical asset-pricing applications. Yet many of the profession’s benchmark specification tests were developed for a much lower-dimensional world.
As the literature increasingly embraces richer datasets and more sophisticated modelling techniques, reliable high-dimensional inference becomes a first-order concern rather than a technical afterthought. The question of whether asset-pricing models successfully explain expected returns remains one of the defining questions in finance. The proposed new test broadens the range of applications where this fundamental question can be addressed rigorously.
More broadly, the findings underscore a simple point: finance has entered an era of increasingly large and complex datasets, so as empirical methods evolve to exploit these data, inference procedures must evolve alongside them.
Featured faculty
Professor of Finance
Featured research

References
Fama, E F and K R French (1993), ‘Common risk factors in the returns on stocks and bonds’, Journal of Financial Economics 33(1): 3–56.
Fama, E F and K R French (2015), ‘A five-factor asset pricing model’, Journal of Financial Economics 116(1): 1–22.

title: Meet the Cambridge MBA class of 2026
author: Cambridge Judge Communications Team
summary: Meet the class of 2026, a diverse group of 222 students with 43 nationalities and an average of 6 years professional experience.
text:
From entrepreneurs and military officers to AI specialists, sustainability leaders and creative industry professionals, the cohort represents an extraordinary breadth of experience and expertise. We meet 7 members of the new cohort and discover the careers that brought them here, why they chose the Cambridge MBA and where they hope it will take them next.
The Cambridge MBA Class of 2026 at a glance

Adiba Arif (Bangladesh)
Adiba Arif joins the Cambridge MBA from a career spanning talent, organisational effectiveness and inclusion, most recently as Head of Talent, Org Effectiveness & Inclusion – APMEA Central.
One of her proudest achievements was leading a cross-geographic, cross-functional team through the largest organisational transformation of the South Asia business of a Fortune 500 company. The experience involved using data to navigate complex decisions, bringing diverse stakeholders together and helping reshape the organisation to become leaner and more future-ready.
Adiba was drawn to the Cambridge MBA by its fast-paced, experiential approach and the opportunity to study within a university ‘steeped in centuries of breakthroughs’.
Ultimately, she wants to leave Cambridge equipped to become a truly global leader, ready to tackle complex problems alongside people with different perspectives.
“A world-class education, meaningful connections with people from all over the world, healthy debates that rewire my brain, and the key to unlock doors I haven’t even thought to knock on yet.”

Cathy Wu (Australia and New Zealand)
AI strategy and product consultant Cathy Wu comes to Cambridge with experience at the intersection of technology, financial services and innovation.
Earlier in her career, Cathy helped launch one of Malaysia’s early end-to-end mobile digital banking experiences. Taking responsibility for digital payments and cards, she worked with teams across more than 5 countries to build the offering in under a year.
The experience sparked an interest in technology that ultimately led her into AI strategy and product management. Cambridge’s technology ecosystem and emphasis on experiential learning were important factors in her decision to join the MBA.
Her next ambition is to move into AI governance, helping organisations interpret emerging regulation and translate it into sustainable practices that support the safe use of AI. Longer term, she hopes to contribute to shaping regulation that genuinely serves the people and organisations working within it.
Cambridge’s technology ecosystem and emphasis on experiential learning were important factors in my decision to join the MBA.
Maria Buzbee (USA and Spain)
US Navy officer Maria Buzbee joins the Cambridge MBA as she prepares to make the transition from military service into finance.
Her career in the US Navy has included serving as a Supply Corps Officer, Executive Assistant to the CEO of NEXCOM and Flag Aide. Among her proudest achievements is earning the Surface Warfare Supply Corps Officer qualification, an intensive process taking approximately 18 months and culminating in an oral examination with the ship’s Captain and senior officers.
At Cambridge, Maria wants to deepen her understanding of financial markets, banking and how capital is invested across different regions of the world, while broadening her perspective on the career opportunities ahead.
She ultimately hopes to take the skills and experience developed during her military career into development finance and international development, with the goal of working for a multilateral institution or development bank.

Enrique Bendana (Paraguay and Italy)
Entrepreneur Enrique Bendana arrives in Cambridge as co-founder and CEO of Paraguayan fintech Vaquita.
What began as an app for collecting money for group activities grew into a financial services business serving more than 150,000 Paraguayans. Of those users, 40,000 had never previously held a bank account.
Building the company meant creating a team from scratch, developing partnerships with some of Paraguay’s leading companies and learning how to adapt his leadership as the business grew.
Enrique sees Cambridge as an opportunity to combine that entrepreneurial experience with new frameworks, perspectives and connections. He is particularly looking forward to the Cambridge Venture Project and Global Consulting Project, alongside the opportunities offered by the wider Cambridge entrepreneurial ecosystem.
He wants to continue building products and companies that create positive change, wherever that path takes him.
“As the only Paraguayan in the cohort, I feel the duty to carry the Cambridge legacy forward by driving positive impact back home.”

Federico Grumo (Italy)
Federico Grumo has taken one of the class’s more unconventional routes to an MBA.
With degrees in performing arts and musicology, his career has taken him from opera houses and live entertainment to international project management, media, marketing and strategic partnerships. Along the way, he has worked with internationally renowned artists including Zubin Mehta and Plácido Domingo. Most recently, he worked in content strategy, marketing and strategic partnerships at Sky Italia.
For Federico, the Cambridge MBA is a bridge between his background in music and the performing arts and a future in business. He was particularly attracted by Cambridge’s combination of technology, entrepreneurship and creative industries, as well as the opportunity to learn through practical projects.
He hopes to build a career in consulting or strategy within media and entertainment, combining his knowledge of the creative industries with stronger managerial and strategic skills.
“Cambridge really is the place where my past and my future meet, but above all, it is a place where I feel I can be myself.”

Mandy Chan (Canada)
Mandy Chan joins Cambridge after 5 years working with international organisations, from the United Nations Human Rights Office to the World Economic Forum.
At the World Economic Forum, she helped build a community of more than 100 chief procurement officers seeking to harness corporate purchasing power to decarbonise hard-to-abate sectors. The community’s members represented approximately $19 billion in annual clean demand by 2030.
She later joined the team behind the GAEA Awards, working to bring together stakeholders including investors, policymakers and public figures and helping award recipients expand their networks, visibility and access to resources.
Mandy chose Cambridge for its focus on responsible and sustainable business and the opportunity to strengthen the commercial knowledge behind her sustainability experience.
Her ambition is to build a career at the intersection of sustainability, finance and policy. In the near term, she hopes to work in impact investing or philanthropy, helping channel capital towards promising sustainability solutions and enabling them to scale.

Solveig Herzum (Italy, USA and UK)
Filmmaker and producer Solveig Herzum joins the Cambridge MBA after building a career across film, media and the creative sector.
A graduate of Northwestern University and the UK National Film and Television School, where she completed a master’s in Directing Documentary, Solveig most recently worked as a Shooting Producer at Into Film.
Since moving to London in 2018 knowing almost no one in the industry, she has built a creative and professional network spanning the UK, Italy and the US. That community has enabled her to develop and produce projects, connect people with opportunities and support emerging creative talent.
The Cambridge MBA’s Creative Industries in the Digital Age concentration was a major attraction, alongside the programme’s global, entrepreneurial and collaborative approach.
After the MBA, Solveig hopes to move into strategic management and leadership within the media, creative and social impact sectors. Longer term, her ambition is to help build sustainable creative organisations that expand opportunities for artists, filmmakers and young people.
