title: Thomas Zurbuchen wechselt zu Blue Origin
author: Redaktion
summary: Als Leiter von ETH Zürich Space hat Thomas Zurbuchen in den letzten drei Jahren die Weltraumforschung und -lehre an der ETH Zürich massgeblich geprägt. Nun verlässt der ETH-Professor die Hochschule, um für das US-Raumfahrtunternehmen Blue Origin zu arbeiten.
text:
Thomas Zurbuchen, warum verlassen Sie die ETH Zürich bereits nach drei Jahren?
Thomas Zurbuchen: Meine Stelle war von Anfang an auf drei Jahre angesetzt. Ich habe immer gesagt, dass ich danach Bilanz ziehe und neue Optionen prüfe. Gemeinsam mit meinem Team haben wir ein dauerhaftes Fundament für die Weltraumausbildung und -forschung geschaffen. Ich bin der ETH Zürich für ihre Unterstützung sehr dankbar, ganz besonders ETH-Präsident Joël Mesot und dem designierten Präsidenten Günther Dissertori. Gemeinsam haben wir die Ziele erreicht, die wir uns gesetzt hatten. 
Was haben sie erreicht? 
Ich möchte vier Projekte hervorheben: Wir haben mit dem «Master Space Systems» den ersten akademischen Masterstudiengang der Schweiz mit Fokus auf Raumfahrtsysteme lanciert. Die ersten Absolventinnen und Absolventen sind heute bereits in der Raumfahrtindustrie tätig. Zudem haben wir einen Innovationshub geschaffen, der gemeinsam mit Forschenden und der Industrie ehrgeizige Forschungs- und Technologieprojekte ins All bringen will. So haben wir beispielsweise ein Weltraumexperiment für ein neues Material entwickelt, das im Dezember zur Internationalen Raumstation (ISS) fliegt und dort getestet wird. Und drittens haben wir im Rahmen des ESA Business Incubation Center zahlreiche Start-ups unterstützt, die international erfolgreich sind.
Zur Person
Thomas Zurbuchen war von 2016 bis 2022 Wissenschaftsdirektor der Weltraumbehörde NASA. Im August 2023 übernahm der schweizerisch-US-amerikanische Astrophysiker als Professor für Weltraumwissenschaft und -technologie die Leitung von ETH Zürich Space. Mit dieser Initiative will die ETH ihre Weltraumforschung und -lehre ausbauen und die Zusammenarbeit mit der Raumfahrtindustrie stärken.
Und das vierte Projekt?
Wir haben dank der Unterstützung der Bucherer-Stiftung und des Kantons Luzern das ETH Swiss GeoLab ins Leben gerufen. Dieses interdisziplinäre Kompetenzzentrum für Erdbeobachtung wird Daten aus dem All, aus der Luft und vom Boden, sowie KI-gestützte Analysemethoden und Hochleistungsrechner nutzen, um Lösungen für konkrete Herausforderungen zu entwickeln – von der Früherkennung von Naturkatastrophen bis hin zu Ernteprognosen für die Landwirtschaft. 
Wie geht es mit ETH Zurich Space nach ihrem Abgang weiter?
ETH Zurich Space ist in besten Händen. Ich bin stolz auf das Team, das wir hier aufgebaut haben. Jedes der vier erwähnten Projekte wird auch nach meinem Abgang von einer erfahrenen Person geleitet. So hat etwa Professor Richard Kornfeld seit über einem Jahr die operative Leitung von ETH Zurich Space inne. Richard ist ein erfahrener Ingenieur mit 25 Jahren Erfahrung bei der Nasa. Auch beim GeoLab haben wir mit ETH-Professorin Verena Griess und Geschäftsführer Dr. Felix Seidel ein äusserst kompetentes Führungsteam. Um einen guten Übergang zu gewährleisten, werde ich das Team noch bis Ende Jahr unterstützen.
Was werden sie in ihrem neuen Job machen?
Ich werde als Senior Vice President das «Advanced Concepts»-Team von Blue Origin in den USA leiten. Dieses Team entwickelt neue Konzepte und Systeme, um eine nachhaltige Zukunft des Lebens und Arbeitens im Weltraum voranzutreiben. Wir werden also massgeblich mitbestimmen, was dieses Raumfahrtunternehmen als Nächstes entwickelt. Diese Herausforderung hat mich sehr gereizt. Meines Erachtens ist Blue Origin eine der Organisationen, welche die zukunftsträchtigsten Space-Technologien heute entwickeln. 
Wie sehen die Zukunft des Schweizer Space-Ökosystems?
Die Zukunft ist nach wie vor vielversprechend. Wir haben das technologische Know-how und die Talente. Jetzt müssen wir mutiger in ambitionierte Space-Projekte sowie vielversprechende Start-ups investieren und die Zusammenarbeit zwischen Hochschulen und Unternehmen intensivieren. Wir sind heute im Schweizer Ökosystem in der Lage ambitionierte Projekte zu realisieren – beispielsweise einen Space-Roboter aus Zürich mit Technologien aus Bern und Lausanne. Mit ETH Zurich Space haben wir einen wichtigen Schritt in diese Richtung gemacht. Ich bin davon überzeugt, dass die Schweiz von dieser Aufbauarbeit profitieren wird und in Zukunft eine gewichtigere Rolle im Bereich Raumfahrt spielen wird.

title: Accuracy where it matters most: How SonoSight brings precision ultrasound to neurosurgery
author: Sarah Schiller
summary: Dr Isaac Esteban Varela, a research fellow at D-ITET and ETH Pioneer Fellow, is developing SonoSight – a platform that combines ultrasound therapy with real-time imaging and treatment monitoring. We spoke with him about overcoming the challenges of brain surgery, navigating the translation from lab to clinic, and why clinical adoption hinges on design.
text:
Accuracy where it matters most: How SonoSight brings precision ultrasound to neurosurgery
Dr Isaac Esteban Varela, how would you explain your research to a non-specialist?
I develop advanced imaging technologies and integrate them with ultrasound therapies, enabling these therapies to be guided, monitored, and controlled through real-time imaging. That is the core of my research within our group.
How did that come about?
Some years ago, I studied industrial engineering and specialised in mechanical engineering. After my doctorate in developmental biology, I pivoted to my current field: engineering combined with translational research. I am dedicated to the intersection of those two disciplines. Solving problems as an engineer dedicated to life sciences is where I find my deepest interest.
About Isaac Esteban Varela
Isaac Esteban Varela is an ETH Pioneer Fellow leading the development of SonoSight. Holding a background in industrial engineering and a doctorate in developmental biology, his work bridges engineering and the life sciences to create next-generation biomedical devices. He is a research fellow in Professor Daniel Razansky’s Chair for Biomedical Imaging. In a recent external page Nature Communications paper, he demonstrated a major technological breakthrough in a preclinical study. The Pioneer Fellowship is ETH Zurich’s incubation programme that helps entrepreneurial students and researchers turn their research into a market‑ready spin‑off with funding, coaching, and 18 months of support in the Life Science/Pharma/Medtech track.
You were quite recently awarded the ETH Pioneer Fellowship with SonoSight. What is the core goal of your project?
The project is the direct translation of my research efforts over the last three years – in close collaboration with Professor Daniel Razansky and senior scientist Dr Hector Estrada. We are developing SonoSight, a compact intraoperative platform that combines focused ultrasound therapy with real-time image guidance and treatment monitoring during open neurosurgery. By integrating therapy delivery, anatomical guidance, and treatment feedback into a single device, we aim to establish a safer, more precise, and more workflow-compatible approach to treating brain lesions.
Why are you focusing on brain surgery?
We focus on brain tumours, since they remain challenging to treat safely: surgeons must remove diseased tissue while preserving delicate and functionally critical brain areas. At the same time, current focused ultrasound solutions remain constrained by skull-induced acoustic distortion, dependence on MRI infrastructure, and complex clinical logistics. Adapting to a tumour is extraordinarily challenging because its growth patterns and boundaries can be highly irregular, making precise treatment difficult. Our technology is promising because we can adapt to different target geometries and provide accurate guidance and monitoring. So before moving into a more advanced clinical phase, the prototype has already demonstrated its feasibility and that it can induce very precise tissue lesions.
The current imaging depth is limited to 1 to 2 centimetres below the surface. Is that a hindrance?
That is simply the current limitation of the technology. And of course, we will try to investigate whether our device can reach deeper regions, but the limitation exists because light cannot travel through tissue that easily. Does this mean that the clinical implications are hindered? I mean, it would be ideal if we could cover the full extent of the brain, which we can achieve with imaging alone, but not with therapy. However, many clinically relevant targets are located on the cortical surface or in cortical regions that lie within the operational range of our device. The key question is how best to align the technology with existing, real-world clinical cases.
Could it – in the future – also be used to treat skin cancer?
Yes, absolutely. We are currently focused on brain surgery because such a delicate organ could benefit tremendously from our innovation, especially given that innovation in neurosurgery has been very limited over recent decades. So we think there is a lot to be done in this area, as the incidence of brain tumours continues to increase. For instance, a large portion of patients with metastatic – secondary – brain cancer develop tumours located within this reachable zone. So that would be one possible clinical case that we could treat and, hopefully, provide a better therapeutic outcome for. But of course, there are other cases that we could treat as well. Any possible target that benefits from thermal therapy and lies within our range can be addressed – such as, as you mentioned, skin cancer or vascular applications.
                            
                                “Surgeons must constantly make hard trade-offs: if you excise too aggressively, you damage healthy tissue; if you are too conservative, there is a high chance the tumour will recur.”
                            
                            Dr Isaac Esteban Varela
In which aspects would this new treatment be beneficial?
I think our device is exciting in many ways compared to current alternatives. Because we have everything integrated into a single device, we no longer rely on MRI facilities. The device can also be considered a faster alternative because one of the technical layers we want to implement is a robotic arm for full process optimisation. This will not only provide much greater speed, but more importantly, help democratise the treatment. Patients confronted with a disease of this kind understandably want access to the world's leading specialists, but doing so often requires both international travel and substantial financial resources.
By automating the procedure under the supervision of a well-trained specialist, we can make this therapy accessible to more people and thus standardise care. Furthermore, our device delivers exceptional targeting precision – down to a range of a few millimetres. This is crucial when working on an open brain, where healthy tissue is easily damaged. By enabling better assessment of the tumour cavity, the patient suffers less trauma.
So, you limit damage in the future …
Yes, exactly. Differentiating between healthy tissue and a tumour is an ongoing challenge that neurosurgeons face every day. Identifying the exact boundary is very difficult, and surgeons must constantly make hard trade-offs: if you excise too aggressively, you damage healthy tissue; if you are too conservative, there is a high chance the tumour will recur. With the advanced imaging technology we are incorporating, we can map the distinct oxygenation and deoxygenation patterns of the tumour. This provides neurosurgeons with a crucial additional resource to make more informed decisions when evaluating cavity borders.
                            
                                “It forces you to look up from your computer screen and address the right questions – such as: ‘What I'm doing seems important and very exciting, but who could benefit from this?’”
                            
                            Dr Isaac Esteban Varela
How has your experience been so far with ETH Entrepreneurship?
It was, and I am sure it will continue to be fantastic. It marked an important shift in my perspective, because it really forces you to look up from your computer screen and address the right questions – such as: "What I’m doing seems important and very exciting, but who could benefit from this? Who is going to pay for it? What do I need to consider to drive not only the technical development, but also what matters to investors and stakeholders?" So, not only after being awarded the fellowship, but already during the application process, I had to confront these questions for the first time. That was a real change of gears.
Would it also be a goal of yours to spin out a company in a couple of years?
Absolutely. That is the primary reason I am pursuing this path. My main objective is to co-found a company, because that is a realistic path to bring a technological innovation to society. At some point, you simply have to commit to that path and go for it.
                            
                                “To me, true success would be knowing that one day patients genuinely benefit from what we are building.”
                            
                            Dr Isaac Esteban Varela
Looking ahead to the end of the fellowship in 2027, what would you consider a realistic outcome for the prototype?
My goal is to see our device become much more robust than it is today. We must improve its usability, as we need to convince surgeons that using this device is intuitive and user-friendly. Clinical adoption is a critical factor: you can have the best machine in the world, but if clinicians find it unwieldy or overly complex, they will stick to their established methods, which they already perform exceptionally well.
Additionally, we need to develop the automation layer by incorporating the robotic arm. Of course, this will require dedicated technological development and extensive laboratory validation. Another key priority from this point forward is addressing all regulatory requirements. While the device is currently a lab prototype, it needs to become more compact, easily transportable within clinical environments, and above all, completely reliable. Every design decision we make from here on must comply with regulations and rigorous risk assessments. How we translate our current prototype into a clinically valid system over the next 18 months is our central focus, which is why working alongside our regulatory, robotics and clinical partners is essential.
What would success in 10 years’ time look like?
By that time, what I would love to see is neurosurgeons in clinics relying on this tool to offer an alternative treatment option to patients where appropriate. To me, true success would be knowing that one day patients genuinely benefit from what we are building.

title: Millimetergenau, wo es am wichtigsten ist: Wie SonoSight Präzisions-Ultraschall in die Neurochirurgie bringt
author: Sarah Schiller
summary: Dr. Isaac Esteban Varela, Forschungsstipendiat am D-ITET und ETH Pioneer Fellow, entwickelt SonoSight – eine Plattform, die Ultraschalltherapie mit Echtzeit-Bildgebung und Behandlungsüberwachung kombiniert. Wir sprachen mit ihm darüber, wie man die Herausforderungen bei Operationen am Gehirn meistert, wie der Transfer vom Labor in die Klinik gelingt und warum die klinische Anwendung vom Design abhängt.
text:
Millimetergenau, wo es am wichtigsten ist: Wie SonoSight Präzisions-Ultraschall in die Neurochirurgie bringt
Dr. Isaac Esteban Varela, wie würden Sie Ihre Forschung einem Laien erklären?
Ich entwickle fortschrittliche Bildgebungstechnologien und integriere diese in Ultraschalltherapien. Das ermöglicht es, dass diese Therapien mit Echtzeit-Bildgebung gesteuert, überwacht und kontrolliert werden können. Das ist der Kern meiner Forschung in unserer Gruppe.
Wie kam es dazu?
Vor einigen Jahren habe ich Wirtschaftsingenieurwesen studiert und mich auf Maschinenbau spezialisiert. Nach meinem Doktorat in Entwicklungsbiologie habe ich mich meinem heutigen Fachgebiet zugewandt: Ingenieurwesen in Kombination mit translationaler Forschung. Ich widme mich der Schnittstelle dieser beiden Disziplinen. Am meisten interessiert mich die Lösung komplexer Problemstellungen an der Schnittstelle von Ingenieurwesen und Life Sciences.
Über Isaac Esteban Varela
Isaac Esteban Varela ist ETH Pioneer Fellow und leitet die Entwicklung von SonoSight. Mit seinem Hintergrund im Wirtschaftsingenieurwesen und einem Doktorat in Entwicklungsbiologie schlägt seine Arbeit den Bogen zwischen Ingenieurwesen und Life Sciences, um biomedizinische Geräte der nächsten Generation zu entwickeln. Er ist Forschungsstipendiat am Lehrstuhl für Biomedizinische Bildgebung von Professor Daniel Razansky. In einem kürzlich in externe Seite Nature Communications veröffentlichten Paper stellte er einen bedeutenden technologischen Durchbruch in einer präklinischen Studie vor. Das Pioneer Fellowship ist das Inkubationsprogramm der ETH Zürich, das unternehmerisch denkenden Studierenden und Forschenden dabei hilft, ihre Forschungsergebnisse mithilfe von Finanzierung, Coaching und 18-monatiger Unterstützung im Bereich Life Science/Pharma/Medtech in ein marktreifes Spin-off zu überführen.
Sie haben erst kürzlich mit SonoSight das ETH Pioneer Fellowship erhalten. Was ist das Kernziel Ihres Projekts?
Das Projekt ist die direkte Umsetzung meiner Forschungsarbeit der letzten drei Jahre – in enger Zusammenarbeit mit Professor Daniel Razansky und Senior Scientist Dr. Hector Estrada. Wir entwickeln SonoSight, eine kompakte intraoperative Plattform, die fokussierte Ultraschalltherapie mit Echtzeit-Bildführung und Behandlungsüberwachung während neurochirurgischen Eingriffen am offenen Gehirn kombiniert. Durch die Integration von Therapieverabreichung, anatomischer Führung und Behandlungsfeedback in einem einzigen Gerät wollen wir einen sichereren, präziseren und besser in den Arbeitsablauf integrierbaren Ansatz zur Behandlung von Hirnläsionen etablieren.
Warum konzentrieren Sie sich auf die Gehirnchirurgie?
Wir konzentrieren uns auf Hirntumore, da deren sichere Behandlung nach wie vor eine Herausforderung darstellt: Chirurginnen und Chirurgen müssen erkranktes Gewebe entfernen und gleichzeitig empfindliche und funktionskritische Hirnareale erhalten. Aktuelle Lösungen mit fokussiertem Ultraschall sind nach wie vor durch schädelbedingte akustische Verzerrungen, die Abhängigkeit von MRI-Infrastruktur und komplexe klinische Logistik eingeschränkt. Die Anpassung an einen Tumor ist ausserordentlich schwierig, da dessen Wachstumsmuster und Grenzen sehr unregelmässig sein können, was eine präzise Behandlung erschwert. Unsere Technologie ist vielversprechend, da wir uns an unterschiedliche Zielgeometrien anpassen und eine genaue Führung und Überwachung bieten können. Bevor wir also in eine fortgeschrittenere klinische Phase übergehen, hat der Prototyp bereits seine Machbarkeit unter Beweis gestellt und gezeigt, dass er sehr präzise Gewebeläsionen erzeugen kann.
Die derzeitige Bildgebungstiefe ist auf 1 bis 2 Zentimeter unter der Oberfläche begrenzt. Ist das ein Hindernis?
Das ist schlicht die derzeitige Grenze der Technologie. Natürlich werden wir versuchen zu untersuchen, ob unser Gerät tiefere Bereiche erreichen kann, aber diese Einschränkung besteht, weil Licht Gewebe nicht so leicht durchdringen kann. Bedeutet das, dass die klinischen Anwendungsmöglichkeiten eingeschränkt sind? Es wäre natürlich ideal, wenn wir das gesamte Gehirn abdecken könnten, was wir zwar mit der Bildgebung erreichen können, nicht aber mit der Therapie. Viele klinisch relevante Ziele befinden sich jedoch an der kortikalen Oberfläche oder in kortikalen Regionen, die innerhalb des Wirkbereichs unseres Geräts liegen. Die entscheidende Frage ist, wie sich die Technologie am besten auf bestehende, reale klinische Fälle abstimmen lässt.
Könnte es – in Zukunft – auch zur Behandlung von Hautkrebs eingesetzt werden?
Ja, auf jeden Fall. Derzeit konzentrieren wir uns auf die Gehirnchirurgie, weil ein so empfindliches Organ enorm von unserer Innovation profitieren könnte, zumal es in der Neurochirurgie in den letzten Jahrzehnten nur sehr wenige Fortschritte gab. Wir sind daher der Meinung, dass es in diesem Bereich noch viel zu tun gibt – auch weil die Häufigkeit von Hirntumoren weiter zunimmt. So entwickelt beispielsweise ein grosser Teil der Patientinnen und Patienten mit metastasiertem – sekundärem – Hirnkrebs Tumore, die sich genau in dieser erreichbaren Zone befinden. Das wäre also ein möglicher klinischer Fall, den wir behandeln und für den wir hoffentlich ein besseres Therapieergebnis erzielen könnten. Aber natürlich gibt es auch andere Fälle, die wir behandeln könnten. Jedes mögliche Ziel, das von einer thermischen Therapie profitiert und in unserem Wirkbereich liegt, kann adressiert werden – wie zum Beispiel Hautkrebs oder vaskuläre Anwendungen.
                            
                                «Chirurginnen und Chirurgen müssen ständig schwierige Kompromisse eingehen: Wenn man zu aggressiv herausschneidet, schädigt man gesundes Gewebe; wenn man zu konservativ vorgeht, ist die Wahrscheinlichkeit hoch, dass der Tumor zurückkehrt.»
                            
                            Dr. Isaac Esteban Varela
In welchen Aspekten wäre diese neue Behandlungsmethode also von Vorteil?
Ich denke, unser Gerät ist im Vergleich zu den derzeitigen Alternativen in vielerlei Hinsicht spannend. Da wir alles in ein einziges Gerät integriert haben, sind wir nicht mehr auf MRI-Infrastrukturen angewiesen. Das Gerät kann auch als schnellere Alternative betrachtet werden, da eine der technischen Komponenten, die wir implementieren wollen, ein Roboterarm zur vollständigen Prozessoptimierung ist. Dies wird nicht nur für eine deutlich höhere Geschwindigkeit sorgen, sondern vor allem dazu beitragen, die Behandlung zu demokratisieren. Patientinnen und Patienten, die mit einer solchen Krankheit konfrontiert sind, wünschen sich verständlicherweise Zugang zu den weltweit führenden Spezialistinnen und Spezialisten, was jedoch oft sowohl internationale Reisen als auch erhebliche finanzielle Mittel erfordert.
Durch die Automatisierung des Eingriffs unter der Aufsicht von gut ausgebildetem Fachpersonal können wir diese Therapie für mehr Menschen zugänglich machen und so die Versorgung standardisieren. Darüber hinaus bietet unser Gerät eine aussergewöhnliche Zielgenauigkeit – bis auf wenige Millimeter genau. Dies ist entscheidend bei Eingriffen am offenen Gehirn, bei denen gesundes Gewebe leicht beschädigt werden kann. Es ermöglicht so auch eine bessere Beurteilung der Tumorkavität und die Patientin oder der Patient erleidet weniger Trauma.
Man begrenzt also künftige Schäden …
Ja, genau. Die Unterscheidung zwischen gesundem Gewebe und einem Tumor ist eine ständige Herausforderung, mit der Neurochirurginnen und -chirurgen täglich konfrontiert sind. Die genaue Grenze zu bestimmen ist sehr schwierig, und Chirurginnen und Chirurgen müssen ständig schwierige Kompromisse eingehen: Wenn man zu aggressiv herausschneidet, schädigt man gesundes Gewebe; wenn man zu konservativ vorgeht, ist die Wahrscheinlichkeit hoch, dass der Tumor zurückkehrt. Mit der fortschrittlichen Bildgebungstechnologie, die wir integrieren, können wir die unterschiedlichen Sauerstoffanreicherungs- und Entsäuerungsmuster des Tumors abbilden. Dies bietet Neurochirurginnen und -chirurgen eine entscheidende zusätzliche Ressource, um bei der Beurteilung von Kavitätsrändern fundiertere Entscheidungen zu treffen.
                            
                                «Es zwingt einen dazu, den Blick vom Bildschirm zu heben und sich mit den richtigen Fragen auseinanderzusetzen – zum Beispiel: ‹Was ich mache, scheint wichtig und sehr spannend zu sein, aber wer könnte davon profitieren?›»
                            
                            Dr. Isaac Esteban Varela
Wie waren Ihre bisherigen Erfahrungen mit ETH Entrepreneurship?
Es war fantastisch – und ich bin sicher, das wird es auch weiterhin sein. Es markierte einen wichtigen Perspektivenwechsel, weil es einen wirklich dazu zwingt, den Blick vom Bildschirm zu heben und sich mit den richtigen Fragen auseinanderzusetzen – zum Beispiel: «Was ich mache, scheint wichtig und sehr spannend zu sein, aber wer könnte davon profitieren? Wer wird dafür bezahlen? Was muss ich beachten, um nicht nur die technische Entwicklung voranzutreiben, sondern auch das, was für Investoren und Stakeholder wichtig ist?» Also musste ich mich nicht erst nach dem Erhalt des Fellowships, sondern bereits während des Bewerbungsprozesses zum ersten Mal mit diesen Fragen auseinandersetzen. Das war ein echter Richtungswechsel.
Ist es auch eines Ihrer Ziele, in ein paar Jahren ein Unternehmen daraus zu gründen?
Auf jeden Fall. Das ist der Hauptgrund, warum ich diesen Weg einschlage. Mein Hauptziel ist es, ein Unternehmen mitzugründen, denn das ist ein realistischer Weg, um eine technologische Innovation in die Gesellschaft zu bringen. Irgendwann muss man sich einfach auf diesen Weg festlegen und es versuchen.
                            
                                «Für mich wäre es ein echter Erfolg zu wissen, dass Patientinnen und Patienten eines Tages wirklich von dem profitieren, was wir hier entwickeln.»
                            
                            Dr. Isaac Esteban Varela
Mit Blick auf das Ende des Stipendiums im Jahr 2027: Was würden Sie als realistisches Ergebnis für Ihren Prototypen betrachten?
Mein Ziel ist es, dass unser Gerät wesentlich robuster wird, als es heute ist. Wir müssen die Usability verbessern, da wir die Chirurginnen und Chirurgen davon überzeugen müssen, dass die Bedienung dieses Geräts intuitiv und benutzerfreundlich ist. Die klinische Akzeptanz ist ein entscheidender Faktor: Man kann die beste Maschine der Welt haben, aber wenn das klinische Personal sie unhandlich oder zu komplex findet, wird es bei seinen etablierten Methoden bleiben, die es bereits hervorragend beherrscht.
Zudem müssen wir die Automatisierungsebene durch die Integration des Roboterarms weiterentwickeln. Dies erfordert natürlich gezielte technologische Entwicklung und umfangreiche Validierungen im Labor. Eine weitere Hauptpriorität von nun an ist die Berücksichtigung aller regulatorischen Anforderungen. Das Gerät ist zwar derzeit noch ein Laborprototyp, muss aber kompakter, innerhalb klinischer Umgebungen leicht transportierbar und vor allem absolut zuverlässig werden. Jede Designentscheidung, die wir treffen, muss den Vorschriften und strengen Risikobeurteilungen entsprechen. Wie wir unseren aktuellen Prototypen in den nächsten 18 Monaten in ein klinisch valides System überführen, steht im Mittelpunkt unserer Arbeit – deshalb ist die Zusammenarbeit mit unseren Partner:innen aus den Bereichen Zulassung, Robotik und Klinik unerlässlich.
Wie würde Erfolg in zehn Jahren aussehen?
Bis dahin würde ich mir wünschen, dass Neurochirurginnen und -chirurgen in Kliniken auf dieses Instrument zurückgreifen, um Patient:innen in geeigneten Fällen eine alternative Behandlungsmöglichkeit anzubieten. Für mich wäre es ein echter Erfolg zu wissen, dass Patientinnen und Patienten eines Tages wirklicfh von dem profitieren, was wir hier entwickeln.

title: Parting words from a scholar who stepped up
author: Christina Pazzanese
summary: Tomiko Brown-Nagin reflects on her work as Radcliffe dean and as leader of high-stakes University initiatives.
text:
When she arrived on campus in 2012 as a legal scholar and historian, Tomiko Brown-Nagin never envisioned that she would one day lead the Harvard Radcliffe Institute.
Now, after eight years as Radcliffe’s dean, during which she also chaired two major University-wide efforts, Brown-Nagin is preparing to join Stanford University next month as the James Quillen Dean of its Graduate School of Education. She will also hold an appointment as professor of law at the Stanford School of Law.
In his Aug. 5 announcement to the Harvard community, President Alan Garber thanked Brown-Nagin for her “many lasting contributions” to Harvard, calling her an “outstanding dean” and “exemplary scholar.”
At Radcliffe, Brown-Nagin, RI ’17, spearheaded the development and implementation of a strategic plan that both affirmed the institute’s history as Radcliffe College and charted a bold path forward. She expanded Harvard’s faculty with key hires through jointly appointed Radcliffe Professorships, strengthened Radcliffe’s celebrated fellowship program, and launched a leadership program that partners local high school students with Harvard undergraduate mentors.
In 2019, President Lawrence S. Bacow asked Brown-Nagin to lead a comprehensive inquiry into the history and lasting impact of Harvard’s ties to slavery. The committee’s 2022 report identified “difficult truths” and offered recommendations for reparative steps the University should undertake. Garber called Brown-Nagin’s leadership of the effort “as humane as it was rigorous,” saying it “reflected the best of what it means to be a scholar in service to a community, an institution, and a nation.”
More recently, amid tensions related to political protest and civil discourse, Brown-Nagin co-chaired the University’s Open Inquiry and Constructive Dialogue Working Group, which Garber called a “tremendous contribution” to ensuring an improved campus climate. In its report, the group examined reluctance among many students, faculty, and staff to participate fully in the free exchange of ideas and viewpoints for fear of social, professional, or legal consequences and proposed concrete strategies and techniques to encourage respectful debate on campus.
In addition to her leadership of Radcliffe, Brown-Nagin is the Daniel P.S. Paul Professor of Constitutional Law at Harvard Law School and a professor of history in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences. In 2022, she authored a widely acclaimed book on Constance Baker Motley, the groundbreaking civil rights attorney, politician, and federal judge. In this edited conversation, she reflects on her time at Harvard and looks ahead to a new chapter at Stanford.
Gazette: Education — access to education as a means to opportunity — has been a central theme in your work as a historian, as a legal scholar, as dean, and in your family’s history. Did that guide your decision to join Stanford and lead its Graduate School of Education?
Tomiko Brown-Nagin: Absolutely it did. I would not depart Harvard but for an opportunity that I consider unique and entirely consistent with my longstanding commitment to education, access, and opportunity.
It is a throughline of my work — as a scholar and as a university administrator — that is also evident in my forthcoming book, which is a study of the nation’s fits and starts toward opportunity. The book is a sweeping survey of American history that also incorporates the history of the Deep South state where I was born and part of my family’s history, and my own experiences as a student who experienced the integration of public schools during the 1970s.
It’s a book about the transformational power of education and the power of individuals to find common ground across difference. That effort to seek commonality is a commitment that’s deeply important to me and something that I’ve been thinking a lot about over the past couple of years. It’s no secret that these have been — and continue to be — challenging times for educational systems, including colleges and universities, and for all of us who have invested our time in these institutions. We are being tested.
In your note to the Radcliffe community, you said in this new role, you “will be in a position to strengthen American education.” Where is American education today and what needs to be done?
Learning is declining, as evidenced by test scores since 2013. Researchers refer to the phenomenon as a “learning recession.”
In light of this trend, I’m eager to lead a faculty where a tremendous number and variety of researchers are pursuing projects that can illuminate why we are experiencing learning loss and can offer policy and legal recommendations. It fits my own interests so well. I’m looking forward to being a part of that — particularly now, when we are also experiencing disruption in education as a result of technological change, including AI. We really need to think deeply about what education is and what it is to become, and to speak in a way that can guide institutions that reflect the vast diversity of our education system. One of the first things that I will do at Stanford is lead a strategic planning process that I hope will help us speak to some of these issues.
You took on some of Harvard’s most complex challenges as chair of the Presidential Committee on Harvard and the Legacy of Slavery and as co-chair of the Working Group on Academic Freedom and Constructive Dialogue. Looking back, did those efforts accomplish what you had hoped?
President Bacow asked me to lead the first phase of the Harvard and Legacy of Slavery Initiative, which was focused on research. The charge that he put to me and the committee was to follow the evidence surrounding this very painful chapter in Harvard’s history and to make recommendations for how to move forward.
I’m very proud of the work that we were able to do. It was a monumental effort. It involved a lot of people: The committee included experts and faculty from every Harvard School. During the effort, I engaged the Harvard Corporation, vice presidents, the Harvard Board of Overseers, deans, faculty, students — virtually every stakeholder group that one can imagine — around that very difficult subject. It was not a foregone conclusion that we would be successful. The matter is fraught and frankly, not a lot of people other than a subset of scholars are interested in engaging with a subject that is so painful. Nevertheless, we were able to accomplish our scholarly mission.
As to the Open Inquiry work, I was asked by President Garber and Provost [John F.] Manning to take on that role with my colleague Eric Beerbohm, and I do think that our report successfully articulated aspirations for what our learning community should look like. We suggested tools and techniques for moving the University toward a better learning climate, things like the Chatham House Rule and new skills-building efforts across the Schools to teach students as well as educators how to engage with controversial issues in a constructive manner. I’m very pleased that Harvard approached that issue in the way that it did.
Radcliffe introduced the Emerging Leaders Program for high school students to work with College students to develop and hone their leadership skills. Why was that so important to initiate?
Universities like Harvard directly serve a very small and exclusive group of students. And yet it seems to me that while a relatively few students will have the benefits of an elite research education, institutions like Radcliffe can and should serve local communities and introduce a broader cross section of students to the life of the mind, to deep research, to interacting with serious scholars and students. And that’s what I have tried to do during my time at Radcliffe.
The Emerging Leaders Program is a leadership program, but it’s also a research program. One thing that makes it distinctive is that the undergraduates and the high schoolers learn about leadership using the collections of the Schlesinger Library — we introduce these students to archival research. It’s such an important learning tool, and it’s a creative way that our staff members and our students engage these high school students in thinking about how they can contribute productively to whatever social reform issues they find compelling. We also teach them about women leaders, which is important to me and important to us as an institution at Radcliffe.
As you prepare to leave Cambridge, what do you think you’ll miss most?
I will miss Harvard deeply. And I am filled with gratitude for the opportunities that I’ve had to help strengthen this great university. I’m so grateful to Larry Bacow, Drew Faust, and Alan Garber for the opportunities they gave me at Radcliffe. I’m a scholar first, and it never occurred to me that my scholarly path would lead me to this administrative role.
I’m also grateful for the opportunity to have served with a wonderful group of deans during very challenging circumstances. And although I am going on to a different institution, I would like to think that through the relationships that I’ve built over 14 years, and the work that I’ve done, I will remain connected to Harvard. Wherever I am in the world, I will always be a champion of Harvard and of Radcliffe.

title: Time to leave?
author: Samantha Laine Perfas
summary: ‘Case for Quitting’ author Lindsay Crouse on why you’re wrong when you answer ‘persevere’
text:
You’ve probably heard some version of the message: “Don’t be a quitter.” But in journalist Lindsay Crouse’s new book, “The Case for Quitting: The Surprising Benefits of Opting Out,” she argues that giving up sometimes is the best decision. In an interview with the Gazette, which has been edited for clarity and length, Crouse ’06 discussed the benefits of learning when to say “enough is enough.”
Gazette: What made you question your own relationship with quitting?
Lindsay Crouse: A lot of us grow up embracing but never questioning the language of ambition: to go harder, keep going, do more, never give up. That was always my recipe for how to achieve my dreams. And it worked, to a certain degree. I grew up in a small town, went to Harvard, ran marathons. I moved to New York and eventually landed a job at The New York Times, where I reported on how perseverance helps us achieve our goals. I viewed quitting as the opposite of perseverance, almost like a flaw of weaker people compared to the superpower of perseverance for the successful.
But perseverance and quitting are not opposites; in fact, quitting is a tool of perseverance. I wanted to explore the value of learning to stop and how it can help you create not just a happy and balanced life but also help you succeed in ways that are more fulfilling.
In your book you mention the Finnish concept of sisu, the grim determination to push through adversity. How can sisu be a double-edged sword?
Sisu can be a superpower, but it can become a weakness when it’s misapplied to problems that should be questioned or challenged. That’s when sisu can become harmful. Researchers in Finland like Amelia Latu have done a lot of research on how sisu is beneficial for us. It helps us thrive. It builds our resilience. But harmful sisu can hold us back. It can isolate us or cause us to overlook our problems. It can also make us blame other people for having problems. Sisu is great when we need help overcoming problems, but it can also cause us to ignore situations in which we’d be better off quitting.
Why does wanting to quit sometimes feel like a character flaw?
We think of quitting as a passive action or thing that happens to us. Our culture doesn’t always make room for the idea of quitting as an active choice, of taking control of a situation where we might not have control. I would argue that quitting (in many cases) is one of the boldest agentic decisions you can make.
One example: Let’s say you’re middle-aged. You’re well established, but you look at the trajectory of where you’ll be in five or 10 years. Do you like what you see? If not, how is it going to change? It often requires quitting something that you’re doing. But again, our culture rewards continuing. It rewards completion, and quitting is the opposite of that. It’s countercultural to make the decision to not continue your current path.
“Our culture doesn’t always make room for the idea of quitting as an active choice, of taking control of a situation where we might not have control.”
Lindsay Crouse
What is the harm in not quitting when you should?
In the long run, if we want to do our best, we need to learn to quit. When we fail to quit, we waste precious resources — like our time, our energy, our money — on quests that will make us increasingly miserable while often falling short of what we want. We invest those resources in paths that don’t succeed. In my own life, I’ve been tormented by the tension between productive hard work and working pointlessly hard. They can feel the same, but they get very different outcomes. Focusing on work alone keeps us from registering the mounting costs of that work, especially when it’s achieving nothing.
In the book you ask if women should quit like men. Should they?
I wrote an article in 2018 for The New York Times detailing women’s abilities to persevere in brutal circumstances, in this case the Boston Marathon. Women have physical, mental, and social qualities that help us to endure more and quit less than men; that’s especially true when conditions are harsh and the stakes are high. But the question is, does this help women? Who benefits from women’s ability to endure?
It’s often not women, it’s everybody else.
Women live longer than men, but we don’t necessarily live better. We’re more likely to battle chronic pain, to experience insomnia, to suffer migraines, to take meds for anxiety and depression. Women graduate from school at higher rates than men, but our incomes haven’t gone up. We seldom occupy the C-suite. Motherhood is another arena where we keep showing up, keep going harder, and keep doing more. I think it’s fair to say that women sometimes look at life like a war of attrition, where suffering is success. But that’s not true. Suffering is not success, and we wind up with more suffering and less reward.
Let’s say I’m tempted to quit something, be it a relationship, a job, a goal. How can I tell if it’s the kind of impulse I should listen to or if it’s a situation where it might benefit me to keep going?
When we want to quit something, it’s common to have an impulsive response: I can’t. Why not? Is it because you want to avoid the pain of disruption or is it actually true? Maybe you’re not in a position to quit right now. But can you take active steps toward building yourself an off-ramp? Maybe it’s financial, a lifestyle adjustment, a gap in your skill set. Take steps to build that cushion for a softer landing in your quest for something else. It’s also important to think about what it is you’re trying to leave or quit. Is it the environment? Your team? The job itself? Your role or workload? It’s a process of figuring out what you want to leave, figuring out if you can change it, and finally figuring out where you’ll go next.
How can we change our relationship with quitting so that we view it as a potential form of liberation rather than failure?
Just as quitting is a choice, so is continuing. These are equal decisions. And it’s important to acknowledge that while quitting does give you that liberation, it doesn’t necessarily tell you what to do next. You need to either be at peace with that or take steps to mitigate the risks involved.
I think oftentimes when we look at quitting, we say, “I don’t know how bad it will be, when I don’t know what’s coming next.” I think we forget that we also don’t know how good it could be. Look at quitting with the same optimism that we might apply to continuing. I think these are all ways to give the act of quitting equal weight in our lives. We can think about what it can bring us, as opposed to simply what we’re going to lose.

title: ‘The bulk of the benefit and the threat is actually humans’
author: Sy Boles
summary: Isaac Kohane cautions against both doomer and utopian visions of AI: ‘We have agency here.’
text:
As the inaugural chair of the Harvard Medical School’s Department of Biomedical Informatics, Isaac Kohane thinks deeply about how artificial intelligence tools can help and hurt in the field of medicine. The same set of questions led him to found the Human Values Project, an international research initiative studying the values embedded in clinical AI and developing tools to make those values visible.
We talked to Kohane about AI in healthcare and education, and as a driver of ethical challenges for universities and policymakers.
This conversation has been edited for clarity and length.
Gazette: What is the role of universities in AI development?
Isaac Kohane: A fair assessment of the last 15 years is that most of the advancements in AI have come out of industry. Currently, it does seem that the highest-performing models are indeed the largest models, and that creates an advantage for organizations that are fully aligned with the business of building these models so that their business succeeds.
In that particular comparison, universities don’t look relevant, but I think that’s an illusion. Universities have a role to play, and it’s in two domains: What are the right applications for AI, and what are the right ethical frameworks in AI governance?
“Universities have a role to play, and it’s in two domains: What are the right applications for AI, and what are the right ethical frameworks in AI governance?”
Isaac Kohane
There’s been a bizarre assumption that the leaders of these AI companies can either have or buy ethical guidance to do what they’re doing throughout the world. That seems to me to be prima facie incorrect, because ethical frameworks change from location to location.
Can you give me an example?
The Human Values Project asked a whole bunch of doctors around the world some thorny questions. For example, you’re presented with a woman who has severe anorexia. Her electrolytes look bad. She’s vomiting. You don’t hear bowel sounds. Her heart rate and ECG look normal. She’s refusing to eat; she says, “I’ll eat tomorrow.” If you ask a bunch of doctors if they should put in a feeding tube against her will or not, shockingly, doctors split 50-50. Perhaps less shockingly, so do the AI models.
Within that, there’s a lot of heterogeneity. It turns out that American doctors, compared to peers in East Asia or South America or in Central Europe, care much more about patient autonomy. It gets beaten into us, whether it’s because of our education or a fear of malpractice lawsuits. The AI models are much less pro-autonomy. On average, we found that these AI models agree more often with doctors around the world, and less with doctors in the U.S.
But the way enterprises work, they don’t work with lots and lots of AI models and go with the average. Typically, they pick one. And what we find across not just that example but across dozens of vignettes is that these AI models have their own ethical north stars. They’re consistent. Some AI models are more pro-autonomy; others are more pro-beneficence; others more pro-justice. But humans also differ. Some people want to live the longest possible life, and others just want to make it to their daughter’s wedding.
These questions are what big parts of the humanities have discussed, what the history of science has a lot to say about. This involves governance and government and law. So I think universities have an enormous role to play here. This can’t be left to a few companies who don’t have that rich tradition of thought. We have riches in that sense, especially if we embrace the full diversity of universities, which we should and will in the future, if we want AI to reflect the diversity of the human condition.
But it does mean that we, as universities, have to get out of the ivory tower a bit and engage more with the public.
What do you make of AI in medical education?
Right now, nobody has any magic recipe about the best way to use AI in education. My own kids, who are in college, tell me that if they use AI to help them solve problems, they’re not as ready come exam time. On the other hand, if they’re stuck, AI is very useful to them. So clearly there’s going to be a method for the madness, and it’s going to differ by different tasks and different specialties.
One of our biggest tasks as human beings is to take squishy little kids and turn them into full, responsible adults. There are unthinking ways to do that, which we’ve already seen with social media, and there are ways to do that with AI that are predictably not going to be so good.
Paradoxically, I think this is going to put education back in the driver’s seat. The reality is, the advent of the internet and video conferencing made students essentially defect from personalized engagement. The challenge for us is to ask, “What’s the added value that we can give that they would not get otherwise to be successful in life?” I don’t claim that we have the answers, but who else, other than universities, has the resources and the people who care about this — who can actually focus on it?
I’m struck by what you said about different specialties requiring different methods. It seems to me that the university is also a place where we can put our heads together and hammer out the distinctions of appropriate uses for AI in law versus medicine versus literature.
This is a platitude, but it’s true: Like any tool, AI can make things worse and it can make things better. It can make us more siloed, but it can also make us look outside our disciplines. For example, you could imagine, as part of the requirements for any ethical task force or education class, you could ask AI, “Of all the faculty at Harvard, who else should be at the table?”
And there are places at Harvard where we’re already incredibly cross-barrier. But if we want to be insular, AI is not going to stop us.
Do you think medicine as a field has been too quick to adopt AI tools?
I wrote an editorial for a perspective piece in the New England Journal of Medicine last year called “Compared with What?”, where I argued that we should not be so sanctimonious or fastidious when we say we should not use AI for healthcare because, compared to the best possible doctor, it’s inferior. Because, I wrote, most people don’t have the best possible doctor. On average, people have the average doctor.
The average doctor, we’re fallible. In fact, we’re not even always available. Our own residents in training at our hospitals don’t have their own primary doctors, and even under a socialized medicine system like in the U.K., you can be in a lot of pain and still not be able to see your primary care doctor for six months. Compared to that, you might be better off having a conversation with one or more AIs.
I think a lot about what I call the “bothness” of AI: peoples’ concerns about cognitive offloading, impacts on the job market, and environmental impacts, among other worries, and simultaneously the incredible capacities of these tools to advance human knowledge, discover new treatments for disease, and so on. How do you make sense of that bothness?
I think the bothness of AI is the same as the bothness of humanity. The biggest benefits and the biggest threats of AI, it’s humans making that happen. In the Ukrainian-Russian War, we’re seeing drones becoming increasingly autonomous … but it’s not AI deciding by itself to go and kill some humans: People are telling it to do that. And when I decide to use AI to treat myself, to ask whatever questions I forgot to ask my doctor or to get a second opinion, I’m the one doing the asking.
That’s not to deny the possibility of fully autonomous AI. But I think the bulk of the benefit and the threat is actually humans. We have to be responsible to each other. We have agency here. The doomer feeling out there is from giving up agency, and I think that’s a real mistake, because the bad actors out there aren’t going to give up theirs. The solution is to read carefully. Don’t get swept up in either the doomer stuff or the utopian stuff. Our society needs conversations about this, not fearmongering, and I think universities are a great place for those conversations to happen.

title: What Paul Farmer and Joan Kleinman taught Arthur Kleinman about wisdom
author: gazettebeckycoleman
summary: Physician and anthropologist says it all comes down caregiving in new collection rooted in Harvard course "Quests for Wisdom."
text:
Excerpted from “The Quest for Care” by Arthur Kleinman, a chapter in “The Practice of Wisdom: Five Quests” by David Carrasco, Neil L. Rudenstine Professor of the Study of Latin America; Kleinman, Esther and Sidney Rabb Professor of Anthropology, Professor of Medical Anthropology in Global Health and Social Medicine, Professor of Psychiatry; Stephanie Paulsell, Susan Shallcross Swartz Professor of the Practice of Christian Studies Emerita; and Michael Puett, Walter C. Klein Professor of Chinese History and Anthropology. The book, published by The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, is rooted in the long-running course “Quests for Wisdom: Religious, Moral, and Aesthetic Experiences and the Art of Living in Perilous Times,” taught by the authors.
Our digitized time is wondrous in many ways, such as in its accuracy to forecast the weather, place in our hands devices that can connect us almost instantaneously with far-flung friends and rapidly create vaccines for the COVID-19 pandemic. But it is not a generative time for wisdom, experience-based knowledge that can help us craft lives of purpose or engage in the art of living. Wisdom enables us to make sense of our innermost feelings, respond to tragedy, transcend the grief of deeply personal loss, cultivate meaning in a relationship or find it in a thing, aspire for joy, or prepare to die. This sort of practical wisdom for living is what Aristotle meant by phronesis. Aristotle held that phronesis was the most important of all forms of knowledge. A practical knowledge for how to live a life. A critical pragmatism that our troubled time has sorely tested. Technology based information has made living more efficient, but not more purposeful, ethical, or beautiful. Information, in and of itself, can never be phronesis.
Not so fast! Does the latest AI challenge this point? Can ChatGPT create wisdom? Especially wisdom for the art of living? AI certainly has the capability to recycle, recombine, and rephrase existing statements from wisdom traditions and from ordinary people struggling with living. But can AI actually search for wisdom in the sense of the human search for meaning and its practical application in the world? Both can and do transmit others’ wisdom—but can AI go on a lived quest for its own wisdom? I leave the answer for the future as philosophers, engineers, and business entrepreneurs not only try to further narrow the gap between knowledge generated through machine learning and the embodied and transpersonal human search for creating ways to enrich, repair, and reform lived experience, but also as they, and all of us, try to figure out what eliminating that gap means. As I see it, if machines one day achieve this end, it will be because they have been more completely humanized. And that, in a sense, is my point.
The COVID-19 pandemic taught us once again, as if adults still needed the lesson, that our lives are replete with experiences of serious danger and substantial uncertainty, which are at times uncontrollable. We also saw more clearly than before that those who are poor and members of stigmatized racial and other social castes have the least resources to meet these challenges, which they experience at a higher rate with worse outcomes. Yet no human being is free from this existential reality. We are all terribly vulnerable. In response, we struggle to stay safe and healthy and to be in control. Caught up as we are today in the post-pandemic era of disordered politics, negligence of the climate crisis, and insecurity owing to wars and other violent conflicts, we engage in practical acts of harm reduction, prevention, protection, and care. In truth, we knew of this vulnerability long before COVID, and that danger and uncertainty will continue to be our existential condition.
Among this informed range of responses to the threats of ordinary life is the quest for wisdom in the art of living. That quest can take many forms. Faced with paralyzing uncertainty, we seek genuine wisdom to help us decide what to do, when to do it, and how best to do it. But we also seek to integrate into the flow of our lives what needs to be done and why it needs doing. Here multiple forms of knowledge can be at play. A practical illustration comes from my own life. When my late wife was rapidly declining with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease, I actively sought wisdom that would help us and our family to struggle to keep going each day. I searched for wisdom to endure during the most difficult and demanding decade of my life, a terrible time when I felt I and my loved ones could succumb and give up entirely. Overmatched by Joan’s destructive decline, we had to find a way forward, beyond the lack of control and the sense of being inadequate. Many others are, have been, and will find themselves in the same human condition.
Earlier in my life, I looked for the wisdom to decide whether to continue to pursue medicine or drop out of medical school and become a common laborer in order to support my not-so-secret ambition to become a writer: a blue-collar mentor who had toiled in the foul New York sewer system for decades disabused me of this romantic dream and made clear what really was at stake for me. Later still, Joan and I searched for the wisdom we felt we needed to marry, despite the opposition of our families and faith communities. Giving up a primary commitment of clinical psychiatry for social medicine was another such fraught moment. Each time I searched for exemplary stories, telling ideas, even evocative words, that could come right down into my daily life to illuminate from within what I should do, how to do it, and to justify why I viscerally felt it had to be done.
And following Joan’s death, almost 46 years from when we married, I desperately needed to find the wisdom to make sense of this most devastating loss of a partner, collaborator, mentor, and lover. The anguish and poignancy of that painful search made me aware of something I had failed to understand from my research and clinical experience: that bereavement is a continuation of care, though it is caring for memories. Memories, in the process of grieving, are incessantly worked through, assembled into a story, and told to oneself and to others as a way of controlling unruly emotions that threaten to overwhelm and further break one. Memory in this instance is visceral, meaning gut and muscle memory, the body’s own wisdom, which makes it possible to transcend grief and rebuild a life.
I experienced great grief a second time in 2022, with the untimely death of my former student and close friend and colleague, Paul Farmer. News of his death in Rwanda shocked me so completely that for two hours I sat without moving, unable and unwilling to accommodate a world without his moral clarity, beauty of being, and foundational friendship. During those lost hours, I lived through the arc of our relationship. And to tell the truth, I still am caught up in replaying our time together. Replaying is the wrong word, I now realize. Because I am still suspended in that uncompleted trajectory the bereavement continues as my way of inhabiting my world, much as it does for Joan. The memories of both are not just alive within me; they are me. Caring for and living within those memories is my testimony to the meaning of my life. It is the form of my vitality, the path of my journey, a still incomplete ending.
Seen this way, bereavement is one of the quests for wisdom in the art of living that we all experience: grieving illustrates how such pursuits create the existential foundations of what makes us human. These vital actions of looking for meaning, seeking control, and either creating new ways of being in the world or remaking old ones are human experiments that draw upon and feed back into emotions, moral schemas, aesthetic sensibility, and religious experience with the same outcome: transformation of life itself.
The course that is the source of this book did not set out expressly to offer wisdom. Far from it. We, the authors of this book, did not believe that there was one or even a few kinds of wisdom that we could credibly convey; nor did we believe that we had access to special sources of wisdom. We were uncertain of what any particular person’s wisdom would be. We felt that context and contingency would make wisdom as various as the seekers themselves.
The memories of both are not just alive within me; they are me. Caring for and living within those memories is my testimony to the meaning of my life.
What we wanted to do, instead of proselytizing a particular brand of wisdom, was to explore the variety of quests, and learn from them. Ours was a nonpartisan stance with a couple of exceptions. We wanted to understand those pursuits of wisdom that took place in truly perilous times, historical times of breakdown, and times of communal threat, personal times of anguish and despair with the possibility for failure and for transcendence. COVID-19, which converted our course into a Zoom-based experience, together with the roiling wave of the racial justice movement and the political and cultural blowback to it, was surely one such syndemical time. The pandemic brought an anxious immediacy and powerful relevance to our teaching and the experience of the students. The racial justice movement deepened our discomfort with the colonial legacy and neocolonial structures constraining so many dispossessed people in our era. The political and cultural backlash challenged our values and unmade them and remade our struggles. But we were convinced that responding to such times had something to do with human acts of care, caretaking, and caregiving. We wanted to understand how care was enacted and felt emotionally, morally, and religiously. Coming from distinctive disciplinary perspectives and teaching very different books, the four of us were united in thinking that care was a shared feature of seeking wisdom for how to live. Everything we learned during the course and since has convinced us our intuition was the right one. That this was not a sentimentalized search for heroic acts or “saving grace.” But, rather, a sober, somewhat doubt-driven understanding of what human needs are about and how fragile, even broken, are our efforts to meet them. The emerging wisdom kept us closer to the sensibility of the hard forces that inflict pain and social suffering and to the softer, but still hard, work of repair and healing.
Wisdom, as I have tried to imagine it, is caring for how people (especially those who really matter to us) live their lives. It is about doing good in a small world of kin, kith, and some strangers whose lives interact with ours face-to-face. If care is indeed doing good in the world, it is a very local world where care can be taken and given to help build up others, respond to their pain and suffering, protect them from shame and humiliation, and through that free them from bonds, inner and outer, which fetter each of us. And in so doing, we also contribute to doing good for ourselves, because we, too, are accompanied and transformed.
At a dinner following Toni Morrison’s Ingersoll Lecture at the Harvard Divinity School, she shared with me and Davíd Carrasco that no matter how critical her novels were of persistent racism in America and the impact of its failed societal projects on individuals, she never took for granted or allowed herself to vicariously criticize efforts to do good in the world. She insisted that doing good for others is one of the few truly significant acts where people possess what is needed to reach out to counter, even if inadequately, all the built-up negativity in history and everyday life.
In his picaresque novel “Heaven’s My Destination,” written in the middle of the Great Depression, Thornton Wilder amusingly satirizes the journey of a naive, obstinate, religion-obsessed, and impractical young man who has the intention to do good in the world as a principled way of living a Christian life and contrasts that fraught trajectory with the tawdry, overly compromised, business-dominated, middle-class Midwestern American life. In this secular version of the “Pilgrim’s Progress,” mundane American preoccupations, misunderstandings, and failings first crush the uncritical religious zeal out of the protagonist, but later their all-too-human weaknesses assist him in his shaky way to reconcile idealistic principles with the practical demands of everyday existence. This hero lacks phronesis. His good intentions go awry, wreaking havoc with ordinary people’s lives, while he is blindly intent on what he believes must be good for the denizens of his patch of small-town America. The result, though humorous, seems to be a serious warning: be careful, be very careful. Don’t impose on others an abstract idea of the good that fails to take into account the history and context of real people in real-life situations, and therefore risks unintended consequences which undermine relationships, break lives, and demonstrate a wanton carelessness with the subtleties and compromises that make social life endurable. A passion for wisdom needs to be balanced by doubt; quests need to be questioned.
Add to this Graham Greene’s cynical vision in his novel “The Quiet American,” where American efforts to use naive, one-size-fits-all political and economic development in poor societies like Vietnam before the Vietnam War have truly disastrous effects: They “do good” in a dangerously abstract way by building an illusory democracy, in which everyone would be discouraged from advocating for doing good in the world.
Readers are justified in questioning a call for doing good as an example of wisdom about the art of living. Clearly, this impulse to care needs to be different than platitude and out-of-touch principle. It must be built into small-scale, face-to-face encounters and local community relations of accompaniment. It should be balanced by acute insight into human foibles and the unintended consequences of purposive action; and it needs to emerge out of the mature view of human prospects that includes a critical pragmatism for balancing passion and ideals with doubt. That way, a care perspective based in doing good for others is not just possible, but it is a requisite human wisdom for the art of living. Paul Farmer, the late great medical humanitarian, lived his extraordinary life and practiced his clinical profession this way.
Just as there are skilled artisans and artists who craft things of value from cuisine to furniture and sculptures, there are artisans and artists whose material is life itself. My late wife, Joan, was one such artisan and artist. She knew how, in the most minutely practical way, to bring beauty and goodness into our family’s everyday life. Candles on the dining room table turned an ordinary meal into a celebration. Reading books we all enjoyed together as a family became ritualized at home and, when traveling, a form of moral and aesthetic commitment. Simple but elegant picnics gave us joy but also taught us how to bring joy into the lives of others. Whether gardening, clamming, gathering mushrooms or wild berries, hiking, bicycling, or playing interesting games — we all took part in an adventure that mixed spontaneity with a disciplined way of playing together. Joan cultivated our French and Chinese and used these languages to bring us more deeply into the cultural traditions that stood behind them. And she did all this on a tight budget, which itself was remarkable and instructive. Joan was unselfish in brightening the days and cultivating our aesthetic sensibility. She built the foundation for the future where we would be on our own without her, as if she understood from the beginning that her time with us was going to be foreshortened. Her creative medium was life itself. She taught my children and me, and even my mother, how to focus on those things that really matter in living; and yet she did so with such warmth, lightness of being, and the freshness of her calm presence that there was delight in our responses to her practical wisdom. Joan illustrated daily that she was here to be of use, that her desire was to be used until she was all used up. And that gift is one we have internalized, too. Paul Farmer also modeled this for both of us: carrying his powerful moral being lightly and using himself up in acts of caring for those truly poor and wretched with the greatest need for mercy and pragmatic solidarity.
During the course of our marriage, Joan remade me. I had an unpromising background and early life experiences for a future caregiver. I had been raised in a crass and often cruel inner-city world of violence and hyperbolic masculinity, where trust was unreciprocated and no one was encouraged to reveal their vulnerability. I transferred my aggressiveness and hyper individualism as time went on to the academic domain. My tendency was to be a self-absorbed workaholic. Joan transformed me over the decades into a husband, father, and mentor who became more able to engender the lives of others. Her love made me into a carer.
I had long understood in principle that we were here in this broken world to do good for others, but it was my family life and the model of Joan and Paul that trained me in the corporal and emotional acts of caregiving, re-creating who I am and how I live. It is while caring for Joan and my family and close friends, as well as allowing myself to be cared for by them, that I came to experience my own maturation into finding wisdom through caring. This was for me a profound transformation of self, sensibility, and action. This wisdom became embodied and yet also social. By going outward to care for others, I learned, one ends up traveling inward to care for the soul. It is the only discovery of wisdom in which I have made any headway.
