title: Selective nostalgia
author: Sy Boles
summary: Half a century after curator’s road trip collecting photos of American life, a look at what’s inside — and outside — the frames.
text:
In the mid-1970s, Harvard curator Barbara “Bobbie” Norfleet crisscrossed America in a red sports car, hunting for photos for Harvard’s collections. She wasn’t interested in the classical fine-art photography that was then beginning to be curated by the big-name museums. She wanted images of everyday life — the wedding portraits, kids’ dance recitals, and other social rituals.
It was an era of change in the photography industry. More Americans owned their own cameras; more companies and government agencies had photographers on staff. The professional photography studio, which had been a mainstay of community life since the late 1800s, was dying out.
Over the course of two years, Norfleet met with photo studio heads, reviewed thousands upon thousands of negatives, and carted her finds — ultimately more than 20,000 images — back to Harvard in the trunk of her car (or in a suitcase on an airplane).
Now, half a century later, a selection of her finds is on display at the Harvard Art Museums in an exhibition titled “The Way We Never Were: The American Professional Photographers Collection.”
“This collection hasn’t received the attention it deserves, and we’re hoping we can at least start to remedy that,” said Audrey Sands, the curator of the exhibition and the Richard L. Menschel Associate Curator of Photography at the museums.
The photos brim with postwar optimism, mid-century domesticity, and sitcom-style humor. But something lurks at the edges of the frames: a nervous escapism, maybe, or a too-effortful performance of domestic bliss.
The exhibition also explores how commissioned photographs helped create a shared visual culture in mid-century America — the white picket fence, the handsome football star at the high school game, the happy family at the fast-food drive-through — and what those photographs omitted.
Norfleet, who is now 100, collected photos taken between the late 1800s and the early 1970s. But Sands, along with her co-curator Madison Brown, focused the exhibition on the postwar boom of the 1950s. That includes the baby boom, but also the explosive growth of highways and car culture and the expansion of suburbia as a result of the G.I. bill.
“The show is really contending in the 21st century with Bobbie’s claim that these photos could serve as a record of American life,” Sands said. “These pictures are fascinating and humorous and nostalgic and meticulously composed, but they don’t stand in for the richness, the diversity of American life during the decades that they represent.”
At its most literal, the exhibition contrasts an image of the baby boom — swaddled newborns in rows of bassinets, taken for a pamphlet for the U.S. Public Health Service — with a photojournalism image of an atom bomb’s mushroom cloud over Nagasaki during the final days of World War II.
“There was another sort of boom, quite literally, overshadowing the whole period,” Sands explained. “That was the constant and persistent threat of nuclear war.”
Sands believes Norfleet’s understanding of the photos evolved throughout her career.
A social psychologist who earned her Ph.D. from Harvard in 1951, Norfleet was always interested in class in the U.S., Sands said. But she wasn’t satisfied with seeing America through the lens of statistics. She later trained as a photographer, producing documentary works on the private lives of the American elite, and from there began an interdisciplinary approach to teaching, research, and curation. In 1972, just three years before she began her cross-country road trip, she became the curator of photography for the Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts.
“What she tapped into was a bigger question in photography that extended far beyond art history, which was, ‘What is the relationship between photography, memory, and selfhood?’” Sands said.
By the end of her career, Norfleet was clearly framing the collection in yet another way: as an inquiry into the relationship between photography, omission, and the truth.
A 2001 exhibition she curated, “When We Liked Ike,” showcased familiar images of white, middle-class America — clean-cut teens engaged in good clean fun, housewives with newfangled kitchen appliances on Formica countertops — with commentary from James Baldwin, Jack Kerouac, and other cultural critics of the same age.
“It was her way of raising questions and pointing arrows to perspectives, concerns that are different than those of the professional photographer, that bring a range of voices and a kind of sociopolitical tension and a sense of unrest to this otherwise tightly controlled world that professional photography helped to create,” Sands said.
As part of a commitment to making the American Professional Photographers Collection available for research and discovery, Sands is currently overseeing a research initiative that will result in a Special Collection website dedicated to the body of work. The site will launch next year and will detail the history of the collection and the specific studios that comprise it, and map Norfleet’s 1975-1977 travels to amass it.
“The Way We Never Were: The American Professional Photographers Collection,” is on display through May 9. See the museums’ website to learn about in-gallery talks and tours and other programs that will take place throughout the run of the exhibition.

title: Who should take GLP-1s?
author: Samantha Laine Perfas
summary: In this episode of the "Harvard Thinking" podcast, experts dig into what we’ve overlooked in rush to embrace "magical" weight-loss drugs.
text:
GLP-1s were created to treat Type 2 diabetes. But since their discovery as a tool for fighting obesity, they have surged in popularity. As of last year, nearly one in eight American adults were using GLP-1s to lose weight. For some, it raises questions about who these drugs are meant to serve.
“I think what we’re not talking about adequately enough is: Who are they for?” said Caroline Apovian, co-inaugural director of the Integrated Mass General Brigham Center for Weight Management and Wellness and a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School. She argues that as the medical field creates guidelines for these new drugs, the highest-risk patients should be prioritized even as the drugs are marketed to the general public. “If you take a GLP-1 to lose 10 pounds, you don’t have the disease of obesity. [You might be] setting yourself up for stopping the medication, gaining even more weight back, and developing a problem that you didn’t have in the first place.”
In this episode of “Harvard Thinking,” host Samantha Laine Perfas talks with Apovian, evolutionary biologist Daniel Lieberman, and obesity medicine physician scientist Fatima Cody Stanford about why we should be excited — and cautious — about the potential of GLP-1s.
Listen on: Spotify Apple YouTube
The transcript
Daniel Lieberman: My real nightmare about GLP-1s is that we end up in a world where we cease to pay attention to the cause of the problem, which is the various reasons that people are struggling with obesity in the first place. It’s like in the supermarket aisle, you can go down one aisle of the supermarket, and there are the companies selling all these foods that are really bad for us. And then the same companies in the next aisle are selling us the weight-loss products that deal with the problem that they caused in the other aisle.
Laine Perfas: GLP-1s have evolved from a treatment of Type 2 diabetes into drugs for weight management, leading to a surge in usage and evidence of promise against a range of other health issues. But given how new these drugs are to the market, medical professionals are only now starting to figure out who should — and should not — be using them, considering downstream risks like muscle loss, which can particularly impact the elderly.
They also raise the question: Do we lose anything when we allow taking a pill to become a substitute for lasting lifestyle changes?
Welcome to “Harvard Thinking,” a podcast where the life of the mind meets everyday life. Today, I’m joined by:
Caroline Apovian: Caroline Apovian. I am an obesity medicine specialist, professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School.
Laine Perfas: She’s also the co-inaugural director of the Integrated Mass General Brigham Center for Weight Management and Wellness. Then:
Lieberman: Daniel Lieberman. I’m a professor of human evolutionary biology at Harvard University.
Laine Perfas: He’s also a bestselling author and recently published “Fed Up: What Evolution Reveals About Food, Diet, Health, and Eating Well.” And finally:
Fatima Cody Stanford: Dr. Fatima Cody Stanford. I’m an obesity medicine physician-scientist at Mass General Brigham.
Laine Perfas: She’s also an associate professor of medicine and pediatrics at Harvard Medical School.
And I’m your host, Samantha Laine Perfas. I’m a writer for The Harvard Gazette. Today, we’ll talk about GLP-1s and why we should be excited about their potential — and also cautious.
And a quick note, Caroline Apovian and Fatima Cody Stanford have worked with pharmaceutical companies, including makers of GLP-1s. Caroline worked as a former consultant and Fatima as a current consultant. Fatima has also received industry funding for her research.
What is so magical about this category of drug?
Apovian: The word magical is a very interesting word to use. We call these drugs game changers because of their robust effects on health and in particular on first, you’re right, Type 2 diabetes, and now obesity. Obesity affects 42 percent of the United States’ population. Fatima Cody Stanford was instrumental in getting organizations to distinguish obesity to be a disease and not a matter of willpower. And once that happened, the race was on to develop these drugs for use in obesity. And the reason why they’re considered magical is because, for the first time in many people’s lives, they take a GLP-1 and suddenly, as they say, the food noise is gone. They eat, they’re full, they feel like eating healthy food, and they feel like exercising. We’ve never had anything like this before to treat obesity, except for metabolic bariatric surgery.
Cody Stanford: I actually push back a little bit on the terms game changer or magical. I do think that they have definitely created an inflection point in how we think about this disease process. Their potency has changed how the world sees or approaches this disease process due to the fact that we’re looking at a total body weight change of either 15 percent or 22 percent, or if we’re looking at the triple agonist, you know, getting closer to 30 percent total body weight loss. When we look at these, people in the world are beginning to realize that this disease process is beyond this idea of willpower and self-control, that there is actual biology behind this disease. It’s not just “Oh, eat less and exercise more.” This inflection point of really thinking about this from a disease process, while we can go back to the AMA declaration in 2013 or the World Medical Association, which just happened in 2025, it’s when people start to become acclimated to the utilization of these medications and say, “Wait a minute, I do feel different. Wait a minute, I am making different choices. Wait a minute, these choices are influencing the way I interact with the world around me,” that they begin to think, “Wait a minute, it must be something in the biology of me and how my biology may differ from those around me.” And that was what really got the conversation moving in a different direction outside of the typical status quo conversation.
Lieberman: If I can just add to that from an evolutionary perspective, I want to remind us all that we never evolved to lose weight. We’re an interesting species. Human beings have a lot more body fat than most other mammals. Most mammals rarely have more than about five percent body fat. But in our evolutionary history, we evolved to put on a lot more fat because it’s really important for feeding our brains, for our reproductive system, for all kinds of reasons. You know, in the past, it was extremely rare that anybody could gain extra weight, and we never evolved adaptations to lose it. And instead, the key adaptations that we have are hunger and appetite, right? So when we lose weight, we go into what we call negative energy balance. We turn on a whole suite of signaling molecules, hormones that signal to our brain that we’re losing weight and make us hungry. That’s why it’s been so hard for so many people for so long to lose weight, because they’re fighting against millions of years of deep and fundamental adaptations. And all of a sudden, for the first time, we’ve got this drug that can turn off some of those adaptations. From an evolutionary perspective, this is really quite astonishing.
Apovian: The reason why I think these are game changers for the field of obesity medicine is because these are not drugs. These are analogs of the hormones that the body makes when you eat food. They have numerous effects on other organs, including the brain. I’d love to know from you, Dan, what you think about this evolutionary process and using these naturally occurring hormones to then counteract what we’ve done to the environment. Because it can’t be purely genetic, because our genes have evolved over millions of years and not over 50 or 100 years. What is it about the environment? Is it the ultra-processed food? Is just the fact that we’ve got all kinds of ways to throw down 3,000 calories by rolling down our window at fast-food restaurants?
Lieberman: Look, everything about our bodies is an interaction between our genes and our environment. Everything, right? This is no exception. But as you say, our genes haven’t changed that much in the last few generations. But in my lifetime, the percentage of Americans with obesity has quadrupled. Obviously, it’s not because some genes for weight gain have suddenly swept through the population in the last generation or two, but it is true that some people have more proclivity than others. The other thing is that, of course, there are many factors that affect weight gain. Your microbiome is one of them; your metabolism. People differ in their metabolic rates. Physical activity has some effect, particularly for weight gain prevention, not so much for weight loss. We could go on for all the various factors, but nobody doubts that the one thing that’s changed the most, of course, is our food. When we walk into a supermarket here in Boston, the average supermarket here has 40,000 different kinds of food — 40,000 different kinds of food, and something between 50 percent and 70 percent, depending upon your definition, are ultra-processed. These are foods where the fiber’s been removed; sugar and fat has been added; they’ve been made hyper-palatable. They’ve got all kinds of tricks and gimmicks to make us eat more. There is an association unquestionably between the proliferation of processed foods and weight gain. And here’s the thing: Most of us, once we gain the weight, because of those adaptations, our bodies then reach a new set point. We now call it a settling point, because for reasons that I don’t think any of us understand, your body fights to put you back at the previous weight, not necessarily your original.
“People are beginning to realize that [obesity] is beyond this idea of willpower and self-control, that there is actual biology behind this disease.”
Cody Stanford: One of the things that I want to bring up, particularly as we think about this from an evolutionary perspective, is I want to think about the group that happens to carry the highest weight, particularly within the U.S. population, which happens to be Black women. I want to take us back to our period of enslavement. And if we really look at when Black women started to accumulate great levels of adiposity, it was actually during our periods of enslavement, which is very interesting because during the period of enslavement, we didn’t have ultra-processed foods. There were high levels of physical activity. But what we don’t account for during that time frame, which really sets us up for the high levels of obesity within this population, the group that I represent, is the allostatic load and stress that started to occur for that population at that time. We have to recognize that early predisposition to obesity within the population that carries the highest burden here in the United States now, and when it started for us, and then bring it over to the high burden that then exists, and particularly think about it now in the context of what we see.
Lieberman: I completely agree. To add to that list, I should have mentioned stress, chronic stress, for example, which is, of course, a function of socioeconomic status and racism. There are epigenetic effects. I 100 percent agree with you. This is a multifactorial problem. There’s no question that our food supply is a major one, but it’s not the only one.
Laine Perfas: One thing about food that I did want to ask about was this idea of food noise. What does that mean, and what is it about GLP-1s that are affecting it?
Cody Stanford: For people who have food noise, they are constantly thinking about food. It doesn’t matter if it’s ultra-processed, it doesn’t matter if it’s not. They have this constant desire to want to eat. For those who are responders to GLP-1s, when they go on something like a GLP-1, they say they no longer think about eating in the way that they did before. That volume that might be really high, you turn that down and they’re like, “Wait a minute, I’m not thinking about food. I actually forgot to eat breakfast, lunch, and wait a minute, it’s dinner time.” I turned down the volume. This thinking about food, it’s no longer a focal point.
Lieberman: For some people, not everyone, GLP-1s also reduce other kinds of noise, other forms of addiction for people who have issues with, say, tobacco or certain pharmaceuticals or alcohol. There’s something just really quite extraordinary about this hormone and its multiple effects. You have to remember that hormones evolved to do multiple things, but I like to think of hormones really as allocators of investment and energy. This is a hormone that’s basically telling the body to turn down stuff. We have hormones that turn things up and hormones that turn things down. It’s a very crude simplification. But what’s amazing is that GLP-1s, normally in human beings, they have very short action. The real turning point for this was that they used essentially the GLP-1 of a lizard that eats only once every three weeks or something. I can’t remember. The Gila monster. That has a much longer-acting effect than the human version. Now we’re finding out all kinds of fascinating things about this hormone.
Laine Perfas: One thing I want to talk about too is that the usage for these drugs has increased significantly. I think as of last year, one in eight American adults was using GLP-1s for weight loss. Dan, you have been vocal about some of your skepticisms with GLP-1s. I would love to hear some of the concerns and/or limitations that we are seeing.
Lieberman: I’m not skeptical. I have two concerns really that are overriding. The first is that the evidence is that a lot of people on GLP-1s are losing a lot of muscle mass. As with bariatric surgery, where you have very extreme weight loss, people can lose something like 20, 30, even more percent of their body weight, and a large percentage of that, maybe up to 30 percent of that, can be fat-free mass. We’re not talking about body fat; we’re talking about other tissues, and some of that’s muscle. One of the big issues for aging in the United States is sarcopenia, which is age-related muscle loss. So it’s not a skepticism, but it’s a concern that individuals who are on GLP-1s and losing a lot of weight, if they don’t include some degree of strength training, they could be at greater risk for age-related muscle loss, for sarcopenia. And that’s really concerning because that becomes a kind of vicious cycle. Once you get very frail, you become less physically active. You become less physically active, you become even less active. I can speak from personal experience with my parents: It’s a challenging thing to watch.
My other concern, of course, is that a lot of people, and Caroline and Fatima will know the data better than I, but there’s a fairly high quit rate for these drugs. I think the latest study I saw, and I’m sure there’s better data now, was that over 50 percent of people are quitting it between one and two years. And then the other concern is what happens when they quit, right? Are they gaining the weight back? But you guys know more about this than I do.
“If you’re going to take a GLP-1 just to lose 10 pounds so you can look good in your dress, you should not be taking a GLP-1.”
Apovian: These are two big areas, Dan. The muscle-loss concept is very much debated. First of all, when you lose any kind of weight by any means, you’re right — bariatric surgery, drugs, diet, and exercise — you don’t lose just fat, right? Because if you have obesity, there’s extra muscle to hold everything together. And the Krebs cycle, metabolism, you need amino acids to burn energy, so you can’t just lose fat. There is always a certain percent that is muscle, and you really can’t go below losing 20 to 25 percent of the total as muscle. So that’s physiology. Yes, there are people who lose more, 30 or 40 percent. We think it may have to do with the rapidity of the weight loss, if they’re not eating enough protein, and yes, if they’re not doing strength training. But I think that the largest concern about muscle mass should be with the older population. The older population is already losing muscle mass at something like 1 percent per year after the age of 40 or 50. And yes, those people on GLP-1s or after bariatric surgery may lose more muscle mass and develop dysfunction and frailty and sarcopenia and also bone loss. So that’s a valid concern, and we’ve already had people in the older population losing 40 pounds on Wegovy and then falling and fracturing their tib-fib because it was fragile.
Cody Stanford: The muscle loss piece is by far more germane to those that are older adults. And particularly with the new Medicare Bridge program that’s just come into place. For those who are unaware, Medicare has decided to start covering these medications for individuals with obesity as of July 1st, which means that there’s going to be a sizable percentage of the population who now have access to these drugs. The program appears to be in place from July 1st of 2026 through December 31st of 2027. We have no idea what’s going to happen after that, but a sizable percentage of the population, particularly those who are 65-plus, will gain access. Now, we also know that population has a higher tendency to have issues like sarcopenia, and we do need to think about protein and muscle retention for that population.
And so this is what I really like to emphasize with my patients, and this is how I bring them into the conversation regardless of age. I say in our 20s and 30s, I like to think of a one-to-one ratio of cardio to strength, so 30 minutes of strength for 30 minutes of cardio. And when we get into our 40s and 50s, where I exist, in that middle-age range, I think of it as a two-to-one strength to cardio ratio. So for every 60 minutes of strength, 30 minutes of cardio. In our 60s and 70s, I like to think of a three-to-one strength to cardio ratio. So for every 90 minutes of strength, we should have 30 minutes of cardio. And if we get into our 80s and 90s, I like to think of it as a four-to-one strength to cardio ratio. So for every hundred and 20 minutes of strength training, 30 minutes of cardio. Now, tell me how many people actually do that.
Apovian: Zero.
Cody Stanford: Exactly. Unless you’re me, right? So this is what I emphasize with my patients. And when they’re getting that mantra, they begin to realize the importance of strength training. Because we’ve been fed this idea that it’s cardio, cardio, cardio, cardio, cardio. But if you’re really strength training in the way that we’re talking about it, you are getting that heart-health benefit from doing the strength training. Now, moving into your second piece, which is how people pull back the utilization. So 50 percent discontinuation of GLP-1s. The number one reason for the discontinuation is cost, access. But what we’ve seen, and I will use Massachusetts as a case in point for discontinuation for these medications, up until January 1st of 2026, Massachusetts had the best utilization and coverage for GLP-1 receptor agonists. If we look at employer-sponsored insurance here in Massachusetts, the big four are Mass General Brigham, Harvard Pilgrim, Tufts, and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts or New England. All of these insurers were covering GLP-1s for patients with obesity. But as of January 1st, they pulled back coverage for this patient population.
What happened was our patient populations got pulled off of these medications. Now, for persons who are high-income earners, they were able to retain utilization of these medications. Price point: between $300 and $450 a month out-of-pocket price. But if you’re a high-income earner, that’s not too much for you. If you’re not a high-income earner, it’s a lot.
Apovian: That’s a very important point. I just saw a patient virtually because he weighs 625 pounds. But he did weigh 725 pounds, and he lost 100 pounds getting ready for bariatric surgery with Zepbound. He lost 100 pounds on the top dose of Zepbound, and then in July it got pulled. He is now gaining weight. And I just messaged the surgeon and said, “You better get him to surgery now because he’s going to gain that weight back. You got to get him to surgery now.” This is the segment of the population, BMI over 60, still rising exponentially in the United States and probably worldwide. So what are we going to do about this weight regain? It’s causing a lot of oxidative stress, especially as you gain it rapidly. So that food noise comes back very aggressively, especially if you’ve lost 100 pounds and you suddenly stop the GLP-1. You suddenly think that you’re starving to death.
Lieberman: My other concern about GLP-1s is about prevention, and it really goes back to what we started off talking about, which is that — so I have this term I apologize for, which I created, called dis-evolution: When we treat the symptoms rather than the causes of a mismatch problem, then we just keep the cycle going. My real nightmare about GLP-1s is that we end up in a world where we cease to pay attention to the cause of the problem, which is the various reasons that people are struggling with obesity in the first place. It’s like in the supermarket aisle, you can go down one aisle of the supermarket, and there are the companies selling all these foods that are really bad for us. And then the same companies in the next aisle are selling us the weight loss products that deal with the problem that they caused in the other aisle. Ultimately, what we should all really want to do is prevent this problem from happening in the first place.
Laine Perfas: That got to another question that I wanted to ask all of you. It is amazing that these medications are able to so effectively help people. And also, what happens when it becomes a substitute for the lifestyle change that needs to happen?
Cody Stanford: I don’t think it’s a substitute for the lifestyle changes. By the time the patients get to us, these patients have tried and failed, or that lifestyle has tried and failed them. They can list 25 to 30 different programs that they’ve tried and failed. It’s like the Biggest Loser concept. It worked for a short period of time, and then it didn’t work, and their bodies came back. And so then they’re coming to us because they’re like, “OK, look, I’ve tried all these things.” Let’s say they go on these medications and they’re like, “Oh, wait a minute, this works.” Now they can actually go work out; they are feeling good about themselves, going to the gym, and seeing the results pay off while they’re on the medications. Because as Dan mentioned, if it pulls back, they’re regaining, and then they’re feeling lack of confidence. Their self-worth and self-esteem unfortunately deteriorate because they’re like, “Here I am. I finally got to the quote-unquote ‘promised land,’ and it was snatched from me.”
Apovian: I always say nobody wants to have obesity. If diet and exercise worked, and they wouldn’t be stigmatized walking down the street because they have obesity, they would have done it. We have a disease. GLP-1s are not removing the cause of the problem. But what it is doing is it is reducing the body weight set point.
Lieberman: I fully agree with you two, but I do want to ask you about children. As I’m sure you both know, there are very scary statistics about the percentage of teenagers in the United States who are classified with obesity. It’s somewhere between 20 and 30 percent, depending upon which study you believe in. Should we be giving GLP-1s to those kids? Me, my concern is, how do we prevent those kids from getting into that problem in the first place?
Cody Stanford: I treat the full age spectrum, my patients go from 2 to 90-plus, and I think about, who are the pediatric patients who actually end up in my clinic? It’s usually the children of my patients. How do I prevent this? If I can get the patients modified preconception, I have a higher likelihood of having children who have a lesser likelihood of obesity. The best study was a study that came out in the Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism back in 2009, which demonstrated that children born to mothers who had undergone bariatric surgery had a threefold decrease in the likelihood of obesity in the mother after she had undergone surgical intervention. So if we can modify the weight status of the parents preconception, we can modify the children’s weight status.
But let’s come back to the question you specifically asked: Do we utilize these medications in children, and how does that work? I do treat patients as young as 12 with GLP-1 receptor agonists. What I have found in treating these patients, first of all, when I get pediatric patients, I find that they actually have health status that’s much worse than my adult patients. Their cholesterol is much worse. Their liver function tests are much worse. Their hemoglobin A1C, which is their blood sugar, is much worse. What I also find when using these medications is that they usually respond much better than my adult patients to the therapy when given to them. That gives them a likelihood of having a much better life moving forward than they did prior to the advent of these medications. I see these patients go from looking down in my visit, not actually making direct eye contact because their self-esteem, their value, their self-worth is so tied into their weight, to making eye contact, having an improvement of their cardiometabolic health, and allowing them to move forward into adulthood with a better life.
“My real nightmare about GLP-1s is that we end up in a world where we cease to pay attention to the cause of the problem.”
Laine Perfas: When we talk about GLP-1s, obviously they’re so new, we’re still figuring out so many things. What do you feel we are not talking about enough? Or what are things that we really should be focusing on as an area of further research?
Apovian: I think that GLP-1s just created this explosion in social media and in research and in the medical community. And I think what we’re not talking about adequately enough is, who are they for? The protocols are not in yet. We’re writing guidelines with the ADA, but we’re not categorizing patients. I think the highest-risk patients should be getting our more potent drugs and be considered for metabolic surgery. The BMI is not an adequate measure of body fat. We still don’t have the right tools to measure who is at risk. And social media now is on a rampage which compounded GLP-1s that people are taking to lose 10 pounds. If you take a GLP-1 to lose 10 pounds and you don’t have the disease of obesity, are you setting yourself up for stopping the medication, gaining even more weight back, and developing a problem that you didn’t have in the first place? If you’re going to take a GLP-1 just to lose 10 pounds so you can look good in your dress, you should not be taking a GLP-1. It’s not for you.
Cody Stanford: One of the key things that we’re not talking about are the potential use-case scenarios for GLP-1s. What we do know is the GLP-1s were initially approved for Type 2 diabetes, and then we moved into obesity and obstructive sleep apnea. But we’re going to continue to see different use-case scenarios for these medications, and there’s a variety of research interests that move outside of the space of cardiometabolic health into looking at rheumatologic conditions like gout and rheumatoid arthritis. We’re looking at disorders like Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s and things of that sort. As we begin to see this blossoming of research, it’s going to be interesting to see how these medications begin to explode beyond the cardiometabolic use and then how the dosing structure will change to accommodate these potential use-case scenarios as we move forward.
Lieberman: My thing that I really hope we can use GLP-1s to talk more about is that they really are game changers for treatment. There’s no question about that. But they’re not game changers for prevention. Wouldn’t the best world be where you didn’t have to use these in the first place? The fact of the matter is we do, and we should, and they are helping a lot of people. And we’ll find out better ways to use them, and maybe other adjuvants that can help us use them better. But hopefully, we can leverage the opportunities that GLP-1s are giving us for treatment to also think more about prevention.
Laine Perfas: Thank you all for joining me for this conversation.
Lieberman: My pleasure. Thank you.
Apovian: It’s been a pleasure speaking to everyone.
Laine Perfas: Thanks for listening. For a transcript of this episode and our other episodes, visit harvard.edu/thinking. If you like this episode, rate and review us on Apple or Spotify, or like us on YouTube. It helps others find us. This episode was hosted and produced by me, Samantha Laine Perfas. It was edited by Ryan Mulcahy, Paul Makishima, and Sarah Lamodi. Original music and sound design by Noel Flatt. Produced by Harvard University. Copyright 2026.
Recommended reading

- “Fed Up: What Evolution Reveals About Food, Diet, Health, and Eating Well” by Daniel Lieberman
- “Eat this. Take that. Get skinny. Trust us.” by The Harvard Gazette
- “Are new weight-loss drugs the answer to America’s obesity problem?” by The Harvard Gazette

title: Boston Children’s Hospital, SEAS, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, and NTT Research Announce THUMPIN’ Initiative to Develop Living, Bioengineered Heart Tissues for Children
summary: Up to five-year and up to $29.6 million project aims to create living cardiac components, and ultimately a complete heart, for infants and young children with congenital heart disease
text:
News
Boston Children’s Hospital, SEAS, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, and NTT Research Announce THUMPIN’ Initiative to Develop Living, Bioengineered Heart Tissues for Children
    
          Up to five-year and up to $29.6 million project aims to create living cardiac components, and ultimately a complete heart, for infants and young children with congenital heart disease
      
Boston Children’s Hospital, Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (SEAS), Brigham and Women’s Hospital, and NTT Research today announced the launch of THUMPIN' (Tissue-engineered Hearts Using Multimodal Printing in Newborns), a Boston Children’s-led research consortium, supported by an up to five-year, and up to $29.6 million contract from the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) and other funders. THUMPIN' aims to bioengineer living cardiac tissues and components, with the ultimate goal of bringing those components together into a complete, functioning heart for infants and young children with congenital heart disease.
The initiative is designed to address one of the most pressing challenges in pediatric heart care: providing lasting treatment options for complex congenital heart defects.
“THUMPIN’ brings together a team of clinicians and researchers to rethink what is possible in pediatric heart care: living hearts and heart parts that grow, function, and adapt throughout childhood,” said Dr. Kit Parker, principal investigator for THUMPIN’. “It is an ambitious challenge, but the scale and importance of the problem demand that level of ambition.”
It is an ambitious challenge, but the scale and importance of the problem demand that level of ambition.
Led by Parker, a Senior Scientist at Boston Children’s Hospital, the Tarr Family Professor of Bioengineering and Applied Physics at SEAS and Director of the DesignBio Group at SEAS, the consortium brings together experts in pediatric cardiac surgery, tissue engineering, stem cell biology, additive manufacturing, and computational modeling.
Over the five-year project, the THUMPIN' team will develop and test the cells, tissues, manufacturing methods, and computational tools required to engineer living cardiac structures, including heart valves, vascular grafts, myocardial patches, components of the conduction system, single ventricles, and ultimately a whole heart. The project will progress from laboratory testing to studies of bioengineered heart tissues in large-animal models, while establishing the manufacturing, safety, and regulatory foundation needed to move the technology toward future human studies.
“Infants and young children with the most severe congenital heart defects may undergo surgery after surgery as they grow, and some ultimately exhaust the options we have available,” said Dr. Pedro del Nido, chair of the Department of Cardiac Surgery at Boston Children’s Hospital and a THUMPIN' investigator who will lead the program’s implantation studies. “The possibility of creating living heart tissue that can grow with an infant could fundamentally change that trajectory. Our job through this program is to determine whether we can make that vision safe, functional, and ultimately translatable to patients.”
Joining Parker and del Nido in this effort are William Pu, MD; Juan Melero-Martin, PhD; Vassilios J. Bezzerides, MD, PhD, of Boston Children’s Hospital; Elena Aikawa, MD, PhD, of Brigham and Women’s Hospital; and Joe Alexander, MD, PhD, FACC, of NTT Research.
The consortium will establish the manufacturing, testing, and regulatory foundation needed to advance these technologies toward an eventual U.S. Food and Drug Administration Investigational Device Exemption, bringing first-in-human clinical studies closer to reality.
Manufacturing efforts will be led in partnership with Landmark Bio, a public-private company co-founded by Harvard University, MIT, and industry partners, with Boston Children’s Hospital and Brigham and Women’s Hospital as collaborating institutions.
“NTT Research is honored to contribute to this groundbreaking effort,” said Dr. Joe Alexander, director of the NTT Research BioMedical Engineering Innovation (MEI) Lab (formerly the NTT Research Medical and Health Informatics Lab). “Our mission is to build computational models that help physicians better understand and treat cardiovascular disease. Through THUMPIN', we’re applying those capabilities to help create a future where infants and young children with congenital heart defects may receive living heart replacements that can grow and adapt throughout their lives.”
“This project challenges us to move beyond repairing damaged cardiac structures and toward engineering living replacement tissues from the ground up,” said Dr. Elena Aikawa, an investigator with the Mass General Brigham Heart and Vascular Institute. “The convergence of biofabrication, regenerative medicine, and computational approaches creates a unique opportunity to develop solutions that have long been considered out of reach.”
“It is not enough to just build the heart. We must build the clinical and industrial capacity to support the THUMPIN’ deliverables as therapeutic options for the patient. We are co-developing the plan for those efforts along with the heart. It’s the only way to make the effort something more than a party trick,” said Parker.
THUMPIN’ is part of the ARPA-H Personalized Regenerative Immunocompetent Nanotechnology Tissue (PRINT) program led by Program Manager Ryan Spitler, Ph.D.

title: Should parents be wary of Silicon Valley’s influence in schools?
author: Max Larkin
summary: Times reporter says students need "tech civics" to understand value, drawbacks amid breakneck advance of tools like AI.
text:
Things move quickly in Silicon Valley. Its now-familiar mantra — “move fast, break stuff” — can suggest either daring or recklessness, depending on where you stand.
It is an attitude that might be expected to sit uneasily in the deliberate, bureaucratic, complex world of public schools.
And yet, leading technologists and executives have been drawn to classrooms in recent decades as laboratories, market opportunities, and above all, problems waiting to be solved — whether with computers, software, or AI chatbots, according to Natasha Singer.
Since 2013, Singer has watched those efforts closely as a New York Times tech reporter. She found them at best quixotic or naive and at worst insidious, threatening to deprive young Americans of their ability to think critically about some of the world’s largest companies.
In her just published book, “Coding Kids,” she presents a panoramic view of a series of campaigns starting in the 1980s to shape the nation’s students into future coders, founders, and technologists.
The daughter of an MIT professor, Singer returns to Greater Boston this week to discuss the book, including in a conversation with Cathy O’Neill, Ph.D. ’99, author of “Weapons of Math Destruction: How Big Data Increases Inequality and Threatens Democracy,” Wednesday night at 6 p.m. at the Science Center.
In this edited conversation, Singer describes how tech companies became decisive players in public education — and why parents and teachers should be wary.
Gazette: One phrase that jumps out from your book is “tech exceptionalism.” When it comes to schools, you argue, we don’t rush to deploy even new cleaning chemicals or sodas. And yet we have done that with new digital technologies, for decades: from the first desktop computers to Chromebooks to AI. Why does tech have that unique level of access?
Natasha Singer: Big tech companies have more power in schools than any other industry partly by virtue of the fact that they now provide the infrastructure that schools run on. Apple and Microsoft provide iPads or Surface tablets; Google provides Chromebooks — and then the operating systems those things run on.
They also provide other kinds of infrastructure — cloud computing, data analytics, and things that kids and teachers use on a daily basis.
For instance, millions of kids use Gmail in school and come to class, and the teacher says, “Open your Chromebooks to Google Classroom,” which is an app that Google made where teachers can make assignments and kids can see them.
If they’re asked to write an essay, they do it in Google Docs; for a presentation, they’ll do it in Microsoft PowerPoint or Google Slides. So these companies are entrenched, the backbone on which schools rely to operate — and essentially utilities.
But then you detail a further step, where the companies that provide these utilities come, in many ways, to shape teaching and learning.
Right. These companies now have an end-to-end influence over nearly every step in the education supply chain that we do not see in other subjects or other industries.
Some train teachers directly or provide funding to third-party nonprofits that do. Some have also gone from state to state, lobbying to get laws passed or to promote subjects that are important to their industry — like AI or computer science.
And some companies have had a seat on state committees that decide what education standards are going to be for a subject like computer science.
One example I give in the book is that when the College Board was trying to expand AP computer science, they decided to approve company-sponsored, branded curriculum.
So there is an AP computer science course that is Apple-branded, that teaches kids to code in Swift, Apple’s programming language for iOS. And there’s another one from Microsoft that uses Minecraft, their popular game, to teach computing.
By comparison, we do not have AP Pfizer Biology, or AP ExxonMobil Environmental Science. And if we did, there would be parents, teachers, and students who thought we shouldn’t let an oil and gas company shape what environmental science looks like.
Speaking of which, you came to the tech beat after years covering big pharmaceutical companies like Pfizer. And in the book you see parallels between the kind of hard and soft influence on industry professionals that the two industries have pursued.
Yes. For decades, the big drug companies have gone into big academic hospitals and brought lunch. Doctors are busy, so are run-down medical students, and they’d bring salad or sandwiches or pizza, and the doctors would sit for 15 minutes and have the industry rep tell them about the latest drug and its benefits.
When bioethics researchers studied these practices, they discovered that doctors who took even one lunch, worth less than $20, were more likely to prescribe the drug that had been pitched to them.
So in medicine, researchers routinely study that kind of influence, and doctors who speak at conferences have to disclose their conflicts of interest. But in public schools, we don’t even ask the question — like it’s impolite.
There is, of course, a cultural or an economic argument behind adding tech to schools. From the first desktop computers to AI, tech executives have argued that making digital tools available in school both introduces young people to the magic of engineering and better prepares the future workforce. And many public officials have agreed.
That’s right. And generally I take the position that most people were well-intentioned — there’s no big conspiracy. The executives I interviewed all thought their ideas would make stuff better.
I do think tech entrepreneurs like to look ahead, though: History isn’t something that many of them love, because it bogs you down. And I do think the framing of education as a solvable problem, when it is so complex, is one big issue here.
I really admire Larry Cuban, now an emeritus professor at the education school at Stanford. He wrote a book in the 1990s, right as computers were being introduced in schools, called “Oversold and Underused.” And he found that teachers didn’t know how to teach with them and that kids weren’t really using them.
Part of his argument was that schools’ most serious underlying problems — like kids who’ve come in without having eaten breakfast or dinner, or the roof is leaking, or there’s no air conditioning — are not going to be solved by technology.
You spoke with many teachers who are trying to navigate this moment, and they emerge as kind of the heroes of your book, trying to mediate between the good and the bad in the digital age.
That’s one of the things that gives me hope: this new generation of teachers with a vision for a broader kind of tech education. On top of using tech and making tech, they say kids need to be able to understand tech, interrogate tech.
There’s all kinds of names for that new approach, but I call it “tech civics.” We already teach government civics, and it’s a discipline about power.
The book ends in Revere High School, in the computer-science class of a teacher named Lisa Black. You watch her class, and she’s showing her students those robotic dogs that can carry weapons, and she’s asking them: “What are the risks of AI?” Or: “Who has your data?” The students said, “Mark Zuckerberg and the bald dude from Amazon” — they couldn’t remember Jeff Bezos’ name.
Now, Lisa Black told me she is grateful for the tools that the tech industry offers her — that she needs these resources. And she’s got a Google poster in one corner of her classroom, and an Amazon poster in another corner.
But she also said that the resources come with costs, and kids need to understand what’s under the hood, and, “As a teacher, it’s my duty to teach them that.”
The book is timely in the sense that communities are starting to raise the alarm about Big Tech. There’s the growing resistance to data centers behind AI models, and some large school districts are moving to ban or restrict AI use.
Earlier this year in Los Angeles, more than 1,000 parents petitioned the schools to stop providing iPads and Chromebooks in pre-K to first grade, and to block YouTube and other things — and the district agreed. New York just introduced some similar restrictions.
The book hopes to explain how we got here, by tracking this cycle: overpromotion of tech in schools, and then a failure to live up to the hype. That’s what parents are now pushing back against.

title: Your neighbor’s no Bezos, but he might be ‘stealthy wealthy’
author: Christina Pazzanese
summary: Insights on tax policy and inequality from economist and co-author of "The Everywhere Millionaire."
text:
A majority of Americans blame billionaires for the nation’s ever-growing income and wealth divide. But economists Eric Zwick and Owen Zidar say there’s a much larger, but little-known cadre of very rich folks who may be even more important in closing the gap.
In a new book, “The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There,” the pair dug through federal tax records to get a fuller, more precise picture of prosperity in the U.S.
What they found was a large and hidden pool of Main Street millionaires. Most often, these are very successful local entrepreneurs who own ordinary businesses like gas stations, supermarkets, plumbing supply companies or car dealerships.
These “everywhere millionaires” collectively hold many times the wealth of the entire Forbes 400 — and wield considerable political power.
In this edited interview, Zwick, M.A. ’11, Ph.D. ’14, explains how this happened and what it can tell us about wealth and inequality in the nation.
Gazette: What makes someone an “everywhere millionaire”?
Eric Zwick: We define an everywhere millionaire as somebody who has a net worth of at least $5 million and has an ownership stake of a private business. That’s a really important part of their wealth.
That definition applies to about 3 million Americans who, collectively, have an average wealth of around $25 million. If you add all their wealth up, it’s more than 10 times the size of the Forbes 400 list in terms of their total wealth combined. So, it’s a much larger amount of resources we’re talking about.
Of course, individually, a typical one is not going to be as rich as Elon Musk or Jeff Bezos. But each of them is quite rich in the way that a normal person might think about what makes somebody really rich.
The book refers to them as the “stealthy wealthy” because these are people who aren’t flashing their cash and often are unglamorous industries, like fast-food franchises and car dealerships. Why did you want to study this particular group?
Three reasons. One is they are central characters in the story of rising income and wealth inequality over the last 40 years.
If we look at the rise of the top 1 percent income share, which is one famous measure of what’s going on with income inequality, more than half of the rise comes from income that flows through pass-through businesses to these private business owners.
It’s not the Elon Musk story. Elon has gotten really rich, and the Forbes 400 has gotten relatively richer, but they still just command a far smaller share of total resources. To understand what’s going on with income and wealth inequality, you need to understand these everywhere millionaires and how they got there.
A second reason is there’s a lot of conversation about the health of the American dream. One version of the American dream is starting a business to get you from the bottom to the top of the income distribution in a generation.
“About a quarter of everywhere millionaires inherited their business. That’s quite a lot. So, it’s an interesting window into upward mobility and opportunity in the country.”
These folks, a lot of them did come from middle-class or lower backgrounds. The typical everywhere millionaire didn’t inherit their firm or didn’t come from a large rich family, and so, it does tell us something about the health of the American dream — that it’s still possible. There are a lot of paths available, even in unglamorous locations and occupations.
At the same time, if you’re born to rich parents, you’re much more likely to be a star entrepreneur. There’s advantages that are quite substantial that accrue to those kids who win the birth lottery.
About a quarter of everywhere millionaires inherited their business. That’s quite a lot. So, it’s an interesting window into upward mobility and opportunity in the country.
And then the third reason is about trying to understand economic and political power in the economy. We tend to focus on the richest and most powerful people and end the conversation there.
There’s an everywhere millionaire in every congressional district.
They have a lot of employees; they pay a lot of sales tax. They’re central figures in the culture, and that means they also have a lot of political power.
In some industries, they’ve used that power to either reduce their tax burdens or protect themselves from competition in ways that are bad for consumers and workers, and we want to interrogate that power when it’s not being used wisely.
Over the last 40 years, you and your co-author say, widespread use of a tax-shift strategy known as “pass-through” businesses has been one of the key drivers of the growth of this cohort of rich folks. What effect has this had and what are some of the other factors?
The tax story is partly a story of them getting richer through being able to keep more of the proceeds of their businesses over time as the tax rates have come down. It also enabled us to see them for the first time.
In the mid ’80s, there was a big tax reform. It was a bipartisan reform — President Reagan and Democrats in Congress.
For the first time it brought the personal income tax rate down below the level of the corporate tax rate. Before, for an entrepreneur, you would have wanted to be a traditional corporation so that you could get that lower tax rate.
Now you want to be what’s called a pass-through business because you pay tax on the personal rate and it’s lower. That led to an explosion and transformation of business activity in the U.S.
Fast-forward 40 years, and more than half of the income, nearly half of the employees, and the vast majority of businesses in the economy are pass-through businesses, which was not at all the case back in 1980. So the tax code played a role in amplifying their growth but also making them visible.
There are a lot of non-tax factors that are important for thinking about why these private businesses have gotten so valuable and why they’re making so much money.
What are some examples of this?
There’s a wave of globalization, which is opening up product markets for not just large multinationals but also for mid-market businesses that can sell and also hire lower-cost workers in the supply chain offshore. These firms benefit in the same way that multinationals do in a lot of industries.
You have deregulation across states that made it a lot easier for these businesses to grow regionally, across state borders.
You have a decline in interest rates, which made it a lot easier to finance growth and also made the businesses more valuable when people turn around to sell them because people are going to pay more. Private equity is willing to pay more when they can finance that purchase with very low interest rates. Those are three examples.
Does the existence and recognition of this large, successful cohort of rich people tell us anything about wealth inequality in the U.S. or the attainability of the American dream?
If you have the view that the American dream is dead, we’re saying it’s more alive than you think. It might not be exactly where you’re looking.
There’s this traditional path to achieving the American dream, which is a very standard credentialed, labor market story — do well in school, get a really high SAT score, go to the best college you can, then go to the blue-chip company to get a job and rise up the corporate ladder or whatever.
That’s a path that works for a lot of people.
But if you have this view that you have to get on that path and if you fall off that path then you’re screwed, that’s definitely not at all supported by the data.
One striking example is if you look at the relationship between SAT scores and the probability of starting a successful business, it’s actually pretty weak. The relationship is much weaker than the relationship between that and your salary at age 35.
So, there’s a different set of skills or abilities or work ethic or whatever that seems to sustain and support successful entrepreneurs that’s much broader than scholastic aptitude by itself, which is another element that’s missing from a lot of American dream narratives that we want to emphasize.
One popular idea to reduce inequality in the U.S. is to focus on the wealth of the biggest billionaires and to constrain the rapid growth of tech and finance-based fortunes. In the book, you say that’s not going to bridge the inequality gap in any significant way. Why not?
Taxing the billionaires is a good idea for closing some loopholes in the income tax that they particularly benefit from. We should have pretty fair tax treatment of people who are high earners, across the types of people that we’re talking about.
The problem with just focusing on the billionaires is that there’s not that much money there, collectively, and so we’re leaving a lot on the table, and we’re failing to recognize other areas where the tax code has been eroded to the benefit of these everywhere millionaires.
They’re individually very rich, but the Forbes 400 is still 4 or 5 percent of total household wealth. There’s this much larger class of people that have really substantial resources, and the book is hopeful, but also shows them with very extravagant consumption habits in some cases.
And I think that’s evidence suggesting that they can afford to pay a little more tax, and they wouldn’t probably notice.
And so, rationalizing the tax burden on this group of people could raise a ton of money and at relatively little economic cost. I think for thinking about our fiscal problems, that should be an important part of the policy tool kit.
Zwick and Zidar will discuss the book with Jason Furman, the Frank and Denie Weil Director of the Mossavar-Rahmani Center for Business and Government and Aetna Professor of the Practice of Economic Policy, on 12:30 p.m. Wednesday at the Malkin Penthouse at HKS. The book also will be the topic of the Stone Inequality Book Talk slated for noon Nov. 3 at the Malkin Penthouse.

title: Rowin’ in the rain
author: Niles Singer
summary: Spirits were high despite gray skies as 12,000-plus rowers from over 30 countries competed in the 61st Head of the Charles Regatta.
text:
The Head of the Charles Regatta got off to a rainy and blustery start this year. But on Friday as announcers mulled how the conditions would affect the race, the rowers and spectators gathering for the launch of the 61st edition seemed undeterred. One rower even defied the weather by breaking into a rendition of, you guessed it, “Singin’ in the Rain” during the race.
The three-day event, the largest rowing regatta in the world, featured 12,000 competitors from more than 30 countries. Against the backdrop of gray skies and vibrant foliage blanketing the banks, sculls raced around river bends as family and friends cheered them on. Harvard photographers were there to capture the action before and during the big event.

title: Predicting weather subseasons with machine learning
author: Matt Goisman
summary: Undergraduate explores weather patterns and precipitation at summer Microsoft Research internship
text:
News
Getting information about tomorrow’s weather can be as easy as tapping an application on your smartphone. Modeling weather patterns years down the line is the job of climate scientists. But what about predicting 2-6 weeks out? These intermediate periods, known as subseasons, are when predictive models are critical.
“This time horizon is very important for farmers who are looking to plan when they want to either plant or harvest their crops,” said Hannah Guan, a fourth-year applied math concentrator. “It's important for city planners who are trying to decide how much energy to allocate to the grid in anticipation of a cold front. This horizon obviously has a lot of very important impacts, but it's also a horizon where there just hasn't been that much research done before, and the models that currently exist just don't reach the same level of accuracy as the short-term or the longer models are able to do.”
Following her sophomore year at the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (SEAS), Guan spent her summer as an intern at Microsoft Research, where she helped develop machine learning algorithms to better predict subseasonal weather and precipitation patterns. Even after finishing her internship, Guan continued her research, eventually becoming first author on a recent publication in Nature.
“There already exist a lot of really big physics-based models or AI foundation models that are pretty good at getting the overall trends, but they still have a lot of errors on the subseasonal timescale,” she said. “Instead of trying to predict the weather directly, we wanted to try to predict where these models that are typically used get it wrong. We're basically trying to build a model that models the error in existing models.”
Guan’s research focused on “probabilistic subseasonal forecasting,” which breaks down a weather prediction into a range of conditions or temperatures, and the percentage likelihood of each scenario. The project focused on correcting existing forecasts, finding potential errors in how the forecast was made, then using their machine learning algorithms to remove the errors.
“There are a few different advantages to this,” she said. “It means that we don't have to build something that's extremely large and compute-intensive. It also means that our method is extremely adaptable, because it can be applied to correct the forecasts from any existing weather model.”
This internship wasn’t Guan’s first research experience, having studied genetic variations and traits at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and worked at the Kempner Institute of Natural and Artificial Intelligence throughout her first two years at SEAS. She sought out the Microsoft Research internship as a way to contrast academic and corporate research experiences.
“I had no clue that this was even a field that people worked on when it came to machine learning and computer science," she said. “After I was accepted to the internship, I got matched with a mentor who had been working on the problem of weather forecasting. A lot of the problems that I find interesting are generally ones where the problem is very applied, and it's very clear what the end result is and how it can help other people. So this was a project that I was immediately interested in.”
Using her interests to benefit her community is a common thread throughout much of Guan’s time at SEAS, and even as a high school student in San Antonio. She served as Co-Director of Programming for the 2025 Women Engineers Code (WECode) Conference at SEAS, and in high school founded Math Include, a now-international STEM tutoring nonprofit. She’s also been a course assistant for several classes.
“That was something I started initially because when I was trying to do math competitions in middle school and high school, there was no existing community in my hometown,” she said. “I wanted to build up this framework that allowed not only me to connect with others, but also for all the students that came after me to connect with other students who were very like-minded. With WECode, there are so many women who are interested in computer science these days, but they're still lacking a lot of venues in which they can connect with each other on a deeper level, connecting over their shared interests and shared challenges that they may have faced in their journeys.”
A high school valedictorian, Guan chose Harvard because it offered more breadth than a more engineering-specific school. She wanted more variety in her courses, but also a more diverse student community with interests and life experiences much different from hers. Similarly, she chose applied math as a concentration because it seemed to offer the broadest range of applications.
“By sophomore fall, I'd taken computer science classes, I'd taken stats classes before, I'd taken a couple of economics classes, and I knew that I was interested in all of these things,” she said. “Applied math was the perfect concentration where I could take all of these classes and combine my interests in each of them to figure out how they all interact with each other and the types of work I can do by combining them.”
Between her research at Harvard Chan School, Kempner and Microsoft Research, as well as her ongoing senior thesis on task memory challenges in artificial intelligence, Guan has devoted much of her time at SEAS to research. She hopes to continue along the same trajectory after graduating, as she’s in the process of applying to Ph.D. programs related to computer science and applied math.
“I really appreciate not only the work itself, but also the community that you are able to foster when you're working on research,” she said. “I've been able to make really close connections to both my mentors and the other students I've also met during this process. What really appealed to me about doing a PhD program was that you're able to make these really deep and close connections with other people just by virtue of being interested in the same problems, and you all have this shared desire to work on the hardest problems in the world and try and solve them for the greater good.”

title: Using AI in the Global Fight Against HIV
author: Anne J. Manning
summary: Harvard computer scientists help incentivize testing, treatment
text:
News
Key Takeaways
- With partners in South Africa, Harvard researchers are testing whether artificial intelligence could enhance a digital health intervention program aimed at generating peer referrals for HIV services.
- A field trial involving a free, confidential AI health coach and chatbot that's now underway in the KwaZulu-Natal province is part of HIV-LIFT, a larger initiative for improving HIV testing and care.
When faced with the possibility of an HIV diagnosis, sometimes the best initial prescription is support from a trusted friend — someone who might offer not just emotional guidance, but also critical, practical health resources.
A Harvard research team thinks artificial intelligence has a role to play in that process.
Led by Milind Tambe, the Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science in the John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (SEAS), researchers are testing whether AI could enhance a digital health intervention program aimed at generating peer referrals for HIV services, especially among populations that have been traditionally harder to reach. South Africa has about 8 million people living with HIV – the highest of any country in the world.
A field trial now underway in the KwaZulu-Natal province of South Africa is part of HIV-LIFT – Leveraging Innovation and Friendships to Improve HIV Testing — a Gates Foundation-funded initiative that includes Wits University in South Africa, Harvard’s Teamcore research group led by Tambe, partners at the World Health Organization, and others.
HIV-LIFT, whose principal investigator is Alastair van Heerden of Wits University, is a multi-year study aimed at improving HIV testing and care in South Africa among populations, such as men and adolescents, who are less likely to seek testing and are more likely to remain undiagnosed or to attend clinics. The Harvard team is contributing a machine learning protocol added to an existing smartphone app that’s designed to incentivize more people from underserved groups to seek HIV services.
“It’s great to see real-world deployments of computer science,” said Davin Choo, a postdoctoral fellow who has led the development of the algorithms and is working closely with partners on the ground running the field trial. “It’s also interesting to see that when real-world constraints come in, you have to adapt. There’s no point in having fancy things look good on paper but cannot be used in practice.”
For example, said graduate student and team member Akseli Kangaslahti, the Harvard team first approached the problem of AI-guided targeting with a more complex simulation algorithm, but they found that results from this algorithm were not easily interpretable for regular users. “I think we learned a lot from that work, even if we weren’t able to directly employ the algorithms that we proposed in them,” Kangaslahti said.
Also collaborating on HIV-LIFT is Cheryl Case Johnson, a technical officer and innovation lead at the World Health Organization’s department of HIV, TB, Hepatitis and STIs with expertise in HIV network-based interventions.
Improving an existing AI health coach
The ongoing field trial focuses on Coach Mpilo, a free, confidential AI health coach and chatbot available through WhatsApp. Designed specifically for South Africans, Coach Mpilo provides information and support related to HIV testing and treatment, as well as other health issues. With more than 150,000 enrolled users, only about 15% of the app’s users are men; men are historically less likely to seek HIV testing and treatment than other groups due to factors like social stigma or long working hours.
Within the Coach Mpilo app is a financial incentive for existing users to send referrals to others who might also need HIV services. The field trial will seek to answer the question: When a program only has the financial resources to encourage a limited number of people to recruit their friends and other contacts, whom should it prioritize?
The Harvard team has developed a machine-learning and optimization approach intended to improve the process of referrals by more intentionally targeting existing users to be “nudged” with an incentive to recruit others. Their AI model discerns which users are most likely to refer people in underserved groups, including men and adolescents.
The work is intended to supplement — not replace — clinics, health workers or the social relationships that make peer referrals possible.
The planned study will compare two groups: one in which eligible users will be selected for outreach at random, and the other, with the added AI filter that further narrows the incentive-eligible pool of users. The AI system will provide a fixed priority list developed in advance from data collected during earlier incentive campaigns.
The Harvard team developed the AI-guided approach based on previous HIV-LIFT incentive campaigns. In retrospective evaluations involving approximately 16,000 historical nudges of existing users collected over two months, this “nudging” approach was estimated to generate more successful referrals than any other strategy.
The prioritization solution the researchers developed demanded transparency so that users on the ground could easily understand it, added Tambe. “Specifically, partners proposed policy restrictions to ensure fairness and equal treatment for users with identical profiles, while maintaining a simple, transparent, and practical framework that works within real-world system constraints.”
Now, with the Harvard team’s AI algorithms generating the right groups to target for incentivizing, the research team will determine whether this priority-group approach could be implemented permanently within Coach Mpilo or potentially other applications.
AI for social good
The current work at Harvard builds on more than a decade of Teamcore research into the use of AI and social networks for HIV prevention. Tambe has worked on leveraging AI for socially meaningful purposes for more than 20 years and began focusing on HIV prevention in 2013, initially through work with youth experiencing homelessness in Los Angeles.
“We hope that our work will ultimately contribute to some improvement in how HIV-affected people may be cared for, or how people can get access to HIV information,” Tambe said.
Beyond his Harvard appointment, he leads the Google Research AI for Social Good initiative, which is separate from the HIV-LIFT work.
