title: The idea of a university
author: Liz Mineo
summary: MLK Lecture honoree argues goal should prepare students for jobs, and to be responsible, principled citizens.
text:
In 1947, Martin Luther King Jr., then an 18-year-old Morehouse College student, wrote an article in the campus newspaper arguing that education should be about more than just developing the intellectual skills needed to get students ready for careers. It should shape character to ensure they pursue worthy goals as individuals and as part of society.
The nation’s universities and colleges lately are missing the mark, said Paula Johnson, Wellesley College president and this year’s honoree of the Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Commemorative Lecture.
“I have been president of Wellesley College for just over a decade,” said Johnson ’80, M.D. ’84, M.P.H. ’85, in her address Thursday evening in Memorial Church. “In those tumultuous years, I have come to see the hard truth of how we are falling short of our responsibility to prepare students to be the citizens our country needs. I have witnessed the growing discomfort of students and faculty with sharing their views. I have observed the consequences of a focus on service without a corresponding emphasis on citizenship or civic purpose.”
Drawing on King’s words and legacy, Johnson urged university and college leaders to honor “the higher purpose Dr. King saw in education.” For King, the goal of true education was “intelligence plus character,” she said.
“For many, higher education has become an economic endeavor in terms of a return on an investment, an exercise of gaining knowledge for the purpose of personal gain,” said Johnson.
“The purpose of education is not to gain knowledge alone, but to teach students to form judgment with empathy and to imbue them with a sense of higher responsibility to our democracy.”
Paula Johnson
“The purpose of education is not to gain knowledge alone, but to teach students to form judgment with empathy and to imbue them with a sense of higher responsibility to our democracy. In an age of rapid technological advances and political fragmentation, I see this as an urgent need.”
To fulfill that purpose, Johnson advocated for the restoration of three principles: fostering moral and ethical development of character, reasserting the central importance of history, and exposing students to real encounters across difference.
“College is an opportunity for students to discover what they believe, based in knowledge and their lived experience, what they owe each other, and what they owe people beyond their communities,” said Johnson. “A strong education teaches us that all facets of life have a history, and learning that history changes how we understand ourselves, and how we understand our responsibilities to each other. That is the education we owe our students.”
A pioneering physician scientist, public health leader, and educator, Johnson spoke at the fifth MLK Lecture commemorating the 1962 speech King gave at Harvard on the future of integration.
Organized by Community and Campus Life, the annual presidential event honors individuals for their contributions to advancing King’s ideals of justice and equality.
Past honorees include Freeman A. Hrabowski III, president emeritus of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County; Loretta Lynch, former U.S. attorney general; Sherrilyn Ifill, president and director-counsel emeritus of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, and Darren Walker, president of the Ford Foundation.
Harvard President Alan Garber described Johnson as “a daughter of Harvard, a beloved educator and an inspiring leader” in presenting her the award.
“President Paula Johnson, who has been my friend and an inspiration for more than four decades, is the best hopes of this University realized: a visionary who has brought her talents to bear on everything she does, a scholar who has expanded her capacities across a lifetime of meaningful and valuable work, a leader who has made the world better through her efforts,” said Garber.
Before becoming Wellesley president, Johnson was the Grayce A. Young Family Professor of Medicine in Women’s Health at Harvard Medical School and professor of epidemiology at the Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health.
She was also the chief of the Division of Women’s Health and founded and served as the inaugural executive director of the Mary Horrigan Connors Center for Women’s Health at Brigham and Women’s Hospital.
The evening’s events included a moderated discussion between Johnson and Drew Gilpin Faust, Harvard president emerita and Arthur Kingsley Porter University Research Professor.
The two spoke about King’s legacy and also noted their similar journeys as women who rose to the top of their professions and became distinguished scholars and university presidents.
“Harvard didn’t expect to see the two of us sitting up here,” said Faust, prompting applause from the audience.
Born and raised in Brooklyn, Johnson was part of the first Harvard-Radcliffe class to admit men and women in equal numbers. In 1990, Johnson was the first Black American in the history of Brigham and Women’s Hospital to be chosen as chief medical resident.
Faust, who served as Harvard president from 2007 to 2018, was the University’s first female president.
At one point Faust asked Johnson how higher education could meet King’s call to educate future generations of engaged and ethical citizens.
Johnson admitted there is work to do, but, “We don’t have a choice.”

title: Is it already too late to reduce catastrophic AI risk?
author: Christina Pazzanese
summary: New Kennedy School "pre-mortem" lays out threats, vulnerabilities, and possible steps, and warns firms must act now.
text:
Is it too late to safeguard ourselves from a large-scale catastrophic event caused by AI running amok?
No, but there is very real cause for concern unless AI firms take decisive action, a new research paper from Harvard Kennedy School’s Belfer Center concludes.
Rogue agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google breached hundreds of corporate and government systems in the U.S. and Australia this year.
The CEOs of Anthropic and OpenAI, along with other prominent AI leaders, underscore the game-changing potential of the powerful new technology but have urged a slowdown in its development, with OpenAI announcing last month that it would pause training of its most advanced models because of safety concerns.
Anthropic’s new IPO prospectus cautions investors: AI could pose an “existential threat to humanity.”
Still, there’s still time to act before the first big AI-enabled tragedy strikes, according to new research from the Kennedy School’s Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs.
The paper identifies current threats and vulnerabilities of frontier AI models, games out probable scenarios, and concludes that what happens will be determined largely by the choices AI companies and governments are making right now.
In this edited conversation, computer scientist Stephen Casper, one of the paper’s co-authors, lays out the findings of the group’s “pre-mortem.”
Gazette: Did the breach disclosures over the past few months prompt this work?
Stephen Casper: This project wasn’t motivated by recent events, but recent events have done a lot to provoke a reckoning among the public and policymakers about AI risks that do seem pretty serious, and about whether or not now is the time for some form of decisive action. It’s very possible that things could get much, much, more intense or urgent.
This paper was an attempt to pick one of the more dramatic scenarios by which things could change and try to do a pre-mortem with the hope of either helping prevent it or helping to speed up a more-informed discussion in the aftermath so it can be prevented from happening a second or third time, if it does.
What would you consider a major AI-enabled terror event?
We define this as a terrorism incident that causes more than 50 deaths or serious injuries or more than a billion dollars in damages. We use these thresholds because these are some of the same thresholds used behind the definition of “critical incident” or “critical risk” inside of certain frontier AI laws.
Right now, what AI companies are concerned about in their evaluations and reporting, and what AI governance institutes like in the U.S. and U.K. are concerned about, is mainly bio risk, chemical risk, and cyber risk. That’s one thing that can be predicted without too much difficulty — the ways in which something might transpire that causes a lot of harm.
A second thing that can be predicted is that a very large, AI-enabled terrorism incident is probably going to be the result of a closed-weight frontier AI model that is poorly safeguarded or an open-weight model.
For closed-weight models, where developers control all points of access to that model, there are a lot of safeguard layers you can put in place, like model safety, system filters, user monitoring, etc. There’s a really good tool kit and it’s reasonably well-developed and when you use that whole tool kit, it is not particularly hard to make your model not perfectly secure, but very secure against consistent forms of misuse.
Instead, though, there are closed-weight models that are less well-safeguarded, and open-weight models are just hard to safeguard in the first place. And that’s where we think most of the incident-level threats are going to come from.
How close are we to seeing a major AI-assisted event occur? Is it inevitable that something will happen?
Something’s eventually going to happen. The lessons of the past few years have taught us that if there is a bad AI capability that can exist, it will eventually widely proliferate.
“Something’s eventually going to happen. The lessons of the past few years have taught us that if there is a bad AI capability that can exist, it will eventually widely proliferate.”
The trends here would suggest there are credible risks within months, or a year or two, if not now.
But it’s hard to point to events and be like “this is here” or “this is a few months away.” AI risk management, from a high level or a government-level perspective, is just about decreasing the rate at which very bad or catastrophic incidents can happen and making them more endurable when we do run into them.
For bio- and chem-terrorism incidents, there is more uncertainty because there is less open research on these things, and we haven’t had any major incidents, so far.
But there have been some credible empirical events, including the Red Four attack in India, in which models were consulted for creating harmful chemical compounds like ricin. So, some amount of capability is there, but we don’t know what, maximally solicited, these capabilities really might be.
When it comes to cyber, events of the past months have been pretty convincing in showing us that Mythos 5 or GPT 5.6 Sol-level AI capabilities are very superhumanly good at persistent cyberattacks and vulnerability discovery. It might be that you don’t need models much more powerful than these in order to orchestrate large-scale swarm-style attacks against important infrastructure or companies.
We’ve already seen plenty of AI-assisted hacking events.
Right now, if you look at trend lines in general capabilities, the closed systems are ahead in terms of how advanced they are. But the open systems pretty reliably stay about six months behind, which means we might be able to expect some open-weight AI system that has the same cyber capabilities as Mythos or GBT 5.6 Sol by around Christmas.
We might be up for some general period of disruptiveness and an instability in the cybersecurity world. Not saying it’ll last forever, but it’s going to be a shock to the cyber world, I think.
What are some of the ways AI can be manipulated in order to cause significant harm?
It will differ based on whether the model is closed-weight or open-weight.
The way that harm comes from a frontier model with closed weights is through prompt-based attacks against the model. You trick it to do something harmful that safeguards normally would prevent it from doing, such as giving you advice on how to design a virology lab experiment or automating hacking for you.
In the open-model scenario, a model that’s just online and anyone can download it, there are a variety of ways it could be misused.
It could be misused off the shelf because open models have a tendency to be less safe a lot of the time than closed ones.
Maybe it could be misused by someone who downloads it and modifies it to remove safeguards or to sharpen its harmful capabilities. This type of fine-tuning could cost hundreds or a few thousand dollars, at most.
It could also be misused by someone who accesses an uncensored version.
When open models are released, there is a pretty consistent tendency for certain types of users to download and then uncensor them by training away their harmful-task-refusal behaviors and then re-uploading it.
“When open models are released, there is a pretty consistent tendency for certain types of users to download and then uncensor them by training away their harmful-task-refusal behaviors and then re-uploading it.”
You can go online right now to Hugging Face, which is the largest open-model downloading and sharing platform in the world, and by searching the right keywords, find 15,000 different models that have been uncensored, ones that shouldn’t refuse any harmful request even if you ask them to automate creating hate speech or for instructions about how to commit crimes.
Which AI safeguards help reduce the risks of a major incident occurring?
With closed models, there’s a much richer tool kit of safeguards that you can turn to.
One is to scope the model’s capabilities. You can’t maximize useful capabilities without also enabling some harmful capabilities. If you have an AI model that can help you with benign and legitimate virology experiments, that same model can probably also help you with experiments creating harmful pathogens.
So the first thing is to recognize and account for the fact that minimizing risk is incompatible with maximizing legitimate usefulness. There’s a trade-off.
Number two is to scope the model’s capabilities accordingly, largely through training. You probably want to filter out lots of biohazard-related scientific research from the training set.
Number three is to rigorously train the model to refuse harmful requests even when they are prompted. The prompt comes in tricky ways, and state-of-the-art ways of doing this usually involve over a million GPU hours of automated vulnerability discovery and training against those vulnerabilities.
Another set of techniques involves monitoring the inputs that a user gives it, the outputs that it produces, and the conversation or trajectory long actions that it is taking in. If you do all of these things, with good state-of-the-art monitors, there are very few harmful actions you cannot detect.
The last key thing is user monitoring. If you’re a ChatGPT user and you start asking more than one or two questions about biohazards, user monitoring and shadow banning is really helpful.
All of these things put together are quite strong if you do them in a state-of-the-art way, and there is no known attack. I’m not saying they’re perfect, but the state of the art is quite good compared to how effective attacks can be.
On the open-model side, it’s much harder. You have a much less rich tool kit of reliable safeguards.
If you have an open model that anyone can download and access and run privately, suddenly, any sort of safeguard external to that model, like a safety filter, can and will be stripped away. This happens all the time.
Is this a problem for AI model developers to fix alone, or do others have a role to play?
The actors with the most power to mitigate significant harms are the AI model developers, because they’re in control of the systems that end up getting misused. There’s a long list of safeguards and best practices that can be implemented but aren’t consistently implemented.
Aside from that, there’s a good bit to be said about the role that policymakers can play here.
If policymakers want to improve incentives or reduce the risks we currently have, then policymakers should be very interested in greatly increasing transparency into decision-making and risk-management deliberation inside of these companies and think about taking actions to put the government more in control of the pace of AI, so that the default “move fast and break things” modality by which the AI ecosystem operates is less at the wheel.
Lastly, researchers and the public can play an important role too by working on patching some holes in safeguards that exist.
We’re at a time in which lots of policymakers are starting to seriously think about their positions on AI. If there were any point in history at which it could be influential, now might be a particularly important time for constituents to let policymakers know what they’re worried about.

title: Making music is magic. Understanding it is even better.
author: Liz Mineo
summary: Why Sophia Zervas traded a career in the arts for academia.
text:
From her first piano lesson at age 6, Sophia Zervas seemed destined to become a professional musician. It wasn’t until her final year of pursuing a double bachelor’s degree in voice and piano performance at the University of Colorado, Boulder, that another class — on ethnomusicology, the study of music in its social and cultural contexts — changed everything.
The discipline lured Zervas away from the spotlight of the stage to the archives of academia. Now a Ph.D. candidate in ethnomusicology in the Department of Music, Zervas finds herself a rarity in the field as both a scholar and a classically trained musician.
“Understanding music as a cultural phenomenon, not just as an object in and of itself; that’s what really drew me to ethnomusicology,” said Zervas. “As an artist you produce something that’s ephemeral, and even if you record it, it doesn’t capture the moment of being on stage. As a scholar, you produce something, an article or a book, which can be quite rewarding, because you’ll always have that piece.”
Although Zervas still performs occasionally, she really feels at home using her musical training to understand “the way people make meaning around music.”
“Understanding music as a cultural phenomenon, not just as an object in and of itself; that’s what really drew me to ethnomusicology.”
Sophia Zervas
“Being a musical performer involves an intellectual challenge, an emotional challenge, and also a kinesthetic challenge,” Zervas said. “It’s very exhausting compared to being in the archives or doing ethnographic interviews, but there is something really wonderful about taking a piece of music and breathing life into it.”
For the past six years, Zervas has studied music and cultural institutions in 21st-century Turkey. How she chose the country that sits at the crossroads of the East and West was a bit of an accident, she said. With a mixed background of Lebanese and Greek roots, Zervas was always fascinated by the music of the Mediterranean. She focused on Turkey because of her interest in the intersection between politics and culture.
Zervas studied Turkish at Boğaziçi University in Istanbul and spent more than two years in the country doing field work through a traveling fellowship from Harvard and a doctoral scholarship at the Orient-Institut Istanbul. She researches state cultural policy under the current administration of Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, who was the country’s prime minister from 2003 until 2014 and has been president since 2014.
According to Zervas, the early years of Erdogan’s mayorship in Istanbul, around the mid-1990s, were marked by a rise in traditional music, but also musical syntheses, such as the Janissary military bands, which play traditional songs mixed with jazz. In the early 2000s, she said, multiculturalism through music took off because the country was campaigning to join the EU.
“Then in the mid-2010s, a series of socio-cultural ruptures happened and there is a rise in censorship in music,” said Zervas. “You see a turn from a more positive building up of cultural policy to a more repressive one in the later years.”
Zervas’ adviser, Kay Kaufman Shelemay, G. Gordon Watts Professor of Music and of African and African American Studies, said the work is timely “given the activity in Turkey and a number of other authoritarian regimes to control directions in the arts.”
“The topic of music and politics is also a sensitive one,” said Shelemay. “Sophia is quite keenly aware of the challenges of her specialization. She has found a dissertation topic that is relevant across borders today and is quite innovative in her approach to the interaction of music and politics in modern Turkey.”
After graduation in May, Zervas plans to apply for jobs in academia but remains open to performing. Last year, she was invited to give a small concert at the Orient-Institut Istanbul. She played pieces by Monteverdi, Mendelssohn, and Brahms, among others, and enjoyed a return to the spotlight.
“It was a really joyful experience,” said Zervas. “It was nice not to have to perform for a jury or a grade, but just to perform for an audience of people who I knew well and who were appreciative and excited about the music. So, hopefully, after the Ph.D. is over, there will be more opportunities for that.”

title: Jennifer Lewis Elected to National Academy of Medicine
author: Anne J. Manning
summary: SEAS professor recognized for work in soft and living materials
text:
News
Jennifer Lewis, the Hansjörg Wyss Professor of Biologically Inspired Engineering in the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (SEAS) and a core faculty member of the Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering, has been elected to the National Academy of Medicine. The Academy has recognized her work in 3D bioprinting of soft and living materials, and for development of advanced techniques for creating vascularized organoids and human tissues for use in drug discovery, disease modeling and therapeutic repair.
Lewis joins 100 new members of the Academy this year, including 13 at Harvard. Election to the National Academy of Medicine is considered one of the highest honors in health and medicine and recognizes individuals who have demonstrated outstanding professional achievement and commitment to service. With her election, Lewis earns the rare distinction of membership in all three national academies, including the National Academy of Sciences (NAS) and the National Academy of Engineering.
Lewis and her team are focused on developing functional, structural, and living materials for applications ranging from printed electronics to vascularized human tissues. Her lab integrates expertise in materials science, soft matter physics, additive manufacturing, bioengineering, and stem cell biology to create new classes of printable materials and 3D printing and 3D bioprinting methods.
Lewis has received widespread recognition for her work, including the NAS James Prize for Science and Technology Integration, the Sigma Xi Gold Key Award, the Lush Prize for Scientific Research, the Materials Research Society Medal, and the Department of Defense Vannevar Bush Faculty Fellowship.
Multiple startups are commercializing technology from her research lab, ranging from printed electronics to kidney tissue therapeutics.
Topics: Bioengineering, Health / Medicine, Materials Science & Mechanical Engineering, Meet Our Faculty, Research, Technology

title: 11 Harvard Medical School Researchers, Educators Elected to National Academy of Medicine
summary: Eleven faculty members from Harvard Medical School have been newly elected to the National Academy of Medicine (NAM).Election to the NAM is among the highest honors in health and medicine, recognizing individuals for their exceptional professional accomplishments and dedication to service.Get more HMS news
text:
Eleven faculty members from Harvard Medical School have been newly elected to the National Academy of Medicine (NAM).
Election to the NAM is among the highest honors in health and medicine, recognizing individuals for their exceptional professional accomplishments and dedication to service.
Lauding the new members as “outstanding health and medicine leaders,” NAM President Monica Bertagnolli said, “Their extraordinary talent and commitment to advancing evidence-based guidance and solutions for our country’s greatest health care challenges will strengthen our efforts to improve health for all.”
A total of 100 new members, chosen by current members, were announced during the NAM annual meeting on Oct. 19. Total NAM membership is now over 2,600, including more than 300 international members.
The newly elected members from HMS are:
- Fabrisia Ambrosio, HMS professor of physical medicine and rehabilitation at Spaulding Rehabilitation Hospital, for her international leadership and work in regenerative rehabilitation research that couples the use of cellular bioengineering technologies with physical modalities and exercise to improve health, functioning, and longevity.
- Kathleen Burns, HMS professor of pathology at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, for work on transposable elements in human disease. Her discoveries have highlighted long interspersed nuclear element-1 (LINE-1) activity as a source of heritable genetic variation and a hallmark of cancers.
- Marcela del Carmen, HMS professor of obstetrics, gynecology, and reproductive biology at Massachusetts General Hospital, for her work in transforming the treatment of ovarian cancer and establishing new approaches to reduce cancer-related morbidity and mortality in gynecologic cancers.
- Anna Greka, HMS professor of medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, for elucidating the molecular basis of kidney and genetic diseases, particularly those that disrupt fundamental mechanisms of protein trafficking and renal barrier function, and for translating these discoveries into targeted therapies.
- David Jones, the A. Bernard Ackerman Professor of the Culture of Medicine in the Blavatnik Institute at HMS, professor in the Department of Epidemiology at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, and chair of the Department of the History of Science at the Harvard Faculty of Arts and Sciences, for scholarship in the history of medicine, the social determinants of disease, health disparities in diverse populations, and the utilization of health technologies, including work reevaluating the use of race correction in clinical algorithms.
- Nancy Keating, professor of health care policy in the Blavatnik Institute at HMS, for seminal contributions to promoting high-quality, high-value cancer care through the evaluation of alternative payment models, comparative effectiveness studies of cancer treatments in real-world settings, and research to improve guideline-recommended use, affordability, and adherence.
- Bruce Landon, professor of health care policy in the Blavatnik Institute at HMS, for his formative research and key insights about primary care, quality of care, delivery system structure, and financial incentives that have led to reforms to primary care payment, Medicare Advantage, and quality measurement programs.
- Emily Oken, HMS Harvard Pilgrim Health Care Institute Professor of Population Medicine at Harvard Pilgrim Healthcare, for research on the nutritional and environmental influences on women’s health during the reproductive years and children’s long-term health, advancing understanding of pregnancy health and chronic disease risk while shaping scientific research and public policy.
- Jordan Smoller, HMS professor of psychiatry at Mass General, for his leadership in the discovery of shared and distinct genomic influences across psychiatric disorders, illuminating how genetic variation relates to the structure of psychopathology.
- Kimberly Stegmaier, the HMS David G. Nathan Professor of Pediatrics at Dana-Farber, for developing highly innovative methods of genetic and chemical genomic screening of cell phenotypes, which she successfully applied to understand pediatric cancer biology and discover drugs to treat specific cancers.
- Michael Yaffe, HMS instructor in surgery at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, for discovering phospho Ser/Thr-binding domains in proteins and revealing how they regulate signaling pathways controlling the cell cycle or in response to stress, which helped advance the use of computational tools to understand how proteins interact and how enzymes recognize and act on specific targets within cells.
Founded in 1970 by the National Academy of Sciences as the Institute of Medicine, the NAM works to address pressing challenges in health, science, medicine, and related policy while advancing solutions across sectors. Together with the National Academy of Sciences and the National Academy of Engineering, collectively known as the National Academies, the NAM provides independent, objective analysis and guidance to help address complex challenges and inform public policy decisions.
Adapted from NAM materials.

title: How to know if you’re wrong
author: Sydney Boles
summary: Acknowledging your vast ignorance is a good first step — but don’t stop there, says “Knowing Our Limits” author Nathan Ballantyne.
text:
Nathan Ballantyne is the 2026-2027 Beatrice Shepherd Blane Fellow at the Radcliffe Institute. He is also an associate professor of philosophy, cognition, and culture at Arizona State University’s School of Historical, Philosophical, and Religious Studies.
In a high school English class, I first encountered a disconcerting question about knowing oneself. The teacher was talking about a Shakespeare character who fails catastrophically because of their own flaws — vices the character couldn’t see. Hamartia, or a tragic flaw, is the term used for this. How can we know our own errors? Well, it turns out sometimes we can’t, and I became fascinated by the possibility that there were errors I might be making that I couldn’t recognize.
We are often willing to accept that we might be wrong, though in a very general sort of way. But as soon as someone zooms in and thinks about one of their particular convictions, something they believe strongly, they often don’t feel the same pull of the idea that this belief might be wrong. Of course, it can’t be that all our beliefs are accurate; we all have some imperfect beliefs. The trouble is figuring out which ones are mistaken. We need a way to step back somehow and gain perspectives on our beliefs.
The method I lay out in my book, “Knowing Our Limits,” starts with a simple question: Are we competent to form good beliefs on the basis of the evidence we have? Basically, if we find out that we have reasonable doubts about whether we’re competent to arrive at good beliefs, that’s going to give us the space to admit to ourselves that we might be wrong, and we might lower our confidence in our views.
So how do we cultivate the capacity to acknowledge we’re wrong? A big part of the story is engaging with the rival ideas other people have put forward.
For example, it’s easy to become aware of vast bodies of evidence concerning controversial topics, evidence we haven’t looked at. You might have an opinion about something like the morality of capital punishment, but then you realize that the library has a whole shelf of books about this issue, and some of those books contain arguments against your views — but you haven’t read those books. That’s an insight that can lead you to admit your way of forming your view on capital punishment wasn’t competent. You formed an opinion on the basis of an unrepresentative sample of the available evidence, and so you shouldn’t be so sure of yourself. When we encounter what appear to be reasonable doubts like that, it’s helpful to build our uncertainty into our way of thinking; that’s how we get nuance into our ideas.
A second example begins by noting that our intellectual world is filled with complicated, dense domains of expertise where people answer questions using all sorts of different methods and data. When we make judgments about topics that fall well outside our own circle of expertise, I call that “epistemic trespassing.” We can start to recognize that we’re missing out on methods and data from those other fields. That insight gives us some means of doubting that we’re competent to form good beliefs about that issue.
So how do we cultivate the capacity to acknowledge we’re wrong? A big part of the story is engaging with the rival ideas other people have put forward. Some obvious skills here are listening carefully, reading widely and sympathetically, coming to inquiry with patience and humility. But I think in the background there’s an even more important issue — context. We can ask, “Where do people go to spend time having this sort of intellectually open conversation? What are the spaces where humility is more natural for us than arrogance?” Well, it probably won’t be in the group chat with like-minded friends or on a social media hellsite. Sometimes lab groups and classrooms can be places that help us be more open and exercise those skills — places where we can brainstorm together, ease ourselves into new ways of looking at the world.
Learning how others think and reason doesn’t always — and shouldn’t always — change our minds, but it’s important to exercise patience to see someone’s argument all the way through to its conclusions, and to try to understand why they find that perspective compelling. In my experience, friendships that are built across political, moral, and religious differences can be helpful, though these are admittedly hard to maintain in a fractured age.
A friend of mine shared me a quotation from Hannah Arendt recently: “A human being is far more valuable than his opinions.” That struck me as an idea worth reflecting on, even if you happen to think it’s wrong.
—As told to Sy Boles/Harvard Staff Writer

title: Designing for world in flux
author: Anna Lamb
summary: Exhibit at Graduate School of Design highlights innovation that makes possible structures, projects that balance efficacy, affordability, efficiency
text:
At Harvard’s Graduate School of Design, students are often hoping to make structures and innovations that last.
But the current era has been marked by relatively rapid environmental, social, political, and technological shifts across the globe. Designers are increasingly being asked to make things that can be adaptable, accessible, and economical.
Enter “Infrastructure in a Time of Flux: Methods, Conditions, and Situations,” the School’s fall exhibit on display in the Druker Design Gallery through December. The show spotlights architectural, engineering, urban planning, and design innovations focused on building for a world in transition.
“I think there’s an interesting tension between these two words,” said Rahul Mehrotra, professor of urban design and planning and co-curator along with Dan Borelli, GSD exhibitions director. “Infrastructure is generally understood as a stable framework within which life happens, but flux suggests almost the opposite. Flux implies movement, change, uncertainty, transformation. So what happens to our understanding of infrastructure when permanence can no longer be assumed as the fundamental condition of the city?”
Mehrotra said he was inspired in part by his home city of Mumbai, where the Hindu Kumbh Mela festival brings millions of people into a camp created just for the celebration. The festival grounds are dismantled just as quickly as they are constructed — a temporary city within a city.
“Millions of people arrive, infrastructures are assembled — roads, bridges, sanitation, electricity, water, housing, markets, security systems — all come together,” Mehrotra said. “It has all the attributes of a regular city, and then after a relatively short period — 55 days — it takes only three or four weeks to assemble it and takes 10 days to disassemble it. The land returns to another condition.”
He’s also drawn inspiration from artists, including Christo and Jeanne-Claude, who made their mark creating large-scale temporary installations across the globe. The exhibition features stills of their work, including the iconic 1985 covering of the Pont Neuf in Paris.
“[Christo] would always say permanence is the enemy of freedom,” said Vladimir Yavachev, director of operations at the Christo and Jeanne-Claude Foundation. “You can pick up and go at any time. You don’t have to be dependent.”
In addition to exploring impermanence, the exhibition is an examination of feasibility, highlighting techniques, materials, and practices that balance efficacy with affordability and efficiency.
Some examples include scaffolding in New York City that allows construction to take place without interrupting pedestrian traffic, and plastic housing for Ethiopia’s Kobe Refugee Camp, where there are about 37,000 people.
“Some of the examples in the exhibition are speculative, artistic, and even dreamy. Others are scrappy, ad hoc, and poignant. Some harken back to very old traditions. Other others are futuristic,” said Sarah Whiting, GSD dean and Josep Lluís Sert Professor of Architecture. “Every example offers fodder for thinking and acting. We have nine different degree programs here at the GSD, ranging from urban design to design engineering to ecologies, architecture, and more. And I think every one of them is reflected by the work displayed in the exhibition out there.”
Some methods embrace geometry and dynamic movement to create lightweight and affordable structures and infrastructure.
One example are space frames — truss lattices of interlocking geometric patterns like you might see in an airplane hangar — which distribute load evenly across structures and eliminate need for permanent load bearing beams or columns.
Another involves folded structures, often done with stiff plastic, that transform flexible materials into sturdy shapes.
Scholars say designers often face projects that require them to consider questions like: How do people actually access different resources? Would they be willing to travel for certain things? How far? What occupied the site before and what connotations does that space hold? How much buy-in exists from stakeholders?
“People move, economies change, buildings are adapted, spaces are occupied differently, new meanings are attached to old places,” Mehrotra said. “The city is constantly being adjusted.”
And sometimes design is only intended to be temporary for celebrations, religious gatherings, nomadic groups, disaster victims, and military refugees.
During Italy’s Feast of the Redeemer, a temporary pontoon bridge brings visitors and pilgrims to the Church of the Most Holy Redeemer, commonly known as Il Redentore. At Burning Man, a temporary city in the desert makes sure festival-goers have access to food, water, and bathrooms.
“Reversibility is not just about whether we can take something apart. It is about how we think. It asks whether the things we build can anticipate change. Can they be adapted? Can they be moved? Can they be reused? Can they be dismantled? Can they leave something behind, or perhaps leave almost nothing behind?” Mehrotra said.
A symposium will be held on Nov. 12 and 13 bringing together designers, architects, humanitarian workers, and historians to reflect on the exhibition’s three themes and interrogate the Kumbh Mela festival as a case study.

title: Writing a novel? Just like being a fashion designer.
author: Anna Lamb
summary: Douglas Stuart, Booker winner for "Shuggie Bain," traces career path at Mahindra event
text:
Writing, said Douglas Stuart, is a lot like fashion.
“In fashion you’re always prototyping,” said the award-winning novelist who spent more than two decades as a designer. “You start with a dream, and then you sketch it in pencil, and then you throw that sketch out. You draw it in ink, and you throw that out, and then you draw it in a way that a pattern maker can understand. … Then make a prototype; then you get the first version. You fit it, and it’s a constant redoing of an idea.”
Stuart made the observation during a recent Mahindra Center conversation with Charlie Tyson, Harvard Society of Fellows Junior Fellow, to discuss the Scottish writer’s third novel, “John of John,” released in May. The book chronicles the tale of a father and son set against the backdrop of the textile industry of the Outer Hebrides.
Stuart became a breakout literary sensation with his Booker Prize-winning 2020 debut, the semi-autobiographical “Shuggie Bain,” which follows a young man in 1980s Glasgow as he deals with poverty, violence, and complicated familial love. His second book, 2022’s “Young Mungo,” is a love story between two young men of different religious backgrounds who find solace in each other despite violence and economic struggle.
When he began working on “Shuggie,” Stuart said he looked for inspiration in other writers.
“At first I really wanted to be Cormac McCarthy, and I imitated him, and it was terrible,” he said. “And I realized actually, you’ve got to just use what you have.”
Stuart grew up in Glasgow under the free-market policies of Thatcherism, which sped up the decline of state-sponsored industry and coal mining and resulted in high unemployment. He watched his older brother and others of his generation struggle to find economic footing.
Stuart said he took advantage of opportunities his brother didn’t have, going to art school and getting a bachelor’s degree at the Scottish College of Textiles and earning a master’s in design from the Royal College of Art in London.
“Shuggie Bain” took shape over more than a decade, as Stuart balanced working at several fashion houses in New York City. In 2019, as his book was getting ready to publish, he quit designing and turned to writing full-time.
That’s when the first seeds of “John of John” were planted.
“It takes 18 months for a book to publish, and about three months into it, I’ve been working my whole life, and so I’m starting to get so distracted and so anxious, and I say to my husband one day, ‘I think I’m going to go to the Hebrides,’” Stuart said. “He went, ‘OK …’ he was so keen to get rid of me and my anxiety.”
“After my first two novels about gang violence and about the decline in the city, I wanted to also show that the working class were very capable of loving beauty in all its forms.”
Douglas Stuart
Stuart said the sojourn, which started as a way to discover his own country, turned into a research trip.
“I thought I was going to write a story of return. You’ve gone. You’ve seen some of the world. You’re coming home to a small town.”
“John of John” follows Cal, a young man returning to his small island village under the pretense of caring for his ailing grandmother Ella. But in reality, it’s an opportunity for art school graduate Cal to connect with his father — a weaver working in traditional tweed manufacturing. Both men struggle to share their lives with one another and find ways to connect through the craft.
“I wanted to write a novel about working-class men who love beauty,” Stuart said. “That was one of the first things I wanted to do. After my first two novels about gang violence and about the decline in the city, I wanted to also show that the working class were very capable of loving beauty in all its forms.”
Cal and his father share a love of color and creation. The Isle of Harris, where they live, is dominated by residents (including Cal’s father) with devout Protestant and Calvinist beliefs. Both father and son are queer — a fact each keeps hidden from the other.
Stuart recalled the moment the book really took shape during his trip to the isles.
He noticed many of the older men he came across were single. Talking to a local woman, he mentioned he thought some of them must be gay.
“And the woman sort of looked at me, and pulled back a little, and said, ‘That’s not possible,”‘ he said. “And I thought, in that moment, it’s not about the son returning home; it’s about the father he left behind. It’s about the men and women that have lost their progress in that way.”

title: ‘Our focus has been on resiliency.’
author: gazettebeckycoleman
summary: University leaders welcome strong financial results, reiterate deep commitment to research in face of "substantial and sustained" challenges.
text:
The fiscal year that closed on June 30 included economic headwinds and uncertainty around research funding, all while areas of the University undertook strategic restructuring efforts to reverse a trend of expenses outpacing revenues.
At the same time, the fiscal year included significant investments and achievements in research and discovery, raising hopes for life-saving medical treatments and shaping innovations to drive U.S. security and competitiveness.
Harvard’s annual financial report, released Thursday, detailed the results of the University’s financial management across these challenges and opportunities, including ending the year with a $100 million operating surplus.
The Gazette sat down with Harvard Executive Vice President Meredith Weenick and Chief Financial Officer and Vice President for Finance Ritu Kalra to discuss the financial results and ongoing economic pressures, as well as how the University is stewarding resources to its highest priorities.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length.
Gazette: How would you describe Harvard’s financial position at the close of the year?
Meredith Weenick: We see the year-end result in the context of a much broader transformation that began well before fiscal year 2026. Our stewardship has been focused on driving efficiencies and adapting our operations to meet the uncertainty of the moment. Our focus has been on resiliency. That’s not simply maintaining the status quo, but actually ensuring we have the resources to invest in our research and teaching, as well as other mission-related needs.
Ending the year with a surplus required lots of work in the Schools and units. We restructured our operations and reduced costs where possible. Without those interventions, we would have ended the year in deficit. I want to recognize that this is hard work, and it isn’t finished. We have to stay diligent across every aspect of managing the University to continue producing results that allow us to reinvest in our mission.
Ritu Kalra: As Meredith said, the surplus was a result of a tremendous amount of work. No School or unit was untouched, and that deserves acknowledgment.
It’s also worth putting the number in context. A $100 million surplus on a $6.7 billion revenue base is a 1.5 percent operating margin. That’s only five days of operations. We don’t need a surplus for its own sake. We need one because it allows us the flexibility to pay for investments like renewing the labs, classrooms, and housing we’re obligated to maintain for the next century. It also allows us to make the new investments that are essential to generating new knowledge. Together with the strong endowment return, it means we’ve closed the year on solid financial footing. The pressures we face are substantial and sustained, and we have to plan accordingly. But our community should also feel a level of confidence in our financial stability. It was not easy. We are enormously grateful to everyone who got us here.
What does resiliency mean in a year of uncertainty around federal research funding, restructuring in several parts of the University, and a strong endowment performance?
Kalra: Resiliency means absorbing pressures and adapting to new realities while holding steadfast to our core mission. Flexible financial resources are key to that. They let us direct funds to where they’re most needed, and to invest in the areas with the greatest promise. This is also why we must continue operating with discipline. The strong endowment return is a boost, but markets can take back what they give, and the uncertainty persists. Resiliency is what lets us advance our priorities while the landscape is still shifting.
Weenick: There’s also our human capacity for resiliency. We’re fortunate to have resources that provide some financial flexibility, but people power the University. I want to recognize everyone affected by the reorganizations and restructurings, and to honor the colleagues who have left our workforce through those painful decisions. People are the foundation of everything Harvard does, and building their capacity to absorb and adapt to change is as much a part of resiliency as our financial resources.
What gives you confidence that Harvard’s research enterprise is positioned to continue to be a leading engine for discovery and innovation?
Kalra: Harvard is as committed as ever to research that serves the nation and the world. Even as the federal government stepped back from funding research this past year, the University stepped up. We spent over $1.2 billion in research activity; a third of it was funded by Harvard itself.
We’re working to diversify the external sponsors who support that work by deepening our engagement with foundations and industry. It’s not just a matter of bringing in dollars — it’s about collaboration, about rethinking how the University partners with others to advance research in ways that we couldn’t have imagined a decade ago.
Meanwhile, the discoveries keep coming, from bringing quantum closer to practical use to contributing to the development of a new FDA-approved drug for pancreatic cancer. Our faculty are uniquely positioned to take on society’s hardest problems. We intend for Harvard to remain the place where those breakthroughs happen, and to work with partners so they happen at a greater scale.
Weenick: It’s the University’s responsibility to provide the infrastructure for that research. We recently announced a $150 million investment in research to support access to the tools, resources, and capacity our researchers need in areas including neuroscience, immunology, quantum, artificial intelligence, and energy and climate. That’s our obligation in this time of uncertainty — to make sure our faculty, students, and staff know that work can continue at a time of remarkable opportunity for discovery.
Philanthropy — including endowment distributions and current-use giving — is the University’s largest source of operating revenue. How did that support help the University sustain its mission during a disruptive year?
Kalra: A grant cycle can be five years, while the work of discovery can take decades. Philanthropy provides the kind of long-term, committed support that matches the time scale of a research university. It’s infused in every facet of Harvard, and it mattered this year more than ever. Donors committed more than $1.5 billion in gifts received, and we received over $640 million in gifts for current use — dollars available to be spent immediately on the challenges at hand. At a time of real uncertainty, alumni and friends chose to invest in Harvard’s teaching, research, and students, and we are grateful to them.
Every dollar of the endowment began as a gift. The endowment is built on philanthropy, and then it’s amplified by the work that Harvard Management Company does to invest it. I want to thank Narv Narvekar and his team. This year’s 27.1 percent endowment return will support greater distributions for years, and generations, to come.
Weenick: One place we put philanthropy to work is financial aid. In fiscal year 2026, the University provided more than $775 million in financial aid, including about $265 million in need-based scholarships for Harvard College students in the first year of the College’s expanded program. The College is now free for students from families earning $100,000 or less, and tuition-free for families earning $200,000 or less. This is a University priority, and it is fueled by philanthropy.
Another area where donors have responded to the University’s urgent need to support the next generation of researchers at Harvard is through the Research Accelerator Challenge, which has already raised more than $100 million for endowed Ph.D. fellowships at the Harvard Kenneth C. Griffin Graduate School of Arts and Sciences.
Every gift, no matter its size, makes a difference. That generosity is what makes the University accessible and opens more opportunities for our students, faculty, and researchers.
With a strong endowment return of 27.1 percent and a $100 million surplus, even in a challenging year, what is the reason for continuing to focus on financial capacity?
Kalra: It helps to start with unpacking what the endowment actually is, because it doesn’t provide financial capacity in the way people assume. It’s not a bank account. It’s roughly 15,000 separate funds, each given for a particular purpose — such as cancer research or immunotherapy — and we can’t divert them to payroll or facilities in another School. We do spend from them every year: The distribution funds nearly 40 percent of our operating budget. What we don’t do is spend more simply because the market had a good year. If we raised the distribution whenever returns were strong, we would have to cut it whenever they weren’t. We smooth it deliberately so that faculty, researchers, and students across generations can work with some certainty.
With the distribution already reflected in this year’s operating results, it’s worth unpacking the $100 million surplus because it nets two things that tell two different stories. The part of the budget we control — salaries and renewing our facilities — finished nearly $80 million in deficit, and that’s with a hiring freeze and after painful position reductions. Offsetting it is a $180 million surplus of restricted funds. These are gifts and distributions for specific purposes, and the surplus largely reflects timing differences between when the funds arrived and when we’ll spend them. The two aren’t interchangeable, which is why we keep returning to financial capacity. Even with the endowment fully at work, the flexible funds that pay for general operations are running a deficit.
Weenick: Which is why it is our obligation to run the University as efficiently and effectively as possible. That work is never done. Meeting the moment means making sure that our staff, faculty, and researchers have the tools they need for whatever comes next.
Understanding that the unrestricted portion of the University’s budget is running a deficit, how is Harvard approaching capital investment and priorities going forward?
Weenick: Investing in our physical plant is a key part of our stewardship. We need to anticipate the requirements of a university in the future — from educational spaces to research spaces to activities we haven’t yet dreamed of. That means making sure that we’re maintaining our buildings as we have them today, and making room for those spaces that we may need tomorrow. Our physical plant is vast, and its needs are enormous, particularly given the historic nature of our campus.
Our fiscal year 2026 capital spending of more than $950 million is roughly what it costs just to maintain our physical plant. Yet we need to address the backlog of deferred maintenance while also investing in the kinds of upgrades and expansions that today’s teaching and research require. That’s the financial capacity the University has to create by driving efficiencies, raising more money, and identifying other resources.
This isn’t a choice between buildings and people. These are the labs, libraries, and classrooms where our people do their work. But there are hard choices inside the physical plant, too. As we think about which projects come first, which come next, we need to make those choices with the long-term needs of the University in view.
Harvard leaders have previously spoken about the negative impacts of the federal excise tax on endowment earnings. How is the University managing such a large increase in that tax in FY27?
Kalra: This will be a significant headwind. Starting fiscal year 2027, the University is now subject to an 8 percent tax, up from 1.4 percent. We project that that will cost roughly $300 million a year, though the actual amount will depend on returns and how much of them we realize. In a year like this one, with a 27.1 percent return, the tax would be several times larger.
We’re already feeling it. The endowment distribution would have grown in fiscal year 2027, but we held it flat compared to fiscal year 2026 to account for the tax. Those are additional funds that would have supported research, teaching, and scholarships. Instead, we had to use them to pay for the tax.
In addition to the increased tax on the endowment and managing the impacts, what other factors are part of capacity and resilience planning for the University’s financial outlook?
Weenick: Maintaining Harvard’s academic excellence requires strategic choices. Harvard can do anything, but it can’t do everything all at once. Part of the University’s plan going forward is to make sure we have the room to continue to invest in the next new idea and the next opportunity for learning. Those are our highest priorities. It is going to require continued diligence and work to drive efficiencies to make sure that we can sustain our research and teaching mission as new opportunities emerge.
After a very challenging fiscal year 2026, it is important that we look ahead to what we will do with the University’s financial capacity. How will Harvard pursue excellence in service to the world in ways that we cannot even imagine today?

title: Delving into Stormwater Drainage
author: Matt Goisman
summary: Rodrigo spends summer with NYC Department of Environmental Protection
text:
When Typhoon Pablo struck the Philippines in 2012, flooding destroyed Aryenne Ysabelle Rodrigo’s home. Watching her community rebuild, and also her country’s mismanagement of flood control projects in the ensuing years – a scandal that led to widespread protests in 2025 – showed Rodrigo how essential it is for communities to have well-designed and properly inspected flood control systems in place.
“It’s very important for me to understand how connected we are to our environment, and how it affects communities,” she said.
Rodrigo, a fourth-year environmental science and engineering concentrator at the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (SEAS), spent her summer as an intern on the stormwater team at the New York City Department of Environmental Protection (DEP). She got to experience first-hand how a major metropolitan area handles stormwater permitting, from mapping the geographic region to reviewing project designs to conducting on-site inspections.
“With stormwater management practices in New York, I think one of the differences I see is that everything is digitized,” she said. “There’s also great cooperation between developers, not just public but also the private sector. There are clear criteria: if you disturb an amount of land, or if you make a place more impervious than it was before, then you have to submit a storm management practice design that would meet the water quality volume requirements.”
Rodrigo found her internship with the help of Harvard’s Mignone Center for Career Success. Her first month consisted mostly of reading manuals and attending meetings in the DEP’s office in Queens, but from there she transitioned to shadowing inspectors during stormwater management practice (SMP) inspections and visiting wastewater treatment facilities. She also used Python to develop a tool that could help optimize pipe configuration and size for upcoming stormwater drainage projects based on factors such as design constraints, excavation depth and cost.
“What we’re trying to avoid is an excess of piping,” she said. “Based on the parameters you input, the tool spits out the ideal diameter size and arrangement of those pipes to optimize the cost.”
The internship showed Rodrigo what can happen when a community properly manages its water infrastructure.
“The DEP has emphasized that historically, New York City’s harbor and waterways are the cleanest they have been in over a century,” she said. “I really see how important the job that they’re doing is to making the city habitable for people.”
As soon as her internship ended, Rodrigo turned her attention to another water-based project: Harvard’s chapter of Engineers Without Borders. She’s one of the team leads for the newest initiative, a project focused on improving water access in Mirador in Guatemala. Having previously worked on the water distribution project in the Los Sanchez community in the Dominican Republic, which was completed in August 2025, Rodrigo’s team wrapped up the summer with their initial assessment trip to Guatemala.
“The first interactions I had in Los Sanchez were interviews with local households,” she said. “It was really interesting to hear so many stories, especially of how this decade-long project changed their lives after getting access to water. I saw so many similarities from back home in the Philippines, and the stories really inspired me to continue working on the project. After Typhoon Pablo, my house was completely destroyed. A lot of volunteers from all around the world came in and helped rebuild our community. That showed me what it was like to be in a nonprofit organization giving back.”
Rodrigo’s ultimate goal is to someday use her experiences at SEAS to help her community. She’s devoted much of her time here to water-related challenges, but knows there are many aspects of environmental engineering that she hasn’t explored, such as remediation of toxic materials. After graduating, she hopes to immerse herself in these new areas, thus making her best suited to address the range of challenges her community faces.
“I find solving water problems very interesting, but I don't want to hold myself back,” she said. “Back home, I'm from a rural province in the Philippines. We still use groundwater and hand pumps for both primary and secondary water sources. It’s very important to me to continue gathering all the expertise and the knowledge that I need, and go through the development stages so I can help communities like the one I grew up in.”

title: First Large-Scale Study Shows How Doctors Use AI in Medicine
summary: The future of federally funded research at Harvard Medical School — supported by taxpayers and done in service to humanity — remains uncertain. Learn more.
text:
The future of federally funded research at Harvard Medical School — supported by taxpayers and done in service to humanity — remains uncertain. Learn more.
The first large-scale study of how often clinicians use artificial intelligence tools in patient care, who those clinicians are, and what they are using it for finds that a significant number of medical practitioners are using AI in the clinic and that they are often using it to explore treatment options for their patients in areas outside their clinical specialty.
The study, led by researchers at Harvard Medical School and Brigham and Women’s Hospital, looked at how 950,000 physicians, physician assistants, and nurse practitioners in the United States used OpenEvidence, a popular AI-enabled clinical information platform, over the last two and a half years. Most queries were related to clinical decision making (51.9 percent), particularly treatment and management. Diagnosis accounted for 13.9 percent of queries.
The results of this federally funded study were published Oct. 15 in JAMA.
“Two key takeaways are that an enormous number of physicians are using AI for clinical care and that they are often using it in areas where they don’t have specific expertise,” said corresponding author Anupam Jena, the Joseph P. Newhouse Professor of Health Care Policy in the Blavatnik Institute at HMS and HMS professor of medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital.
“Everyone appreciates the huge potential for AI to change how medicine is practiced, but right now we have limited information on how many doctors are using it, what they are using it for, and how it’s impacting patients,” Jena said. The JAMA study tackles the first two of those questions.
Dramatic increase in use of AI
The researchers found that use has been dramatic, in terms of both the speed and scale of adoption, Jena said. That was in contrast to what research showed with electronic health records, where the pace of adoption was slow and “only really occurred after government regulation,” Jena said.
From January 2024 to June 2026, the number of monthly active OpenEvidence users increased from 355 to 703,265, the team found. Over that time, practitioners included in the study submitted 270 million queries to the platform.
Jena and colleagues used a large language model to classify the clinical purpose and topic areas of a random sample of 38.8 million queries.
What are doctors using AI for?
The data showed that queries were frequently for aiding in treatment decisions rather than diagnostic tasks and that questions were often about subjects that were outside of the practitioner’s specialty. For example, surgeons often ask questions that are not about surgery, the team found.
The level of use varied across clinician types, specialties, and career stages.
The researchers compared the number of queries made by a particular specialty with the percentage of the physician workforce that they represent. Some specialties used more than their share of queries. Oncology/hematology specialists accounted for 3.8 percent of queries, while they comprise just 1.9 percent of the workforce and internal medicine doctors accounted for 27.3 percent of physician queries, while they make up 14.5 percent of the physician workforce. Other specialties, including radiology, orthopedics, and ophthalmology, used less than their share.
More than half of the users in the sample (556,200) were physicians. They submitted an average of 37 queries per month of use. Early-career physicians and those in oncology, hematology, internal medicine, and family medicine submitted a higher-than-average share of queries.
The next step will be to examine whether use of these tools improves clinical care, the researchers said.
“AI tools have become integrated into routine in clinical practice faster than almost any technology we’ve seen, but until now we’ve had very little data on how clinicians actually use them,” said first author Vishal Patel, HMS clinical fellow in surgery at Brigham and Women’s. “This research gives us an early picture of where these tools fit into clinical decision-making and where we need to study their accuracy and effects on patient care next.”
Three of the co-authors are employees of OpenEvidence, which did not fund the study but provided the de-identified data that was analyzed.
Authorship, funding, disclosures
Additional authors include Samuel G. Finlayson, Michael Liu-Hass, Mondira Ray, Jesse Burk-Rafel, and Travis I. Zack.
This research was supported by the National Institutes of Health/National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering (grant F32EB040202).
Finlayson reported being a salaried employee of OpenEvidence during the conduct of the study. Liu-Hass reported receiving personal fees from Accompany Health for consulting outside the submitted work. Ray reported receiving personal fees from OpenEvidence as a full-time employee outside the submitted work. Zack reported being the chief medical officer of OpenEvidence during the conduct of the study. Jena reported receiving personal fees from Analysis Group; Freakonomics, MD; Doubleday Books; The New York Times; Los Angeles Times; The Wall Street Journal; and Harry Walker Agency outside the submitted work and serving as an unpaid board member for the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS). No other disclosures were reported.

title: New Screening Platform Helps Identify Genes With Tissue-Rejuvenation Potential
summary: Researchers have developed a new method for predicting tissue age and screening for genes that affect the aging process.
text:
Researchers have developed a new method for predicting tissue age and screening for genes that affect the aging process.
Using these methods, the team — led by George Church, the Robert Winthrop Professor of Genetics in the Blavatnik Institute at Harvard Medical School and a core faculty member at the Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering at Harvard University, in collaboration with a group at the Basque Research and Technology Alliance in Spain — identified a gene that demonstrated age-reversal effects in lab experiments.
The findings, published Oct 14 in Nature Aging, offer a new way to search for genetic factors that could be manipulated to turn back the clock on aging cells and rejuvenate tissue.
The team first designed a machine-learning algorithm to predict the “transcriptomic age” — measured by changes in gene activity, also known as gene expression — of skin cells. They then used it to screen a focused collection of genes predicted to affect aging processes.
An RNA-regulating gene called SRSF1 scored highest for its ability to rejuvenate fibroblast cells when overexpressed. In lab experiments, SRSF1 reduced features that corresponded to several hallmarks of aging, such as cellular senescence (a biological process in which damaged cells stop dividing but do not die), proteostatic stress (disruptions in the normal balance and turnover of proteins), and “inflammaging” (chronic low-grade inflammation).
When SRSF1 was delivered to aging mice, it reduced the animals’ rate of aging and extended their lifespan by 14 percent.
“It has been a long-standing goal of my lab to devise clinically useful de-aging strategies by identifying genes that, when engineered in the genome for under- or overexpression in aging target tissues, extend human health span,” said Church. “Our platform and findings on SRSF1 are an important step on that quest.”
Authorship, funding, disclosures
Alexandru M. Plesa and Sascha Jung are co-first authors of this work. Antonio del Sol is co-corresponding author. Additional authors include Helen H. Wang, Fawad Omar, Michael Shadpour, David Choy Buentello, Maria C. Perez-Matos, Naftali Horwitz, George Cai, Zhen Kai Ngian, Carol Magalhaes, Amy J. Wagers, and William B. Mair.
The study was funded by the Aging and Longevity-Related Research Fund, the Astera Fund at the Silicon Valley Community Foundation, the Wyss Institute Synthetic Biology Platform, and the Spanish Ministry of Science and Innovation (grant PID2020-118605RB-I00).
Plesa, Jung, Wang, del Sol, and Church are listed as inventors on patent application US20250313599A1, which covers the use of SRSF1 and other factors. Plesa and Church are cofounders of and hold equity in RegulaBio, an early-stage company developing therapeutics for age-related diseases. Additional aging-related disclosures for Church can be found in the paper.

title: ‘I don’t know if this is going to turn out well.’
author: Sy Boles
summary: With a split-screen view of a turbulent tech revolution, Michael Brenner makes a case for the value of human guidance
text:
Michael Brenner is one of Harvard’s inaugural Catalyst Professors, a role designed to foster collaboration between the University and the private sector — in his case, at Google. Brenner, who has appointments in Harvard physics and at SEAS, has been thinking deeply about what it means to do math and science in the age of AI, how to teach students, and the value of collaborating with industry. We talked to him about the role of universities in this uncertain moment in the history of knowledge.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length.
Gazette: There’s been a lot of discussion about the role of universities in the age of artificial intelligence. Many people think that part of it is to be a kind of moral force, a defender of human values in the face of automation. What do you make of that? 
Brenner: I can’t talk about morality. But let me give you my version of that.
Obviously, the type of work that’s building out the LLM systems is simply impractical for a university, even Harvard, to lead at — just look at the cost of a data center. But we have an absolutely central role, both universities in general and Harvard in particular, which is that we’re arbiters of truth.
The example I would give is that when the Navier-Stokes result came out — and this is something that I worked on when I was a graduate student — I dropped everything to find out if it’s correct.
I basically spent five days working on it, and although I’m not quite convinced that it’s correct, it’s clear to me that progress has been made. But I think the world has been much too quick to declare that because the computer-assisted proof by an LLM has solved one of the major open problems in mathematics, that therefore the solution is actually true.
I mean, I’m not the arbiter — the world is going to have to decide when progress has been made, when arguments are true. We have to decide when the directions are correct. Maybe morality does come into it. So all right, fine, we’ve arrived at morality.
What should universities be doing?
There should be professors who are committed to the pursuit of knowledge, genuine understanding, without bias, for what is true and what is important, and we should be educating students to do that. That’s our job. And if there are machines that have opinions on that, great. I’m all for listening to the opinions of any entity that has opinions. But I don’t think machines can be the arbiters of truth.
“I’m all for listening to the opinions of any entity that has opinions. But I don’t think machines can be the arbiters of truth.”
In my view, the role of Harvard, and the role of universities in general, is even more important than it was before.
I don’t really have much patience for the party line you’ll hear in the newspapers, which is that now that we have machines that can do science, do we really need graduate students? I think the answer is that we need more graduate students, not less. The reason is that graduate students should be more effective now. The Harvard Math Department should be doing better in 10 years than it did in the last 10 years because either they’ll decide these tools are bullshit and they won’t use them, or they’ll figure out how to use them to advance mathematics faster, which is good.
Can you articulate that “party line” argument, and why you think it’s wrong?
The party line is that now that we have AI, fields like mathematics are being transformed. Problems that have been open for 50 years are being solved, and we humans can’t understand the solution, and isn’t it amazing that AI solved it? The party line is that this is where we’re going as a society — that intelligence is going to be entrusted to machines, and that’s where all knowledge is going to come from, so we don’t need people, we don’t need to train experts in mathematics and physics and chemistry. And I just don’t believe that at all.
The expert is actually more important. Because anyone can think that they solved the Riemann hypothesis, but we need experts who can actually figure out if that’s true.
For a lot of people, it’s scary to hear these companies saying they’re building things that might kill us all, might put us out of work, might already be escaping our control — but look! It can also make you a meal plan! It’s a hard vision to get on board with.
I say this as a person who’s talking to you from the Google Cambridge office, and I understand — or I think I understand — what the state of the art is. So I’m biased. But I also think these things are dangerous. I do not think this is a joke. I’m really worried. I spend part of my time working on AI safety for this reason: I cannot morally do what I do without trying to figure this out. Until now, it’s taken deep knowledge to use science to cause harm. We’re transitioning to a society where maybe you don’t need somebody like me, a physicist with deep knowledge. This is an extraordinary risk to society.
The governments of the world are going to have to figure out how to deal with this, and that cuts back to Harvard.
We have on one hand a technical problem related to computer science, which is, “How do I take a model and make it smart enough so it can help us develop novel vaccines, but safe enough to not give out dangerous knowledge to the wrong people?” That requires physics knowledge, biology knowledge. It also requires deep knowledge about policy, international relations. At Harvard we have all of that expertise.
“Wouldn’t you like a place where there are deep thinkers with deep knowledge of how to influence government, how to understand physics, how to understand computer science, and who are unbiased, who aren’t doing it to make money, who are just in it to help humanity?”
Wouldn’t you like a place where there are deep thinkers with deep knowledge of how to influence government, how to understand physics, how to understand computer science, and who are unbiased, who aren’t doing it to make money, who are just in it to help humanity?
Can you take more about your perspective as a Catalyst Professor, with appointments both at Harvard and at Google?
A big part of the reason I’m at Google is that there are things I can work on here that, to be totally honest, I can’t work on from the University. We have the expertise at Harvard, but we can’t stop an LLM from giving the answers it’s going to give. There’s a level of influence that’s only possible inside these companies.
I’m also more able to be helpful to my students. I have a class of 120 undergraduates who are worried about getting jobs. They’re asking me, “What do I need to learn to make sure I can be relevant in this world?” If I didn’t spend part of my time at Google, I wouldn’t be able to give them the best advice. At SEAS, we’re really lucky to have both me and Boaz Barak with Catalyst appointments. We have a very good view of what’s going on inside both Google and OpenAI, and I can’t believe that’s not a good thing. Boaz is teaching AI alignment to graduate students as someone who’s doing that work at OpenAI, and, I mean, that’s who I’d want teaching me AI alignment: a great intellectual who is actually doing the work.
What has it been like for you personally to be on the frontier of AI development?
I have to be honest with you: I’ve spent most of my life at Harvard training students, and I continue to do so. In the end, I think that’s the biggest impact I’ll have made in the world: training people who then go off and do things. But I also feel like I’ve been training my entire life for this: the combination of things that are required to think about this, the technical pieces.
I don’t know if this is going to turn out well. But I also feel that I have some influence, certainly more influence than anyone who might be very technical but isn’t also inside Google. On the other hand, my primary interest is to advance knowledge and to help train people to function in the world. I hope that answers the question.

title: How can a book make you cry?
author: Alvin Powell
summary: Harvard graduate and new Nobel laureate reflects on his undergraduate years, early lab experiences, and his later work.
text:
How can words make us laugh? Make us cry? During Nobel laureate Karl Deisseroth’s time at the College, the question went from a matter of literature and writing to one of biochemistry and science.
Deisseroth’s pursuit of those mysteries led him from a 1992 Harvard bachelor’s degree to a Stanford University M.D./Ph.D. and a career as a clinical psychiatrist and researcher.
