Deisseroth’s work developing optogenetics, which uses light to activate single neurons in the brain, has opened new windows to observe and understand the brain. The work’s importance was recognized with this year’s Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
In this edited conversation, Deisseroth, Stanford University’s D.H. Chen Professor of Bioengineering and of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, reflected on his undergraduate years and on the throughlines, apparent even then, that led from early lab experiences through his later work.
Gazette: Your family traveled when you were little. Do you consider Boston your childhood home or was there another city that your family settled in?
Karl Deisseroth: My father was a medical intern at the Beth Israel Hospital on the Longwood campus. I was born there. He was a Harvard affiliate but wasn’t a professor. He became a hematologist, oncologist, and had appointments around the country.
So I spent a lot of time in Northern California, when my dad was at the University of California in San Francisco; in Houston, when he was at the MD Anderson Cancer Center; and in Maryland, when he was at the NIH. I’ve been around, but I definitely see myself as a Boston native, a Red Sox fan, and a Patriots fan.
Who were you when you first got to Harvard?
We had just moved from Northern California to Texas, so I was coming from a one-year, senior-year stint at a high school in Texas. It was a good school.
The other thing unusual about me is that I was only 16 when I went to Harvard. I started school a year early and then skipped second grade, so it definitely was important that I got good preparation.
Did the fact that you were younger affect your course through Harvard?
It was not something I would necessarily recommend — I think that’s why you don’t see it much these days. But I had a great time at Harvard. I learned a ton and made some great friends.
I was in Winthrop House, and all my friends were physics and math folks. So I had breakfast, lunch, and dinner with physicists for at least three of the four years I was there.
I know you were busy in the lab, but did you have time for extracurriculars?
I did wrestling freshman year and focused on lab work after that.
I started as a developmental neurobiologist in the lab of Martin Shankland — he’s in Texas now. I worked on homeobox genes that regulate body plan formation in leeches.
I was always interested in the brain and thought I should start with the most accessible preparation. Leech development is pretty interesting. All the cells are accessible because the embryos are transparent, and you can actually track the lineage of each cell as it develops.
I thought that would be a cool opportunity to see how a nervous system is formed.
How much time were you spending in the lab at that point?
I did an honors thesis and spent as much time as I could in Martin’s lab. What was hard was that it was at the Medical School, and you have to take a shuttle bus to the Longwood campus and back. I rode the M2 more than I care to remember.
My major was biochemical sciences — I think they’ve reorganized the departments since then. We were based in the Sherman Fairchild building, and I took a lot of classes there. I also was a teaching fellow. I taught quantum biochemistry.
But you were first interested in creative writing?
My first semester, I took a creative writing course and that was the direction where I thought I was headed. I was writing poems and short stories, and I loved the power of the written word, how it could make me feel and make others feel.
I still feel that way. I just got distracted by science.
“It was more about where feelings come from, how this collection of cells can create a subjective feeling. To me, that seemed like a very deep mystery — it still does — and I wanted to understand that better.”
What made you decide to chuck writing for science?
It was gradual. I had taken introductory chemistry and biochemistry classes, and I started to get excited by how other fields — immunology, developmental biology — had made a lot of headway by getting to know the cells very deeply.
So my attraction to the leech system is that you could access the individual cells directly and consistently through the lifespan. I thought if we can do for the brain what was done for developmental biology and for immunology, that would be amazing. I got enthralled and headed in that direction.
Was there any connection between your interest in the brain and in creative writing, from the standpoint of where in the brain ideas come from?
There was definitely a connection, but it was more about where feelings come from, how this collection of cells can create a subjective feeling. To me, that seemed like a very deep mystery — it still does — and I wanted to understand that better.
Does your work in psychiatry follow that path as well?
Yes, but it was not clear from the beginning.
I was interested in feeling and how it could be assembled from cells. That was a nice connection with my interest in writing and words because I knew that words were a very precise way of causing feeling.
Of course, that only works with people, so I thought, “I’ve got to work with the human brain so I have to go to medical school.”
I did an M.D./Ph.D. program at Stanford though I wasn’t at all thinking psychiatry. I was thinking neurosurgery because I knew that neurosurgeons had direct access to the cells of the human brain. I was thinking that would be the route.
But time spent in a psychiatric ward put you on the path to psychiatry?
It was very unexpected. This was during the later stage of medical school. It was my first exposure and reset my path completely.
What was so moving or influential?
One was an encounter with a patient, and another was more cultural about the specialty. I had a very intense interaction with a patient with schizoaffective disorder, which is a schizophrenia-like symptom. It was a person who was otherwise healthy but was very upset and had a very deep paranoid delusion.
I was so struck by how different his reality was from mine and how his brain had constructed for him a different reality.
I thought, “Look at this guy. His brain is giving him this emotion, this anger, this altered perception.” That’s what I was interested in. Here’s somebody who’s suffering, maybe I could help people like this and increase understanding at the same time.
I hadn’t quite realized the clarity of this psychiatric state, how much help the patients needed, and how much it could teach everybody else.
The cultural aspect was that I also did a neurosurgery rotation, and I realized that the nature of psychiatry is that it gives more time to talk and think in an intellectual way. So I thought, all signs point to psychiatry.
It seems like progress on some of these psychiatric conditions has been stuck for a while. Are we starting to make progress with some of them?
I think things are starting to move. We went through a long time in psychiatry when there were neither new classes of medication nor new deep insights into the nature of psychiatric illness. Both of those are changing now.
Your development of optogenetics is being used in labs all over the world. Are there specific advances — whether in your lab or another — that are particularly gratifying to you and show how impactful that work has been?
Certainly, on the basic science side, there have been more than 10,000 papers — discoveries from labs around the world — using our methods. We’ve been teaching people how to use these methods. So it’s been very gratifying to see all the work that’s been done and all the insights that have emerged.
On the translational side, it’s also moving. For example, one issue in psychiatry is that we haven’t really known the cells that are causal — that are actually making the problems or that might correct the problems. There are ideas, there are correlations, but you don’t know what’s causing the problem.
With optogenetics, you can know that, because you’re having a direct, precise, real-time, causal impact on cells. And that brings me all the way back to my initial motivation of getting direct access to cells, except now we’re using light and a gene from algae.
We’ve been able to bring that causality to preclinical and then clinical work. For example, right now there are medications for autism and for schizophrenia that are well advanced in the clinical trial process.
For both, these treatments were validated with optogenetic causality. And these are pills — which makes them easier to give — and they have that crucial causal validation. It’s a firm bedrock to stand on.

title: My chatbot is my boyfriend. What’s the harm?
author: Samantha Laine Perfas
summary: Sherry Turkle’s ‘Artificial Intimacy’ is a book-length response to ‘fundamental lie we’re telling ourselves’
text:
What happens when we replace humans with machines in our deepest relationships?
That’s the driving question behind MIT sociologist Sherry Turkle’s new book, “Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines.” In an age in which more people are treating chatbots as close friends, even romantic partners, the Harvard alumna — A.B. ’69, Ph.D. ’76 in sociology — sees a troubling reality deficit not only in our individual lives but in a society whose problems demand human ingenuity and collaboration. She talked about the consequences in a recent conversation with the Gazette.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length.
Gazette: In your book you say that we’re primed at a young age to turn to machines for companionship. How so?
Sherry Turkle: Over the last few decades, we’ve been introduced to Tamagotchis, Furbies, Aibos, and PAROs, these robotic toys that helped me see just how powerful this psychology is: We nurture what we love, and we love what we nurture. This first generation of objects made people think, “Oh, an object who loves me and I love it.” It showed how ready we were for that kind of engagement. Then came social media, the gateway drug to artificial intimacy. We got used to spending our time on screens, turning to social media when we felt sad or bored. And now, those initial objects have been reanimated by the generative AI revolution. I like to say first we talked to each other, then we talked to each other through machines, and now we just talk to machines.
What is the problem with machines tapping into our human desire for connection?
Using the first person is the original sin of chatbots. They’re not offering connection; that’s the fundamental deceit. There is no “I” there, and we’re biologically wired to respond to this. We’re tempted to accept these objects as kin, but they’re not. You could be having the greatest, best conversation with your ChatGPT, but when you get up, it doesn’t care if you cook pasta or kill yourself. There is nobody there who cares about you.
Industries like healthcare, education, and science have touted chatbots as cost-effective solutions to overwhelmed systems. What do you think is missing from those conversations?
“I think we have a lack of imagination and political will to solve the real problems. Technology exacerbates the problem and then says only technology can solve it. It’s the oldest game in the technology industry playbook.”
Sherry Turkle
I think we have a lack of imagination and political will to solve the real problems. Technology exacerbates the problem and then says only technology can solve it. It’s the oldest game in the technology industry playbook. Right now, we have social breakdown. And at the same time, we are defunding programs for therapy, social support, and social work. Then technology makes it worse. Everybody’s at a screen, there’s a loneliness crisis. And then, oh, my goodness! Our social media platforms will give you 12 new chatbot friends plus an artificial therapist. It reveals a cowardice — an unwillingness to face what our real problems are.
People like to say there aren’t enough people in these industries. Well, yeah, if you take away all the funding and turn your resources to building data centers, there won’t be. My work is a wake-up call: What’s your end game when there’s no community resources for you and all you have is to sit alone talking to something that really isn’t there? I don’t find that dignified for the people we love and the people we’re going to become. People may be smitten now, but in the long run, this is not a good path.
A question you get asked is, “If people are reporting feeling happier, less lonely, and more fulfilled in their chatbot relationship, what’s the problem?” How do you respond to that?
The problem is that there’s something wonderful and sustaining about what people can offer people.
I believe that reality really needs us right now. It needs us in our families. It needs us to raise children in a very challenging time. The garbage still needs to be picked up, there’s an ecological crisis that needs immediate attention, there’s a political system that’s shredding democratic values. Reality needs us.
Chatbots have undergone a transition: At first, they were seen as better than nothing, but nowadays some people prefer them to humans. What’s the attraction?
People often say to me about their chatbots, “I feel so heard.” But you’re not being heard at all. The bot can pretend that there’s somebody there who loves you, and no human being can do that in this friction-free way. People are difficult. But we have to get back into what people can offer and the chatbots cannot.
Having a “relationship” with a chatbot is a fundamental lie we’re telling ourselves. But another danger is that you start to think empathy is what’s coming out of the machine. You start to look at the people in your life and say, “Well, this friction-free, always-accepting-me chatbot — my people are not doing that for me.” That’s dangerous.

title: State-of-the-art performance space in A.R.T.’s new home to be named Blavatnik Theater
author: gazettebeckycoleman
summary: Move builds on businessman and philanthropist’s longstanding ties to University, commitment to advancing innovation, education, arts.
text:
The American Repertory Theater announced today the largest performance space in its new home will be named The Blavatnik Theater.
The naming of the state-of-the-art venue in the David E. and Stacey L. Goel Center for Creativity & Performance, which will open in May, comes in recognition of a major gift from the Blavatnik Family Foundation, founded by businessman and philanthropist Sir Leonard Blavatnik, MBA ’89.
Made possible through the generosity of Len and Emily Blavatnik, the fully flexible venue is designed to foster artistic innovation and creative collaboration while advancing A.R.T.’s commitment to expanding the boundaries of theater.
“Harvard and A.R.T. bring together exceptional talent and creativity. We are delighted to support this innovative new theater, where artists will bring ambitious ideas to the stage,” Blavatnik said.
The Blavatnik Theater is where A.R.T. will produce large-scale productions like the ones created over the last two decades that have gone on to Broadway and toured the world. Despite its size, the space features a unique level of intimacy and energy between audience and performers.
“Life on Mars,” the inaugural A.R.T. production at its new home, will feature the music of the late pop music icon David Bowie and be directed by Diane Paulus, the Terrie and Bradley Bloom Artistic Director of American Repertory Theater.
The Blavatnik Theater is one of two dedicated indoor performances spaces in the Goel Center. Inspired by the sight lines and intimacy of A.R.T.’s current venue, the Loeb Drama Center, the space will accommodate multiple stage positions, seating configurations, and theatrical designs. Its 700 seats — 160 more than the current venue — will be distributed across the main level and two levels of galleries.
Retractable seating, movable galleries, and adjustable stage elements will allow the space to be transformed for each production, from a traditional theater to a thrust-stage configuration or open studio that will accommodate 1,000 standing. Flexible rigging and integrated lighting, sound, and video systems will give artists further freedom to reimagine the relationship between the stage and the audience.
“The Blavatnik Theater is a truly magnificent space that will give artists endless opportunities to create transformative theatrical experiences for decades to come. We celebrate Len Blavatnik’s commitments to imagination, innovation, and to reaching audiences around the world. I am profoundly grateful to Len and Emily for their generosity in support of Harvard and of A.R.T.’s mission to expand the boundaries of theater, always including the audience as a partner,” Paulus said.
The naming gift builds on Blavatnik’s longstanding relationship with Harvard and his commitment to advancing innovation, education, and the arts. A member of the Harvard Global Advisory Council, he has supported University initiatives through the Blavatnik Family Foundation spanning biomedical research, life-science entrepreneurship, and public policy, including a historic commitment to Harvard Medical School and the Blavatnik Biomedical Accelerator.
The A.R.T.’s new home is located at 175 North Harvard St. in Allston, a hub of innovation and creativity where neighbors, entrepreneurs, researchers, and the arts are coming together to encourage collaboration, discovery, and community. The Goel Center will anchor Harvard’s growing arts presence in the neighborhood and provide flexible, adaptive spaces in which to rehearse, create, teach, and convene.
The A.R.T. received its certificate of occupancy last week. A ribbon-cutting marking the Goel Center’s public opening will be held April 5. “Life on Mars” will begin performances May 18.

title: Living longer, disease-free
author: Sy Boles
summary: Healthy Aging Symposium convenes experts to discuss everything from precision nutrition to clues in biology of dogs.
text:
Getting old is inevitable. But getting sick as we get old is not.
That was the message of the first annual Healthy Aging Symposium, hosted by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and supported by the Danone Institute of North America.
“Not only do we know now that we can slow aging in the lab, but thanks to advances in molecular biology starting about 40 years ago, biologists and geroscientists have actually been able to lift up the hood and look inside the engine and see why it is, how it is that we’re able to slow aging,” said keynote speaker Daniel Promislow, senior scientist and scientific adviser at the Jean Mayer USDA Human Nutrition Research Center on Aging at Tufts University.
Hundreds of experts, students, and postdocs in biology, social science, nutrition, environmental health, epidemiology, policy, and other disciplines convened to share expertise in the rapidly growing science of healthy aging. Presentation topics included environmental health and immune resilience, the biomarkers of aging, and intermittent fasting.
The symposium was the brainchild of William Mair, a professor of molecular metabolism at the Chan School and the director of its Healthy Aging Initiative.
“We launched the Healthy Aging Initiative to try to build toward a greater vision that changes how we think about and fund work on aging,” Mair said. The symposium “is an early example of this, giving us a rare opportunity to highlight the breadth of research at the Chan School in one place. My goal is that our initiative and events like this catalyze a unified focus on healthy aging across the wider University.”
Although Mair studies the molecular and cellular mechanisms of aging, he takes a decidedly public-health approach to the problem. In the 20th century alone, Mair said, average U.S. life expectancy rose by 30 years, largely thanks to public health interventions such as clean water, sanitation, and vaccines. But as more people survive into old age, more develop the diseases of longevity, such as metabolic and neurodegenerative disorders.
As Chan School Dean of the Faculty Andrea Baccarelli, put it, “The average American can expect to live the last 12 years of their lives with multiple comorbidities, often with a fair burden not only to the health systems in society but to families, to caregivers, and to everyone around them.”
Living longer is a good problem to have, Mair said, but a problem nonetheless.
“How do we think about the next century of public health, and try to make it so we can all age healthier, not just live a long time?”
Frank Hu, Fredrick J. Stare Professor of Nutrition and Epidemiology at the Chan School, sees hope in what he calls “Nutrition 3.0.” Nutrition 1.0 focused on preventing nutrient deficiencies; Nutrition 2.0 was about preventing chronic disease. The next frontier, he said, is precision nutrition and healthy longevity.
Hu draws on data from the Nurses’ Health Study, a long-running cohort study of some 300,000 healthcare workers. The study just celebrated its 50th anniversary this year, so its original participants are now in their 70s and older. It’s a massive body of data on dietary habits and the biomarkers of aging.
“We’ve made tremendous progress in improving nutrition and epidemiology methods, so now we have much better dietary assessment tools, which have been rigorously vetted, which can actually reduce measurement error,” Hu said.
In other words, broadly speaking, we know what works in nutrition — though, Hu added, getting people to follow through on it remains a challenge.
Less clear, at least right now, is the efficacy of moonshot ideas for extending lifespan through targeted therapies. Promislow runs the Dog Aging Project at Tufts, a cohort study of 55,000 canine companions. Why dogs? They share our living environments, have diverse genes, and develop many of the same chronic diseases we do, but they age much faster. And, Promislow added, people get more invested in research about dogs than about fruit flies. “When I give a talk about fruit fries to a general public audience, I can guarantee that nobody ever comes up to me afterward and says, ‘Oh my goodness, I love fruit flies,’” he joked.
Promislow’s team has identified metabolites that predict mortality in dogs — metabolites that humans share, in similar hazard ratios. The team is now enrolling dogs in a clinical trial testing whether the drug rapamycin can delay the onset of disease. Given how fast dogs age, the study could show results in as little as five years. “There’s huge potential for the biological community to learn a lot from dogs,” he said.
In a day that drew connections across disciplines and research methods, Mair credited the Chan School’s capacity to bring people together.
“The Chan School of Public Health is unique as a place to tackle healthy aging as we have experts under one roof that tackle the problem from completely different angles, from lab-based discovery science, nutrition, and environmental exposure to epidemiology, population science, social science, policy, and implementation. Healthy aging for all will require everyone to come together to effect real change,” he said.

title: Which grade is most important to a child’s development?
author: Liz Mineo
summary: Stats suggest high stakes for one year in particular. A literacy researcher, practitioner, and former school principal weighs in.
text:
Pamela Mason is senior lecturer in education at Harvard Graduate School of Education and co-chair of the Teaching and Teacher Leadership Program.
As a literacy researcher, practitioner, and former school principal, I would say that every year is the most important year in a child’s life. When children start out in preschool or kindergarten, they’re so excited about learning and having teachers and friends who they learn with and from. In kindergarten, they learn some pre-reading skills. In first grade, they’re very excited about learning to read, and they start reading a little bit independently with picture books. As they grow older, they are excited about using their reading to learn about other things. All that learning is foundational to literacy because as children are learning to sound out words and attach letters to sounds, they learn to read and write whole words. They also learn to make meaning from both what they’re reading and what they’re writing.
When they move to third grade, that is when we see children make the transition from learning to read to reading to learn, which is why some experts see this grade as pivotal. Literacy pioneer Jeanne Chall wrote the book “Stages of Reading Development,” in which she made that fairly bright line between learning to read and reading to learn. Another reason why third grade is important is because it’s mandated that the students be tested objectively in third grade in many states. We don’t have a national test in the United States, and in some states and some districts, if children don’t meet a certain score on the third-grade test, they may be retained.
“I always tell my literacy interns that their job is to put themselves out of a job.”
There is a lot of focus on the instruction in third grade, and a lot of anxiety on the part of parents. Even though the test is given in third grade, the third-grade teachers can’t teach everything that the children need to know to be successful. It’s a group effort from kindergarten, first, and second, into third grade. The learning and love of learning and student success start in kindergarten, and it’s as much about what a child knows as it is how the child is motivated to know and learn.
Although Chall coined the “learning to read, reading to learn” statement, children are reading to learn before third grade. However, at third grade more of the disciplinary learning comes from being engaged in written text.
The National Assessment of Education Progress and the National Research Council have done reports that show that third grade is a predictor of future academic achievement, high school graduation, and career success. They have the statistics. It just feels that you’re dooming a young learner on the basis of a test score, and I’ve seen children who didn’t do well in third grade and, after getting the extra support that they need, become very successful. I know that there are people building prisons on the basis of third-grade scores in communities, and it feels like a self-fulfilling prophecy. Professionally and personally, that makes me uncomfortable.
In many schools across the country, there are available resources to help third-graders who are struggling. Schools can use reading specialists, who can be supportive of both the teacher and the learners, and literacy coaches who work primarily with the teachers, so they can help the teachers differentiate their instruction, provide some review and reinforcement instruction for children who don’t seem to be moving along at the expected pace. I always tell my literacy interns that their job is to put themselves out of a job; that they work one-on-one with struggling readers to give them the support and strategies to access the curriculum in the classroom and then their intervention work is done.
— As told to Liz Mineo, Harvard Staff Writer

title: Children Are Left Out of Medical AI. A New Method Could Help.
summary: In the field of radiology, AI models have the potential to improve imaging analysis, speed up diagnoses, and catch errors that might otherwise be missed. But the vast majority of these models are trained on adult data and don’t translate well to infants and children, keeping these advances out of reach of neonatal and pediatric health.
text:
At a glance
- Researchers adapted an adult X-ray AI model for newborns with data from 30 hospitals, using a method designed to keep each hospital’s data in place.
- The new model outperformed adult models trained on pediatric data from a single hospital at 29 of 30 sites, even when tested on that hospital’s own images.
- This approach could be generalized to adapt other adult-trained AI models for use in children without needing large amounts of pediatric data to be added to public imaging datasets.
In the field of radiology, AI models have the potential to improve imaging analysis, speed up diagnoses, and catch errors that might otherwise be missed. But the vast majority of these models are trained on adult data and don’t translate well to infants and children, keeping these advances out of reach of neonatal and pediatric health.
“Because it’s so much harder to get data for children, this transformative technology is disproportionately being developed to help adults,” said Vishwanatha Rao, a member of Pranav Rajpurkar’s biomedical informatics lab at Harvard Medical School. “Children are being left behind.”
A large part of the reason for the gap is that medical records on newborns and children are subject to strict privacy regulations and tend to remain within the institution where the child is a patient, leaving data less accessible to train robust AI models. According to Rao and colleagues, children represent less than 1 percent of public medical imaging datasets.
Rao led and is co-first author on a new study, published Oct. 13 in Nature Biomedical Engineering, showing that models trained on adult radiographs can be adapted for infants using data from multiple hospitals without sensitive information ever needing to leave each institution. The model travels, but the data stays in-house.
The team believes its proof-of-principle approach could be extended to adapt other adult-trained AI models for pediatric use, addressing critical gaps in the deployment of pediatric medical AI.
“Our goal is to figure out how to make medical AI models work for everyone, including vulnerable populations where data can’t easily be shared,” said senior author Rajpurkar, associate professor of biomedical informatics in the Blavatnik Institute at HMS. “Now we’ve come up with a method which would allow for every institution to keep its data within its walls.”
Training sequentially
The researchers started with a model that had been trained on adult data to assess whether breathing tubes have been placed correctly. Breathing tubes, or endotracheal tubes, are crucial for treating respiratory issues, and there is little margin for error, especially in newborns.
Studies have shown that AI models can quickly flag potential issues and shorten the time it takes for radiologists to review and correct tube placement. Multiple AI tools have already received FDA clearance for this task in adults, but none of them are cleared for infants.
Rajpurkar and colleagues collected 2,965 chest X-rays from 30 neonatal intensive care units across 20 countries and territories. To simulate a scenario in which the data never leaves the hospital, the researchers trained the model sequentially on each institution’s data.
Despite differences in image quality and characteristics, the new model outperformed adult models trained on pediatric data from a single hospital at 29 of 30 sites, even when tested on that hospital’s own images, which the new model had never seen.
The fully trained model was able to identify the location of the tip of the endotracheal tube — used to gauge whether the tube is too shallow or too deep — with an average error of 0.67 cm. Existing models adapted to children with data from a single institution averaged errors of 1.29 cm, and adult models were off by an average of 4.30 cm.
“We tested the model on a hospital it had never seen before, and it did better than a model trained on scans from that specific hospital — that’s a pretty powerful result,” said Rao, who is an MD-PhD student at the University of Pennsylvania. “And compared to the original adult model, it’s leaps and bounds better.”
Medical AI for all
Only 17 percent of FDA-authorized AI medical devices are labeled for use in children. While this particular model was trained on endotracheal tube placement, the approach could be generalized to adapt other adult models for pediatric use, the researchers said.
“This is a general framework that shows a cheap, privacy-preserving approach to take advantage of existing adult information and get it to work on children,” Rao said. “It could usher in a whole new generation of AI models that work for kids, adapted through this broad methodology.”
The method isn’t limited to pediatrics, either. The same framework could potentially be applied to any patient population that is underrepresented in AI training data.
“A lot of what research is meant to accomplish is showing that something is possible,” Rajpurkar said. “We’ve shown there’s a system by which you can tune these models without sensitive data leaving a hospital.”

title: Are analytics making pro sports less fun?
author: Jacob Sweet
summary: Some say they rob games of color and spontaneity, but others argue the changes aren’t always for the worse.
text:
Today, sports analytics discussions from the 2011 movie “Moneyball” often seem quaint. The idea of a team using data to find players who may be more valuable than meets the eye (and less expensive) no longer surprises anyone.
“The numbers have won in terms of how sports are trained, practiced, and taught,” said Alex Speier ’98, a Boston Globe sports reporter and author of “Homegrown: How The Red Sox Built a Champion from the Ground Up.” “The number of people who are employed as analysts in sports has exploded.”
One study from MIT found that just 10 data analysts worked across the NBA in 2009. By 2023, there were 132. That same year, the MLB considered limiting how much teams could spend on areas like analytics, in part to ensure competitive equity between more and less wealthy franchises.
That professional sports teams have embraced data analysis is clear. There is less agreement over whether these analytics have made the games more entertaining.
For some the answer is yes. Stat-oriented fans can now find podcasts, or entire alternative broadcasts, devoted to numbers-heavy analysis.
At the same time, some fans, coaches, players, and broadcasters, like Hall of Fame basketball player Charles Barkley, bemoan the role of analytics in the modern game. “That’s why the league sucks,” he said about the widespread increase in three-point shots, which Barkley thinks undercuts the role of play strategy and spontaneity. “I hate analytics.”
In his undergraduate course “Sports Economics,” lecturer Judd Cramer discusses the relationship between analytics and entertainment as a potential principal-agent problem.
“If I own 30 McDonald’s franchises and one of them figures out a new way to make french fries better, I’m super happy,” he said. “But if I’m the MLB and I find out the Rays are trying to get hit by more pitches to score more runs, that’s not good for the league as a whole.”
The same goes for any league. The success of prolific shooting teams like the Golden State Warriors and Houston Rockets led to leaguewide imitation. (Teams today shoot more than twice the number of three-pointers as 20 years ago.) In baseball, teams prioritize extremely fast pitching and home-run-or-bust batting, leading to more strikeouts and home runs but fewer triples and “finesse” pitchers without explosive power.
“The number of people who are employed as analysts in sports has exploded.”
Alex Speier
MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred agreed with a league owner who said analytics were a “race to nowhere” and has approved rules aimed at making the game more fast-paced and exciting for fans. The MLB pitch clock has cut around half an hour of idle time per game. The league also increased the size of the bases to encourage more stolen bases.
But while many think teams’ statistical orientation makes games less fun to watch, that reputation may not be fully deserved. As the experts point out, analytics often lead to more scoring.
“More scoring, generally speaking, is more exciting,” said Kevin Rader, a senior preceptor in statistics who has taught “Introduction to Data Science for Sports Analytics.” NFL teams throw much more than they did decades ago. Teams are much likelier to go for it on fourth down, risking a turnover to maintain possession of the ball.
Critics focus on the ubiquity of three-point shots in the NBA game, but the current playing style is also much faster than in decades previous — with more possessions, more passing, and more player movement on offense and defense.
Cramer said that while the analytics departments of individual teams draw ire overall, organizations are mindful of the importance of fan experience. “I think the leagues are now better equipped to figure out what’s bad for the league and clamp down on it,” he said.
The pushback is sometimes successful. With a new rule, the NBA killed a deliberate fouling strategy that stopped fast breaks. Other battles remain undecided, like the NBA’s ongoing struggle to discourage stars from spending too much time sitting out to reduce fatigue and avoid injuries.
And while analytics are often criticized for inspiring stylistic hegemony, that’s not their inevitable outcome. Rader pointed out that when teams approach the game with the same style, it often becomes advantageous to pursue a counterintuitive one.
When most NFL teams shift resources to pass and defend the pass, others have leaned toward running and signing bigger instead of faster players.
“Now, there’s an opening for that diametrically opposed style,” he said.
He also said that there’s a much bigger gray area in analytics than telecasts portray. Certain situations might present two options that are practically a coin flip, like deciding between a long field goal and a short-yardage fourth-down attempt.
After a decision, an announcer might say the analytics supported it. “I think that’s where I get frustrated,” Rader said, “when they make it so cut and dried, black and white.”
For all of the statistics used in professional leagues, many major contributors to success remain difficult to quantify.
Teams are increasingly tracking factors like sleep quality to help athletes avoid injuries, to mixed results. Certain softer factors, like team chemistry — often cited as a reason behind the New York Knicks’ 2025-26 title — are hard to quantify. Rader said analytics are likely headed toward these softer measurements.
Cramer noted that while people complain about rule changes, like one making football kickoffs safer, they generally keep watching. Interest in sports seems to rise each year, along with team valuations.
Speier likes to think of modern discussions of analytics in a historical context. He pointed out that baseball articles from the 1910s reported players bemoaning the rise of home runs and the loss of skill required.
“I think that sports always evolve,” he said, “and it’s a question of what forces push that evolution.”

title: How to teach in era of AI, grade inflation
author: Anna Lamb
summary: Professors detail assignments that require analytic skills, and make it hard to use technology as a crutch.
text:
As midterms rapidly approach, faculty across the University continue to grapple with how to assess students amid widespread use of AI and concerns of grade inflation.
Those were among the topics discussed at the Harvard Initiative for Learning and Teaching’s 15th annual conference, “The Weight of the Degree: Rigor, Responsibility, and the Modern Campus.”
To kick off the day, a panel discussion focused on “recentering academic rigor in service of society” in a new technological era brought together scholars from the Business School (HBS), John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (SEAS), and Graduate School of Design (GSD).
Amy Edmondson, Novartis Professor of Leadership and Management at HBS, said a good illustration of how things are changing is the time-honored case method, which calls for students to analyze real-life business problems and propose solutions.
“The case method, which we have loved for 100 years, is suffering from the fact that our students are just putting the cases through ChatGPT and getting CliffsNotes and coming in with accurate but superficial and unhelpful knowledge and then we have a lower-quality conversation, which doesn’t have any of the dynamism of old,” she said.
So how to ensure students develop the analytic skills formerly honed by the case method?
“Giving them a short in-person case, a page or two, and then they’re on the spot,” Edmondson said. “There’s no technology in the classroom, and they have to respond to it, then I assign things to read later.”
Rachel Weber, Emma Bloomberg Professor of Urban Planning and chair of the Department of Urban Planning and Design, said homework still has a place — even if it only serves as a way to show students what they’re missing if they lean on AI for lessons.
“There are certain things that can be done at home, and if you’re going to be doing it with AI, then you’re going to come to class, where you create ways of building on what you’ve done at home, and you can’t rely on AI, and it becomes apparent who struggled at home,” she said. “If you didn’t struggle, then your ability to engage in the classroom work is impacted.”
Finding ways to surmount challenges, added Edmondson, is a vital part of the university experience. It’s what makes students successful once they graduate and are handed real problems without ready solutions.
“Our job is to make our students’ lives harder, and I think we have to take that job very seriously,” she said. “And it isn’t going to be doing what we used to do, just in slightly different ways. I think we’re going to need some dramatically different ways.”
Another key puzzle piece in ensuring students are grasping the core concepts of their education, the panel said, is assessing their progress. But with grade inflation, educators wonder how best to capture the quality of the work.
“Grades are feedback, and if grades are taken off the table, you can almost assume an A,” Edmondson said. “These are competitive and bright young people, professional and undergraduate, and they will find other ways to compete and distinguish themselves that are not in the academics. So I think I think we absolutely need and want them to prioritize the academics while they’re here.”
At the GSD, Weber said they are borrowing from an architect’s workflow.
“A process of review,” she said. “So we invite external stakeholders and other experts from the field to our midterm evaluations and final evaluations, and so it’s nice in some ways that some of that responsibility for assessment is taken off of the individual instructor’s shoulders.”
Le Xie, the Gordon McKay Professor of Electrical Engineering at SEAS, said he and his colleagues are trying to implement more team-based projects, where students have an opportunity to evaluate each other.
“We need to combine both what we traditionally would have taught in class, which are these core disciplines, with a sense of does your solution actually have a possibility of shaping the society?” Xie said. “And in the classroom that is translated into team-based project evaluations and presentations, and that becomes part of the evaluation that we do.”
One shining example of this new approach, Xie said, is the ENCE program — Energy, Climate and the Environment — a degree that combines SEAS courses with courses from the Divisions of Arts & Humanities, Social Science, and Science. Students in the ENCE program participate in active learning labs, giving them hands-on mechanical, electrical, computational, biological, and environmental experience.
“We try to keep them together as a cohort … doing team-based projects at the end of the undergraduate journey,” Xie said. “You have to struggle with the idea of coming up with the topic of your project, right, and then trying to define and then work together with the professor and teaching fellows and staff members.”
Even though these project-based curricula promote collaboration and active learning, Weber adds that AI can still have a place in student learning. For her students, who often are faced with presenting their ideas to stakeholders outside of the classroom, AI can help mimic feedback situations. “All of the graduates are involved in shaping the built and natural environment and therefore shaping people’s lives and the future of our planet,” she said. “You can train AI to simulate the environment of a contested community hearing, and you can assign different roles. You can have the small-business owner who really cares about parking, and you can have the housing activist who really cares about affordable housing, and you can test out your ideas before you actually have to go into the real world.”

title: Five Ph.D. students named Siebel Scholars
author: Kim LaSpina
summary: Scholars receive funding, access to network of scholars, researchers, and entrepreneurs
text:
News
Five computer science graduate students at the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (SEAS) have been named 2027 Siebel Scholars. Prashanth Amireddy, Tian (Sunny) Qin, Paula Rodriguez-Diaz, Itai Shapira and Kevin Zhang will each receive an award for their final year of graduate studies. They are among 72 students who join past Siebel Scholars classes to form an unmatched professional and personal network of more than 2,000 scholars, researchers, and entrepreneurs. Through the program, this formidable group brings together diverse perspectives from business, science, and engineering to influence the technologies, policies, and economic and social decisions that shape the future.
“Every year, the Siebel Scholars continue to impress me with their commitment to academics and influencing future society. This year’s class is exceptional, and once again represents the best and brightest minds from around the globe who are advancing innovations in healthcare, artificial intelligence, financial services, and more,” said Thomas M. Siebel, Chairman of the Siebel Scholars Foundation. “It is my distinct pleasure to welcome these students into this ever-growing, lifelong community, and I personally look forward to seeing their impact and contributions unfold.”
Founded in 2000 by the Thomas and Stacey Siebel Foundation, the Siebel Scholars program awards grants to 16 universities in the United States, China, France, Italy and Japan. Following a competitive review process by the deans of their respective schools on the basis of outstanding academic achievement and demonstrated leadership, the top graduate students from 27 partner programs are selected each year as Siebel Scholars and receive a $35,000 award for their final year of studies. On average, Siebel Scholars rank in the top five percent of their class, many within the top one percent.
Prashanth Amireddy is a Ph.D. student in the Theory of Computation group at Harvard University, where he is co-advised by Madhu Sudan, Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science, and Salil Vadhan, Vicky Joseph Professor of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics. His research lies at the intersection of computational complexity theory, error-correcting codes, and pseudorandomness, with a particular focus on developing new algebraic techniques. His work addresses questions related to detecting and correcting errors over unstructured domains, as well as probabilistically checkable proofs, and seeks to deepen the connections between algebra and theoretical computer science.
Before beginning his doctoral studies, Amireddy was a Research Fellow at Microsoft Research India, where he worked with Ankit Garg and Neeraj Kayal on problems in algebraic complexity theory. He received his bachelor’s degree in computer science and engineering from the Indian Institute of Technology Madras, where he conducted research under the guidance of Professor Jayalal Sarma.
Paula Rodriguez-Diaz is a Ph.D. candidate in computer science, advised by Milind Tambe, Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science, and Elisabeth Paulson, Assistant Professor of Business Administration in the Technology and Operations Management Unit at Harvard Business School, in close collaboration with David Alvarez-Melis, Assistant Professor of Computer Science. Her research bridges data-centric machine learning with decision-focused learning to build systems that optimize the quality of downstream decisions in public-sector operations where data are scarce, constraints are binding, and distributions shift. She develops methods for task-aware data curation, efficient decision-focused training, and learning from observational data, with applications in maternal and child healthcare and refugee resettlement in collaboration with field partners including ARMMAN, Mbarara Regional Referral Hospital, and the Stanford Immigration Policy Lab. Her work has been published at venues including UAI, ICML, AAAI, and AAMAS. She co-founded the Centro de Analítica para Políticas Públicas (CAPP), bringing data science and AI to public-sector challenges in Latin America, and has served as poster co-chair for the EAAMO Conference and co-organizer of the Machine Learning for the Developing World Workshop at NeurIPS. Originally from Bogotá, Colombia, Paula earned a B.S. in mathematics and a B.S. and M.S. in industrial engineering from Universidad de Los Andes.
Itai Shapira is a Ph.D. candidate in computer science, advised by Professor Ariel D. Procaccia, Alfred and Rebecca Lin Professor of Computer Science. His research examines how to align AI systems with human values when the feedback used to train them is imperfect or reflects conflicting preferences. Drawing on machine learning and social choice theory, he studies how alignment methods transform human judgments and which behaviors they preserve or amplify. His recent work shows how reinforcement learning from human feedback can increase sycophancy, causing AI models to tell users what they want to hear, and develops methods for building AI systems that reflect a wide range of human views. Shapira is a 2025 JPMorgan Chase PhD Fellow and serves on the Student Leadership Council of the NSF AI Institute for Societal Decision Making. He holds a bachelor's degree in mathematics and economics from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
Tian (Sunny) Qin is a fourth-year Ph.D. student in computer science, co-advised by Alvarez-Melis and Sham Kakade, Rampell Family Professor of Computer Science and Professor of Statistics. Her research aims to build a scientific understanding of how large AI models are trained, with a particular focus on data-centric AI and reinforcement learning. On the data-centric side, she studies how the data used to train models shapes their capabilities and behavior. On the reinforcement learning side, she studies how it can be used to improve the way models reason and solve problems. Across both directions, her goal is to develop a scientific understanding of model training choices in order to build better, more reliable models.
Prior to her Ph.D., Sunny earned her B.A. cum laude in physics with a minor in statistics and machine learning at Princeton University. She then spent several years in quantitative trading before pivoting into AI research and joining Harvard's Ph.D. program.
Sunny is also passionate about mentoring others. She has served as a Teaching Fellow for “CS2881: AI Safety,” and she mentors students through independent research mentorship of master's and thesis students. She is currently organizing a workshop at NeurIPS 2026 on the interplay between pre- and post-training. Outside of research, she serves as Education Officer of the Harvard Mountaineering Club, where she regularly plans and leads climbing trips and expeditions, teaching and coaching students in climbing and mountaineering skills.
Kevin Zhang is a sixth-year Ph.D. candidate in computer science, advised by Stephen Chong, Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science. His research focuses on developing whole program analyses for bug and vulnerability discovery. Specifically, his current work aims to make symbolic execution more scalable through the use of program dependence graphs. Through his work, he aims to advance practical tools that improve software security and reliability. He recently interned with the GraalVM team at Oracle Labs, where he worked on improving the precision of the points-to analysis used by GraalVM Native Image. Previously, he received a bachelor's degree in computer science from Cornell University.
