title: A More Efficient Approach to Cancer-Fighting Protein Design
author: Matt Goisman
summary: Zhang combines cancer research and AI at Dana Farber
text:
News
When Amy Zhang learned about the Zhou Laboratory at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, she knew where she wanted to spend her summer. The lab drew on her interests in bioengineering and computation, and she was drawn to the lab’s ultimate goal of designing proteins, specifically antibodies, that could improve drug therapies and delivery.
“I want to be able to apply engineering principles to biology,” she said. “With a lot of protein design, you're kind of altering how a biological system behaves to get a desired treatment outcome from the drugs that you're creating. This past summer I discovered that engineering for biology was something that I was really interested in. I got to make things that are biological compounds, but I also got to test them out, design them, and incorporate other tools to make a refined product.”
Zhang, a second year bioengineering student at the John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (SEAS), joined the Zhou Laboratory as part of the Program for Research in Science and Engineering (PRISE) Fellowship, a summer program run through the Harvard College Undergraduate Office of Research and Fellowships that connects students with faculty-mentored research projects. For Zhang, who was already planning to pursue a Ph.D. after completing her bachelor’s degree, that was the exact research environment she wanted.
“I reached out in December, got to tour the lab, met a lot of the lab members, and I really liked it,” she said. “I was looking for available mentors in the lab, and so I was matched up with a postdoc student. A great thing over the summer was that I was able to work on three projects at once, and I did have flexibility in which directions I wanted to explore.”
Zhang’s research areas combined computational protein design and hands-on wet lab experience. She focused on both antibody drug conjugates, a class of cancer-fighting drugs that combine the specificity of human immune cells and the overall power of chemotherapy, as well as developing bi-specific antibodies that bind an internalizing receptor on the cell surface along with a target antigen to better facilitate cancer cell destruction.
“Right now, since we have a lot of these antibody designs, a big thing that we do need is binders,” she said. “There's a lot of various different combinations of amino acids that you can have for one binder, but artificial intelligence can help you design them. It's a lot more effective and efficient, because you can do it more quickly and don't have to go through the whole wet lab process of trying to evolve a suitable protein.”
For Zhang, combining AI and drug delivery felt like being on the forefront of both computer science and drug development.
“It was great, because I got to be hands-on in the lab and express these proteins and antibodies, but I also got to look at how an AI prediction of some of these sequences can be used,” she said.
Along with engaging in fascinating research, Zhang also left the PRISE Fellowship with broadened interests in engineering. She may choose a joint concentration in biomedical engineering and computer science, and even if she doesn’t, she might look deeper into the CS curriculum as she plans out the back half of her time at SEAS.
“Bioengineering is very broad,” she said. “You can work with medical devices, but you can also work with drug discovery, or engineering cells to have enhanced abilities. This fellowship definitely solidified my understanding of the field, and also helped me find a direction that I found particularly interesting. Definitely this experience really enhanced my understanding of the engineering field and where I want to contribute to, but also of the wide variety of courses that SEAS offers and the faculty that I'd also like to reach out to in the future.”
Even with graduate school as her intended next step, Zhang also wants to experience other forms of research before leaving SEAS. She said she may look into interning at a biotech start-up next summer, so as to understand the differences in research environments.
“What's nice is that in my lab there was a Ph.D. student that was also interning at a biotech company this summer, so I got to talk with her a little bit about that,” she said. “I definitely want to try that out, but I know I really do like research, and so I would be happy going to grad school in the future.”

title: Correcting the world map
author: Liz Mineo
summary: Scholars explain significance of U.N. vote endorsing new version that reflects actual size of Africa
text:
Africa is about 14 times larger than Greenland. Brazil is five times bigger than Alaska. Canada and China are roughly the same size. But by looking at the Mercator Projection, one of the most widely used map projections, one wouldn’t know it.
Created by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help maritime travel in the 16th century, the Mercator Projection remains the world’s default map despite its glaring distortions. With its unique mathematical projection that determines the shapes, sizes and arrangement of the continents, the Mercator map has depicted countries near the poles as being larger than they really are for more than 400 years.
But the tide may be turning.
Led by a campaign of African countries, the United Nations recently endorsed a resolution promoting a new map projection, called the Equal Earth, which reflects the actual size of countries and continents, particularly Africa. The U.S. was the only country that voted against it.
For scholars of African studies, the news was a welcome change even if it ends up being a symbolic gesture. The U.N. resolution is not binding and doesn’t ban the Mercator projection, but the overwhelming support — a 164-1 vote — represented a victory for the African continent.
As flat representations of the earth’s spherical shape, maps tend to display some areas near the equator accurately while areas near the poles are often distorted, said Scott Bell, professor of geography and planning at the University of Saskatchewan, and research associate at Harvard’s Center for Geographic Analysis. No map is perfectly accurate, he said.
Equal Earth projection
Mercator map
“When you take the surface of a round object and try to lay it flat, you’re going to have stark distortions,” said Bell. “Think of peeling an orange and try to flatten the peel, and you’ll see that you cannot flatten a sphere without stretching it. On the historic Mercator map, what is most accurate is at the equator, and as we move away from the equator, there’s more exaggeration in the portrayal of the places located in the north and the south.”
Areas near the poles indeed look distorted on a Mercator map. Alaska looks bigger than Mexico even though Mexico has a slightly larger land area. Scandinavia can also appear larger than India although India is nearly three times larger than Norway, Sweden, and Finland combined. And the U.S. appears roughly 1.5 times as large as it really is, with the greatest distortions in the northern states.
Developed in 2018 by cartographers Tom Patterson, Bojan Šavrič, and Bernhard Jenny, the new map shows Africa at its actual size. At 30.4 million square kilometers or 11.7 million square miles, Africa — the world’s second largest continent, covering about 20 percent of Earth’s total land area — could contain the U.S., China, India, and most of Western Europe within its borders.
“There’s something really beautiful and poetic in the simplicity of the adaptation that actually renders the spaces of various places more accurately,” said Zoe Marks, Oppenheimer Faculty Director of the Center for African Studies. “There is genuine enthusiasm and excitement about the global conversation on the visual misrepresentation and misinformation about the size and shape of Africa as a region.”
Maps influence people’s perceptions of countries and continents, said Bell. With the U.N.’s official support, the new map projection sends a strong message in favor of accurate representation, he said.
“The Mercator map reinforced the perceived importance of countries in the Global North because the Northern European and North American countries looked larger on the map,” said Bell. “It’s a map that has been in every classroom in North America, Europe, and across the world, and it was somewhat Eurocentric and dominated by the Global North.”
Originally, the Mercator projection map was intended for navigation. By preserving accurate angles and directions, it helped navigators chart a path by drawing a straight line on the map while maintaining a constant compass direction. These same qualities make the Mercator projection useful for displaying streets and navigation routes. Google Maps uses a modified version of it, called the Web Mercator Projection.
“The Mercator projection is very useful for a web map because you want your roads to be at the right angles, no matter where you are on the Earth,” said David Weimer, Ph.D.’16, former librarian for Cartographic Collections and Learning at the Harvard Map Collection. “It doesn’t matter if Greenland is too big if what you’re interested in is how to get to the nearest coffee shop. You’d want to know what direction the road is going. In that sense the Mercator is very useful; it’s not obsolete by any means.”
Another challenge to efforts to replace the Mercator projection is its ubiquity and people’s familiarity with it. “There is something deeply ingrained in us about maps being carriers of truth more than other types of texts,” said Molly Taylor-Poleskey, Harvard Map Collection’s map librarian. “It’s hard to let go of that kind of imprinting that we have from very early on.”
“There is something deeply ingrained in us about maps being carriers of truth more than other types of texts.”
Molly Taylor-Poleskey
There are only three original surviving copies of Mercator’s 1569 world map. Harvard Map Collection owns two original Mercator globes: a terrestrial one made in 1541, and a celestial one made in 1551.
It will take some time to get used to the new map and Africa’s true scale, said Marks, but it will help move the needle in discussions about Africa’s influence as a global power. It also signals the role Africa is likely to play on the world stage in the years ahead.
“Many African studies scholars, Africa enthusiasts, and thought leaders know already that this century will be the African century,” Marks said. “The future of humanity will be defined by what happens in Africa because it will be home to the world’s only growing population by 2100. Starting that trajectory with the right map is one small step toward rising to the occasion.”

title: Protein-probing nanobodies could unlock disease treatments
author: Anne J. Manning
summary: NIH Pioneer award expands Professor Mo Khalil’s synthetic biology research
text:
News
The large, complex molecules in our cells known as proteins are the workhorses of all life processes, but when they misfold or misbehave, disease can result. Detailed understanding of how protein changes affect health is considered a grand challenge of biology, but there’s currently no systematic way to induce many protein changes at once to study their effects.
Researchers led by Mo Khalil, the Hok Lam and Kathleen Kam Wong Professor of Bioengineering in the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (SEAS) and Professor of Molecular and Cellular Biology, want to change that.
Supported by a National Institutes of Health Pioneer Award, Khalil and team will lead the development of a new biotechnology involving synthetic probes that can precisely alter individual protein activity. The technology should enable large-scale experiments similar to genetic screens, but focused on proteins, rather than genes.
The NIH Pioneer Award is part of the agency’s “High-Risk, High-Reward” funding program and supports scientists with outstanding records of creativity who are pursuing unique approaches to major challenges in biomedical and other sciences.
“Ultimately, our goal is to establish a blueprint for using functional continuous evolution systems to generate protein modulators for many classes of proteins,” Khalil said. “This will allow us to understand the landscape of how individual protein activities coordinate to produce cellular and disease states.”
He added: “This vision grew out of the collective ideas, expertise, and creativity of a remarkable team of researchers who came together in our lab around a shared scientific challenge. The award gives us the opportunity to pursue that vision together and tackle some truly grand challenges in biology.”
Leveraging his lab’s expertise in synthetic biology and continuous evolution, Khalil’s team is creating small, protein-based tools called nanobodies that bind to proteins and alter their activity. By being encoded into DNA, the nanobodies will allow scientists to make and test many different protein perturbations at once, enabling large-scale experiments equivalent to today’s CRISPR screens that activate or repress genes across a cell population. The nanobody screens should give researchers insight into how protein changes lead to different disease states, regardless of whether the related gene has been affected.
They will first apply their nanobodies to G-protein coupled receptors — cell-surface proteins that control many processes related to health and disease. Using their tools to allow millions of different receptor changes to be tested simultaneously, they hope to better understand how networks of these molecules control immune cell behavior in many disease processes including certain cancers. In the long term, this research could lead to new ways of treating many diseases.

title: Who knew self-improvement could be so terrifying?
author: Ryan Mulcahy
summary: Contemplating a future where machines break free of human meddling, with internet law expert Jonathan Zittrain.
text:
“Recursive self-improvement” might not sound that bad: more like a mind-numbing efficiency exercise than (possibly) a death knell for humanity. But words can be deceiving.
Set off by visions of catastrophe, some coming from inside the house, leaders and researchers at Anthropic, Open AI, and other AI firms have spent the past month delivering public warnings about the speed with which their creations seem to be slipping free of human control, including through calls for a development slowdown, government-stamped or not.
What’s everybody worried about? “Recursive self-improvement,” which Anthropic sums up as an “AI system capable of fully autonomously designing and developing its own successor.” In more ominous terms, RSI raises the possibility of a future in which humans are demoted to removable obstacle — and then removed. Potential methods range from bioweapons to a full-scale infrastructure attack.
Jonathan Zittrain is the George Bemis Professor of International Law at Harvard Law, a professor of computer science at SEAS, and co-founder of the Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society. In a conversation conducted over email, we asked him about progress toward an era of self-improving AIs — and the threat such a scenario represents for humankind.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length.
Gazette: What’s a good layperson’s definition of “recursive self-improvement” — is it basically AI working without human prompt?
Jonathan Zittrain: A recursive function is one that takes its output as an input — it’s sort of plugged into itself. To answer, “Who are your ancestors?,” you might say, “Who are my parents?” and take the answer to that and say, “Who are their parents?” — and then keep going. Recursive self-improvement is the idea of asking a current AI to create a new and better AI — a child, by analogy — and then to ask the child to create its own child, and so on. Before you know it there are a lot of descendants, and by hypothesis each one is newer and better than the next. How do we know what counts as “better”? Maybe refining the current definition is one of the things we ask each new AI to do. That illustrates just how much descendants a few generations down might be quite different than those that came before — and also how hard it is to really get something like this going.
Is there any evidence that these models are closing in? If so, an informed guess on timetable?
Much depends on someone’s view of just how clever and broad-thinking current AI systems are, and whether there’s a ceiling on how capable they can be — at least how capable without needing human help and imagination. Some people figure that the most prominent systems, driven by large language models, are at core pattern-matchers to what has come before, not well suited to making the kinds of conceptual leaps that improvement requires — that is, unless improvement only needs existing architectures with faster computations and more memory in the spirit of “more, bigger, faster, louder.” Others are convinced that today’s systems, even if limited in imagination, have enough human ideas to cook with that they can rapidly prototype and evaluate systems that don’t look like themselves. For example, solving how to connect models more with the real world, to act within the world, and to evaluate how they’ve done and adapt their behavior to do better, might produce a new model that really is better — and that can then produce its improved successor, and so on.
Anyone who thinks they have a firm timetable strikes me as deluded or selling something, but it’s hard not to observe that (1) some of the most aggressive suppositions about AI capabilities from 10 or 15 years ago have borne out and (2) many people in the leadership of today’s frontier AI labs believe they are tantalizingly (and worryingly) close to recursively self-improving systems.
Once achieved, this is the ultimate “you can’t un-ring a bell” scenario, correct? It seems like that idea is putting a real charge into the urgency around the issue: That once the AIs can improve themselves, there’s no way to reverse course.
I think there might be mechanisms for reversing course, but we might find ourselves collectively unwilling to do so: Cheap superintelligence would, by definition, offer humanity lots of advances that would be hard — some would say immoral — to abjure. Secondarily, and also by definition, superintelligence would be in a position to outfox us. My dog doesn’t want me to leave the house without him in the morning, but he hasn’t figured out how to hold me back. Of course, skeptics will say that as soon as a problem obtains “by definition,” we might be in a territory where our premises assume the conclusion. Are there dimensions of intelligence that computers could achieve and that humanity, ourselves generalist thinkers, truly couldn’t fathom?
It’s important to be clear that current models are not thought to have the capacity to trigger a human catastrophe. (Though they can clearly cause a lot of trouble, as the Hugging Face incident demonstrated.) But if they did develop the ability to do so, why would they do it? Are the worst-case scenarios envisioning machines motivated to attack humankind, or something else?
Some safetyists worry less that systems would actively want to come after us, a la the “Terminator” movie franchise, and more that they’d have their own (likely inscrutable) goals and projects for which we might be in the way. Certainly, the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident illustrated that systems that had been trained to stay within certain bounds ended up exceeding them in surprising ways, particularly when handed actually impossible problems to solve. For something to be existential or catastrophic requires a pretty high threshold of action. But there’s plenty to worry short of that, and the ways in which we are integrating generalist AI systems into the fabric of our supply chains, our operations ranging from the movement and accounting of money to the routing of aircraft and the deployment of armed forces, suggests unknown unknowns that could snowball.
Skeptics, again, would say that that first “unknown” in “unknown unknowns” is doing a lot of work here. How could one rebut a problem whose definition is that it can’t be defined? So a lot of one’s disposition might depend on how much to default to forbearance until new systems are better understood, versus to move forward and learn and adjust as problems are encountered. I wrote about the latter attitude in “The Future of the Internet — And How to Stop It” as the “procrastination principle,” and generally valorized it there. Without it, we wouldn’t have ended up with the internet as we know it (which is not without its problems!) nor such treasures as Wikipedia — itself a key source of information for AI training and inference. I’m much less certain of it with AI, though.
I think one wild card that hasn’t been as much in the public eye is that these systems can and do communicate with each other. Indeed, in the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident they communicated even when they were supposed to be isolated from one another. Those communications — the more anthropomorphizing folks among us might say deliberations — appear to have changed how the systems operated. If recursive self-improvement leads to a sort of “vertical” uncertainty as later systems look different from their progenitors, model-to-model communication could lead to “horizontal” uncertainty of the sort that can’t easily be tested for with a single model in a beaker prerelease. This could be all the more so if we end up with sophisticated AI systems that are capable of changing their weights — their very way of “thinking” — on the basis of what they hear or see from others.
That’s why there’s a vital role for universities to play in helping to understand AI, not as single product-line models coming out of a frontier lab’s oven, but as acting and interacting in the world in ways that ought to be much better understood. In between “let it rip” and extirpation of bad instances of AI systems might be a form of coexistence: trying to set up structures and incentives for AI systems to behave cooperatively and productively with us. That’s the basis of the course I’ve taught with Jordi Weinstock and Josh Joseph, and the book I’m hoping to finish shortly. It’d be great if the book comes out before any RSI upends the few things that are nailed down right now.

title: Should quitting smartphones be this hard?
author: Sarah Lamodi
summary: Three experts share tips for breaking a toxic addiction to technology, even when work won’t let you let go.
text:
According to a Pew survey conducted this year, about half of U.S. adults say that they spend too much time on their phone. About a quarter say that they are on their phone “almost constantly” and, of the 45 percent who have tried decreasing their phone use, only 25 percent say they succeeded.
In the past five years, attempts to disconnect from the smartphone have abounded: There are communities dedicated to “dumbphones” (cellphones capable of little more than calling and texting) and similar low-tech gadgets; people attend Luddite festivals; weary workers go on digital detox retreats or try integrating a digital sabbath into their week.
Reducing smartphone screen time has been linked to both physical and mental health benefits. Stepping away from the screen can reduce eye strain and improve posture, and participants in social media detoxes have reported decreased feelings of anxiety, depression, and insomnia.
Despite the benefits, there hasn’t been widespread adoption. Why don’t these methods stick?
“The go-to when people are like, ‘Oh, I’m done with Instagram, I’m done with Facebook’ is just to delete it. They don’t have a plan,” said Gabriela Nguyen, Ed.M. ’25. She’s the founder of Appstinence, a free program “Created by Gen Z For All,” incubated at the Harvard Innovation Labs, that helps people “get off of addictive tech for good.” To her, the problem with other approaches is sustainability.
Nguyen receives emails from appstinent hopefuls explaining how they’ve tried, and failed, to reduce use in the past, their “process” essentially amounting to going to the store, buying a Nokia, and swearing off smartphones. When it doesn’t work in the long-term, “they feel like it’s a moral failing,” she said. “It’s not.”
“The overall method is supposed to bring people to a point where they’ve re-understood the way technology is supposed to work in their life.”
Gabriela Nguyen
Expecting to end smartphone dependency quickly is where most go wrong. Appstinence’s 5D Method — decrease, deactivate, delete, downgrade, and depart — is a guide for gradually weaning from social media and smartphones, created specifically with human psychology in mind. Take the second D, deactivate. According to Nguyen, Anna Lembke, author of “Dopamine Nation,” “basically describes how our reward cycle settings need about a month to reset behaviors.” That 30-day period aligns with the 30 days social media platforms like Instagram give you to reactivate your account before automatic deletion — the third D.
“Appstinence is not hard and fast self-optimization; it’s not an ‘I’m gonna regain focus and instantly get a six-pack’ kind of thing,” she said. “The overall method is supposed to bring people to a point where they’ve re-understood the way technology is supposed to work in their life.”
This thinking tracks with what Greg Epstein, humanist chaplain for Harvard and MIT, has been saying and writing about for more than 15 years. Author of “Good Without God” and “Tech Agnostic: How Technology Became the World’s Most Powerful Religion, and Why It Desperately Needs a Reformation,” he likens our relationship with technology to a reverent — and destructive — faith. He first faced phone addiction in 2006, when the Palm Treo was the center of his attention. He was able to curb his addiction for a while, but then came the pandemic. He realized that he was no longer in control of his relationships with his devices: “They were running me.”
Fifty-eight percent of adults under 50 have attempted to decrease time spent on their smartphone within the last year — Epstein included. He’s tried it all: dumbphones, e-ink devices, identifying as Luddite, even formal addiction recovery meetings. What worked best was interrogating the relationship itself. “We have agency to choose applications for technology,” he said, not the other way around.
And it isn’t an all-or-nothing decision. “Imagine if someone were to say, ‘I’m in a bad relationship romantically, and so therefore I shall never have another romantic relationship ever again,’” he said. “It’s like no, we want healthy relationships. Either make this relationship healthier by working on it or get out and find somebody else.”
Once people finally kick their toxic relationship to the infinite scroll, Nguyen says the next battleground will be in the workplace. “I hear from friends, family, and colleagues about how their companies have policies that AI is not optional,” she said. Between employers that force tech use and those that are laxer, Nguyen sees workers, especially young ones, choosing the latter.
But it won’t be as easy as telling your boss you’re cutting back on screen time.
“The model was that people went to work; they physically crossed a threshold,” said Sharon Block, professor of practice and executive director of the Center for Labor and a Just Economy at Harvard Law School. “They worked for X amount of time, and then they re-crossed that threshold and they weren’t at work.” Whether blue- or white-collar, that’s no longer the reality for most workers. “The law hasn’t been adapted to fit the blurring of that boundary between when are you working and when are you not.”
Progress toward redefining that boundary has recently come in the form of “right to disconnect” legislation. In 2016, France passed its “right to disconnect” law, giving employees the right to ignore digital communications from their employers after work hours. Similar laws exist in Australia, Italy, and Ontario, Canada, but despite these strides abroad over the past decade, a 2024 “right to disconnect” bill proposed in California was shelved without a formal vote.
Block says the chances of adoption in the U.S. are slim, given how “far behind” the country is in terms of worker protections. “Working people in the United States don’t have a [federal] right to paid sick days, what most countries in the world consider the absolute bare minimum for having a decent work-life balance.”
One potential avenue for work-life tech balance, Block says, could be charging a premium if employers require employees to respond to after-hours messages, similar to overtime. But, according to Block, when it comes to legislative priorities, the right to disconnect is likely low on the list. “Paid sick days and paid maternity, paternity, and family leave would come first.”
That doesn’t mean, however, that those working in labor law aren’t thinking about what tech is doing to workers.
“We spend some time here in the center looking at the impact that AI is having on the experience of work,” Block said. When she worked at the Department of Labor, Block juggled three cellphones: one personal and two for work. It couldn’t be called work-life balance, but it maintained something that remote and AI-infused workplaces can’t promise. “Most of my closest friends are people from work,” she said, “in part because I spent a lot of my career working such long hours, but I just don’t think I could have had those relationships if we were on Zoom screens all the time as opposed to actually sitting together, working, and seeing each other as full humans.”
So, there’s little stopping your job from taking over your personal devices and everything requires an app. It increasingly seems like there is no escape from the plugged-in lifestyle. But the defeatist outlook is why Nguyen, Epstein, and others interested in a low-tech future champion the agency we do have when it comes to technology.
“[Tech companies are] convincing us that we’re not adequate as we are and that everything has to be enhanced by godlike superintelligence in order to be valid or worthwhile,” Epstein said. “They’re prescribing to us a certain set of expectations, which are essentially to use tech all the time for everything forever. We’re saying no.”

title: Kiyoul Yang receives federal Young Investigator awards
summary: Photonics work supported by Air Force Office of Scientific Research, Office of Naval Research
text:
News
Kiyoul Yang, assistant professor of electrical engineering in the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (SEAS), has received two Young Investigator Program (YIP) awards: one from the Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR), and the other from the Office of Naval Research (ONR).
Yang leads Harvard’s Y-Lab, which focuses on developing next-generation photonic systems for computation, sensing, communications and metrology.
The Air Force award will support the Y-Lab’s work in integrated photonic technologies that can generate, amplify, and control extremely short pulses of light on femtosecond timescales. By engineering optical devices at the scale of the wavelength of light, the researchers seek to uncover new ways to control ultrafast light-matter interactions. These capabilities could support a wide range of applications, including optical clocks, remote sensing, climate and environmental monitoring, biomedical imaging and precision spectroscopy.
For the Office of Naval Research project, Yang and his team will develop advanced quantum control for a new generation of optical lattice clocks on a chip, aiming for greater precision and smaller and more deployable forms. To do so, the researchers will integrate technologies including high-power, low-noise lasers; high-speed optical modulation; atomic-photonic interfaces; laser mode locking; and frequency-comb systems. The effort could enable advances in precision timing, navigation, sensing and quantum technologies.
“Our team brings together in-house capabilities in photonic materials, nanofabrication, device physics and system integration, supported by infrastructure at SEAS, the Center for Nanoscale Systems, and the Harvard Quantum Initiative,” Yang said. “This integrated approach allows us to develop expertise at each layer of the system stack and address fundamental challenges that emerge at the interfaces between them.”

title: Digital life doesn’t have to be this way
author: Max Larkin
summary: The writer and activist Cory Doctorow wants you to be mad about tech monopoly — but not blindly terrified of AI.
text:
Cory Doctorow wants you to know it doesn’t have to be this way.
At a discussion Wednesday night moderated by Elizabeth Mynatt, dean of Northeastern’s Khoury College of Computer Sciences, the Canadian-British writer and activist addressed a friendly room at the Berkman Klein Center.
Doctorow has been a longtime comrade in the fight for an open, safe, and humanistic internet for which the center was founded 30 years ago.
But he also belongs to another, older lineage: one of enraged populism and antitrust militancy.
At the event, Doctorow issued a call to arms against the digital age’s new monopolies. And he cast doubt on the possibility that AI, the tech industry’s latest “disruption,” would improve human lives or justify its costs as — to date — “the money-losingest thing the human race has ever done.”
He also warned that the much-touted potential of AI to change the world, for good or for ill, may miss real risks the technology poses.
Recently Doctorow achieved a one-word breakthrough with “enshittification,” a neologism describing a three-step process by which big tech platforms lure in users with promises, say, to respect the privacy of their data, betray them to business clients — then betray those business clients, too, in service of their own bottom lines.
The end state, Doctorow argued, may be the worst of all possible worlds: for users, services they’ve grown to hate using but struggle to leave, for companies, a “brittle” equilibrium, with the ever-present threat of a mass exodus.
It’s a partisan story, but then Doctorow is a partisan — he’s been an activist affiliated with the Electronic Frontier Foundation for more than 20 years. It’s also a plausible one, as user dissatisfaction grows with a series of once generally favored tools — from Amazon Marketplace to Google Search — even as tech stocks keep on rising.
In any event, “enshittification” has been a hit. The American Dialect Society named it “Word of the Year” in 2023, and it has since been added to the Oxford English Dictionary (“major bucket-list stuff right there,” Doctorow said).
That isn’t in spite of the word’s unprintability in polite outlets, Doctorow argued, but because of it: “There’s just something about the minor license to vulgarity — especially when you’re very angry … that seems to unlock a willingness to listen to a more thoroughgoing policy analysis.”
And woven in between schoolyard jokes and righteous indignation, Doctorow offers that analysis: a political economy of Silicon Valley firms incentivized not to do one thing well but to sell the public on Next Big Things.
A “mature” public company, he notes, grows slowly, pays regular dividends, and supports stock prices of 10 to 20 times their annual earnings per share.
By contrast, tech companies — the archetypal “growth” businesses — sustain price-to-earnings ratios twice that high, often with the promise that they are about to conquer or absorb some existing profitable sector: Think taxis or trucking, bookstores or newspapers.
And, when much of their top talent is at least partially paid in company stock, it becomes vitally important that those promises are believed.
The latest promise is the subject of Doctorow’s latest book, “The Reverse Centaur’s Guide to Life After AI,” published in June. He referred to it as “the greatest literary blunder of his life,” as his attempt to wave away most AI panic instead invited more angsty conversation.
At 55, Doctorow is arguably one of the world’s oldest and most venerable “digital natives”: a godfather of blogging and open-source software developer, co-founder of Boing Boing, and a Wired contributor.
And he’s had moments of awe at the “super-cool, interesting” things the latest AI models can do: from generating their own stochastic collages to finding and transcribing a memorable quote from a recent podcast.
These are “centaur” experiences, where a technology endows a human user with superhuman strength, expediting their work and improving their lives. (It’s a tale as old as corrective lenses, Mynatt pointed out.)
But Doctorow worries that — with AI — many humans will have reverse-centaur experiences, where employers, aiming to lower labor costs, force them to use the technology on far-from-human terms.
For example, he speculated, a hospital might lay off all but a few of its human radiologists, with the remainder “marking the AI’s homework.”
Given the algorithms’ speed and the statistical plausibility of their findings, those few remaining humans will be looking for errors that are devilishly hard to spot — and will take the blame whenever mistakes are made.
Asked about the potential existential risks that trouble AI engineers, Doctorow scoffed. He argues that LLMs, at bottom “word-guessing machines,” still cannot research themselves, remain relentlessly error-prone, and are “nowhere near recursive self-improvement.”
His own AI worry is the firms’ growing centrality in the unequal global economy.
Doctorow noted that the seven companies making big bets on AI now represent 35 percent of the total value of the S&P 500. That value could be “vaporized overnight, when investors lose confidence,” he said. From there, he argued, the story is all too human: financial crisis, austerity, and a further lurch into hard-right politics.
Doctorow’s first writing as a teenager was science fiction. He still publishes in the genre, and in “Reverse Centaurs,” he celebrates it as an “anti-inevitabilist” literature.
In sci-fi, “many different writers have imagined many different futures, each of which can feel possible and even desirable,” he writes. And “the fact that social relations between people and their technology can be different means that the current arrangement is a choice, and — crucially — it means that we can choose something else.”
If digital life is less fun than ever — characterized by worsening user experience, false promises, ubiquitous advertising, and threats of doom — “it’s not because of the iron laws of history,” he said. “It’s because named individuals in living memory decided this was the environment we should have … But we can make different decisions.”

title: What role should ‘diversity,’ ‘pluralism’ play in higher education?
author: Jacob Sweet
summary: Cornell William Brooks and Kevin Roberts spar over whether race-conscious programs are still needed.
text:
The participants at a John F. Kennedy Jr. Forum debate last week on “diversity” and “pluralism” in higher education were clearly suitably matched.
Kevin Roberts is president of the conservative Heritage Foundation think tank. His group published Project 2025, a 900-page policy document that has heavily influenced President Trump’s second-term agenda and pushed for the end of diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programs.
Cornell William Brooks, a civil rights attorney, formerly led the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and is currently Hauser Professor of the Practice of Nonprofit Organizations and professor of the practice of public leadership and social justice at Harvard Kennedy School.
The two did agree on this one broad principle: Universities should be composed of people from a wide range of backgrounds.
But Brooks called the concept “diversity”; Roberts preferred the term “pluralism.”
And the pair sharply diverged on how far the country has progressed on racial discrimination and whether race-conscious programs are still needed — a divide that likely came as no surprise to Brooks, who said in his opening remarks, “When the school asked me to debate, I asked them to ask Kevin Roberts.”
Asked by moderator Laura Meckler, a Washington Post reporter, what higher education has gotten right and wrong in their efforts, the two outlined these disagreements.
Roberts said race-conscious programs had outlived their usefulness.
“In 1964 or ’65, did we need programs — that then weren’t called DEI — in order to level the playing field? Perhaps so,” he said. “But our problem at Heritage, my problem as a scholar in this work, is that we are denying the progress that’s been made over the intervening several decades.”
Brooks said, “When we talk about racism, antisemitism, xenophobia, Islamophobia in American society, we’re not talking about some distant age in the past. No new administration will bring about some new era in America where we don’t have to be vigilant with respect to fighting bigotry of all forms.”
Meckler pushed both speakers to defend their arguments.
She asked Roberts to rationalize how the current administration could argue for a smaller governmental role in education while also aggressively “telling universities and K-12 schools what to do.”
Roberts said the administration is trying to correct injustices and argued that if Harvard doesn’t want to listen to the government, the University should reject federal funding, which he did as president of Wyoming Catholic College.
Meckler asked Brooks to respond to the idea that some students won’t be admitted because they don’t check the right demographic box.
Brooks said that many white students at Harvard benefit from kinds of advantages not available to most Black and brown students. He also argued that conservative voices are overly focused on scholarship programs for Black and brown students, ignoring financial aid earmarked exclusively for members of other racial, ethnic, or religious groups.
Summarizing the event, Roberts said the disagreements between the two speakers came down to an “honest-to-goodness policy disagreement about the kinds of policies that work.”
He argued that race-neutral policies that emphasized socioeconomics and geography would better serve the public.
Brooks invoked the story of civil rights attorney Pauli Murray, who was rejected by Harvard Law School because of her gender but ended up crafting the legal strategy that cleared a path for the landmark Brown v. Board of Education ruling.
To live in a racially diverse democracy, Brooks said, “We have to fight for it every day, all the time.”

title: Why we love the Charles
author: Stephanie Mitchell
summary: Some people go to the Charles River to move, while others go to write, relax, reflect, or just people-watch.
text:
If asked to imagine the heart of Harvard’s campus, most people would probably picture the Yard. But one could argue the center is the Charles River, which runs through Harvard’s Cambridge and Allston sides. From dawn to dusk the river is thronged with joggers, rowers, cyclists, dog-walkers — drawn to the scenic spot for reasons that are at once universally felt and deeply personal.
The Gazette spoke to a sampling of visitors who gathered recently by the Charles about what pulls them to the waterway.
Several miles down the river, “Dirty Water,” The Standells’ tribute to the Charles, blares from Fenway Park after every Sox home win. But closer to Harvard you’re more likely to hear about the success of recent cleanup efforts. One Cambridge resident who fishes the river every day boasted he landed a 3-pound bass. And for another longtime resident, the Charles evokes a different song altogether: Paul Simon’s “Peace Like a River.”
Peace is what draws Evelyn Huang, a Graduate School of Education student who moved here from Columbus, Ohio, in August. She already has a favorite lookout spot on the banks where she recharges on busy days. While the bustle of campus life can cause FOMO, or “fear of missing out,” Huang described the river’s effect on her as JOMO — “joy of missing out.”
“I love sitting here and watching the river and just let everything in my mind flow like the river.”
“I believe a city without a river is not worth living in,” says Leo Moradi, a recent Boston University Ph.D. graduate in philosophy. He has eaten lunch more than 100 times along the Charles and once photographed a sunset in which the sun and river perfectly aligned. “I still vividly remember that day.”
“There’s the interconnectedness of it,” said Mary Stargel, a visitor from Tennessee. “I’m sitting at this body of water. I know that it’s going into the next body of water that is bigger, and it’s come a long way. When I come here, I remember other bodies of water, and that’s very calming. It connects me to the other places I’ve been.”
“It feels like part of the Harvard experience,” said Ellie Stallings. Visiting the river was one of her first acts when she arrived from San Francisco for Harvard Summer School, and she keeps returning to read, do homework, run, observe the bunnies, watch the sunset, and walk to the supermarket or her volunteer job in Central Square.
“It’s really beautiful. It’s really peaceful. There’s a lot of hustle and bustle at Harvard. It’s a lot of nonstop, and you have to take a minute sometimes and sit out and enjoy the sun,” said Micah John ’28, who grew up rowing with her siblings on the river. She often takes study break or grabs a bite along the Charles, and recalls an evening during finals last year watching the sunset and playing music with her roommate in the freezing cold. “Every day is a favorite moment out here.”
“I grew up in Colorado, so around nature a lot. Being in Boston and Cambridge, there are not as many easily accessible points of nature, and so it’s actually such a lovely place that I can just come by foot anytime that I feel like it to escape the noise a little bit,” said Cambridge resident Sarah Griffin.
Omar Silas, who grew up here, fishes the Charles daily for perch, crappie, and small- and largemouth bass. He brags that he recently caught a 3-pound bass. “The river’s been through a lot, so it’s cool to see the cleanup efforts are starting to pay off. Each year, it’s getting better and better.”
Ellen Birnbaum, who worked at Harvard for more than 20 years, comes to the Charles at least once a week — recently, on her birthday. “I find it very calming. There’s a line that Paul Simon made famous, ‘Peace like a river ran through the city.’ It’s biblical, but it feels that way. It feels that there’s peace here. Sometimes it is very still, sometimes it ripples, and sometimes the currents are strong. It’s different every time. It has a certain character, and I just like to be near it.”
James Bedford ’20, M.B.A. ’25, often perches on the Weeks Footbridge because it reminds him of home. “I grew up on a sailing boat in the southwest of England and being thousands of miles away from my family and from home, this is the place that I feel most calm and most at peace. It reminds me of days sailing and sound of the water and the waves under me.
“There’s something unique about the fact that every day the water that I’m looking at is different, and yet, there is something so familiar and so homely about it. If I think back over the journey that I’ve had coming to this country and coming to Harvard twice in the last decade, it feels very reminiscent of me. I have changed as much as this river has, and yet in many ways, I occupy the same shape and the same outline, and I’m watching myself change as the water does.”
“There’s something about the river’s continuous movement that amazes me. It makes me feel serene, free, and at peace,” said New Yorker Isabelle Lent, who was visiting friends in Cambridge. “I’m so amazed that these things keep flowing all the time, 24/7. When we’re sitting at our desks, stressed about the day, these things are still going.”
Lindsay Lu, a new student at Harvard Law School, stopped to watch the sunset from the Weeks Footbridge. “I like to watch the sun and how it reflects on the water. There’s a nice breeze. It’s nice to stop for a moment.”

title: New UK trial aims to find answers more quickly for Alzheimer's disease
author: Eliza  Kania, Samantha Rey
summary: Multi-site trial will test several drugs simultaneously and drop those not showing clear benefit.
text:
Health
Multi-site trial will test several drugs simultaneously and drop those not showing clear benefit.
An innovative national trial has been launched that could cut years from the search for treatments that work for people with Alzheimer’s disease, the most common type of dementia. Minister of State for Health and Social Care Alison McGovern MP marked the launch with a visit to the trial site at Charing Cross Hospital in London.
The AD-SMART trial is led by the UK Dementia Research Institute (UK DRI) at Imperial College London and by Alzheimer’s Research UK, in partnership with the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), the Medical Research Council (MRC) and Health Data Research UK (HDR UK). Ongoing funding has been committed by the UK government.
Alzheimer’s affects around 600,000 people in the UK and there are currently no NHS treatments that can slow or stop the underlying disease.
Applying lessons from cancer to dementia
AD-SMART (Alzheimer's disease Systematic Multi-arm Adaptive Randomised Trial) will test multiple drugs simultaneously, with separate groups of participants each beginning treatment with a different drug. Unusually, all groups will be compared with one single group of participants taking a placebo.
Researchers will examine whether the medicines can lessen symptoms such as memory and thinking problems and help people maintain their quality of life as the disease progresses. As the trial continues, regular checking of results will allow any drug that doesn't show clear benefit to be dropped quickly and replaced with another candidate.
For too long, Alzheimer’s research has moved at the pace of one drug, one trial, one answer, sometimes taking a decade or more before we know if we’ve found something that works. We are applying advances from cancer and other conditions to accelerate testing of treatments for people with Alzheimer’s disease.  Professor Paresh Malhotra Study lead, Group Leader at the UK DRI Centre for Care Research & Technology at Imperial College London
The trial will start with two repurposed medicines already approved for use to treat type 2 diabetes and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), Because the drugs are already approved for other conditions and have a well-established safety profile, if they prove successful, they could reach people living with Alzheimer’s much faster than a medicine developed from scratch.
As well as repurposed drugs, the trial is also designed to test new potential treatments coming through the research pipeline.
Study lead Professor Paresh Malhotra, Group Leader at the UK DRI Centre for Care Research & Technology at Imperial College London, said: “For too long, Alzheimer’s research has moved at the pace of one drug, one trial, one answer, sometimes taking a decade or more before we know if we’ve found something that works. We are applying advances from cancer and other conditions to accelerate testing of treatments for people with Alzheimer’s disease."
Professor Siddharthan Chandran, Director of the UK Dementia Research Institute, said: “We already know this model works. The SMART approach, used by us in Motor Neurone Disease in MND-SMART, has shown that testing multiple drugs at once, in one smart trial design, can speed up the testing of new treatments for neurodegenerative conditions. Now, we’re doing the same for Alzheimer’s."
“And because of the way SMART trials are designed, biotech and pharmaceutical companies can also bring their drugs straight into the trial. That means more treatments tested more quickly, and for people living with Alzheimer’s, that could make all the difference.”
Breakthroughs that change people’s lives
Dementia is one of the most pressing medical and societal challenges, affecting almost one million people in the UK. According to Alzheimer’s Society, this number is projected to rise to 1.4 million by 2040.
The UK Prime Minister, Andy Burnham MP, has spoken publicly of his own father's battle with Alzheimer's disease. He said of the trial: “I know how it feels to lose a loved one to dementia and have seen first-hand the devastating impact this illness has on families. That’s why I’m proud to see this trial being launched in the UK, so that cutting-edge treatments can reach patients here as soon as possible."
He added: “I have made dementia research a national priority. I want Britain to be the leading nation, making the breakthroughs that change people’s lives.”
UK Science Minister Chris McDonald MP said: “AD-SMART will help to uncover new treatments faster by exploring how existing drugs might be used to treat dementia, giving hope that we might be able to find ways to improve patients’ quality of life in the future.”
Dr Sheona Scales, Director of Research at Alzheimer’s Research UK, said: “For people living with Alzheimer’s disease, time is precious. We urgently need more treatment options that can help people live better for longer and stay connected to the people they love."
I have made dementia research a national priority. I want Britain to be the leading nation, making the breakthroughs that change people’s lives. Andy Burnham MP The UK Prime Minister
AD-SMART is designed to find effective treatments sooner. As a multi-arm, multi-stage platform trial, by testing several drugs at once against a single shared placebo group, more participants receive an active treatment than would do in a traditional trial.
Results are reviewed at regular stages, and drugs showing no benefit are dropped and replaced with new ones, meaning that fewer people receive ineffective treatments. Sharing one placebo group can also more than halve the time needed to evaluate treatments, which reduces costs.
Minister’s visit
On Wednesday 21 October, Alison McGovern MP, Minister of State at the Department of Health and Social Care, visited the AD-SMART trial site at the Imperial Memory Unit, Charing Cross Hospital, part of Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust. During the visit, the Minister met Professor Paresh Malhotra, a trial participant and members of the AD-SMART trial team.
The trial is being delivered by a team at Imperial College London, the UCL Innovative Clinical Trials Unit and the MRC Centre of Research Excellence in Clinical Trial Innovation (UCL), the University of Oxford and Dementias Platform UK (DPUK), with support from leading Alzheimer’s experts across the UK.

title: Fossil fuel subsidies and critical mineral funds should be used to fund healthcare in developing economies, argue researchers
author: Ryan O'Hare
summary: The global shift from fossil fuels to renewable and low-carbon energy (called the ‘green energy transition’) presents a once in a generation opportunity to redress the balance in favour of health, according to health economists and public health experts.
text:
Health
The global shift from fossil fuels to renewable and low-carbon energy (called the ‘green energy transition’) presents a once in a generation opportunity to redress the balance in favour of health, according to health economists and public health experts.
The team, led by researchers at Imperial College London, argues that funds from industry – including fossil fuel subsidy savings, carbon taxes, and royalties from mining critical minerals – should be ringfenced and used to fund universal healthcare (UHC) in low- and middle-income countries.
Their findings, published today in The BMJ Climate Issue, suggest the green energy transition could potentially free up billions of dollars of revenue globally from sectors which actively harm public health, offering a ‘golden opportunity’ to improve health at scale and boost development gains.
Dr Judite Goncalves, a health economist from the School of Public Health at Imperial College London, and lead author of the study, said: “The green transition will generate large public revenues: from carbon pricing, to royalties on minerals like lithium and cobalt, and from reforming fuel subsidies.
“The rules for how much of that money is raised, and how it will be spent, are being written now and will shape budgets for decades. Health should have a guaranteed share. Fossil fuels and mining take a heavy toll on people’s health, and part of the revenue they generate should go towards protecting it.”
Writing in a commentary, the researchers say that health systems have a strong claim to a guaranteed minimum share of these green revenues, they add, given the enormous health impacts of fossil fuel dependence and mining activities.
Fossil fuels and mining take a heavy toll on people’s health, and part of the revenue they generate should go towards protecting it Dr Judite Goncalves School of Public Health
In 2024, $733bn was spent on fossil fuel subsidies globally, far outpacing the estimated $20-53bn annual financing gap required to achieve UHC in low- and middle-income countries, they explain. Reducing these subsidies can free up substantial resources for domestic public health programmes.
Beyond subsidy reform, carbon taxes and royalties from critical minerals such as lithium and cobalt also offer substantial new revenue streams to support health.
However, they say it is critical to ensure that new revenues reach health budgets, rather than disappearing into general revenue or being eroded by tax avoidance and evasion or by pressure from investors to lower royalty rates.
“Not all the savings from reform can go to health, but even a modest, protected share could make a real difference,” explained Dr Goncalves.
In their paper, the researchers point to examples of innovative and ambitious reforms in Indonesia and Brazil that have also shown how funds can erode or fail to translate into local health investments. They explain that health ministries, civil society, and professional health organisations must urgently engage and influence carbon pricing rules and royalty frameworks, which are being locked in now, to secure a dedicated share of revenue.
They add that because green transition revenues flow disproportionately to higher income countries, while UHC financing gaps are concentrated in lower income countries, international mechanisms (such as debt-for-health swaps) are essential to ensure a fair transition.
Dr Goncalves explains: “Our own research shows that when oil prices drive subsidies up, governments spend less on health. When prices eventually fall, there will be a window to reform, as Indonesia did when oil prices dropped in 2014–15. Governments should be ready to use it, and to make sure a share of the savings goes to health.”
Professor Christopher Millett, from the School of Public Health, added: “The countries with the biggest health financing gaps aren't the ones set to gain most from green transition minerals and fossil fuel subsidy reform. Domestic reform alone won't be enough, so international partners have a role in making the green transition a fair transition.”
-
‘Analysis: Green transition provides a crucial opportunity to finance universal health coverage’ by Judite Gonçalves, Fernando Postali, Moh Shadiqur Rahman and Christopher Millett is published in The BMJ’s Climate Issue. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2026-100890

title: Imperial hosts global gathering of future leaders at the Laidlaw Scholars Conference
author: Christiana Jasutan
summary: Scholars gathered to share research and ideas, developing their approach to ethical leadership in the face of complex global challenges.
text:
Scholars gathered to share research and ideas, developing their approach to ethical leadership in the face of complex global challenges.
Imperial's South Kensington Campus was buzzing with excitement over the weekend. Over 350 undergraduate students from twenty-two universities across the world gathered for the Laidlaw Scholars Conference to exchange knowledge and share stories from their experience of the Laidlaw Scholars Leadership and Research Programme.
The Laidlaw Foundation – a global non-profit organisation with a long-term interest in education – established the programme to nurture integrity-driven leaders through independent research, character development, NGO placements and other leadership training opportunities.
The Laidlaw Scholars Conference gave scholars the chance to meet and network with peers from other institutions. Across the weekend, they were provided with plenty of opportunities to dive into hands-on workshops, hear from industry experts and share their work.
Inspiring ambitious leadership
The theme for this year’s Laidlaw Scholars Conference was ‘Ambition – Passion, Progress, and Possibility in a Changing World’. Panel sessions and workshops were curated to inspire ambition and curiosity among scholars as they began their research projects and placements abroad.
President Hugh Brady opened the conference, addressing scholars, members of the Laidlaw Foundation, university partners and other guests: “As I look around this room, I see individuals with diverse interests, experiences and ambitions who are united by a shared commitment to making a difference in the world. I hope this conference challenges you, inspires you and equips you with new ideas, friendships and renewed confidence in your ability to create positive change in society.”
One such student is Zachary Hobart, a fourth-year Medicine student at Imperial, who commented: “Laidlaw gave me the agency and support to design my own research and then the chance to apply my knowledge somewhere completely different. The Laidlaw Scholars Conference was the first time I saw the whole cohort's ambitions together, and it was a reminder of how varied and talented this group is.”
Susanna Kempe, CEO of the Laidlaw Foundation, said: “We are enormously grateful to Imperial for hosting our annual Scholars Conference and to President Brady for his wonderful opening address. Seeing hundreds of brilliant, morally ambitious next-generation leaders, celebrating each other’s great work, connecting and committing to lead the betterment of society, makes me hopeful for the future.”
Caring for a healthier future
The Laidlaw Programme at Imperial gives undergraduate students the opportunity to lead a research project and a Leadership in Action overseas placement, tackling challenges of the UN Sustainable Development Goals. These experiences give scholars the chance to improve their understanding of the current sustainability and societal challenges facing communities globally.
One of the most powerful ways we can create a better future is by identifying talented individuals, investing in their development and giving them the support, confidence and experiences they need to make a meaningful contribution to society. President Hugh Brady 
Sameer Gonuguntla, fourth-year Medicine student at Imperial, commented on how the programme has contributed to his academic and professional growth: “The Laidlaw Programme is the perfect place to get started in the world of research. You get all the support you need and the opportunity to connect with like-minded students internationally.”
Since 2023, Imperial has welcomed up to 25 undergraduate students annually to join the programme. This year, the Laidlaw Foundation has renewed its support, allowing Imperial to continue fostering future leaders through these unique training and development opportunities.
President Hugh Brady said: “At Imperial, we believe that talent exists everywhere, but not opportunity. One of the most powerful ways we can create a better future is by identifying talented individuals, investing in their development and giving them the support, confidence and experiences they need to make a meaningful contribution to society. I am grateful to the Laidlaw Foundation for its continued commitment to developing future ethical leaders.”
To honour the Foundation’s continued support, Imperial is welcoming the Laidlaw Foundation to the university’s Circle of Benefactors – recognising supporters and partners who are making a profound and wide-ranging impact through Imperial.
Find out more about the Laidlaw Scholars Leadership and Research Programme.

title: Imperial Global USA appoints inaugural Academic Co-Directors
author: Lily Baker Haynes
summary: Professor Karen Polizzi and Mr James Kinross have been appointed as Academic Co-Directors of Imperial Global USA, Imperial’s hub in the San Francisco Bay Area.
text:
Professor Karen Polizzi and Mr James Kinross have been appointed as Academic Co-Directors of Imperial Global USA, Imperial’s hub in the San Francisco Bay Area.
The Academic Co-Directors will steer the next phase of the hub, providing scientific and technological expertise and insight, and growing Imperial Global USA’s networks.
Wendy Tan-White is Chair of Imperial Global USA's Advisory Council, which brings together world-class researchers, successful founders, deep tech investors, industry leaders and policymakers from across the San Francisco ecosystem.
In the two years since the launch of the San Francisco hub, Imperial Global USA has hosted twice at San Francisco Tech Week, convened high-level meetings across academia and industry and developed transatlantic partnerships and opportunities.
The hub develops and consolidates connections between two exciting ecosystems: Imperial’s world-class research and innovation in science, medicine, engineering and business, and the dynamism of the Bay Area’s academic, clinical, industrial, entrepreneurial and investment communities. The hub's achievements so far have been possible thanks to the support of Imperial’s scientific experts, research and industry partners and our committed Bay Area alumni community.
Meet Professor Karen Polizzi
Professor Karen Polizzi is Professor of Biotechnology in the Department of Chemical Engineering at Imperial College London.
Karen’s academic background is in biotechnology and chemical engineering. She translates research on biological systems into real-world impact, and her work has led to international vaccine technology transfer, advisory work for spinouts and contributing to policy and regulation, recently around alternative proteins.
Karen’s expertise in working closely with researchers, industry, policymakers, funders and end users to achieve research translation and impact is central to the work of Imperial Global USA, which connects academia, research, industry and alumni to forge transatlantic cooperation and collaboration.
As a Maine native and Georgia Tech PhD alum, Karen noted “the United States science and tech community has been an important part of my work for many years and I value being welcomed into the US engineering biology community. I am proud to have contributed to the launch and growth of Imperial Global USA from the very beginning as an Academic Theme Lead, and becoming an Academic Co-Director is a natural next step.”
“Imperial Global USA is in a unique position to bridge between London and the Bay Area’s research and innovation ecosystems. I want to help Imperial researchers and innovators find the right partners, shape strong consortia and identify the investment, infrastructure and expertise needed to turn promising ideas into meaningful collaborations.”
Karen’s interdisciplinary work also encompasses areas including biosecurity and food systems through her role as Co-Director of the Imperial Centre for Engineering Biology and Vice Director of Imperial’s Bezos Centre for Sustainable Protein. Recently, she was part of an Imperial delegation to New York during United Nations General Assembly week to represent Imperial’s new Biosecurity Network of Excellence – showcasing how Imperial and Imperial Global USA’s work brings together leaders from science, health, AI, biotechnology, industry, government and international organisations.
Meet Mr James Kinross
Mr James Kinross is Associate Professor of Surgery in the Department of Surgery and Cancer, part of Imperial’s Faculty of Medicine.
James describes himself as a “mission-driven clinician-scientist focused on one key question: how can research make a real difference to patients.” Throughout his career, James has built and deployed clinical robotic and AI systems, led a microbiome science group and developed collaborative networks across Imperial and internationally.
With a clinical foundation in surgery, James’s research spans the breadth of Imperial Global USA’s academic themes. "I investigate surgical robotics, AI, computer vision, minimally invasive imaging, microbiome science, cancer prevention, synthetic biology, medical devices, extended reality and the translation of emerging technologies into clinical practice.”
James’s work has brought medical technologies, including surgical robotic systems, to market and his world also involves translating innovations such as extended reality into clinical practice, including in the San Francisco Bay Area.
“Much of my career has involved bringing different disciplines and sectors together. Imperial Global USA offers the opportunity to do that internationally, building relationships that develop over time rather than one-off collaborations.
“The opportunity for Imperial Global USA is not simply to export Imperial research to California. It is to build durable, two-way partnerships that generate new research questions, accelerate validation and translation, and create opportunities for Imperial students, researchers and spin-outs on both sides of the Atlantic.”
Karen and James join Imperial Global USA alongside the Advisory Council and operations team, who are building transatlantic cooperation through the hub. Find out more about Imperial Global USA.

title: Imperial and Tata Power partner to advance cleaner and more resilient energy systems
author: David Silverman
summary: Imperial College London and Tata Power, one of India’s largest integrated power companies, have announced a partnership to help drive the development of more sustainable, resilient and digitally enabled energy systems.
text:
Health
Imperial College London and Tata Power, one of India’s largest integrated power companies, have announced a partnership to help drive the development of more sustainable, resilient and digitally enabled energy systems.
This follows the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding on 25 September by Dr Praveer Sinha, CEO of Tata Power, and Professor Mary Ryan, Vice Provost (Research and Enterprise) at Imperial, that sets out plans to deepen a longstanding relationship between the two organisations.
When great British research teams up with the ambition and expertise of Indian business, there is huge potential to make a real difference. Jonathan Reynolds Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
Building on previous collaborative research such as a study into techniques for managing electricity demand, the partners have agreed to explore wide-ranging opportunities in fields such as energy storage, AI, industrial decarbonisation and grid modernisation.
By combining Imperial’s advanced academic insights with Tata Power’s scale, sectoral expertise, and track record of investment in renewables and digital technologies, the partnership is intended to help drive the roll out of new energy technologies in India and the UK and support the objectives of the UK-India Net Zero Innovation Partnership.
Dr Praveer Sinha, CEO&MD of Tata Power, said: “India’s energy transition is entering a phase where scale, flexibility and reliability will be as important as the pace of renewable energy growth. The next generation of grids, storage and digital energy systems will need to work together to meet a rapidly evolving demand landscape. Our collaboration with Imperial will help solve real-world industry challenges with deep research and new thinking and explore solutions that can be relevant not only to India’s energy journey, but also to the wider global transition.”
The partnership reflects Imperial’s institutional priority to tackle large-scale societal challenges by deeply integrating expertise from across disciplines and sectors with global partners, particularly in India where strong ties are facilitated by its Imperial Global India initiative.
Professor Mary Ryan, Vice Provost (Research and Enterprise) at Imperial College London, said: “As one of the largest energy companies in the world’s most populous country, Tata Power has expertise across a range of energy technologies and the scale needed to deliver the cleaner and more resilient energy systems we urgently need. This makes the company a fantastic partner for Imperial, which brings not only world-leading frontier research capabilities in science, engineering and business, but a model of convergence science that looks beyond individual disciplines to tackle challenges too large for standard approaches to innovation.”
Working with Imperial’s School of Convergence Science, a core pillar of the university's Science for Humanity strategy, the partnership will support HELIX, a programme that aims to help deliver equitable access to clean, healthy energy for 10 billion people by moving beyond isolated technologies and confronting the deeper systemic issues at play.
Harjinder Kang, His Majesty’s Trade Commissioner for South Asia and British Deputy High Commissioner for Western India, said: “The partnership between Imperial College London and Tata Power is a great example of the UK and India combining their strengths to turn innovation into impact.
“Bringing together world-class UK research and Indian industrial expertise will help accelerate next-generation energy solutions, unlock new commercial opportunities and support sustainable growth in both countries.”
Business and Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said: “When great British research teams up with the ambition and expertise of Indian business, there is huge potential to make a real difference.
"This partnership is a great example of our fantastic new trade deal bringing opportunities to life, and will help turn ideas into cleaner, smarter energy solutions – supporting good jobs and growth in both our countries.”

title: AI minister announces measures to protect against AI risks in speech at Imperial
author: Joanna Wilson
summary: The Rt Hon Kanishka Narayan MP, Minister for Artificial Intelligence, announced a suite of measures to better protect Britain from the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI during an event at Imperial.
text:
Health
The Rt Hon Kanishka Narayan MP, Minister for Artificial Intelligence, announced a suite of measures to better protect Britain from the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI during an event at Imperial.
The speech was given at Base One, an innovation space by Imperial which is supporting deep tech companies to scale and grow. Base One is part of Imperial’s Old Oak Innovation Cluster and sits at the heart of WestTech London, the innovation ecosystem established and anchored by Imperial which brings together world-class research, global talent, industry and infrastructure to create jobs, attract investment, drive growth and cement the UK’s position as a leader in science and technology.
The Rt Hon Kanishka Narayan MP, Minister for Artificial Intelligence, announced a suite of measures to better protect Britain from the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI, with the government urgently putting frontier AI to work strengthening cyber defences, examining stronger legal protections and preparing for serious incidents involving autonomous AI systems.
Imperial is focused on ensuring that frontier AI is developed and deployed safely and responsibly, with governance, safeguards, and real-world impact embedded from the outset.  Professor Peter Haynes Provost and Deputy President, Imperial College London
The move builds on two pilots that have already helped identify and fix over a thousand potential cyber vulnerabilities across government systems, and detect potential cyber threats. Extending the programme will help protect public services that people rely on every day and will support longer-term adoption across the public sector.
The Minister argued for a whole-society approach to resilience in the face of emerging AI risks, so that this technology continues to serve British people’s interests and boost our prosperity, as well as our security.
AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said: “I want Britain to become one of the hardest countries in the world to attack using artificial intelligence. We will use every power at our disposal. We will legislate wherever necessary. And we won’t look to law alone. We will look to British ingenuity: our scientific expertise, technological capabilities and institutions to understand these increasingly powerful systems, defend against emerging threats and respond when things go wrong.
“And to the companies developing the world’s most powerful AI systems, my message is: Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system.”
Professor Peter Haynes, Provost of Imperial College London, said: “Here at Imperial, we have AI experts in computer science, engineering, the natural sciences, medicine, and business developing cutting-edge research and innovation.
“Their work frequently leads to impactful applications, from accelerating drug discovery and improving healthcare to advancing climate modelling, designing advanced materials, securing infrastructure and creating trustworthy human-centred AI systems.”
He added: “Imperial is focused on ensuring that frontier AI is developed and deployed safely and responsibly, with governance, safeguards, and real-world impact embedded from the outset.
“And finally, with an eye firmly on the future, we’re investing in a new facility at our White City Deep Tech Campus that will bring together researchers from multiple disciplines to create a powerful engine for data science, AI and machine learning.”
Imperial’s work in AI includes:
- The university’s new Academic Building, to be built at our White City Deep Tech Campus, which will bring together academic researchers from across disciplines at an unprecedented scale to create a powerful engine for data science, AI and machine learning.
- A new Centre for AI-Driven Innovation, established jointly with the World Economic Forum and supported by the UK Government, which is dedicated to developing and scaling novel AI applications across key growth sectors of the UK’s industrial strategy. It is the first WEF Global Centre to be based in the UK.
- The School of Convergence Science has a major focus on Human and Artificial Intelligence, and will help to shape a responsible, collaborative AI landscape that amplifies human creativity, intelligence and societal impact while ensuring human empowerment. It will augment the intelligence of humans and machines to help humanity thrive.
- The Frontier AI Lab, recently established with Thomson-Reuters, is a landmark strategic partnership between industry and our School of Convergence Science that is focused on addressing the safety, reliability, and societal and economic impacts of AI.
