title: Imperial visits San Francisco to showcase quantum and deep tech expertise
author: Conrad Duncan
summary: Senior leaders from Imperial College London have travelled to the US to highlight the university’s expertise in quantum research and deep tech entrepreneurship for San Francisco Tech Week.
text:
Senior leaders from Imperial College London have travelled to the US to highlight the university’s expertise in quantum research and deep tech entrepreneurship for San Francisco Tech Week.
As a world-leader in deep tech, Imperial is home to researchers working at the cutting-edge of quantum technology which could lead to major advances for secure communications systems, ultra-sensitive sensors and computing.
The trip to San Francisco provided an opportunity to showcase how Imperial is using quantum technology to discover practical solutions to real world challenges, and building partnerships across academia, industry, tech, philanthropy and government in the UK, US and beyond.
San Francisco Tech Week is a city-wide technology festival which provides a space for independently hosted events, attracting an audience of global entrepreneurs, startups, industry leaders, tech commentators and investors from around the world.
Imperial hosted and participated in a range of events and activity during the week, including:
- An alumni and startup roundtable on Imperial Innovation in the Bay Area.
- An in-conversation event with PsiQuantum and tour of their facilities in the San Francisco Bay Area.
- A panel on London’s AI and deep tech ecosystem, featuring Imperial’s Vice-President (Strategic Engagement and Communications) Amanda Wolthuizen.
- Engagement with some of the Bay Area’s biggest tech companies and US national labs and academic partners.
- Convening tech and industry leaders, Imperial Global USA board members and venture capitalists at the GBx Gala.
- A five-day programme of activity for a cohort of Imperial startup founders.
The trip was led by Imperial Global USA - Imperial’s science and tech hub in San Francisco which acts as a platform for partnerships and connections between innovation ecosystems in the UK and US.
Vice President (Strategic Engagement and Communications) Amanda Wolthuizen speaking on a panel for London’s AI and deep tech ecosystem
The quantum frontier
While quantum computing is moving at increasing speed from theoretical promise to industrial reality, experts still do not know which approach will lead to the first scalable and commercially viable machine.
"Quantum technologies will reshape a great deal about how we live and work, and Imperial has the people, the facilities and the partnerships to help lead that change." Professor Peter Haynes Provost of Imperial College London
For San Francisco Tech Week, Professor Terry Rudolph, from Imperial’s Department of Physics, Co-Founder and Chief Architect of the technology company PsiQuantum, joined Imperial’s Provost Professor Peter Haynes for an event on the potential applications of quantum computing and how deep tech research can create high-value startups and spinouts.
PsiQuantum is one of the few companies working to build a large-scale, error-corrected quantum computer using photons of light.
Professor Peter Haynes said: “Quantum technologies will reshape a great deal about how we live and work, and Imperial has the people, the facilities and the partnerships to help lead that change.
“Through QuEST, our Centre for Quantum Engineering, Science and Technology, we are working right across that span. From discovery science at the frontier, to quantum navigation that can deliver precise positioning, to the expertise government now draws on directly.
“The same community doing the fundamental physics is building the applications and helping shape the policy, and that combination is what makes Imperial unique.”
Professor Terry Rudolph giving a presentation on PsiQuantum in San Francisco
The event also highlighted the importance of the new Centre for AI-Driven Innovation (CADI) - a partnership between Imperial and the World Economic Forum, supported by UK’s Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, which will work to accelerate the adoption and diffusion of high-impact AI across critical sectors.
Through CADI, Imperial aims to connect cutting-edge AI innovators with the partners and resources needed to make sure their ideas have the greatest possible impact, with an initial focus on life sciences, robotics in advanced manufacturing, and clean energy.
Professor Peter Haynes visiting PsiQuantum's facilities in the San Francisco Bay Area
Supporting future tech leaders
Alongside its world-changing research, Imperial also plays a role in preparing future leaders for industry and innovation and nurturing entrepreneurship in its staff and student community.
As part of San Francisco Tech Week, founders from five startups developed in the university’s entrepreneurial ecosystem travelled to the US to build international connections and tap into new channels of investment.
The startups for the San Francisco Venture Trek, led by Imperial Enterprise Lab and Imperial Global USA, were selected for their work in deep tech – a category of innovation rooted in substantial scientific discovery or complex engineering.
The centrepiece of the Venture Trek trip was a roundtable event called From Research to Real-World Impact: Imperial Innovation in the Bay Area, hosted by Professor Haynes, which explored the practical realities and opportunities presented by launching or expanding a company in the Bay Area.
The startup founders from Imperial taking part in the Venture Trek to San Francisco
The startups were joined by Imperial alumni who have established successful companies in the Bay Area, alongside Imperial research and innovation partners and representatives from across the San Francisco UK tech community, including London & Partners, for a wide-ranging conversation covering technical aspects of entrepreneurship, such as legal structures for international expansion, and cultural differences between US and UK investors.
The founders were also encouraged to define clearly what return on investment will look like from their startups and how this will be achieved, and reminded to be bold with setting out what they need from funders, rather than only responding to investor expectations.
The five startups travelling to the US were:
- Brilliant Dyes – a sustainable dye technology using microalgae which offers a sustainable alternative to conventional textile colourants, represented by co-founder & CEO Redwan Rahaman.
- Cardiovolt.ai - a system to teach artificial intelligence to read electrocardiograms (ECGs), providing a tool for identifying cardiovascular risk earlier, represented by co-founders Boroumand Zeidaabadi and Libor Pastika.
- Embed Biotech - a bioelectronics company which is developing smart implants to enhance bone healing after orthopaedic surgery, represented by founder & CEO Tom Hall.
- EvoTouch – an interactive soft-robotic simulator which offers realistic touch, diverse virtual patients and sensor-driven feedback for clinical education, represented by co-founder Elyse Marshall.
- Sealeo - a seaweed-based alternative to single-use packaging for temperature-sensitive medicines like vaccines and insulin, represented by co-founder Diana Epel.
Imperial and GBx
Through Imperial Global USA, Imperial is a member of GBx - a network that brings together British founders, technology executives and investors based in, or expanding to, the Bay Area.
Founded in 2016, GBx exists to support British entrepreneurs in the region, giving new UK founders a network to plug into as they establish themselves in the US, and provides a forum on emerging tech issues that can inform UK Government policy thinking.
As part of San Francisco Tech Week, Imperial Global USA Chair Wendy Tan White co‑hosted Imperial tables at the GBx Gala, alongside Imperial leadership, to celebrate UK‑US tech partnerships.
At the Gala’s Best in British Tech Awards, the technology company Starcloud, co-founded by Imperial alum Dr Ezra Feilden, won the Trailblazer Award in the growth‑stage category. Dr Feilden completed both his MSc in Materials Science & Engineering and his PhD in Materials Engineering at Imperial.
Starcloud is building data centres in space to address the energy bottleneck facing AI. The company has launched the first Nvidia H100 GPU into space and trained the first AI model in orbit, and became the fastest ever Y Combinator company to reach unicorn status, doing so in just 17 months. It recently raised $250m at a $2.3bn valuation, with backing from Benchmark and Nvidia.
Imperial Global USA Chair Wendy Tan White
More on Imperial Global USA
Earlier this week, Imperial Global USA announced that two new Academic Co-Directors have been appointed to help steer the strategy and evolution of the hub.
Dr James Kinross, from the Department of Surgery and Cancer, and Professor Karen Polizzi, from the Department of Chemical Engineering, will use their expertise to support the hub’s work on enhancing Imperial’s research partnerships with US academic and industrial partners.
Read an introduction blog from Dr James Kinross here and Professor Karen Polizzi here.
To find more information on the hub's work, visit Imperial’s website and follow Imperial Global USA’s activity on LinkedIn.

title: New technique reveals hidden losses in solar water splitting
author: Sanjana Kakar
summary: A new technique developed at Imperial College London measures oxygen production in real time, revealing hidden losses in solar water splitting.
text:
Engineering
A new technique developed at Imperial College London measures oxygen production in real time, revealing hidden losses in solar water splitting.
Researchers at Imperial team found that electrical current did not always correspond to oxygen generation in hematite, one of the most widely studied materials in the field, revealing a previously unknown limitation in the reaction.
The study was led by Dr Flurin Eisner, formerly a Research Fellow in Imperial's Department of Materials and now at Queen Mary University of London, together with Dr Daniele Benetti from Imperial's Department of Chemistry. Collaborators included Professor Ifan Stephens from the Department of Materials and Professor James Durrant from the Department of Chemistry.
Revealing a hidden stage in the reaction
The team identified what they described as a "selectivity switch". At low current levels, much of the electrical charge was diverted into competing surface reactions rather than oxygen production. Once enough positive charge accumulated at the material's surface, oxygen generation became far more efficient, with oxygen-production efficiency rising to around 80%.
The same behaviour was observed when the reaction was driven electrically in the dark, suggesting it is a fundamental property of hematite rather than something specific to light-driven reactions.
The findings challenge the widespread assumption that electrical current always reflects how much oxygen is being produced, giving researchers a more accurate way to identify and improve materials for future solar fuel and green hydrogen technologies.
Royce-enabled instrument development
The discovery was made using a custom photoelectrochemical mass spectrometry (PEC-MS) platform developed at the Royce at Imperial facility in White City.
Access to the EC-MS equipment at Royce Imperial, together with support to develop a light-compatible cell, made this study possible. Dr Flurin Eisner Former Research Fellow, Department of Materials at Imperial
Supported by the Royce Small Equipment Fund, the researchers adapted an electrochemical mass spectrometry system into a platform capable of operating under illumination and measuring oxygen production in real time with exceptional sensitivity. The resulting PEC-MS platform enabled the team to simultaneously illuminate a sample, measure photocurrent and directly monitor oxygen generation as the reaction proceeded, making it possible to compare oxygen production with electrical current and reveal behaviour that would otherwise have remained hidden.
Dr Eisner said: “Access to the EC-MS equipment at Royce Imperial, together with support to develop a light-compatible cell, made this study possible. Its sensitivity allowed us to measure oxygen at reaction rates where current alone would have given an incomplete picture."
It is also very pleasing to see how well Flurin used the Royce Small Equipment Fund. Professor Ifan Stephens Professor in Electrochemistry, Department of Materials at Imperial
Professor Ifan Stephens said: "I am very proud to have played a small role in this paper. It is amazing to see how multiple techniques together, in this case electrochemistry, operando optical spectroscopy and electrochemistry mass spectrometry, can make us rethink our mechanistic understanding of a reaction." He added, "It is also very pleasing to see how well Flurin used the Royce Small Equipment Fund."
Improving solar fuel technologies
The findings could help researchers develop and evaluate new materials for solar fuel production more accurately.
The team now plans to apply the approach to other metal-oxide materials and explore its potential in a wider range of energy-conversion reactions, including carbon dioxide and nitrogen reduction.
The paper is published in Journal American Chemical Society. Link to publication: https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.6c11949

title: MintNeuro raises $5 million to scale-up chip platform for neural devices
author: Ian Mundell
summary: The spinout’s semiconductor chips are purpose-built to work in the brain, enabling implants and other innovative devices that promise better management of conditions such as stroke, epilepsy and depression.
text:
Engineering
The spinout’s semiconductor chips are purpose-built to work in the brain, enabling implants and other innovative devices that promise better management of conditions such as stroke, epilepsy and depression.
MintNeuro, an Imperial spinout developing specialised chips that enable devices to connect with the brain and nervous system, has raised $5 million from European and US investors. The money will be used to accelerate product launches, build new partnerships and support international expansion.
Neurological conditions such as stroke, epilepsy, Parkinson’s and motor neurone disease affect over one billion people worldwide. Many of these conditions are underserved by current treatments, and neural implants offer a promising alternative route to develop effective, long-term solutions.
Today, most device and therapy developers still have to choose between generic components that were never designed for the body and years of custom chip development. We are building the chips that end that trade-off. Dr Dorian Haci Co-founder, MintNeuro
However, these devices require very small semiconductor chips that can function optimally in the special conditions found inside the human body.
“Today, most device and therapy developers still have to choose between generic components that were never designed for the body and years of custom chip development,” explains Dr Dorian Haci, co-founder and Chief Executive of MintNeuro. “We are building the chips that end that trade-off.”
“Neurotechnology is entering a phase where specialised hardware will determine how far, and how fast, the field can go,” said Professor Tim Denison, Chair of MintNeuro and a specialist in emerging biomedical technologies at the University of Oxford. “MintNeuro’s semiconductor technology is well-placed to remove the key obstacle to industry scale, which could dramatically accelerate the pace of innovation.”
MintNeuro’s implantable chip technology originated in the Next Generation Neural Interfaces Lab, led by Professor Tim Constandinou in the Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering at Imperial. He and Dr Haci, then a postdoctoral researcher, started the company in 2022, building on a business case developed through the MedTech SuperConnector (MTSC), an accelerator run by Imperial that supports promising innovations in medical technology.
The company went on to raise £1 million in 2024, supported by an investment from the Imperial College Enterprise Fund and the conversion of a loan note issued through the MTSC Seed Fund.
"MintNeuro is a standout example of what the MedTech SuperConnector Seed Fund exists to do: back exceptional deep tech founders early and help them reach their next stage,” said Hiten Thakrar, Head of Imperial SuperConnector. “Going from Imperial spinout to delivering working silicon for neural devices is a major achievement, and we congratulate Dorian and the team on this raise."
The $5 million in funding announced on 7 October takes the company to the next stage of its journey. “This funding moves us from technology validation to commercial scale-up, with more customer programmes, faster product launches and our chips in the hands of many more developers,” Dr Haci said.
MintNeuro has the technology, market pull and ambition to become a globally important semiconductor company. Michelle Robson Founding Partner, Odyssey Ventures
The company has already delivered functioning chips and reached key integration milestones with research and development partners, including Motif Neurotech in the US and Amber Therapeutics in the UK. Earlier this year, it announced a partnership and multi-year commercial chip supply agreement with Motif, supporting the development of a minimally invasive neurostimulator initially targeting treatment-resistant depression.
“Neural devices such as brain-computer interfaces represent one of the most exciting frontier technology opportunities today, and significant value will accrue to those solving the foundational infrastructure challenges that stand between innovation and widespread adoption,” said Michelle Robson, Founding Partner at Odyssey Ventures, which led the latest investment round.
“MintNeuro has the technology, market pull and ambition to become a globally important semiconductor company,” she went on, “and we are backing this exceptional team as it scales from the UK into global markets, including Silicon Valley.”
Other participants in the funding round include 33East, JSK Investments and Alumni Ventures, along with Empirical Ventures, Jumpspace Ventures and other first-round investors.

title: New Scale-up Pathway connects regional strengths to keep British innovation growing in the UK
author: Claire Burgess
summary: The UK today welcomes a new Scale-up Pathway to enable the scaling of sovereign innovation and manufacturing.
text:
Health
The UK today welcomes a new Scale-up Pathway to enable the scaling of sovereign innovation and manufacturing.
The Scale-up Pathway will help more British innovations to scale here in the UK, supporting a new era of industrial growth and strengthening our competitiveness on the world stage. Professor Hugh Brady President, Imperial College London
WestTech London and the West Midlands have joined forces to deepen the connection between the two leading regional innovation ecosystems. Convened by Imperial College London and the University of Warwick, the new Scale-up Pathway strengthens the UK’s ability to commercialise its research, grow innovative companies, retain strategically important manufacturing and production capability, all of which will enhance UK global competitiveness.
The Pathway has been created to address one of the UK’s biggest innovation challenges – Britain is home to world-leading research and produces pioneering technologies and businesses across energy and climatetech, defence and security, medtech and biotech. But these innovative companies face structural challenges as they move from discovery and R&D to commercial production and scale.
The new initiative will bring together deep tech innovation and commercialisation as well as broad industrial and advanced manufacturing capabilities. It will provide companies with the tools, expertise and capabilities they need at every stage of growth, including access to investment and highly skilled talent, specialist spaces, manufacturing facilities and supply chains. The Scale-Up Pathway will enhance collaboration between the two regions and support growth across the UK.
By working together, we can support growth and create good jobs across both regions. Howard Dawber Deputy Mayor for Business and Growth
The Pathway is supported by the West Midlands Combined Authority and the Greater London Authority, together with Ealing Council, the London Borough of Hammersmith & Fulham, Solihull Metropolitan Borough Council, Birmingham City Council, Coventry City Council and Warwickshire County Council.
In addition to Imperial College London and the University of Warwick, the two regions house other leading knowledge and research institutions, including the University of Birmingham, the University of West London, Brunel University, Aston University, Coventry University, Birmingham City University and the University of Wolverhampton.
WestTech London, established and anchored by Imperial College London with the support of key partners including Imperial College NHS Trust, is unlocking the potential of West London to deliver a thriving, globally competitive innovation ecosystem. WestTech London is home to 1,000 frontier innovation companies which generate more than £9 billion in annual turnover and employ over 20,000 people.
 By working together, we can support growth and create good jobs across both regions.  Howard Dawber Deputy Mayor for Business and Growth
The West Midlands, the UK’s core engine of advanced manufacturing, generates over £22 billion annually in manufacturing output and supports hundreds of thousands of jobs. The region is actively transitioning into next-generation manufacturing, focusing on Electric Light Vehicles, battery technology and smart energy systems.
The Scale-up Pathway announcement comes as the West Midlands prepares to unveil new plans surrounding ‘reindustrialisation’. The region will bring together a number of existing and new initiatives linked to investment, innovation and business support, with the aim of strengthening Britain's productive capacity, accelerating industrial renewal and creating the industries, investment and high-value jobs of the future.
The Scale-up Pathway will be further enhanced by the arrival of HS2, creating an even stronger physical connection between the two ecosystems. Anchored by Old Oak in WestTech London and Birmingham and Arden Cross in the West Midlands, HS2 will become an ‘innovation line’ connecting major growth locations, supporting development and regeneration, and helping to power a UK-wide innovation economy.
Commenting on behalf of WestTech London, Professor Hugh Brady, President at Imperial College London, said: “The UK already has all the ingredients needed to be a global science and technology powerhouse. The opportunity now is to connect these strengths more intentionally, recognising what different places do best and enabling businesses to access the expertise, infrastructure and investment they need as they grow. The Scale-up Pathway will connect our complementary ecosystems and in doing so, help more British innovations to scale here in the UK, supporting a new era of industrial growth and strengthening our competitiveness on the world stage.”
This will further position the UK as a world-leading destination for innovation, investment and scale-up success. Professor Stuart Croft Vice-Chancellor and President, University of Warwick
Howard Dawber, Deputy Mayor of London for Business and Growth, said: “By connecting West London’s research and technology expertise with the West Midlands’ manufacturing strengths, this partnership will help innovative businesses access what they need to grow. London has close ties with regions across the country, including the West Midlands. By working together, we can support growth and create good jobs across both regions, helping to build a better, more prosperous London for everyone.”
Richard Parker, Mayor of the West Midlands said: “For generations the West Midlands has been a powerhouse of innovation and technology, manufacturing the products that built Britain's economy. Today, that pioneering, tech-first mindset persists and is shared, alongside world-class universities and companies, with West London. This is the region where breakthroughs begin and this unique collaboration will attract even greater investment, create high-value jobs and retain more of the economic value generated by British innovation. With HS2 set to bring the West Midlands and West London within a few minutes of each other, this partnership shows how strategic infrastructure can amplify the strengths we share and unlock new opportunities for growth across the UK.”
Professor Stuart Croft, Vice-Chancellor and President, University of Warwick, added: ‘Universities have an important role to play as engines of inclusive economic growth. Here at Warwick, we have a long history of partnering with industry and businesses translating our research into real world impact through education, skills training and business support. The Scale-Up Pathway will build on these strengths. By working together, we can help even more businesses expand, resulting in greater growth across the UK and our region. This will further position the UK as a world-leading destination for innovation, investment and scale-up success”.
Stephen Cowan, Leader of Hammersmith & Fulham Council, said: “This partnership builds directly on Upstream London, our pioneering industrial strategy developed with Imperial College London to drive innovation-led, inclusive growth. With White City Innovation District at its heart, Upstream London has helped create one of the UK’s leading clusters for frontier industries, attracting billions of pounds of investment and thousands of new jobs. Its next phase is focused not only on helping innovative businesses start and grow, but on ensuring they can access the space, skills, connections and supply chains they need to scale – while creating clear pathways for local people into the high-value jobs that growth generates. The new Scale-up Pathway extends that approach beyond the borough, connecting H&F’s innovation ecosystem with the West Midlands’ advanced manufacturing strengths and creating a route for companies to grow and manufacture in the UK.”
Peter Mason, the leader of Ealing Council said: “From South Kensington, Old Oak to the West Midlands, WestTech London is proving that a pipeline of innovation, start-ups, scale-ups, and full manufacturing can deliver huge benefits for the country. For our residents, this means great jobs in high skilled, high paid sectors, at the cutting edge of new technology and production. This partnership builds on that opportunity, extending incredible possibilities to even more people and communities.”
Dame Karen Buck, Chair of OPDC, said: "This partnership between two of the UK’s leading innovation ecosystems is perfectly timed to capitalise on the opportunities HS2 and the new West London district at Old Oak will bring. Old Oak sits at the heart of WestTech London, connecting Imperial's research excellence with Park Royal's industrial strengths to create a place where innovation drives jobs, entrepreneurship and inclusive growth. With unrivalled connectivity and the ability to accommodate innovation-led growth at scale, Old Oak will provide the space, talent and connections that will see West London integrate with the West Midlands to anchor a network of innovation districts of national and international significance."

title: Imperial researchers win international award for advances in lightweight magnesium materials
author: Meg Orpwood-Russell, Sree Jagadeesan
summary: Researchers from Imperial College London have won an international award for research that could help make future aircraft, cars and spacecraft lighter and more energy efficient.
text:
Researchers from Imperial College London have won an international award for research that could help make future aircraft, cars and spacecraft lighter and more energy efficient.
The team, from Imperial’s Departments of Aeronautics, Chemistry and Materials, received the LMD Magnesium Technology Best Paper Award for Fundamental Research from The Minerals, Metals and Materials Society (TMS). The award recognises outstanding fundamental research in magnesium technology presented through the TMS Magnesium Technology symposium.
The award-winning research focuses on lightweight magnesium composites reinforced with tiny silicon carbide (SiC) structures known as nanowhiskers. Magnesium is much lighter than commonly used metals such as aluminium and steel, making it attractive for industries where reducing weight can cut fuel use and emissions.
Although similar magnesium materials have been studied before, scientists have not fully understood what happens where the metal meets the reinforcing SiC nanowhiskers during manufacturing. This boundary, known as the interface, is crucial because what happens there can strongly affect the material’s internal structure and ultimately its mechanical performance.
Using advanced imaging and microscopy techniques, the Imperial-led team studied the materials across multiple length scales and in both two- and three -dimensions. Their work included powerful synchrotron-based methods that allow scientists to see inside materials at very small scales in 3D.
The researchers identified previously overlooked chemical reactions taking place at the interface between the magnesium alloy and the SiC nanowhiskers. In particular, they found a complex compound known as a ternary carbide forming at this boundary. This finding provides new insight into what happens during processing and how certain reactions influence the material internal structure.
This improved understanding is important because it shows how carefully controlling these reactions can lead to better materials. The study demonstrates that managing the interface can help distribute the reinforcing SiC nanowhiskers more evenly and refine the internal structure of the magnesium.
 This award reflects the collaborative nature of our research and our shared aim of understanding how design at the nanoscale can improve the performance of structural materials. Dr Qianquian Li Associate Professor in Lightweight Materials and Composites
Dr Qianqian Li, Associate Professor in Lightweight Materials and Composites at Imperial, said: “It is a great privilege to be recognised by TMS for our work on nano-reinforced lightweight magnesium composites. This award reflects the collaborative nature of our research and our shared aim of understanding how design at the nanoscale can improve the performance of structural materials. I am very grateful to TMS for supporting a community that drives materials innovation.”
The research was carried out through an international collaboration led by Imperial researchers Qianqian Li, Milo Shaffer, Christopher Gourlay, Zhuocheng Xu and Xinyi Hao. They worked with colleagues at the Technical University of Darmstadt and Karlsruhe Institute of Technology in Germany, and the Paul Scherrer Institute in Switzerland. The project highlights the importance of combining expertise across disciplines and borders to tackle complex scientific challenges.
Professor Milo Shaffer, Professor of Materials Chemistry at Imperial, said: “It was a wonderful surprise to receive this award. It reflects the team’s collective effort to use advanced analysis techniques to better understand these complex materials.”
The award-winning conference presentation was based on a peer-reviewed paper published in Materials Characterization. The study shows how relatively simple and scalable manufacturing methods, such as stirring reinforcements into molten metal, can be combined with advanced techniques to better understand how these materials form and develop. The findings could help support the future industrial production of high-performance, SiC reinforced magnesium composites.
By revealing what happens at the smallest scales inside these materials, the research provides new ways that could help guide the design and manufacture of high-performance lightweight metal composites. These advances could play a role in future developments in aerospace, space exploration and low-emission transport.

title: At MIT, Martha Minow speaks on sustaining democracy, both by using and overcoming AI
author: Peter Dizikes | MIT News
summary: Harvard Law School Professor Martha Minow delivered MIT’s Compton Lecture, examining the current threats to democracy, the challenges to it present by AI, and possible ways that AI could better inform people and have civic value.
text:
Legal scholar Martha Minow delivered this fall’s Compton Lecture at MIT on Thursday, examining the civic foundations of democracy — and describing how artificial intelligence is undermining it, but could be used to help reinforce traditional U.S. governance.
“It’s not a good time for democracy or constitutionalism,” said Minow, who is the 300th Anniversary University Professor at Harvard University, and a prominent expert in constitutional law and human rights. She noted a litany of challenges to democracy in recent years, including violations of laws and norms, the stifling of free speech, a diminution of congressional authority, disregard of legal rulings, the common vilification of others in society, and more.
Recent Gallup polling, Minow observed, shows 77 percent of people saying that the founders of the U.S. would be disappointed in the contemporary condition of the country.
“Many people genuinely wonder whether this nation’s system of government and rule of law, ignited 250 years ago, will survive,” Minow said.
Her remarks assessed the state of the U.S. in terms of what she called four key “ingredients” of democracy: education, reliable and accessible information, security from violence, and fairness. Minow evaluated how AI has, among other things, influenced these areas of life — but also suggested ways people could use contemporary technology to help.
“It’s very familiar to hear blame attributed to digital technologies and experts of all stripes, but a turnaround, I believe, is genuinely possible if people at MIT and elsewhere pour time and talent towards real and much-needed solutions,” Minow said.
A substantial portion of her remarks focused on the pitfalls of AI in education. That issue compounds some other troubling trends: The U.S. already has large local and regional disparities in educational funding, Minow noted, while schools have actually become significantly more segregated in economic and ethnic terms over the last three decades.
In this context, AI threatens to further weaken independent-thinking skills, Minow suggested, just when greater understanding of civic issues is absolutely vital.
“As AI surges, I think we have to learn to be smarter about how to use it, how to regulate it, and how to actually educate people about the costs of mindless using,” Minow said. She added: “Dominant AI platforms supercharge the strategies that are deployed by social media companies, inducing passivity in people … Leading AI models and interfaces and sycophantic elements endanger the development particularly of young people’s capabilities to think, to remember, and to engage in critical thinking.”
That trend away from cognitive effort, she suggested, can be changed — perhaps through AI tools that act more like tutors and are designed to enhance people’s deep thinking.
“Existing LLMs, model training, and interface design can offer nudges and questions and hints rather than replacing student work, but there’s so much more that could be developed, and more effectively, to be trustworthy, and to deepen human activities and curiosity, rather than replacing people,” Minow said.
To the audience, she added, “AI tools could do much more of that … And I believe that you, the people here, could develop better tools than the ones that are out there. And make better assessments, more meaningful and cheating-resistant.”
Minow’s talk, “Constituting Democracy in the Era of AI,” was delivered to a large audience in MIT’s Huntington Hall, Room 10-250 on campus.
MIT President Sally A. Kornbluth delivered introductory remarks to the audience. The Karl Taylor Compton Lecture Series, introduced in 1957, is the highest-profile event of its kind at MIT. Karl Taylor Compton was MIT’s ninth president, serving from 1930 to 1948, and then becoming chair of the MIT Corporation from 1948 to 1954.
“He guided MIT through the Great Depression and World War II,” Kornbluth said, “transforming the Institute from an outstanding school for training job-ready engineers to a great global research university.”
She added: “He was also a deeply committed patriot who helped harness the intellectual power of America’s research universities to serve the nation during World War II.”
Kornbluth called Minow “a legal scholar of extraordinary intellectual scope,” and a “dedicated educator whose work has shaped how we think about the law and our own humanity, as individuals and as a society.”
Minow has been a faculty member at Harvard Law School since 1981, and served as dean of the school from 2009 through 2017. Minow earned her BA in history from the University of Michigan, an MA in education from Harvard, and a JD from Yale University.
Minow’s books include “Making All the Difference” (1990), “Partners Not Rivals” (2002), and “When Should Law Forgive?” (2020).
In her talk, Minow also discussed the civic effects of misinformation, threats of violence, and multiple dimension of societal fairness. Modern media technology has led to a 75 percent reduction in journalists in recent decades, Minow observed, with an attendant rise in corruption in places without local media. Civic-minded technologists, she proposed, should work towards establishing a widely-used “information commons,” or many forms of them, to help people access more reliable information.
Meanwhile, when it comes to basic security in society, Minow warned, “We’re on the brink right now. I know a lot of judges, and every one of them has a credible threat of violence against them. In America. This is not acceptable.”
For all the challenges to democracy and traditional civic norms, however, Minow sounded positive notes throughout her remarks, pointing out that there are many opportunities to create new forms of reliable information, education, and community relations.
“We have to actually invent the world that we want to live in,” she offered.
Minow’s remarks were followed by a Q&A session in which Kornbluth read aloud questions submitted by the audience — and asked her to characterize her concerns about present trends.
“I worry about the loss of the Enlightenment,” Minow said. “I worry about the loss of the belief that reason, and testing hypotheses, and rejecting myths in the face of evidence, and the toleration and rights and expansion of participation that came along with the Enlightenment, that’s what concerns me the most. That’s why the disinformation issue for me is so important, that’s why the loss of critical thinking in schools is so important.”
She added: “I’ve spent much of my own career thinking about mass violence. What happens when people don’t understand each other, and are afraid. And it’s terrible, and we don’t want to be there. And I do view the Enlightenment as a time when people learned that actually having mass wars is a bad thing, and coming up with toleration is a good thing, and testing our ideas in light of evidence other people can share can produce a better life for everybody. I worry we’re abandoning that right now.”

title: Reinforcing the value of human understanding at MIT
author: Benjamin Daniel | School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences
summary: During the MIT School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Science's 75th Anniversary Symposium, scholars, students, and performers from across SHASS gathered to celebrate its legacy and contributions.
text:
At the MIT School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS) 75th Anniversary Symposium, speakers celebrated the school’s value and contributions, while exploring how artificial intelligence is transforming many aspects of teaching, research, and society.
The symposium was held Sept. 24-25 in the Linde Music Building’s Thomas Tull Concert Hall. Scholars, students, staff, and alumni from across SHASS and MIT gathered for the event, which kicked off with welcoming remarks from MIT leadership.
“How should we think about MIT’s School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences? With enthusiastic appreciation and gratitude,” said President Sally Kornbluth.
The school’s origins date back to the Lewis Committee Report, commissioned by MIT and published in 1949, which called for stronger integration between scientific and technical topics and humanistic scholarship and teaching.
Kornbluth noted that, much like when the school was founded just after World War II, the world faces uncertainty as it grapples with the broad implications of artificial intelligence.
“AI has suddenly arrived with enormous consequences for both research and education,” she said. “As we face the challenges of our own time, and our own society, it’s clear that MIT has never needed your particular insight and guidance more than we do now.”
In opening remarks, Provost Anantha Chandrakasan described the importance of a human-centered approach to technology, one that considers both its efficacy and its impacts. He lauded many of the new research projects happening through the MIT Human Insight Collaborative, a strategic initiative launched in 2024.
“Today — a time of rapid, AI-driven change — the arts, humanities, and social sciences are as important as ever,” he said. “To be able to contribute effectively to solving the world’s great challenges, it is not enough to gain technical mastery.”
Chancellor Melissa Nobles recalled how, during her tenure as SHASS dean from 2015 to 2021, reading the positive feedback from students in their SHASS course assessments reinforced the value of the school’s teaching.
“MIT students have a range of interests that draw them to our classes that may be invisible to their STEM professors, but that we very well know our students have,” said Nobles, who is also a professor of political science.
Agustín Rayo, the Kenan Sahin Dean of SHASS and professor of philosophy, noted that, while research in the school plays a key role in addressing global issues such as climate change and AI, the value of the work in SHASS should not be measured by practical application alone.
“Education should also help us ask what is worth doing, what do we owe one another, and what makes a life worth living,” Rayo said. “Some research matters because it helps us understand the histories, cultures, and social structures that have made us who we are. Some things matter because they enrich human life.”
Scholarship from across SHASS and beyond
Over the symposium’s two days, research presentations, panel discussions, and performances offered attendees opportunities to engage with the role of SHASS in exploring today’s biggest societal questions.
“We gather not so much to look back over the past 75 years, but to showcase where we are now, and share what we urgently aim to tackle together in the years ahead,” said David Kaiser, Germeshausen Professor of the History of Science and professor of physics at MIT, who also served as chair of the symposium planning committee.
The first day included a session on teaching and learning innovations. Faculty presented on the success of educational programs housed within SHASS, including the MIT Indigenous Languages Initiative Master's Program, the Master in Data, Economics, and Design of Policy (DEDP), and MISTI, the hub for global experiences for MIT students.
Stephanie Seed, associate professor of literature, spoke about why she and others are working to reintegrate classic books into their teaching.
“MIT, of course, is an institution unusually oriented towards the future,” she said. “Our students are trained to imagine and create worlds that don’t yet exist. And it’s precisely this future orientation that makes reading the past especially important here.”
Eric Klopfer, professor of Comparative Media Studies/Writing and co-author of MIT’s recent report on AI and instruction, said this is a moment when instructors must reassess how courses are taught.
“I don’t know exactly what that looks like, but I do think it means something that’s more than modifying our curriculum. I think it really means rethinking what the educational experience is,” he said.
During a session on computing and society, panelists described different views and research into technology and how it affects humans.
“We project aspects of ourselves onto computational systems,” said MIT Professor D. Fox Harrell during his talk about seeing “selfness” in machines.
“What makes an AI system is not just the code, not just the programming or the algorithm, it’s the fact that we narrate it as being intentional,” he said.
Program in Science, Technology, and Society Professor Sherry Turkle offered a skeptical view of human-technology interaction, particularly with AI chatbots, which she describes as “intimate machines.”
“If social media came for our attention, I argue that chatbots are coming for our capacity for attachment, which is deeper and much more troubling,” said Turkle.
Professor David Autor, head of the Department of Economics, said it’s an exciting time to be working at MIT, where scholars are collaborating to explore AI’s impact on society.
“I don’t think there’s a close analogy to a moment when everyone felt the world change so quickly,” he said. “The stakes feel incredibly high.”
Celebrating the arts and engaging with the future
The first day concluded with a rousing Music and Theater Arts performance showcase, which began with an excerpt from Stan Lai’s “A Dream Like A Dream,” a play directed and performed by students and instructors in class 21T.100 (Theater Arts Production).
“Variations on the Theme of SHASS 75,” a piece choreographed by Dan Safer, senior lecturer and director of dance programs, combined movement, lighting, and music in a celebration of both the human body and the school’s milestone anniversary.
Student and faculty musicians from a variety of styles and disciplines shared the stage, including Rambax MIT, MIT Concert Choir, and the MIT All-Star Jazz Combo. The showcase included stirring renditions of “Madrigal,” composed by Vice Provost for the Arts Keeril Makan, and “Prayer for Peace.”
On the second day of the symposium, several alumni presented on their current work and the impact of their SHASS experiences.
Jessica Coon PhD ’10, now a professor of linguistics at McGill University, spoke about the leading role MIT Linguistics plays in preserving endangered languages, and how her studies at MIT prepared her to carry on that work.
“SHASS gives us the tools not just to conduct research, but to communicate the impacts of this research across a variety of different audiences and in different ways,” she said.
Ankita Reddy ’19 double-majored in anthropology and biology and is now an MD/PhD student at the University of Pennsylvania. She highlighted her most impactful SHASS courses, including 21A.308 (Global Mental Health).
“This was the first time I was forced to consider how good health care looks different based on social systems and cultural practices,” she said. “SHASS made me more comfortable with, and more curious about, complexity.”
During the symposium’s final session, panelists engaged in a conversation about AI, art, and the implications for creatives in an era where their art can be co-opted and copied.
“There’s so much praise for new and upgraded technologies,” remarked associate professor of literature Sandy Alexandre. “The question I consistently have is: What does it mean to be an upgraded human being? How are we innovating as technology is innovating?”
Philosopher Justin Khoo said AI’s role in art could be considered a “giant paint brush you don’t have much control over,” adding he could see the creation of new sub-genres of art that are human-only, AI-infused, and purely AI, for example.
Khoo closed by saying he encourages students to “think broadly, and really take seriously the humanistic education here at MIT.”
“A broad understanding of a set of concepts which are widely applicable, not just narrowly applicable, I think that’s what we need more than ever now,” he said.
As the symposium came to a close, attendee Kent Sahin praised the event.
“I’ve attended every session, and this is a fantastic program and a great celebration of the 75th anniversary,” he said. “Clearly, whether it’s AI impact, the impact of climate change, or the impact of political and social change, SHASS is in the right place at the right time.”

title: Gunter Stein, control systems and theory expert, dies at 84
author: Jane Halpern | Amanda Moore | Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science | Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems
summary: Gunter Stein, an expert on control systems and theory whose work helped usher in an era of robust multivariable control, recently died at 84. He spent nearly 30 years as an MIT adjunct professor and researcher, while working at Honeywell.
text:
Gunter Stein, an expert on control systems and theory who was a longtime MIT adjunct professor and researcher who also worked at Honeywell Labs, died on July 11 in his home state of Minnesota. He was 84 years old.
Throughout his career, Stein helped to reconcile competing schools of thought surrounding automated control systems, and he worked helped usher in an era of robust multivariable control.
Born in Germany, Stein emigrated with his family to the United States at a young age. The son of a tool and die maker at Fisher Body Works, Stein earned his BS from the General Motors Institute (now Kettering University) in Flint, Michigan, and his MS and PhD in electrical engineering from Purdue University in 1966 and 1969, respectively. He then joined Honeywell Labs, where he spent a more than 50-year career developing systems including aircraft flight controls, spacecraft altitude and orbit controls, and other navigation and control systems for applications as varied as launch boosters, reentry vehicles, ship positioning systems, torpedo engines and autopilots, and precision guided weapons.
As an engineer at Honeywell, Stein’s incisive and rigorous way of approaching problem-solving quickly garnered attention, catching the eye of the then-director of the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS), Michael Athans, when the laboratory and Honeywell began cooperating on a NASA contract to design the controls for the F-8 aircraft. Stein’s submission on behalf of Honeywell was, at the time, labeled the “most conservative” of the potential submissions, but eventually became the only control system successfully flight-tested.
Noting Stein’s talent, Athans approached Stein with a pitch to join MIT in 1977. As Stein’s career and personal life were by that point deeply rooted in Minnesota, he was not interested in relocating full-time, but agreed to an adjunct position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), where he would spend one week per month giving lectures, helping advise graduate students, reading PhD theses, and acting as a principal investigator in LIDS. This arrangement would continue for the next 30 years, and would deeply shape MIT’s overall approach to control theory.
“Stein immediately struck me as a brilliant engineer,” says Munther Dahleh, the William A. Coolidge Professor in EECS and a member of LIDS, who at the time of Stein’s arrival was a newly hired junior member of the faculty. “As a naive researcher who was more of an applied mathematician than a real engineer, I was struck by how Gunter could see through the mathematics and distill what was truly essential for applications.”
As Dahleh’s career developed — he would eventually become an associate department head of EECS and the founding director of the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society — his regard for Stein only grew: “Through Gunter’s work at Honeywell and his collaborations with students and faculty at MIT and other universities, robust control entered virtually every area of control applications. He shaped the direction of our field for decades, and his ideas remain a driving force behind many of today’s control applications.”
“Gunter came to LIDS at a propitious time,” says Nils R. Sandell Jr. SM ’71, EE ’73, PhD ’74, who co-taught class 6.291 (Classical and Modern Methods for Control System Design) with Stein. “With the experience on the NASA project and on others, the emphasis had begun to shift from optimal control to robust control. Gunter was a key part of this evolution, with his keen insight, based on extensive experience, of how classical frequency domain control techniques for single-input, single-output systems dealt with model uncertainty.”
Over the course of the next decades, Stein would work on systems for the B-2 bomber and F-47 aircraft, and for many years would serve as a member of the U.S. Air Force Scientific Advisory Board. “I can attest that, decades later, the flight control design methodology that Gunter and his colleagues at Honeywell developed is still being applied to our most advanced aircraft,” says Sandell.
Alan Willsky, the Edwin Sibley Webster Professor of EECS (Emeritus), remembered his colleague at LIDS as both a practical and a theoretical force: “Gunter was one of the giants of automatic control. His work at Honeywell on advanced control systems is legendary, but what is equally impressive is his impact on control theory and his influence on generations of control researchers. The period of years when he split time between Minneapolis and MIT had major influences on how control is taught and researched here at LIDS.”
Years of working with uncertainty and multivariable systems led Stein to think carefully and deeply about famous failures of engineering, including the nuclear reactor disaster at Chernobyl that captured the world’s attention in 1983. Stein saw the disaster as a stark warning to all designers of control systems, not only for nuclear power plants but for aircraft, spacecraft, and indeed all systems “with automatic controls that cannot be done manually and that, if done improperly, can have dire consequences for property, the environment, and human life.”
In his highly influential 2003 Bode Lecture and essay for Control Systems Magazine, entitled “Respect the Unstable,” he wrote: “We must place renewed emphasis on stating and teaching the principles of our subject clearly and well. The applications out there are simply too serious for us to hide from responsibility under a cloak of mathematics.” Of that famous lecture, Dahleh muses, “his Bode Lecture, which marked the first time the award was given, solidified my view of his remarkable ability to understand very different applications from a common fundamental perspective ... He showed how the challenges posed by complex control engineering systems, from agile aircraft to the Chernobyl disaster, could be understood through the same fundamental ideas that explain the difficulty of controlling an inverted pendulum. Thirty years later, his lecture remains one of the most-cited Bode Lectures and one that has had a clear impact on our community.”
Among other honors, Stein was elected fellow of the IEEE in 1985; awarded the IEEE Control System Society's first Hendrik Bode Prize in 1989; elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1994; and awarded the International Federation of Automatic Control's Nathaniel Nichols Prize in 1999.
His impact on the field of control engineering is also measured by the regard of his colleagues, who uniformly remember him as warm, social, and deeply conscientious.
“Gunter was a great engineer — the greatest I have known — and he was also a great human being,” says Sandell, who notes the great passion with which Stein, in the Bode lecture, enumerated his responsibilities toward society as an engineer.
“On a personal level, Gunter was incredibly humble and unassuming, and always ready to offer help and support whenever asked,” says Dahleh. “He was a giant in our field and played a major role in shaping it. I am deeply grateful for the opportunity to have learned from him and to have had him as a colleague. He will be dearly missed.”
Predeceased by his parents and wife Nancy, Stein was survived by partner Ann Wynia, siblings Gerry (Lynn) Stein and Gisele Davis, and by many nieces and nephews. A skilled sailor and lifelong outdoorsman, Stein spent much of his life exploring the various coastlines and seas of the world, and the forests and lakes of his native Minnesota. Memorial donations can be made in Stein’s name to the Minnesota Nature Conservancy.

title: Q&A: How AI came to model the “messy” human mind
author: Jane Halpern
summary: Assistant Professor Benjamin Lindquist studies how engineers deliberately injected randomness into early AI, giving rise to deep-learning models that sometimes…
text:
Q&A: How AI came to model the “messy” human mind
Generative artificial intelligence models are rooted in ideas of mid-20th century engineers who thought some amount of irrationality was essential for a machine that could think like a human, contends Benjamin Lindquist, an assistant professor in the MIT History Section, who holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and is a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. To mimic creative thinking, these AI pioneers intentionally injected randomness into algorithms designed to deterministically solve problems, Lindquist writes in a new paper that appears in the journal Past and Present. In the paper, he traces the origins of AI hallucinations back to this early research and suggests there will be inevitable tradeoffs between creativity and predictability when trying to build machines that mimic human behavior. MIT News spoke with Lindquist about these ideas.
Q: Why did early computer engineers believe they needed to inject randomness and irrationality into AI systems designed for logic and calculation?
A: There is a long history of many figures in the world of science and art theorizing that chance plays an important part in discovery and creativity — in the ability to originate ideas. They equated creativity with unexpected leaps of logic, or even a dream-like state that allows you to think about things from a new perspective.
In the early 1950s, one popular idea from John Pierce, who was a prominent electrical engineer at Bell Labs, was about math being valuable in the world of art. The idea was shared by a lot of people working in early computing. When we think of artwork that includes math, we may think of something very orderly and precise, but Pierce came to the opposite conclusion. He concluded that the utility of math is that it could remove order from art. Then in a very calculated way, math could add a burst of the unexpected as a means to deviate from clichés and add an element of irregularity which just might lead to insight.
One popular way to add irregularity into otherwise predictable computers was through artificial (or random) neural networks. Many early neural networks were built by psychologists, who thought that by enabling scientists to build a model of the brain, artificial neural networks allowed scientists to observe what is happening inside, including how brains make productive mistakes. Rather than being black boxes, researchers believed these systems could open this black box of the mind and let scientists peer inside and see all the messy stuff that was really happening.
But there was another camp in the world of AI who thought that creative thinking was just “normal” thinking done better. It is interesting to look at these two very simplistic heuristics for understanding intelligence and creativity, and how they do and don’t mesh. The debate, then, was about trying to determine what human inventiveness boils down to, and then how to reconstitute human inventiveness in machine form.
Q: How did these early computer engineers view AI, and how is it different from the way we think about AI today?
A: When we think of AI systems, we think of ChatGPT or Claude. We value and use these systems because they give answers that, most of the time, are correct. One of the things that was most interesting to me in this research was finding out that a lot of the early advocates of these systems valued them for exactly the opposite reason. They wanted a system that, on occasion, gave answers that deviated from their expectations. They already had systems that could deliver reasonable and expected answers. They saw neural networks as valuable because they could give unexpected, perhaps even strange and bizarre answers.
One reason we might view these systems differently today could be because of how they operate. Early on, these systems were confined to laboratories, so there weren’t really any real-world consequences of a system that gives a strange, or wrong, output. But now there are legal and monetary reasons why OpenAI or Anthropic doesn’t want a chatbot that gives unexpected or creative answers. There has been a “sanding down” of strangeness in these systems. They still potentially have that at their core, but it is something that is now largely suppressed.
Q: How did early neural networks that incorporated randomness to simulate human creativity evolve to become the dominant paradigm in AI?
A: For a long time, a specific kind of AI called “symbolic AI” was the dominant approach. Essentially, symbolic AI says the world is based on rules. The role of the AI researcher is to try and reconstruct the knowledge of the world in facts and propositions and feed it into a computer.
Neural networks, with their use of randomness to solve problems, started to gain traction in the 1950s but fell out favor early on. Frank Rosenblatt, a psychologist who was a very important early figure in neural networks, died prematurely; he died accidentally on his 43rd birthday in 1971. He was quite a charismatic and forceful personality, who made a lot of grand promises about what systems based on neural networks could do. By the time he died, a shift toward symbolic AI was already underway. It is possible if, had he lived, things might have turned out differently.
But neural networks never went away. By the 1980s they had shifted more into the world of cognitive science. To become more powerful, and more useful, neural networks needed a lot of data and computational power. That didn’t really arrive until the advent of the internet, when a lot of data became available and computing started to power up. Around 2012, neural networks started to outperform and outpace a statistical form of machine learning, and they kept growing from there.
Q: What lessons can we learn from studying AI’s history that could inform its development?
A: I think there is a cautionary lesson here. The ideas and experiences of these early engineers tell us that we can work toward quashing hallucinations — we can work toward making AI perform a certain way so it doesn’t produce unexpected or unwanted answers — but there are going to be other consequences of that. These historical figures were onto something. There is a connection between the surprising and creative conclusions AI can offer and errors or hallucinations. There are tradeoffs when we build our systems to behave one way or the other. Maybe it is impossible to be completely at either end of the spectrum, but when we work toward one thing robustly, we often sacrifice something else unintentionally.
