title: Giving AI a “crystal clear” view of the materials world
author: Zach Winn | MIT News
summary: MIT researchers created an AI model that can identify optimal crystalline materials for various applications. The model combines 3D atomic structures with natural language descriptions to characterize crystal structures from research papers and computational databases.
text:
In principle, artificial intelligence could make finding the right material for an application as simple as ordering dinner: Scientists would tell a large language model what they want, and it would serve them the perfect material for the job.
Unfortunately, that approach doesn’t work well yet, and the problem comes down to data: Most materials consist of 3D arrangements of crystals, not the text streams that today’s large language models are trained on. The experimental literature is also heavily biased toward a few popular classes of crystals, making AI outputs skew toward those materials.
Now MIT researchers have created a multimodal AI model that tackles these problems. The model combines 3D atomic structures with natural language descriptions to create rich linguistic descriptions about the structures from experimental research papers and first-principles computational databases. The unified description outlines not just the chemical composition and structure, but also its properties, processing considerations, and potential applications, helping AI learn more about what makes materials impactful.
In a new paper in Nature Communications, the researchers showed their system could identify better material designs than models trained on text streams alone by allowing the model to “see” the atomic arrangements and bonding patterns. For example, when the researchers asked the model to identify materials suited for solid-state lithium-ion battery electrolytes, its top results included materials that had been independently identified as promising candidates. The researchers also showed their model learned geometric representations of material structures in ways text-only models could not.
“Structure is really at the heart of the materials science field,” says Ju Li, the Carl Richard Soderberg Professor in Power Engineering in the departments of Materials Science and Engineering and Nuclear Science and Engineering. “If you understand the structure, you can infer quite a lot about the properties and performance of materials. We wanted to build the connection between a material’s atomic structure and its properties and processing for the model.”
Joining Li on a paper about the model are Yang Jeong Park, first author and former MIT postdoc; Mayank Kumaran, a recent University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign computer engineering graduate; Chia-Wei Hsu SM ’26; and Elsa Olivetti, the Jerry McAfee (1940) Professor in Engineering in DMSE.
Getting models to see in 3D
Materials scientists are always on the hunt for new crystals that will lead to the products of the future. Over the last decade, AI has reshaped that process, proposing and designing new crystalline structures, which have highly ordered atomic structures and make up more than 90 percent of solid materials on Earth. Most of those models treat solid crystalline materials as 3D graphs.
The rise of large language models has given researchers another tool for innovation. But existing large language models rely heavily on text from published papers and books, limiting their knowledge of the physical world, since many potential crystal structures are stored in computational databases. Text-based models also lack understanding of visual geometry.
To overcome those challenges, the researchers decided to create a vision-language model for crystalline materials.
They trained a language model to create textual descriptions of crystal structures using an approach known as contrastive learning, in which models compare similar and dissimilar examples of structures and textual descriptions to achieve a unified understanding. This is similar to aligning the visual and language regions of the brain.
Following training, the researchers compared the predictions of two versions of the model: one trained on a dataset containing the AI-generated descriptions and the other trained on a dataset containing text from papers only. They found that the model trained on AI-generated descriptions successfully learned how to align geometric structures with text descriptions while the other did not.
“We wanted to create an AI model that works broadly across materials,” Li says. “That’s why we decided to synthesize narratives rather than rely solely on existing papers. We found when we used that narrative dataset, the models are better at predicting the function.”
Accelerating materials science
The researchers then showed their model could be given a natural language query describing a property and identify crystalline materials with that property, outperforming a baseline.
“There are sometimes these step changes within materials science around algorithmic integration toward useful tools, which the community uses to further advance the field,” Olivetti says. “This approach helps us see more deeply into three-dimensional structures and link structures to property and processing. I hope this can be one of those step changes.”
Li compares the model to AlphaFold, an AI model that links protein structures with function that has helped advance biological research and drug development.
The researchers believe their new approach can work with many crystalline materials, and they hope other material scientists will use it to accelerate their work.
“Being able to see a three-dimensional crystal and how its atoms are connected is super foundational,” Li says. “I think this will be useful to anyone who practices materials science.”
The work was supported, in part, by the U.S. Defense Threat Reduction Agency through the University Research Alliance; the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency; and the National Research Foundation of Korea.

title: MIT affiliates named 2026 Schmidt Sciences AI2050 Fellows
author: Jane Halpern
summary: Five MIT faculty members and three alumni are honored with fellowships to advance research on beneficial AI.
text:
MIT affiliates named 2026 Schmidt Sciences AI2050 Fellows
Five MIT faculty members and two additional alumni were recently named to the 2026 cohort of AI2050 Fellows. The honor is announced annually by Schmidt Sciences, Eric and Wendy Schmidt’s philanthropic initiative that aims to accelerate scientific innovation.
Conceived and co-chaired by Eric Schmidt and James Manyika, AI2050 is a philanthropic initiative aimed at helping to solve hard problems in AI. Within their research, each fellow will contend with the central motivating question of AI2050: “It’s 2050. AI has turned out to be hugely beneficial to society. What happened? What are the most important problems we solved and the opportunities and possibilities we realized to ensure this outcome?”
The 2026 AI2050 Senior Fellows include:
Sendhil Mullainathan is the Peter de Florez Professor at MIT with dual appointments in the departments of Economics and Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, and a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). His current research is at the intersection of algorithms and people, with a central focus on launching The Bike Shop@MIT, a new research center which works towards more human-centered AI through scalable bicycles for the mind, and innovative new gears for machine learning algorithms. Mullainathan is the cofounder of a non-profit to apply behavioral science (ideas42); a center to promote the use of randomized control trials in development (the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab); and Dandelion Health, and is the co-author of Scarcity: Why Having Too Little Means So Much.
Among other awards, he is a recipient of the MacArthur “Genius Grant,” has been designated a “Young Global Leader” by the World Economic Forum, was labeled a “Top 100 Thinker” by Foreign Policy Magazine, and was named to the “Smart List: 50 people who will change the world” by Wired Magazine (UK). He serves on the board of the MacArthur Foundation, is affiliated with the NBER and BREAD, and is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. His AI2050 project focuses on the translation of patterns detectable by AI into testable theories.
The 2026 AI2050 Early Career Fellows include:
Alex Damian is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Mathematics, holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). His research focuses on the mathematical foundations of deep learning, with an emphasis on optimization dynamics and representation learning. He was previously a research fellow at the Kempner Institute at Harvard University. He received his Ph.D. in Applied and Computational Mathematics from Princeton University and his B.S. in Mathematics from Duke University. His AI2050 project focuses on effective AI model training.
Bailey Flanigan is a Theodore T. Miller (1922) Career Development Assistant Professor in the Department of Political Science, holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of EECS, and a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). She received her PhD in computer science from Carnegie Mellon University in 2024. From 2024-2025, she was a Harvard Data Science Initiative Fellow, hosted at the Harvard Ash Center for Democratic Innovation. Her research combines tools from across disciplines (including social choice theory, game theory, algorithms, statistics, and survey methods) to advance political methodology and strengthen public participation in democracy. She is specifically interested in sampling algorithms, opinion measurement/preference elicitation, and the design of democratic innovations like deliberative minipublics and participatory budgeting. Her AI2050 project focuses on gathering structured public input which lawmakers can use when making complex decisions.
Yunha Hwang is the Samuel A. Goldblith Career Development Assistant Professor in the Department of Biology, holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of EECS. She is also a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). Hwang serves as the Co-founder and Chief Scientist at Tatta Bio, a scientific nonprofit dedicated to advancing genomic AI for biological discovery. She received her PhD in Biology from Harvard University and B.S. in Computer Science from Stanford University. Her research interests span machine learning for microbial evolution, biomanufacturing, and open science. Her AI 2050 project focuses on determining biological enzyme functions.
Manish Raghavan is the Drew Houston (2005) Career Development Professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management, holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, and a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). Before that, he was a postdoctoral fellow at the Harvard Center for Research on Computation and Society (CRCS). Raghavan received his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and computer science from the University of California, Berkeley, and PhD from Cornell University. His research interests lie in the application of computational techniques to domains of social concern, including algorithmic fairness and behavioral economics, with a particular focus on the use of algorithmic tools in the hiring pipeline. His AI2050 project focuses on mitigating negative effects, and strengthening positive aspects, of widespread AI reliance.
Alumni Irene Chen PhD ’22 and Allison Z. Koenecke ’14 and former postdoc Juan Carlos Perdomo were also named AI2050 Early Career Fellows.
Media Inquiries
Journalists seeking information about EECS, or interviews with EECS faculty members, should email eecs-communications@mit.edu.
Please note: The EECS Communications Office only handles media inquiries related to MIT’s Department of Electrical Engineering & Computer Science. Please visit other school, department, laboratory, or center websites to locate their dedicated media-relations teams.

title: Fostering community amid Kendall Square’s innovation
author: Zach Winn | MIT News
summary: The 18th annual Kendall Square Association Annual Meeting explored how new technologies could be a force for shared prosperity in society.
text:
Kendall Square in Cambridge, Massachusetts, is often cited as the most innovative square mile in the world. But when the Kendall Square Association gathered local stakeholders for its 18th Annual Meeting Thursday, the conversation focused on innovation primarily in the context of community.
The event, which took place at the nonprofit startup incubator The Engine, attracted people from across Cambridge, including business leaders, elected officials, local residents, and students, for a night of local food and conversation about the advance of technologies like artificial intelligence and what they mean for society.
“How can we make AI not an enemy of work, but a tool for workers to expand their capabilities and build new expertise or do new things?” asked MIT Institute Professor Daron Acemoglu in a keynote talk. “The world is at a point in time where we need new innovations and new adaptations to growing challenges.”
Acemoglu’s keynote was one of several presentations at the event, which also featured music from the Kendall Square Orchestra, a vote on new KSA board members, and awards for organizations making a positive impact through innovation.
KSA is a nonprofit made up of over 150 organizations across Kendall Square, from major companies to universities, research organizations, and the independent shops and restaurants that give Kendall Square its distinct character.
“People come to Kendall Square to make the world better,” said KSA Executive Director Beth O’Neill Maloney in her opening remarks. “People come here to improve the human condition, people come here to solve big problems, and people come here to innovate for good.”
Acemoglu, who shared the Nobel Prize in economics in 2024 for his work studying how institutions affect prosperity, spoke on the subject of his new book, “What Happened to Liberal Democracy?”
Acemoglu says liberal democracy is under siege as trust in liberal institutions decline, political polarization rises, and people lose faith in elected officials. He acknowledged that the shared prosperity liberal democracy promised has not always been delivered, especially over the last 50 years, but insisted it is the best path forward and in need of renewed support.
“I believe liberal democratic institutions, together with the norms that support them, are one of the greatest human achievements,” Acemoglu said. “It would be unthinkable for people who lived 300 years ago that we could live in societies consisting of hundreds of millions of people with diverse interests, different views, doing different things, and people still participate in politics and reach compromises, and we have state institutions that, by and large, actually provide services and do things for the people, and that we build opportunities for prosperity from which most people benefit while social freedoms are largely upheld.”
Cambridge Mayor Sumbul Siddiqui also spoke at the event. Siddiqui began her talk by telling the story of Cambridge residents working with biotech labs in the 1970s to create a groundbreaking policy on recombinant DNA research, which helped turn Kendall Square into the life science hub it is today.
“All these years later I think that story captures what makes Kendall Square so special: It’s our willingness to work together even when we face big challenges,” Siddiqui said. “It isn’t just the universities or labs, it’s also the culture of collaboration among nonprofits, governments, and residents.”
Broad Institute Chief Communications Officer Lee McGuire started his talk by reviewing a 2009 report on what made Kendall Square such a powerful driver of innovation, noting that factors like talent density, education, and a collective voice remain strong in the area today.
“This report was brilliant in that it captures so many of the special things that matter for a place like Kendall,” McGuire said. “It is the job of the Kendall Square Association and all of us to help protect those things, make sure we name them, understand them, and see them as essential elements of making sure this community stays what it is no matter what happens. As long as there’s a good idea, this is the place that’s going to get that idea moving and scale it up to change the world.”

title: Suzy Nelson transformed student life at MIT
author: Division of Student Life
summary: Over the last decade, MIT Vice Chancellor Suzy Nelson has refocused the Institute’s approach to student life to center on student well-being.
text:
Suzy M. Nelson, MIT vice chancellor for student life since 2016, will retire from the Institute this month. Nelson leaves MIT with a strong, coordinated Division of Student Life (DSL) built from years of close partnership with student leaders. One of her most noteworthy contributions is the elevation of student well-being, now integral to the Institute’s educational mission.
Under Nelson’s leadership, MIT created a culture of well-being, building out a strong support network, enhancing health promotion efforts, and expanding spaces dedicated to student wellness. These efforts emphasized the importance of students finding a sense of purpose, developing positive relations, and flourishing in mind and body.
Working with colleagues from across campus, DSL advanced new ways to coordinate student support services for undergraduate and graduate students experiencing significant challenges. MIT students now increasingly turn to programs such as Student Support Services (S3), which serves 82 percent of all undergraduates by the time they graduate, and 60 percent every year. A new CARE team coordinates resources that undergraduates, graduate students, and the MIT community rely on in a crisis, and has quickly become the thread that weaves together offices caring for students.
Nelson prioritized student residences as the cornerstone of the MIT campus experience. She led an effort to develop architectural principles for housing to guide construction and renewal planning; partnered with alumni from fraternities, sororities, and independent living groups to undertake a comprehensive review of chapters’ deferred maintenance and facility needs; expanded services to the residential communities; and developed close working relationships with the faculty heads of house.
“Suzy has been a wonderful leader and humane presence on our campus,” says David Mindell, head of house for Edgerton House. “She has partnered with the heads of house through trying times, as well as triumphs, and for that we are grateful. The students and their welfare have always been her first priority.”
Additionally, Nelson oversaw the construction of three new campus residences: Graduate Tower at Site 4 in 2020; New Vassar in 2021; and Graduate Junction in 2024, an innovative third-party partnership. The additional on-campus graduate housing increased capacity to accommodate nearly half of MIT’s graduate students and exceeded MIT’s commitment to the City of Cambridge. The division also worked on the renewal of four residences — New House (completed 2018), Burton Connor (completed 2022), East Campus (completed 2025), and now McCormick Hall (targeted for completion in 2028).
Beyond housing, Nelson advanced a major transformation of the core of the Stratton Student Center, leading to the opening of the Wellbeing Lab, new dance studios, improved lounge spaces, and refreshed offices for student organizations.
The Department of Athletics, Physical Education, and Recreation has played a critical role in MIT’s well-being efforts, incorporating wellness modules into physical education and wellness classes and offering recreation, intramural, and club sports opportunities to both undergraduates and graduate students. Additionally, the Institute’s athletics programs thrived during Nelson’s tenure, with MIT Engineer teams earning four national championships in 2024-25 and the number of All-Americans increasing significantly over the last five years. MIT remains the all-time leader in Academic All-Americans across all NCAA divisions. Nelson also encouraged expansion and renewal of athletic facilities, providing all students the opportunity to train using state-of-the-art equipment.
Nelson’s leadership shaped the Institute’s approach to community standards. She helped refine student conduct processes and streamline the Committee on Discipline process. She also championed new policies supporting free expression and launched a new Dialogue Collaborative focused on coordinating efforts that promote dialogue across the campus.
“Suzy is a remarkable leader and she has been a potent positive force within the MIT community. Her fusing of strategic vision, collaborative skill, and deep commitment to the students, DSL staff, and broader MIT community have been the hallmark of her extraordinary leadership,” says Erich Caulfield, chair of the Student Life Visiting Committee. “She has been a joy to work with, and her incomparable wisdom has been invaluable during this unprecedented period in student life at MIT and in higher education nationally."
Highly responsive to the changing needs of students, Nelson partnered closely with the Committee on Student Life and student leaders from the Undergraduate Association, Graduate Student Council, Dormcon, and the Graduate Housing Advisory Committee, as well as student representatives for individual projects. For example, Nelson created a working group to improve how student organizations gain recognition, manage membership, and apply for resources. She has worked closely with students on expanding access to nutritious food and supporting food security, and, this past year, she engaged students to help assess MIT’s dining services.
“Suzy brought her visionary leadership and humanity to DSL over this past decade to create profound, positive, and lasting change. All of us at the Institute, and especially our students, have benefited — and will continue to benefit — from the Nelson Era,” says Chancellor Melissa Nobles.
Throughout her career at MIT, colleagues and students came to know Nelson for her collaborative style. As she navigated crises over the past decade, most notably the Covid-19 pandemic, she always convened students, faculty, and staff. And she found new ways of elevating staff, creating the Staff Engagement Advisory Board, a group of 45-plus volunteers who support the division’s positive work environment and promote professional development opportunities. Her team in DSL is grateful for the many ways she strengthened and professionalized the division, and they will continue to abide by her unwavering belief that students should help shape the communities where they live and learn.
Nelson says of her retirement, “I am grateful to have served with so many exceptional faculty, staff, and students over these past 10 years. Because of their focused dedication to being here for students, I have every confidence that the transition to new leadership will be seamless.”
MIT will soon welcome Akirah Bradley-Armstrong as the next vice chancellor for student life. She most recently served as the vice chancellor for student affairs and success at the University of California at Santa Cruz, and has more than two decades of experience working in student affairs. She will start in the position on Oct. 19.

title: MIT student leaders: Q&A with Association of Student Activities president Hana Sousa
author: Chad Galts | Division of Student Life
summary: Hana Sousa, an MIT senior in chemical engineering, volunteers with the Association of Student Activities as a way to advocate for students and to strengthen bridges between MIT and its student clubs and groups.
text:
Hana Sousa, a senior in chemical engineering who grew up at the confluence of the Rio Negro and the Amazon River, learned some important lessons as the leader of MIT’s Brazilian Students Association. Now president of the Association of Student Activities (ASA) — the organization that oversees all student clubs on campus — she is using what she’s learned to help hundreds of student groups navigate the intricacies of Institute policies.
The ASA serves as a bridge between MIT and all 359 of the Institute’s student clubs and groups, which are organized around topics ranging from acroyoga to model railroads to yearbook. Sousa likes to focus on how to get things done; in this interview she talks about how she works closely with Institute staff and her fellow students to help club leaders, and also takes part in water-treatment research that can be applied to the Amazon River and her hometown.
Q: How did you get involved in the ASA?
A: I was president of the Brazilian Club. I'm from Manaus, a 2-million-person city in the North region [of Brazil]. You can only get there on a boat or an airplane; there is only one road, and it goes to Venezuela. It’s in the middle of the Amazon, but Manaus feels very urban.
When I arrived on campus, Brazilians didn't have a club. The seniors didn't re-register the year before, which is something you have to do, so we lost it — even though Brazilians have been at MIT since 1892!
My class has only four Brazilians, but in my sophomore year my friend and I realized we were losing the connections we had to each other. We could go to the dining hall and get dinner, but clubs give you a lot of perks — like access to funding and renting spaces on campus. We decided to recreate the club, but we made a few mistakes along the way in terms of club rules, because we didn't know.
I got involved with ASA while I was the co-president of the Brazilian Club because I wanted to understand how things work. I learned a lot about other student organizations, the staff, and how the financial systems work. I wanted to share this knowledge, so I ran to become the ASA president.
Q: What’s an example of something you learned in terms of running the club?
A: We wanted to put on a Brazilian harvest festival in the first term we were recognized. It was our first time hosting a large event. We didn’t know that, at MIT, especially if you're running a large event, you have to register at least 10 days in advance. Also, we had live music; you need to have a permit from the City of Cambridge for that.
In the end, the event was beautiful and people had a very nice time. But the next Monday, we received an email explaining what we should have done differently. I apologized and said these were rookie mistakes. We learned what the MIT policies were, and the next year, we didn't make any of the same errors.
This really helped me understand MIT. The staff knows what resources are available, and they want students to have whatever MIT can give them. They don't just tell us about the limits, they say why we are limited, and they offer another solution — when they can.
That's mainly how I advocate for students. If something is not standard, but it's possible, I ask, “How can we do that?”
Q: How do you balance the needs of students and MIT?
A: The ASA is a student organization, so we are their peers. If we say no to someone's application for a new club, that might be our friends. We also try to be their advocates. Because we have constant conversations with MIT staff, we mostly know what's possible and whose door to knock on.
Recently, the staff asked if we could move the ASA Midway — a big fair for student organizations that happens during orientation and campus preview weekend. The clubs set up booths; some of the performance groups have presentations. It's a way for students to understand clubs and organizations. We have a database people can use to look them up, but it's better to let students interact with them. We do it inside the ice rink, but our advisors on the staff thought it would be more visible outside.
I went back and talked with the ASA board, and we all agreed it was not a good idea. We weren't sure we would have enough space, and there were other things — some groups bring projectors, cultural groups like to have heaters for food to give out, performance groups need a lot of power outlets. Most of all, we thought the change would stress the students, and we already know how to do it in the ice rink, so we said no. They were fine with it.
Q: What was your path to MIT? What are you working on outside of the ASA?
A: I loved chemistry growing up, and I got a scholarship to go to a school in another city; I was 16 years old and I had to move there by myself. I got a bronze medal in the International Chemistry Olympiad, so I decided to go to college in the U.S., but my English was very poor. I knew how to read English because of chemistry — after a point, there are no more chemistry books in Portuguese. But conversation? Listening? Not so good. I spent a gap year in a program that helped with my applications. They asked me to apply to 10 schools. I just wanted to go to MIT.
I chose to study chemical engineering because chemistry folks are very focused on reactions and understanding how systems work. The engineers want to apply this.
This summer, for instance, I'm working on water treatment for the Amazon River. In my hometown, even though we are on the largest river in the world, some people don't have access to clean water. Chemists know a lot about colloid suspensions — how clay interacts with water. As an engineer, I need to know this and use it to make informed decisions about how to improve water treatment systems.
This is just like what got me to the ASA. I wanted to understand how things work at MIT. Getting involved and going every week to meetings helped me learn, and it helped me run the Brazilian club. Now I can do that for others, too.

title: State of Supply Chain Sustainability Report finds corporate commitment at record high, but governance lags behind
author: Mackenzie Berry | MIT Center for Transportation and Logistics
summary: The 2026 State of Supply Chain Sustainability Report from MIT's Center for Transportation and Logistics surveyed 1,810 supply chain professionals across 91 countries. While 83% prioritize sustainability, tariffs, geopolitical conflict, and weak governance prevent meaningful progress.
text:
When corporate leaders discuss climate strategy, the message that still dominates is that, despite competing priorities and external pressures, sustainability matters.
According to the 2026 State of Supply Chain Sustainability Report from the MIT Sustainable Supply Chain Lab, which surveyed 1,810 supply chain professionals across 91 countries, 83 percent rate sustainability as important or very important to long-term business success, the highest level in the report's seven-year history.
But commitment, the report reveals, is not the same as capacity. While 59 percent of respondents report becoming more committed to sustainability following recent U.S. policy shifts that deprioritize environmental concerns, the same organizations are being forced to compromise those commitments. Sixty-eight percent report that tariff uncertainty has compelled them to delay, scale back, or abandon sustainability strategies. Nearly one-third have seen tariff-related disruptions actually increase their operational emissions.
"Commitment is strong, measurement is expanding, and AI is accelerating," says Sreedevi Rajagopalan, director of the MIT Sustainable Supply Chain Lab and lead author of the report. "What comes next is harder: converting commitment into accountability, operational integration into strategic decision-making, and incremental decarbonization into genuine transition."
The result is a supply chain sustainability agenda stuck between conviction and constraint.
Beyond tariffs, more than eight in 10 respondents across North America, Europe, and Asia agree that ongoing geopolitical conflict is reducing the effectiveness of their organization’s climate action. Organizations built decarbonization plans on assumptions of stable trade and relative peace, yet neither assumption is holding.
The external disruption reveals an internal vulnerability. Among companies with publicly stated sustainability goals, only 51 percent have established a formal cross-functional sustainability team, which is the governance structure most strongly associated with embedding sustainability into daily decisions. In addition, only 33 percent place sustainability oversight at the board level. Public ambition, in other words, is vastly outrunning internal accountability infrastructure. Companies with formal cross-functional teams report sustainability is "frequently or always" built into decisions 57 percent of the time. Where responsibility sits in a single function, that drops to 13 percent — a 44-point gap illustrating the return on governance investment.
Sustainability is embedding most deeply where companies make daily operational choices: transportation and logistics (39 percent), procurement (35 percent), warehousing (34 percent), and product design (33 percent). However, it thins out dramatically in decisions that lock in long-term emissions: capital investment, network design, and supply chain risk planning. This reveals that companies are becoming better at operating more sustainably, but not at designing sustainable supply chains in the long term.
The artificial intelligence story compounds this tension. Seventy-eight percent of North American organizations report current use of AI in sustainability initiatives, and 87 percent of adopters report positive impact on sustainability goals. Eighty-six percent have reduced material waste, 81 percent have reduced energy use, and 63 percent use AI to estimate missing supplier emissions data. However, among mature agentic AI users, only 53 percent report a reduction in total greenhouse gas emissions. Twenty-nine percent report an increase, suggesting that operational efficiency does not automatically translate into lower net emissions.
This tension is particularly visible in warehousing. Among advanced and fully automated warehouses using AI, 78 percent report higher energy use since implementing AI, and 76 percent report higher waste, yet only 24 percent use AI-driven real-time monitoring to track environmental consequences. Many organizations may not realize their energy footprint is climbing until well after implementation.
Another key area of the report is freight transportation. Nearly every freight company is reducing emissions through route optimization, load consolidation, and driver-behavior programs. However, 43 percent of fleets still operate mostly or entirely on conventional diesel and only 8 percent have completed a full transition to low-emission energy. The divergence between regions reveals why: In Europe, 84 percent of freight companies report that recent policy changes have positively affected decarbonization strategy. In North America, only 44 percent do. When policy signals are unclear, capital-intensive technology transitions stall. For example, battery-electric vehicles are at scale in 60 percent of European companies, but only 36 percent in North America.
The report reveals that one bright spot has emerged in Scope 3, or indirect, emissions collaboration. Participation in joint supplier engagement and decarbonization programs surged from 31 to 58 percent in a single year. In addition, partnerships to manage shared suppliers' emissions more than doubled, from 23 to 55 percent. The share working entirely alone collapsed from 18 to 6 percent. The report, supported by the C.H. Robinson Foundation, Breakthrough, and CO2 AI and Dassault Systèmes, reveals that companies are recognizing that Scope 3 cannot be solved in isolation.
Across all these areas, the consistent pattern the report reveals is that corporate commitment is not the prevailing constraint to ongoing sustainability efforts. Rather, governance, accountability structures, technology infrastructure, and measurement capabilities are the current obstacles. Organizations that close the external gap by building resilience against disruption and the internal gap by hard-wiring accountability into structure will be the ones whose commitments survive. Those that do not will find that ambition without accountability moves the needle very little.

title: AI model decodes the language cells use to communicate
author: Shafaq Zia | Whitehead Institute
summary: Researchers at the MIT Whitehead Institute developed a powerful computational  approach to understand how cells communicate with each other to assemble into tissues and organs. Their framework has the potential to accelerate stem cell engineering, improve disease models, and even inform cancer treatments.
text:
As an embryo develops from a small cluster of stem cells, those once “blank slate” cells begin to take on more specialized roles like brain, liver, or muscle cells, and organize themselves into three-dimensional structures such as tissues and organs.
The fate of each cell — what type of specialized cell it will become — depends on which genes are turned on or off in the cell. These patterns of gene activity shape the cell’s structure and function, enabling it to take on a specific role in the body.
But this decision isn’t up to individual cells. They constantly send and receive chemical signals to and from neighboring cells, which help them understand where they are, what stage of development they are in, and what they should become. These messages spread through multi-step sequences called signaling pathways, which translate external signals into specific changes in gene activity in the cell.
For researchers, being able to retrace the sequence of instructions a cell has received would offer a powerful way to understand how tissues develop and how these processes go awry in disease.
But this has been difficult to achieve because scientists have long assumed that the effects of signaling pathways vary widely across cell types, meaning they would need to map each pathway separately in each cell type — an arduous and painstaking process.
Now, in a new study led by MIT assistant professor of biology and Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research member Pulin Li and graduate student Nicholas Hutchins, researchers have discovered that each signaling pathway leaves behind a unique “fingerprint” — a distinctive pattern of gene activity that reflects the particular signals the cell has encountered.
Importantly, these fingerprints are consistent across different cell types for the same signaling pathway, which means that instead of mapping each cell type separately, scientists can reconstruct signaling histories across many cell types using these pathway-specific fingerprints.
This discovery was made possible through a machine learning model called IRIS. This model can detect fingerprints of different signaling pathways and pinpoint which signals a cell received at different stages of development inside an embryo, even for cell types it hasn’t encountered before.
This artificial intelligence-driven approach marks a major advance over traditional methods, which require researchers to experimentally test every pathway in every possible cell type, and opens up the possibility to comprehensively map the signaling histories of every cell inside a mouse or human embryo at an unprecedented scale.
“Think of voice recognition systems like Siri, which are trained mainly in English, but then use that training to help them recognize other languages,” says Li. “This is called transfer learning, and this is why IRIS can work across many different cell types.”
The researchers’ detailed open-access findings, published in the journal Nature Methods on Sept. 8, could accelerate stem cell engineering for regenerative medicine and improve the creation of organoids — miniature, 3D models that mimic real organs — for studying disease mechanisms and testing new drugs. This is because once researchers learn the pattern of signals that drives a stem cell to become a specific cell type, they can recreate those signals to control the fate of stem cells in a lab or medical setting.
IRIS is a neural network-based model, which, in essence, is an AI-driven system designed to recognize patterns in complex data, similar to how our brains spot patterns. It examines a cell’s overall gene activity and estimates which signaling pathways were likely “on” at specific times during development.
Li and Hutchins trained IRIS on a large experimental dataset that measured how thousands of human embryonic stem cells responded to dozens of combinations of six major signaling pathways at multiple stages of development. This created a comprehensive map, or atlas, of how signaling combinations influence cell behavior.
The team then tested IRIS using single cells from mouse embryos during gastrulation, a stage when cells are rapidly branching into different fates. IRIS could accurately predict when and where specific signaling pathways would activate in cells destined to become part of heart, gut, muscle, and spinal cord tissue. This variation in signaling molecules is what guides cells to form the right structures in the right places.
With this approach, scientists can not only begin to understand the fundamentals of cell-to-cell communication, but also gain a practical roadmap for guiding stem cells into specific, functional cell types in the lab.
When the researchers employed IRIS to identify signals needed to create a cell type critical for lung development, the model predicted that activating a specific signaling pathway would encourage lung-specific development. Experiments in mouse embryos confirmed the model’s prediction. By identifying the precise combinations of signals that drive lung cell development, they can more reliably generate accurate, lab-grown models of lung tissue.
“In these ways, IRIS is helping us decode the language cells use to talk to each other at a much faster rate than we could realistically achieve through experiments,” Hutchins says.
These improved models would allow researchers to study diseases like asthma, lung cancer, and pulmonary fibrosis, in which lung tissue becomes scarred, often without a known cause. They can then use these models to test potential therapies, and ultimately design regenerative treatments that can repair the damaged tissue.

title: Gunter Stein, Control Systems and Theory Expert, Dies at 84
author: Jane Halpern
summary: Gunter Stein, an expert on control systems and theory who helped reconcile competing schools of thought surrounding automated control systems…
text:
Gunter Stein, Control Systems and Theory Expert, Dies at 84
Gunter Stein, an expert on control systems and theory who helped reconcile competing schools of thought surrounding automated control systems, and whose work helped usher in an era of robust multivariable control, died on July 11th, 2026 in his home state of Minnesota. He was 84 years old.
Born in Germany, Stein emigrated with his family to the United States at a young age. The son of a tool and die maker at Fisher Body Works, Stein earned his BS degree from the General Motors Institute (now Kettering University) in Flint, Michigan, and his MS and PhD in electrical engineering from Purdue University in 1966 and 1969, respectively. He then joined Honeywell Labs, where he spent his more than 50-year career developing systems including aircraft flight controls, spacecraft altitude and orbit controls, and other navigation and control systems for applications as varied as launch boosters, reentry vehicles, ship positioning systems, torpedo engines and autopilots, and precision guided weapons.
As an engineer at Honeywell, Stein’s incisive and rigorous way of approaching problem-solving quickly garnered attention, catching the eye of the then-director of LIDS, Michael Athans, when the laboratory and Honeywell began cooperating on a NASA contract to design the controls for the F-8 aircraft. Stein’s submission on behalf of Honeywell was, at the time, labeled the “most conservative” of the potential submissions, but eventually became the only control system successfully flight-tested. Noting Stein’s talent, Athans approached Stein with a pitch to join MIT in 1977. As Stein’s career and personal life were by that point deeply rooted in Minnesota, he was not interested in relocating full-time, but agreed to an adjunct position with EECS, where he would spend one week per month giving lectures, helping advise graduate students, reading PhD theses, and acting as a principal investigator in LIDS. This arrangement would continue for the next thirty years, and would deeply shape MIT’s overall approach to control theory.
“Stein immediately struck me as a brilliant engineer,” says Munther Dahleh, the William A. Coolidge Professor in EECS and a member of LIDS, who at the time of Stein’s arrival was a newly hired junior member of the faculty. “As a naive researcher who was more of an applied mathematician than a real engineer, I was struck by how Gunter could see through the mathematics and distill what was truly essential for applications.” As Dahleh’s career developed (he would eventually become an associate department head of EECS and the founding director of the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS)), his regard for Stein only grew. “Through Gunter’s work at Honeywell and his collaborations with students and faculty at MIT and other universities, robust control entered virtually every area of control applications. He shaped the direction of our field for decades, and his ideas remain a driving force behind many of today’s control applications.”
“Gunter came to LIDS at a propitious time,” said Nils R. Sandell, Jr. SM ’71, EE ’73, PhD ’74, who cotaught 6.291 Classical and Modern Methods for Control System Design with Stein. “With the experience on the NASA project and on others, the emphasis had begun to shift from optimal control to robust control. Gunter was a key part of this evolution, with his keen insight, based on extensive experience, of how classical frequency domain control techniques for single-input, single-output systems dealt with model uncertainty.” Over the course of the next decades, Stein would work on systems for the B-2 bomber and F-47 aircraft, and for many years would serve as a member of the U.S. Airforce Scientific Advisory Board. “I can attest that, decades later, the flight control design methodology that Gunter and his colleagues at Honeywell developed is still being applied to our most advanced aircraft,” said Sandell.
Alan Willsky, Edwin Sibley Webster Professor of EECS (Emeritus), remembered his colleague at LIDS as both a practical and a theoretical force: “Gunter was one of the giants of Automatic Control. His work at Honeywell on advanced control systems is legendary, but what is equally impressive is his impact on Control Theory and his influence on generations of control researchers. The period of years when he split time between Minneapolis and MIT had major influences on how control is taught and researched here at LIDS.”
Years of working with uncertainty and multivariable systems lead Stein to think carefully and deeply about famous failures of engineering, including the nuclear reactor disaster at Chernobyl which captured the world’s attention in 1983. Stein saw the disaster as a stark warning to all designers of control systems, not only for nuclear power plants but for aircraft, spacecraft, and indeed all systems “with automatic controls that cannot be done manually and that, if done improperly, can have dire consequences for property, the environment, and human life.” In his seminal 2003 Bode lecture and essay for Control Systems Magazine, entitled “Respect the Unstable”, he wrote: “We must place renewed emphasis on stating and teaching the principles of our subject clearly and well. The applications out there are simply too serious for us to hide from responsibility under a cloak of mathematics.” Of that famous lecture, Dahleh mused, “His Bode Lecture, which marked the first time the award was given, solidified my view of his remarkable ability to understand very different applications from a common fundamental perspective […] He showed how the challenges posed by complex control engineering systems, from agile aircraft to the Chernobyl disaster, could be understood through the same fundamental ideas that explain the difficulty of controlling an inverted pendulum. Thirty years later, his lecture remains one of the most cited Bode Lectures and one that has had a clear impact on our community.”
Among other honors, Stein was elected Fellow of the IEEE in 1985; awarded the IEEE Control System Society’s first Hendrik Bode Prize in 1989; elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1994; and awarded the International Federation of Automatic Control’s Nathaniel Nichols Prize in 1999. His impact on the field of control engineering is also measured by the regard of his colleagues, who uniformly remember him as warm, social, and deeply conscientious. “Gunter was a great engineer – the greatest I have known – and he was also a great human being,” said Sandell, who noted the great passion with which Stein, in the Bode lecture, enumerated his responsibilities towards society as an engineer.
“On a personal level, Gunter was incredibly humble and unassuming, and always ready to offer help and support whenever asked,” said Dahleh. “He was a giant in our field and played a major role in shaping it. I am deeply grateful for the opportunity to have learned from him and to have had him as a colleague. He will be dearly missed.”
Predeceased by his parents and wife Nancy, Stein was survived by partner Ann Wynia, siblings Gerry (Lynn) Stein and Gisele Davis and by many nieces and nephews. A skilled sailor and lifelong outdoorsman, Stein spent much of his life exploring the various coastlines and seas of the world, and the forests and lakes of his native Minnesota. Memorial donations can be made in Stein’s name to the Minnesota Nature Conservancy.
