I used to get emails from people saying, “For the first time in my life, I see myself as an entrepreneur,” or “I see economic security.” At MIT, we often say, “MIT in the world, for the world.” At the Trust Center, we see our mission as, first, train people here at MIT, but also to create more entrepreneurs outside of MIT.
The platform was inspired by the vision of Audrey McLoghlin, the founder and CEO of apparel brand Frank & Eileen and president of the Frank & Eileen Foundation. In my first meeting with Audrey, we were already asking ourselves, “How do we make more entrepreneurs in the world?” I showed her Jetpack, MIT’s generative AI tool trained on disciplined entrepreneurship, which walks MIT students through the entrepreneurial process, and her eyes lit up. She said, “This is how we create more entrepreneurs: We make the work that you guys are doing here accessible to young people.” She wished she had a tool like this when she first started. She also said her daughter wants to be an entrepreneur, but students don’t get much guidance on entrepreneurship at school. MIT has been a great place to keep making this more accessible.
Q: How does the platform work?
A: It takes the core disciplined entrepreneurship curriculum that we know works from our data, and makes it more interactive and engaging for young people. We spent a lot of time working with younger students to figure out how to make it more digestible to a 10-year old, 12-year old, or 14-year old. We put in different case studies and examples for each step of the framework, and we’ve designed the user interface to make it more like Instagram or YouTube, with videos featuring people that students can relate to. But ultimately the content follows the same path we know works; it’s just presented differently from what you would present to an MIT MBA or PhD.
Q: How might learning about entrepreneurship benefit students?
A: Entrepreneurship is a mindset, a skillset, and a way of operating. It allows you to deal with change, and the world’s rate of change is going faster and faster. It’s really not just about founding companies. Founding companies is a great way to learn the mentality that, ‘We can be different. We can build something. We can achieve a lot.’ Someone once said, ‘If you give a person a job, you give them dignity.’ But if you make someone an entrepreneur, it’s like giving them super dignity. They go from a job seeker to a job creator, and they can focus on the things that they’re most interested in, working with the people they want, in the culture they want. We teach students the entrepreneurial mindset and we train them to systematically take an idea and then come up with a solution in an ambiguous, uncertain environment, and iterate on that.
Everyone might not start a company, but even if they go to work at bigger companies, there are a lot of benefits to the entrepreneurial mindset. I’m an entrepreneur now and I’m at MIT, which is not a startup. In a world that’s moving faster and faster, everyone has to deal with change and ambiguity. Starting companies is just a great way to learn. It’s kind of like learning to paint from a blank canvas.

title: MIT class project turns into an FDA-cleared treatment for tremors
author: Zach Winn | MIT News
summary: Encora Therapeutics, which developed a wrist-based device that reduces essential tremor, started as a project in MIT’s famous product-design class, 2.009 (Product Engineering Processes).
text:
In 2017, a man named Michael walked onto stage in front of a packed Kresge Auditorium at MIT and attempted to draw a spiral, a common test doctors use to diagnose Parkinson’s disease. His tremors, caused by the disease, made the exercise difficult.
Then, Michael put on a wristband device made by a team of MIT students as part of 2.009 (Product Engineering Processes), who were presenting their prototype that evening.
Michael pressed a button and the device produced a subtle vibration. The vibration sent signals up his wrist and into his brain. His tremors dramatically decreased, and within seconds he was able to draw the spiral with much more precision, to a roaring ovation from the audience.
“When this device is turned on, I feel like I used to feel when I didn’t have Parkinson’s disease,” Michael told the crowd. “It’s an amazing, amazing feeling.”
The performance was so impressive that the student team received requests from classmates and others asking where they could buy the device for family and friends living with tremors. Unfortunately, the students had to explain there was only one — for the time being.
The event set off a near decade-long journey that began by leveraging MIT entrepreneurial resources like MIT Sandbox, MIT FUSE, and the MIT Venture Mentoring Service. In 2020, the student team turned into an official company, Encora Therapeutics. But there were still dozens of hardware iterations ahead. Then there were clinical trials. In one trial, 78 percent of patients reported benefits after 90 days of home use.
This February, nine years after Michael’s brave demonstration, all that work finally paid off: The FDA cleared Encora’s device to help adults with essential tremor, a condition similar to Parkinson’s that causes shaking, often in the hands.
“It’s been a long and difficult — very difficult — journey, but also very rewarding, especially when we get feedback from patients,” says Daniel Carballo ’18, SM ’20, an Encora co-founder and vice president of strategy. “We hear stories from patients about how they’ve struggled with their condition and how much they benefit from this. It reminds us why we keep going.”
From classroom to commercialization
The three founders of Encora who are still with the company are Carballo, Allison Davanzo ’18, and Kyle Pina ’18. They were each seniors in 2017 when they enrolled in 2.009, MIT’s popular product-design class.
The semester began with a brainstorming session in which groups of about 17 students were asked to come up with dozens of potential product ideas. Carballo proposed a wearable device that used mechanical vibration to send signals to the brain to reduce tremors. The initial idea was to help patients with Parkinson’s disease.
“It was one of hundreds of throwaway ideas,” Carballo recalls. “The initial concept was inspired by classes I had taken in robotics around neural control of movement. I had a preliminary understanding of how an electromechanical device might interact with the body’s control systems and feedback loops that control movement to relieve pathological control of movement.”
The team eventually whittled their long list of ideas down to a few. Carballo’s idea was finally selected by a vote of 16-1 — with Carballo the only dissenting vote.
“I tried to explain to the team that this was so far-fetched that there was no way, in one semester, we would be able to make anything,” Carballo recalls. “Thankfully, I got outvoted.”
Through most of the semester, Carballo’s pessimism looked justified. At every class milestone, the team lagged behind other teams. Then, the week before final presentations, they met Michael, whose severe hand tremors were the result of early-onset Parkinson’s.
“He was a home renovator, so he worked with his hands, but his tremors had progressed to the point that he struggled to turn a screwdriver, use a drill, or even fill out paperwork,” Carballo recalls. “He had become reliant on his wife and daughter not only to run his business, but to help him with everyday activities.”
By this point, the 2.009 team had a prototype that would vibrate to send mechanical feedback to the brain. Carballo described it as “a foamcore box with a Raspberry Pi chip and some wires coming out.” When Michael put on the device and turned it on, his tremors dramatically decreased.
“It was like a light switch turned on and his tremors stopped,” Carballo says. “His wife and daughter started crying. A week later, he was gracious enough to repeat the process on stage for the final presentations.”
The presentation — and the outpouring of interest from people who wanted it for loved ones with Parkinson’s — made the team determined.
“It showed us there were a lot of people with this problem that could really benefit from this,” Carballo says. “A subset of the team became possessed. It would have been such a shame to know this could exist and to have it never leave the classroom.”
Some team members began using MIT’s entrepreneurial resources to commercialize the technology, initially focusing on Parkinson’s. They ran their first clinical trial with 20 Parkinson’s patients in 2022 in collaboration with MassGeneral Brigham. But they soon learned more patients are living with essential tremor.
“It was a greater unmet need,” Carballo says. “There are a lot of drugs being developed for Parkinson’s disease, but essential tremor hasn’t experienced that same innovation.”
Today scientists think tremor is caused by malfunctioning signals in the regions of the brain responsible for interpreting sensory input and coordinating movement.
“In these diseases, neurotransmitter deficiencies result in this pulsed signaling in the brain that manifests as tremors that are basically pulsed motor outputs,” Carballo says.
One current approach to target those signals is surgery that involves drilling holes in the skull to insert electrodes that drive new electrical patterns in the brain. Encora’s watch-like product targets the same brain regions with mechanical vibrations at the wrist.
“We’re applying mechanical stimulus, basically vibration, to stretch receptors in the wrist, which tell your body where it is in space,” Carballo explains. “The stimulation causes the receptors to activate and send a patterned signal to peripheral nerves of the wrist, that then carry the signal to the peripheral nervous system and into the central nervous system, to the same regions of the brain targeted by surgery.”
In 2024, Encora ran a randomized control trial with 47 patients living with essential tremor. Last year, the team ran a 59-person trial where patients used the devices at home. In both trials, more than 70 percent of patients experienced meaningful improvement.
The results were promising enough to gain what’s known as 510(k) clearance from the FDA for use as a medical device, in February of this year.
Helping patients
Most patients see rapid benefit when using Encora’s device. Patients have described the device as life-changing. Some say it allows them to do tasks they haven’t been able to do in years.
“We see some patients using the device 12, 14 hours a day,” Carballo says.
Today, Encora is focused on building a national sales force and working to secure coverage from insurers. As the company ramps up production, the product will finally become available for patients who qualify.
Further down the line, Encora hopes to fulfill its original mission of helping mitigate tremors in patients with Parkinson’s. Carballo believes the approach also holds promise for many other patients.
“There is a surprisingly long list of diseases that this could work for,” Carballo says. “The most obvious are neurological movement disorders, but the bigger picture of wearable neuromodulation is a rapidly growing field that has seen therapeutic benefit across a broad range of diseases. We see this as a platform technology.”

title: New tool lets users repair AI-generated 3D models, then fabricate them just the way they want
author: Alex Shipps | MIT CSAIL
summary: The InstructMesh generative AI tool helps users 3D print working, real-world items with ease by understanding how designs should look and which edits users truly want. You can prompt the system to produce a 3D model, then ask it to edit specific parts.
text:
“What you see is what you get” is a guiding principle for many software engineers — create programs where the content you’re editing looks the same as the final product. But when you’re using generative artificial intelligence systems to 3D print, say, a mug, you’ll likely get a cup that can’t hold your coffee. Why is that?
The issue is that AI models understand how an object should look, but not how it works, leading to impractical designs that undermine an item’s intended use. Even if you want to fix these errors, the models are typically hard to edit, especially for users new to 3D design.
A new approach called “InstructMesh” makes it much easier to design and print household items, accessories, and robots that work in the real world. The design software, which was developed by researchers at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), Google, and Northeastern University, can be prompted to generate a 3D design for a pair of glasses, for instance, and users can then highlight specific parts of the blueprint they’d like refined before 3D printing. It’s an AI-driven interface designed to understand how these designs should look and which edits experts and novices alike want to make, helping them create the objects they actually want to see.
CSAIL researchers used InstructMesh to put a personalized, creative spin on otherwise regular items. For example, the tool produced a mug that appears to be enveloped by a dragon, with its tail being the handle. It also fabricated a shiny blue whistle resembling a shell and a pair of glasses with butterfly wings spreading out just above the lens. Getting even more creative, it made an octopus-like dispenser, with liquids flowing out of each tentacle to distribute drinks into several cups at once.
What makes InstructMesh so adept at following such unique prompts? It pairs Microsoft’s TRELLIS system, which creates 3D models from text and image prompts, with the large language model (LLM) GPT-4, which supports ChatGPT — in other words, visual and textual knowledge combined.
“We wanted to bring together the talents of 3D generators and the reasoning skills of LLMs in an interactive space to make objects that people actually want,” says Faraz Faruqi SM ’22, PhD ’26, lead author on a paper presenting the project, graduate of the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, and recent CSAIL affiliate. “Language models are great at text and images, while TRELLIS’s talent lies in its ability to create 3D models, since it’s seen so many.”
InstructMesh’s strengths come in handy in other, more surprising areas. MIT scientists used the program to fabricate a knee brace that looks like denim to match a patient’s jeans. InstructMesh can even help create robots — that is, clever enclosures that house wireless components. The researchers made a “bristle bot” that resembles a colorful shrimp to demonstrate this. It has a motor hidden inside, and when switched on, it can slide across surfaces, sort of like a wind-up toy.
Faruqi and his colleagues found that InstructMesh could easily make their desired items. But what would someone who’s never 3D modeled anything think of their program? And could they really detect design flaws before fabrication?
The team has TRELLIS recreate popular 3D models found on Thingiverse, a platform home to millions of 3D printable models, to help them find out. Nearly 80 percent of the models it generated were structurally flawed in some way. CSAIL researchers then asked novices to identify and fix these issues in InstructMesh — and they were able to do both around 90 percent of the time, as reviewed by an expert. What these newcomers lacked in expertise, they made up for in intuition.
InstructMesh scaffolds the actual modeling process, which previously required domain expertise in 3D modeling tools. “With manipulation happening in the latent space of the generative model, InstructMesh supports natural language description of issues, and creates interpretive changes in the geometry for the user to evaluate and approve,” says Faruqi.
Users then created items resembling things like phone stands and vases, noting that InstructMesh was easy to use. They also found that InstructMesh enabled them to express a wide range of ideas, while the sliders gave them more precision to make certain tweaks, such as enlarging or extruding a particular part of the model.
“The users got what they prompted for and easily tweaked designs where needed,” adds Faruqi. “What they saw is what they got, and the items worked as advertised, so to speak.”
While users enjoyed using the InstructMesh, Faruqi has an even grander vision for the project. He now works at Google, where he may soon incorporate InstructMesh into an augmented reality (AR) platform. The idea: Prompt the system by explaining what you need using the context of your surroundings, then it’ll rapidly 3D print it (e.g., making a phone case that matches your wallet).
InstructMesh may also begin to incorporate physics simulations to model how your design may react to specific uses, such as whether a bowl breaks when dropped, and which materials would work best. The software might also integrate the more recent TRELLIS.2 to refine even smaller features in 3D models.
Stefanie Mueller, an associate professor of electrical engineering and computer science (EECS) and mechanical engineering at MIT, and a member of CSAIL, is a senior author on the paper. Faruqi and Mueller wrote the paper with Google researchers Ahmed Katary ’23; Fabian Manhardt; Vrushank Phadnis MEng ’13, PhD ’20; Ruofei Du; and Federico Tombari. Other co-authors were Northeastern University Assistant Professor Megan Hofmann along with several CSAIL colleagues: Demircan Tas SM ’24 and SMArchS ’24, a PhD student in EECS and architecture; former visiting researcher Theresa Hradilak; Ning Zhang ’25, a graduate student in EECS; postdoc Jiaji Li; and Martin Nisser SM ’19, PhD ’24.
The researchers’ work was supported, in part, by Google and the MIT-HPI Collaborative Research Program. They will present it at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology in November.

title: Governor Healey and President Kornbluth launch MIT Future Fest
author: Peter Dizikes | MIT News
summary: MIT Future Fest launched with a visit from Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey. Featuring talks from leading MIT scholars, panel discussions, open labs, exhibitions, performances, screenings, and more, the five-day event adds up to a demonstration of MIT research, teaching, thinking, and discovery.
text:
MIT Future Fest launched on Wednesday afternoon, featuring a visit from Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey before an opening panel at Kresge Auditorium.
Both Healey and MIT President Sally Kornbluth emphasized the power of curiosity and innovation during introductory remarks, while formally kicking off MIT Future Fest as a new kind of event that opens MIT’s doors to the world.
Spanning five days and featuring talks from leading MIT scholars, panel discussions, open labs, exhibitions, performances, screenings, and much more, MIT Future Fest adds up to a demonstration of campus research, teaching, thinking, and discovery.
“MIT and Massachusetts are known around the world as leaders in innovation,” Healey said. “Future Fest is a chance to celebrate that. But it’s also a chance to connect with each other. To learn from each other, and to imagine what comes next. In life sciences and biotech, robotics, advanced manufacturing, in energy and climate technology and quantum, and in the people who make it all happen.”
In remarks preceding Healey’s talk, Kornbluth observed that “in a world as complex and interconnected as ours, we aim to invent the future. We need all the help we can get, and that’s why it’s so important to have all of you join us over the next five days in exploration, conversation, and curiosity.”
Future Fest also underscores that at MIT, as Kornbluth put it, “We feel a drive to explore, to understand, to solve, to invent, to design, all in service of society.”
Since its founding, “MIT has long stood at the forefront of innovation and invention,” Healey noted. “‘The future starts here’ isn’t just a fitting theme for the next few days. It’s something we’ve been doing for the better part of 250 years in Massachusetts.”
Healey later appeared at an event about ocean sciences at the MIT Museum, whose staff have helped develop and organize MIT Future Fest.
All told, MIT Future Fest features over 100 speakers at more than 50 events, among many other activities. The MIT Museum is free to the public during Future Fest; MIT’s newly opened Met Warehouse is hosting its first public events on Saturday; and Sunday features the Cambridge Science Carnival, a series of family activities.
The remarks by Healey and Kornbluth were followed by a panel discussion, “The Future Begins Here,” featuring participants Noubar Afeyan PhD ’87, founder of Flagship Pioneering and co-founder of Moderna; Sangeeta Bhatia SM ’93, PhD ’97, the John J. and Dorothy Wilson Professor of Health Sciences and Technology and of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at MIT, and director of MIT’s Marble Center for Cancer Nanomedicine; and Bob Mumgaard PhD ’15, CEO and co-founder of Commonwealth Fusion Systems.
Massachusetts Economic Development Secretary Eric Paley moderated the wide-ranging discussion, which touched on the cutting-edge Massachusetts innovation ecosystem, the implications of artificial intelligence for research and industry, and more.
The panelists noted that a confluence of ingredients — universities, other research institutions such as hospitals, venture capital, and more — has helped make Massachusetts the world leader in biotechnology and other forms of innovation.
“You can’t be here and not feel like things that the rest of the world feel are not possible are possibly possible,” Afeyan said. “It’s really interesting how the environment makes you feel like you should also do something special.” He added that the various ecosystem elements have created a “critical mass” needed to sustain broad-ranging innovation.
“This critical mass accumulated between the academic science, the hospital research, the entrepreneurial companies, large companies moved in, the government stepped in, state level, to try to help this community,” Afeyan observed. “It’s an inherent advantage of any ecosystem, it’s the co-location, it’s the connections.”
Mumgaard, whose company is building the first fusion power plant in the U.S., concurred that the combination of elements available in the state ecosystem is crucial for advanced innovation.
“In many ways the challenge is simply scale,” Mumgaard said. “How do you get enough capital, how do you get enough smart people, how do you get enough people that are hard workers, how do you get the alignment from the institutions that can give you the permissions and tailwinds to be able to go and do that? And we did find that in Massachusetts.”
He added: “You could not have really have built this company outside of Massachusetts.”
For her part, Bhatia, a leader in developing nanoscale technologies that have made inroads in battling numerous forms of cancer, observed that part of the inspiration for her career came from visiting the MIT campus as a high school-age student.
“It was just that idea that you could engineer things, you could create instruments to improve human health, that started me on my journey,” Bhatia said.
As a faculty member, she has helped found eight spinoff companies and helped direct an MIT study about how the Institute — which has already helped generate about 30,000 new companies — can do even more to produce startups and technology transfer. Ultimately, she has concluded, teaching researchers about the tools and skills they need to found companies can help generate even more productive networks of entrepreneurial activity.
“We can be more intentional. We can create communities. … There are all kinds of ways to do more,” Bhatia said.
The panel discussion included reflections on AI and forecasts about the future of technology 20 years out, while ending with a reminder from Afeyan that, while the future is hard to forecast, it is at least partially shaped by people working consistently hard in pursuit of their goals.
“We can envision the future a lot better than we can predict it,” Afeyan said, when asked to forecast the effects of technology in a couple of decades, near the end of the discussion.
Afeyan concluded: “My parting thought on this would be to say … I think you can either live in the present, do the things you do, and get the future you deserve, or you can envision the future you want, and do everything in service of that.”

title: Craig Rowe soars to new heights
author: Ariana Gaines | MIT Lincoln Laboratory
summary: Aircraft mechanic Craig Rowe of MIT Lincoln Laboratory's Flight Test Facility is lead crew chief of the Gulfstream IV and oversaw its major modification over the past seven years — a leadership role that earned him a 2026 MIT Excellence Award.
text:
Working on airplanes is a profession that runs in the Rowe family. Craig Rowe, his twin brother, and his older brother are all aircraft mechanics. His father was an aircraft technician installing systems on military aircraft during the Vietnam War, after serving with the U.S. Navy in the Korean conflict.
"We are mechanically inclined," says Rowe, who since 2015 has been the lead crew chief of the Gulfstream IV, part of the aircraft fleet at MIT Lincoln Laboratory's Flight Test Facility (FTF) on Hanscom Air Force Base. As lead crew chief, he manages the inspection, maintenance, and servicing of the aircraft to ensure it is fully operational and safe for flight.
"Since I was a kid, I've had an interest in building and getting things running. I've also always been interested in airplanes, but this job involves more than just working on airplanes. These aircraft are test beds for the U.S. Department of War," Rowe says.
A career takes flight
Rowe began his career in 1985 as an automotive mechanic. From 1986 to 1988, he completed a certification program at Hanscom to obtain his airframe and power plant license. Issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), this license authorizes individuals to inspect, maintain, and repair aircraft. Around that time, the major historic American commercial carrier Eastern Air Lines went out of business, flooding the job market with aircraft mechanics and thereby complicating Rowe's search for an airline job. After two years in general aviation, Rowe returned to the automotive world until 1999, when he joined United Airlines operating out of Boston.
For nearly a decade, he worked side by side with his twin, maintaining mostly wide-body aircraft. In 2008, a position opened at the Flight Test Facility for a mechanic to support a Boeing 707 — the same position held for 25 years by Rowe's older brother, who was moving on to another opportunity to work on government aircraft. That aircraft, like all at the facility, had been modified from its original manufactured state to support development and testing of airborne systems for the U.S. government.
"My previous experience in the automotive and aviation fields helped me get the job, which not only required maintaining the aircraft itself, but also up to 30 pieces of ground support equipment in the hangar, from tractors and AC units to power systems," Rowe says.
Within six months of being hired, Rowe was promoted to senior mechanic. By 2010, he was overseeing a Falcon 20 jet that had hosted the Airborne Sensor Testbed (ASTB), used by the laboratory's Tactical Defense Systems Group (TDSG) to assess and mitigate threats to U.S. Air Force aircraft. Rowe served as lead crew chief of the Falcon 20, which largely served as a "chase" plane (flying alongside other test aircraft to observe their operation), for five years. In 2015, the laboratory purchased a Gulfstream IV (G-IV) to replace the Gulfstream II that had been the second platform to host the ASTB, and that was decommissioned in 2023 after 30 years in service.
"The G-IV is the first Gulfstream to digitally display critical flight data," Rowe says. "It's a far cry from the analog steam gauges of the Boeing 707. The newer technology of the G-IV is more in line with what I was trained on while working for the airlines. Even though the G-IV was built in 1999, that's not old by aircraft standards. These aircraft will fly 30, 40, 50 years, as long as you maintain them properly."
Crews cross the border
When the G-IV arrived at the Flight Test Facility, the team there, led by engineers from the Tactical Defense Systems Group, began developing the engineering plans to modify the G-IV into a test bed. Meanwhile, the laboratory's Contracting Services Department started searching for a contractor to design, manufacture, and install the modifications. They selected Field Aviation, with whom the laboratory had been contracting since the early 1990s for aircraft modifications, including those on the Boeing, two Falcons, and the G-II.
After FTF mechanics stripped the aircraft's interior — leather seating, kitchen cabinetry, and other luxury features — the G-IV headed to Field Aviation's 40,000-square-foot hangar at Toronto Pearson International Airport in Canada in December 2018. Field Aviation technicians stripped the cockpit and removed electronics racks and external fairings (structures that make the plane aerodynamically favorable) so they could visualize the aircraft shell.
After scanning the exposed aircraft structure, staff from the TDSG, along with Rowe and other FTF subject-matter experts, worked closely with Field Aviation engineers through preliminary and critical design reviews to verify that the proposed structural, aerodynamic, and electrical system changes would allow the aircraft to operate as required by the Air Force and FAA. These changes included installing load-bearing pylons under the wings, external mounts for sensors, and antenna farms on the roof and belly — all powered by a commercial-scale auxiliary power unit enclosed in a custom-built fireproof titanium box for flight.
Taking turns with his TDSG program manager, Rowe flew up monthly to Canada to oversee the disassembly, modification, and ongoing maintenance of the aircraft. At the end of 2019, Rowe and two other mechanics boarded the 45-minute flight to Toronto to remove the two engines from the G-IV and load them onto tractor-trailer trucks bound for engine manufacturer Rolls-Royce in Montreal.
"Engine parts can degrade over time, so they undergo calendar-based inspection and maintenance to ensure they can still safely power flight," Rowe explains. "The G-IV was due for its 20-year engine overhaul, which took three months for both motors."
When Rowe and his team reinstalled the overhauled engines on March 20, 2020, little did they know that a pandemic was about to cause a worldwide shutdown. They left Canada with six hours to spare before the border closed. A work stalemate ensued until early fall, when they were permitted to return to Canada. The modifications continued through 2023, when Field Aviation started reassembling the aircraft, assisted by Rowe and two or three mechanics on each trip.
"The engines had sat idle on the airplane for well over five years because we had no cockpit to start them," Rowe says. "We had to rebuild the cockpit from scratch, from a yoke [control wheel] and hanging wires. Everything down to the frame, including all radio racks, was gone. When you fly the aircraft for the first time after 2,200 parts were put back on, you pray you did it right. The reassembled aircraft not only powered on, but also took its first flight without a hiccup, which is a testament to the team's work. When the pilots and flight-test engineer returned, they gave me a big hug. I was very emotional."
An asset comes home
In April, the G-IV returned to the Flight Facility, after nearly seven-and-a-half years. Rowe had taken 80 roundtrip flights to Toronto, with stays spanning two to three weeks at a time. Sometimes, he stayed straight through weekends without returning home to his wife and two sons, who were in elementary school when the G-IV was brought to Canada and in high school when it returned to the laboratory. Rowe missed many weeknights of homework help and holidays.
For his leadership role in the G-IV modification effort, Rowe was recognized with a 2026 MIT Excellence Award in the Outstanding Contributor: Working Behind the Scenes category.
"Craig is a humble, confident, and approachable 'rock star' aircraft mechanic. His commitment to the G-IV modification program largely contributed to its success, and will leave a lasting impact as the aircraft returns to service on behalf of the Air Force," says David Culbertson, manager of the Flight Test Facility.
Rowe's work behind the scenes continues with supporting flight testing to validate the safety and functionality of the G-IV before the Tactical Defense Systems Group begins running Air Force-sponsored programs. This airworthiness testing involves test pilots flying the plane in military-designated no-traffic areas (usually over the ocean) to evaluate aircraft performance and handling qualities to ensure FAA standards are met.
The first step is calibrating instrumentation readings at different altitudes. As Rowe explains, the structural additions to the G-IV changed the airflow over its airframe, where ports sense air pressure, temperature, and angle of attack (angle between the aircraft's wing and oncoming wind) — measurements used to calculate critical flight parameters like altitude and air speed. A truth source for calibrating cockpit readouts can be established by placing a nose boom (an extension projecting from the aircraft's nose) housing sensors in front of the plane to measure unperturbed airflow. Those sensor outputs are sent to a separate screen mounted in the cockpit, enabling comparisons with the baseline aircraft instrument readings on the cockpit displays.
Hundreds of hours of computational fluid dynamics analysis by the laboratory’s Engineering Division at the Lincoln Laboratory Supercomputing Center to refine the aerodynamic designs of the modifications paid off when the cockpit displays matched nose-boom truth measurements almost exactly. Test pilots are also conducting in-flight vibration and flutter testing with accelerometers mounted throughout the airframe and control surfaces. These sensors track how the airframe structurally responds to aerodynamic forces; aircraft parts can crack, bend, or, in extreme cases, catastrophically fail if they vibrate at their natural frequency.
"The smallest detail can derail a carefully planned flight test, especially on an aircraft as heavily modified as this G-IV," says G-IV modification program manager Paul Mancini of the TDSG. "I spend a lot of my time thinking about what can go wrong and how to mitigate it. But with Craig as the crew chief, backed by the rest of the Flight Test Facility, the one thing I don’t worry about is having a good jet ready to go when we need it."
The G-IV is expected to be mission-qualified to operationally support the Air Force by 2027. "Our next step is getting the G-IV working for the government like it's supposed to," Rowe says. "I plan to retire in about six years, at which time the G-IV will be handed over to someone else to take care of for the next 20 years. This transition will be bittersweet; you get attached to your airplane like you do to a house or car."

title: YST Cube opens at NUS, broadening horizons in music education
author: National University of Singapore
summary: NUS unveils the YST Cube, a flexible arts space that supports music education, performance and collaboration.
text:
YST Cube debuts new possibilities for music education and performance at NUS
Reimagining YST's former Orchestra Hall, the new flexible arts space gives students more room to learn, create and present their work.
For years, the Orchestra Hall at NUS' Yong Siew Toh Conservatory of Music (YST) served primarily as a venue for rehearsals and masterclasses. Now, the familiar space has been given a new lease of life.
Officially opened on 22 October 2026, the YST Cube is a 254sqm flexible arts space where students and faculty can explore different ways of creating, performing and experiencing music — part of YST's broader efforts to keep up with changing approaches to music education and artistic practice.
“The YST Cube will create new and exciting possibilities for students and faculty to experiment and push the boundaries of artistic practice,” said NUS President Professor Tan Eng Chye at the launch of the Cube during the opening ceremony of Performers(’) Present, YST's triennial international artistic research symposium.
“It will also be a convening space for visiting artists, educators and researchers from around the world to converge, create and showcase.”
Akin to black box performance spaces, the Cube can be reconfigured for different performance formats, including arrangements where audiences surround performers. Its integrated lighting, projection and acoustic systems also support multimedia performances and other artistic activities.
More room to create
For third-year Composition student Joel Tan, the Cube offers possibilities for exploring different ways of presenting music.
“Having the Cube would mean that the school has the capabilities to host much more ambitious projects and performances,” he said.
He is particularly interested in its lighting and projection capabilities, having had limited opportunities to explore these elements previously at YST.
Joel's interest in how audiences experience music is also reflected in a piece he is developing, which explores the individual components of sound, and how different parts of sound can come together as a whole. Using three speakers placed in separate rooms connected by a hallway, the piece allows listeners to experience the different sounds individually and how they merge, depending on how they move through the space.
For fourth-year student Chan Chen, who is pursuing Music, Collaboration and Production with a Second Major in Audio Arts & Sciences, the Cube has the potential to bridge the gap between developing artistic ideas and bringing them to life, while allowing him to further hone his technical skills.
Having previously experimented with audio-reactive visuals and soundscape installations in his first two years at YST, he is now developing an immersive multimedia concert experience that integrates live chamber music with real-time audio-reactive visuals for his final-year project.
Finding a suitable venue with the necessary technical infrastructure has been a challenge, particularly when multiple projectors are involved.
“The new YST Cube potentially addresses many of these challenges through its integrated projection capabilities and flexible performance configurations. It presents an exciting opportunity to explore ideas that might otherwise be difficult to realise within a traditional concert setting,” he shared.
Amplifying the arts
The Cube's opening coincided with the Performers(’) Present symposium, taking place from 22 to 25 October 2026. The symposium will occupy the main venue and its adjoining pre-function area, which can also function independently as a smaller event space.
Beyond music education, the Cube will broaden the range of artistic experiences available to students across different disciplines, in line with the university’s Arts for All framework.
It will also welcome arts organisations and external hirers for performances, rehearsals, creative residencies and collaborative projects, fostering artistic exchange and partnerships between YST and the local arts sector.
“The arts is a deeply fascinating and enriching discipline, and we want every student, whatever their discipline may be, to discover and learn about the arts,” said Prof Tan.
“They stretch our imagination, give us new lenses to see the world and deepen our understanding of the human experience.”

title: YST Cube opens at NUS
author: National University of Singapore
summary: NUS unveils the YST Cube, a flexible arts space repurposed from its former Orchestra Hall to support evolving approaches to music education and performance.
text:
YST Cube opens at NUS as a new space for evolving approaches to music education and performance
The space will offer students a future-ready environment for learning, artistic creation and collaboration, while supporting NUS’s wider commitment to the arts.
The Yong Siew Toh Conservatory of Music (YST) at the National University of Singapore (NUS) unveiled the YST Cube today, transforming its former Orchestra Hall into a flexible, reconfigurable arts space for music education, artistic creation, and performance. 
As approaches to artistic creation, learning and performance continue to evolve, students are exploring broader possibilities in how music can be created and presented, while taking greater ownership of their work. The transformation forms part of YST’s broader academic and artistic development, including reimagining how its physical spaces can support these changing approaches. By building on an existing space while expanding what it can enable, the Cube provides YST with greater capacity to respond to developments in music education over time. 
The Cube was officially opened by NUS President Professor Tan Eng Chye at the Opening Ceremony of Performers(’) Present, YST’s triennial international artistic research symposium, on 22 October 2026. 
“The YST Cube will create new and exciting possibilities for students and faculty to experiment and push the boundaries of artistic practice,” said Professor Tan. 
“It will also be a convening space for visiting artists, educators and researchers from around the world to converge, create and showcase.” 
The opening of the Cube strengthens YST’s role in the arts at NUS, advancing the University’s Arts for All (AFA) framework by broadening the range of artistic experiences that can take place on campus. While primarily serving NUS’s Music students, the new venue will also welcome the wider NUS community through public performances, presentations and other activities, creating further opportunities to engage with the arts at NUS. 
A flexible space for 21st century music education 
The Cube reimagines the Conservatory’s former Orchestra Hall – previously used primarily for orchestra rehearsals and masterclasses – as a purpose-built, flexible space for music education and performance. The transformation comes 20 years after the Conservatory building first opened. 
The Cube’s 254 sqm adaptable configuration, akin to black box performance spaces, allows it to be tailored to different uses, accommodating a range of performance formats, audience layouts and production requirements. For example, the Cube can shift between conventional performance formats and 360-degree arena-style setups where audiences surround the performers, or for multimedia work incorporating projection and lighting. 
Not only can it support conventional teaching, rehearsals and recitals, the new space can also accommodate workshops, presentations, multimedia events and performances that make use of space in more creative ways. The transformation also incorporates sustainability considerations through adaptive reuse, retaining key elements of the former Orchestra Hall while introducing new infrastructure and building systems to improve functionality and operational efficiency. 
This flexibility allows the space to evolve with the needs of its users, providing a future-ready environment that can adapt to changing approaches to how students learn, collaborate and present music as part of their education. 
“As music education evolves, we need spaces that allow students to move beyond fixed performance formats and encourage students to rethink how music can be created, presented and experienced,” said Professor Peter Tornquist, Dean of YST. 
“The Cube brings these possibilities together under one roof, giving students the freedom and flexibility to experiment with new ways of learning, collaborating and performing, while preparing them to navigate and shape the future of music.” 
Creating opportunities for applied learning 
The Cube will provide students with opportunities to apply their learning in a practical environment that mirrors real-world artistic practice. The venue features state-of-the-art audio, visual and lighting systems that brings professional production capabilities that is on par with world-class venues into the student learning environment. 
The Cube’s variable acoustic system allows the room’s acoustic response to be adjusted to suit different uses, while its lighting and multi-projection systems give artists greater flexibility in how performers and audiences are positioned within the space. 
For students, these capabilities provide hands-on opportunities to work with different acoustic conditions, technical setups, spatial configurations and modes of presentation, helping them understand how these choices can shape an artistic outcome. This supports YST’s continued development of its curriculum, including areas that place greater emphasis on student-led performance projects and collaborative music-making. 
“Applied learning is central to the YST experience,” shared YST Assistant Professor Jonathan Shin. 
“The Cube allows for different modes of learning—it gives students a playground to dream in, a laboratory to try practical and creative ways to bring their dreams to life, and a space to learn through the process.” 
The launch of the Cube at Performers(’) Present will demonstrate the versatility of the new venue, with the symposium making use of both the main space and its adjoining pre-function area. Designed as an extension of the Cube, the pre-function area can operate independently as an intimate event space for smaller audiences. 
By hosting activities of this nature within YST, the Cube brings professional artistic and research practices directly into the student learning environment, creating opportunities for students to encounter and engage with different approaches to artistic practice as part of their education. 
Supporting the arts ecosystem at NUS and in Singapore 
The addition of the Cube creates a new focal point for artistic activity within NUS, strengthening the University’s Arts for All (AFA) framework by bringing students across different faculties and disciplines together through the arts. 
“The arts is a deeply fascinating and enriching discipline, and we want every student, whatever their discipline may be, to discover and learn about the arts,” said Professor Tan. 
“They stretch our imagination, give us new lenses to see the world, and deepen our understanding of the human experience.” 
Beyond NUS, the Cube will provide Singapore’s arts community with a new purpose-built platform for performances, rehearsals, creative residencies and collaborative projects. The venue will welcome arts organisations and external hirers, fostering artistic exchange and partnerships between YST and the local arts sector. 
The Cube joins YST’s existing Concert Hall and Recital Studio, expanding the spaces available at the Conservatory to support different scales and forms of artistic activity. Together, these venues reflect YST’s commitment to shaping the future of music education, strengthening connections between students and the professional arts sector while contributing to the cultural landscape of NUS and beyond.

title: NUS researchers thread the world’s first touchscreen into a garment
author: National University of Singapore
summary: Researchers at the National University of Singapore’s College of Design and Engineering (CDE) have developed a fibre that functions as pixels and senses touch at the same time, integrating 54 of them into a sleeve to create the world’s first touchscreen built into a garment.The sleeve displays images and video, responds to finger presses and...
text:
NUS researchers thread the world’s first touchscreen into a garment
Researchers at the National University of Singapore’s College of Design and Engineering (CDE) have developed a fibre that functions as pixels and senses touch at the same time, integrating 54 of them into a sleeve to create the world’s first touchscreen built into a garment.
The sleeve displays images and video, responds to finger presses and connects wirelessly to other devices, yet stays as washable, breathable and flexible as ordinary clothing. The team’s invention enables the creation of garments that act as a direct interface to a wearer’s health data and their digital devices, with no rigid screen involved.
The screens that we are familiar with, such as those on phones and laptops, typically present graphical user interfaces (GUIs) on flat, rigid panels that display information and enable interaction. Textiles, woven from one-dimensional fibres, have never matched this capability. A full-colour, touch-sensitive display that can be threaded like yarn was, until now, out of reach.
“What made this possible was our ability to construct the GUI system from electronic building blocks in fibre form — similar to traditional yarn, but with the sophisticated electronic functionality built directly into the fibres,” said Asst Prof Khudiyev.
The team, led by Assistant Professor Tural Khudiyev from the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at CDE, published their findings in Nature on 21 October 2026.
Interconnecting thousands of chips along a thread
To build a fibre-enabled garment display, the NUS team developed a programmable method that creates connection points along tiny, insulated wires exactly where each microchip needs them. A laser exposes these locations, while controlled surface wetting guides molten solder to bond only at the programmed points. This enabled the team to integrate more than 5,000 chips through over 20,000 electrical connections.
The strip of interconnected digital LEDs was then integrated into a multilayer fibre using a thermal drawing approach, which allows precise formation of the touch-sensitive and pixel layers within a thread just a millimetre thick and 10 metres long. A layer beneath the LEDs senses touch — pressing the fibre completes a circuit, and the signal reveals exactly where your finger landed so the nearest pixel lights up.
“A fibre has a one-dimensional, axially symmetric geometry, which makes it difficult to build complex circuitry using approaches developed for conventional two-dimensional electronics,” added Asst Prof Khudiyev. “We overcame this limitation through a new interconnection architecture, which enables thousands of microelectronic devices to be integrated and interconnected along a fibre.”
Beyond the touchscreen: Wear your apps on your sleeve
In the team’s prototype, 54 pixel fibres, each carrying 96 LEDs, were threaded into the forearm of a sleeve to form a 96 by 54-pixel display measuring 168 mm by 105 mm, refreshing 30 frames per second with 8-bit colour depth. Each fibre has its own control channel, so a fault in one line leaves its neighbours working normally, and the system can register several touches at once. Alongside the pixel fibres, the team integrated peripheral fibres made the same way, carrying a microphone, a speaker and sensors that track movement, find magnetic north, measure temperature and gauge how bright the surroundings are.
Together, the fibres support the functions early generations of smartphones could perform: run a calculator, show a photo gallery, play a video at 30 frames per second (25 frames per second with synchronised audio), work as a compass, respond to voice commands, and receive images over Bluetooth. They can even rotate the screen and adjust brightness automatically. When positioned under the arm, the temperature-sensing fibre lets the sleeve read and display body temperature.
Importantly, the garment still behaves like fabric. Light output and touch response were nearly unchanged after 50 detergent washes in a typical washing machine, and after 1,000 bends around a 5 mm radius. In addition, the built display is as breathable as cotton, polyester and denim, and stays within established safety limits for skin contact.
Clothing as an interface
Smaller microchips and thinner fibres, both compatible with the team’s method, offer a route to sharper and larger displays. Furthermore, as the display and sensing elements sit along the length of the fibre, the thinner fibres can be knitted, weaved and embroidered using standard industrial machines. The same technology could one day perform other functions such as tracking health signs and delivering touch-based feedback.
“Healthcare is one particularly promising application,” said Asst Prof Khudiyev. “A garment could continuously collect physiological information through fibre-based sensors and allow the wearer to access and interact with that information directly through their clothing. Combined with artificial intelligence (AI), this could enable personalised health monitoring, feedback and assistance. Just as smartphones enabled applications that were difficult to imagine when they first appeared, garment GUIs could ultimately enable entirely new applications that do not yet exist.”
What’s next
The research team’s next step is to push the textile touchscreen further—towards higher resolution, integrated sensing and on-device AI, bringing display, touch, sensing and intelligence together within the same textile platform. This convergence could take the technology far beyond a wearable screen, towards clothing that understands both the wearer and their surroundings, providing information or interaction when and where needed.
The researchers are now developing a new interface between people and digital intelligence—one that extends beyond a device users carry to become a natural part of what they wear.

title: NUS outstanding professors on what makes great teaching in the AI era
author: National University of Singapore
summary: Two NUS professors who won the Outstanding Educator Award 2026 share the importance of nurturing students' character and critical thinking in the age of AI.
text:
What makes great teaching in the age of AI
Associate Professor Stephen Tay still remembers a lesson his father brought home from night class. His father’s teacher had said: “If you fail to learn…”.
Young Stephen guessed the ending: “Study more or read for another hour?” But his father revealed a different answer: “If you fail to learn, then I have failed to teach.”
That lesson has shaped Assoc Prof Tay’s approach to education at the NUS College of Design and Engineering, where he teaches in the Department of the Built Environment. He was one of two faculty members recognised as exemplary educators at the University Teaching Award Ceremony and Outstanding Educator Award (OEA) Public Lectures 2026 last month. In his lecture, he shared his Contextualised Learning via Enquiring, Answering, and Reflecting (CLEAR) pedagogical framework, which encourages curiosity and critical thinking and has since been adopted across Singapore and five other countries.
Learning by questioning
Early in his career, Assoc Prof Tay was troubled by students’ feedback that theoretical equations were difficult to follow.
“I began to question my efficacy as a teacher,” he told more than 100 participants.
Determined to improve, he acquired knowledge on pedagogy at the Centre for Teaching, Learning and Technology (then the Centre for Development of Teaching and Learning) to develop the CLEAR framework.
“Instead of giving students the tutorial questions, I guide them to generate the tutorial questions,” he explained. “Then we ask them to develop the answers to their tutorial questions using real-world examples before they teach their peers with the questions and answers developed.”
In one class, a group turned urban sustainability challenges into a game, casting classmates as adventurers solving real-world problems. The exercise helped students connect theory with practical applications.
CLEAR has since reached younger learners. Mr Ng Ee Noch, Head of Department of Information Communication and Technology at Boon Lay Garden Primary School, credited Assoc Prof Tay’s guidance in introducing the approach to primary school students.
“Assoc Prof Tay challenged me with thoughtful, critical questions as I explored using CLEAR with my students, and provided invaluable feedback on an application I developed to support the approach. I have learnt tremendously from the way he continually encourages me to reflect, question and improve,” said Mr Ng.
Teaching that changes you
Meanwhile, Associate Professor Robin Loon from the Department of English, Linguistics and Theatre Studies, NUS Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences, believes education should shape character, not just impart knowledge.
While skills can be forgotten, dispositions — the habits of mind that guide behaviour — take longer to develop but endure. And as AI makes information readily available, critical evaluation matters more than ever, though it also requires an open mind.
“You cannot make a wise critical judgement if your mindset is closed off,” Assoc Prof Loon said.
This philosophy underpins GEN2001 Theatre and Community Engagement, a course he co-designed. Through role play, process drama and community observation, students examine their assumptions and responses to everyday situations.
During a workshop exploring a moral dilemma, one student reflected on failing to offer a seat to a pregnant woman on a crowded train. “All I did was look and think: If neither she nor her partner asked for a seat, fine,” she wrote in a reflection. “That was what I convinced myself to think.”
That experience in Assoc Prof Loon’s class prompted her to question her response and consider whether she would act differently next time, demonstrating how this teaching approach can reshape how students engage with self and community.
After all, as Professor Peter Ho, Vice Provost (Undergraduate Studies & Technology-Enhanced Learning), said in his opening address, educators must place greater emphasis on nurturing critical thinking and character as AI increasingly takes on tasks from drafting syllabi to synthesising literature and generating content.
“What an algorithm cannot offer our students is judgement, resilience and character,” he said. “An algorithm does not care. It has syntax, but no stakes. Humans can care and we must care.”

title: Why humans must learn to learn in the age of AI
author: National University of Singapore
summary: At the NUS Lifelong Learning Festival 2026, experts explored why human judgement, adaptability and lifelong learning matter more as AI reshapes work.
text:
The human edge: Why learning to learn matters more than ever in the age of AI
As AI becomes more capable, knowing how to use it will not be enough. At the NUS Lifelong Learning Festival 2026, educators and industry leaders explored why judgement, adaptability and the ability to keep learning will become increasingly important — and how education and work will need to evolve.
The smarter machines get, the more distinctively human skills matter.
This is the paradox of the age of AI and one reason why lifelong learning is becoming increasingly important, said NUS President Professor Tan Eng Chye.
“AI can give us answers, but learning is actually more than just providing solutions,” he said. “It is about learning to learn. It is about the struggle of learning, asking questions, making detours, failing and then trying again, and the eureka moment when something finally clicks.”
The same applies to the workforce: as AI reshapes jobs, people need to embrace its capabilities while retaining the ability to understand and critique it, and apply good human judgement and sensing.
Prof Tan was speaking at the third NUS Lifelong Learning Festival on 28 September 2026. Themed “Human in the Age of AI”, the Festival brought together educators and industry leaders to explore how AI is reshaping work and learning, and what people need to do in response. It also marked the 10th anniversary of the NUS School of Continuing and Lifelong Education (SCALE).
Across the discussions at the Festival, a broader shift emerged: as AI makes knowledge and certain capabilities more widely accessible, the advantage will increasingly lie not simply in what people know, but in how they think.
Raising the ceiling as AI raises the floor
AI has already raised the “floor” of what people can accomplish, said Professor Tulika Mitra, NUS Vice Provost (Special Projects), Dean of the School of Computing and Provost’s Chair Professor of Computer Science.
Knowledge, analysis, coding and content creation are now far more accessible — even to novices. But rather than lowering human expectations, Prof Mitra said that this should prompt people to raise the ceiling.
“When AI can answer questions, who asks the right question? Who frames the right question?” she asked, highlighting the growing importance of discernment and the ability to imagine new possibilities.
This also means moving beyond using AI simply to perform existing tasks faster. Prof Mitra described this as accelerating “yesterday’s work”: useful for productivity, but not necessarily transformational. The larger opportunity is to redesign workflows and ask what can now be achieved that was previously impractical or impossible.
The shift is already playing out in workplaces. Panellists from Singtel, Raffles Medical Group, ST Engineering and NUS-ISS described approaches ranging from workforce-wide AI training and experimentation to deploying AI agents and developing specialist capabilities. Mr Victor Chua, Deputy Chief Executive Officer of NUS-ISS, described AI as a “force multiplier” — a co-partner or co-pilot rather than an autopilot.
The next wave could take these capabilities from the digital into the physical world. Professor Jochen Wirtz, Vice Dean (MBA Programmes) at NUS Business School, highlighted how the convergence of large language models, large behavioural models and agentic AI could transform service robots, enabling them to converse more naturally, remember previous interactions, reason and plan, and autonomously execute service transactions.
No-code programming could also make it easier for employees to teach robots new ways of performing tasks, with that learning potentially shared across an entire fleet. Such technologies could help alleviate labour shortages while freeing employees for higher-value human interactions.
The question, then, is not simply which tasks AI can perform, but how work can be redesigned around new combinations of human and machine capabilities.
Accountability matters more, not less
Greater AI capability does not mean people can relinquish responsibility.
Professor Simon Chesterman, NUS Vice Provost (Educational Innovation), offered a colourful analogy: generative AI should be treated as a “very smart intern with a drinking problem” — capable of impressive work, but prone to hallucinations and requiring supervision. Humans remain responsible for deciding what to delegate, scrutinising the results and intervening when necessary.
Prof Mitra made a similar point about AI agents. Once tasks are delegated to them, she said, the ownership still belongs to the user: “We can delegate the actions to AI agents, but accountability needs to really stay with the people.”
These questions become even more consequential as AI moves into physical environments. Prof Wirtz highlighted risks involving ethics, fairness, privacy, agency, and health and safety. Managing increasingly autonomous systems would therefore still require human oversight, including for exceptions, auditing, errors and escalations.
This places an increasing premium on expertise and judgement.
While degrees will remain important, Prof Chesterman observed that as AI enables people to perform some cognitive tasks at a higher level, credentials and grades alone may become less effective differentiators. The “human edge” will increasingly encompass soft skills including creativity, empathy, teamwork and leadership.
This does not diminish the importance of disciplinary expertise. Prof Mitra stressed that strong foundations remain essential for evaluating AI’s outputs: “If you have zero foundation, you multiply it by AI, you still end up with zero foundation.”
Prof Chesterman described NUS’ approach as “X plus AI” rather than “AI plus X” — starting with a person’s expertise and asking how AI can enhance it, rather than treating AI as the starting point.
How workers can open up new career possibilities
If the capabilities required at work are changing more quickly, careers themselves may also become less linear.
Ms Aileen Tan, Group Chief People and Sustainability Officer at Singtel, suggested that workers with longer careers may need to pivot into different areas several times rather than expect to progress continuously up a single career ladder.
Instead of thinking only about promotion, employees should consider “career optionality” — building skills that allow them to move between different roles and domains. Curiosity, a growth mindset and the ability to keep learning will be crucial to navigating those transitions.
More fundamentally, Prof Mitra suggested that lifelong learning in the AI era should not be seen simply as reskilling or upskilling to catch up with technological change, but as continually “discovering new possibilities” as AI opens up new ways of working.
This changes the role of universities too.
“The idea that... a few years at university will give you everything you need for a career, that ship has sailed,” said Prof Chesterman. In an AI-mediated world, universities will increasingly need a “lifelong conversation” with their graduates, with stackable credentials and other opportunities enabling them to acquire new capabilities and reinvent themselves.
Senior Parliamentary Secretary for Education and National Development Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi said Institutes of Higher Learning need to do more than simply offer more courses. They must help learners acquire deep and relevant skills that employers recognise and value, design flexible pathways for diverse adult learners, and partner with companies on workforce and enterprise transformation.
“New skills deliver their greatest value when companies are also ready to redesign jobs, adopt technology, and deploy workers differently,” he said. “The next frontier is to help individuals and businesses adapt and grow together.”
This closer partnership between learners, employers and universities has underpinned NUS’ approach to lifelong learning. Over the past decade, the number of NUS schools and institutes working with the Skills and Workforce Development Agency to offer courses has grown from two to 14, with some 550 courses and more than 130,000 training places offered today. Collaborations with employers have also strengthened. At this year’s Festival, NUS recognised four organisations through the inaugural NUS Lifelong Learning Industry Partner Award for their strong commitment to the learning and growth of their workforce, and for driving innovative approaches to workforce transformation.
Yet amid changing technologies, skills and careers, one constant remains.
“As AI grows more capable, our job is to keep growing ourselves alongside it. Education starts with something intrinsically human, which is curiosity. Technology will change. New skills will emerge. The way we learn must also evolve,” Prof Tan said.
“But our desire to learn — this has to stay with us always.”

title: Temasek-NUS Heritage Champions document Singapore's lesser-known past
author: National University of Singapore
summary: The Temasek Foundation-NUS Heritage Champions Programme celebrates a year of empowering youth to document and share Singapore’s lesser-known heritage stories.
text:
Temasek Foundation-NUS Heritage Champions Programme marks a year of documenting lesser-known stories of Singapore’s past
“Aren't libraries supposed to just shelve books and collect resources? Why run a youth heritage ambassador programme?"
These are common questions that NUS University Librarian Associate Professor Natalie Pang, from the Department of Communications and New Media at the NUS Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences, is used to fielding. To her, however, shelving books and collecting resources are merely functions of a library — not its fundamental purpose.
“Functions are not the same as purpose. The purpose of a library, like many other cultural institutions, is to connect communities and ensure equitable access to knowledge. By using research and library resources to catalyse community action, we play a part in heritage and cultural preservation,” she said at the Temasek Foundation-NUS Heritage Champions Showcase on 5 September 2026.
Held by NUS Libraries at the Temasek Shophouse, the event was the culmination of the year-long Temasek Foundation-National University of Singapore Heritage Champions Programme (TF–NUS Heritage Champions Programme), which drew over 100 students from various institutes of higher learning in Singapore.
The programme enabled youths to document and preserve Singapore’s diverse heritage through training workshops, a heritage ideathon to develop solutions to conservation challenges, and a project incubation phase where groups implemented their proposals with guidance from mentors. Ten of these student-led community heritage projects offering fresh perspectives on Singapore’s heritage and history were spotlighted at the showcase event.
The featured projects showcased Singapore’s diverse, lesser-known heritage, from hidden communities such as Southern Islanders and the Bras Basah Hainanese enclave, to food culture, biodiversity heritage and maritime histories. Through innovative approaches such as stamp rallies, walking trails, mobile games and hands-on workshops, the projects collectively engaged over a thousand members of the public.
For participant Totaan Aljean Choong, who recently graduated from Ngee Ann Polytechnic with a Diploma in Mass Communication, his project aimed to preserve the voices and memories of a disappearing trade. His group, “Scoops of Memory”, focused on the stories of ice cream uncles — the iconic pushcart hawkers who have been a fixture of Singapore's streets for decades.
“Interviewing ice-cream hawkers and working with my teammates taught me valuable lessons in research, collaboration and perseverance,” he recalled. “I learned to triangulate sources when documenting this vanishing trade, by combining interviews with vendors and suppliers, governmental records and quantitative data to paint a more holistic picture.”
Several groups are maintaining the momentum beyond the showcase. Rachel Lie, a Year 4 Global Studies student from the group “Shore to Shore”, which documented Singapore’s Southern Islands’ communities, shared, “The response to our tours and workshops encouraged us to continue building on the project. We are in the process of applying for a grant to continue our work with the community so that more people can experience the islands for themselves.”
One year in, the heart of the programme — to document and preserve Singapore’s history — remains unchanged, though discussions between NUS Libraries and potential partners on its future direction are underway.
As Assoc Prof Pang emphasised, "Singapore's heritage is not only found in monuments and historic buildings. It also lives in everyday experiences, memories, food, places and the stories of communities. When young people take ownership of these stories and find new ways to share them, they ensure that our heritage remains relevant and meaningful to future generations.”

title: NUS launches Singapore’s first accelerated clinical psychology pathway
author: National University of Singapore
summary: NUS launches Singapore’s first fast-tracked clinical psychology programme, integrating undergraduate and master’s studies to meet rising mental health needs.
text:
NUS launches Singapore's first accelerated clinical psychology programme to boost practitioner pool
The five-year programme integrates undergraduate and master’s studies, shortening the usual seven-year route to five as part of a national push to strengthen support for mental healthcare in Singapore.
Since the launch of the National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy in 2023, there has been a stronger national push to expand mental health services and strengthen support across healthcare facilities and within communities. With this comes the need to develop a strong pipeline of clinical psychologists.
NUS Psychology’s response to this growing demand is an accelerated training pathway that allows eligible undergraduates to qualify as clinical psychologists in five years – instead of the usual seven.
Launched in August 2026, NUS Psychology’s Concurrent Degree Programme in Clinical Psychology (CDP-CP) follows a “three-plus-two” structure: three years of undergraduate study tightly focused on clinical foundations, followed by the same two-year Master of Psychology (Clinical) that all NUS-trained clinical psychologists complete.
This new five-year track does not replace the standalone Master’s programme, which continues to train clinical psychologists who choose to pursue post-graduate studies after gaining relevant work experience. The latter is suitable for those who prefer to explore their interests before committing or who come to clinical psychology later in their careers.
Dr Lohsnah Jeevanandam, Director of the Clinical Psychology programme at the NUS Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences, who led the CDP-CP’s design, together with Dr Matthew Lim and the rest of the clinical psychology faculty, said the two cater to different groups of aspiring clinical psychologists.
“We’re not replacing one pathway with the other,” she said. “Rather, we’re giving more people more options to meet the same growing need.”
From freshman to clinical psychologist
The CDP-CP programme aims to train more clinical psychologists without compromising on the quality of preparation and training.
“There’s a significant national demand for clinical psychologists and we needed to think about how to make the whole pipeline more efficient, so that we can produce more qualified clinical psychologists, faster, without compromising on training,” said Dr Jeevanandam.
Apart from the shorter time needed to complete both degrees, the programme also brings clinical psychology learning and clinical internship into the undergraduate years.
Students who register interest in the CDP-CP get priority access to a focused set of clinical psychology courses, including Introduction to Clinical Psychology, Counselling Psychology and Psychological Assessment, giving them a stronger theoretical grounding earlier than most of their peers. The aim is to better prepare them for the Master’s coursework ahead.
Another key feature is a six-month supervised clinical internship that is also embedded into the undergraduate years — designed to fulfil the relevant work experience typically required for entry into the traditional Master’s programme. During this period, students gain exposure to real client work, conducting basic mental wellness screenings and helping to run group wellness programmes under close supervision.
Together, these enable students to connect psychological theories to the realities of practice early on and develop an early appreciation of the responsibilities involved in supporting people dealing with mental health challenges.
“The internship is a shorter, more concentrated experience than the year of work experience it replaces, but one deliberately designed to give students a meaningful first encounter with clinical practice,” said Dr Jeevanandam, adding that students must still complete the same advanced coursework and further clinical training for their Master’s.
A selective pathway
Entry into the programme is competitive. Of the more than 60 students majoring in Psychology who have registered their interest, only around 10 will ultimately be admitted.
Alongside academic performance, the selection process considers whether students have the aptitude for the demands of clinical psychology, which involves working ethically and responsibly with people facing difficult times.
“We’re talking about developing clinical psychologists who are going to be talking about life and death matters, so we need to make sure we pick the people who have the aptitude for it,” said Dr Jeevanandam.
She added that the Department plans to grow the cohort size as the programme matures, while keeping the same careful selection process.
For prospective students like Wu Tong, a first-year Psychology major who has registered her interest in the CDP-CP, the appeal lies in getting to real clinical work sooner.
“The traditional path works well for many, especially those who want time to gain experience before committing to a Master’s. But for me, I felt ready to commit early… It meant I could move through my training with a clear, structured timeline, and start practising sooner rather than waiting longer to get there,” she said.
Building capabilities across the mental healthcare system
CDP-CP builds on NUS’ longstanding efforts to strengthen Singapore’s mental healthcare workforce.
Since 2010, the NUS Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine has offered the Graduate Diploma in Mental Health (GDMH) in collaboration with the Institute of Mental Health to equip medical professionals with additional knowledge and skills to support people with mental health conditions.
The new NUS Psychology programme extends this work by developing a pipeline of future clinical psychologists to complement the capabilities of professionals already providing mental healthcare.
It also joins a small but growing group of CDP programmes at NUS built around national workforce priorities in areas such as healthcare, public policy, management, environmental management and digital transformation.
By shortening the runway into the profession without shortening the training itself, the CDP-CP is designed to get more qualified clinical psychologists into the workforce sooner — a step towards closing the gap between how many psychologists Singapore needs and how many it has.
More information on the CDP-CP programme can be found here.
