title: NUS student finds home on exchange at University College Utrecht
author: National University of Singapore
summary: Discover how an NUS student found belonging, growth and cross-cultural friendships during her exchange at University College Utrecht in the Netherlands.
text:
How an NUS student found a second home at University College Utrecht
From learning to cycle and cook to forging friendships across cultures, NUS Arts and Social Sciences undergraduate Long Wen Xi reflects on five transformative months at University College Utrecht in the Netherlands. Through NUS’ Student Exchange Programme (SEP), she discovered how embracing the unfamiliar and finding joy in simple moments turned a foreign place into home.
Name: Long Wen Xi 
Faculty: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences and NUS College 
Host Country/University: The Netherlands, University College Utrecht 
What was your first week like in the Netherlands?
It was both scary and exciting. I remember the journey from the airport to school feeling incredibly long. My friend and I were struggling with all our luggage on the trains and buses, and we even took the wrong bus. After such a long flight, we were completely exhausted by the time we reached our dorm.
The next few days were mostly settling in, meeting my unit and orientation mates, exploring the campus and city and buying everyday essentials I couldn’t bring from home. I also wandered around Utrecht’s quaint streets, shops, library and canals.
Everything felt quite surreal. I couldn’t believe I was so far from home and would be there for five months. I was definitely nervous, but I kept reminding myself to live in the present. As the week went by, the uncertainty slowly faded, and Utrecht started to feel a little more like home.
Why did you choose University College Utrecht for your exchange?
I was drawn to University College Utrecht (UCU) because it reminded me of NUS College. It has an interdisciplinary curriculum, small seminar-style classes and a close-knit student community living together on campus.
I also liked the variety of modules offered. One of the classes I took was on activism, which was something I had never explored before. The small class sizes were also great because I could interact more closely with my classmates and professors. As an exchange student, taking classes alone can feel intimidating, so having that intimate setting made things much more comfortable.
But one of the biggest reasons I chose UCU was the residential experience. I really wanted the chance to live with people from completely different cultures and backgrounds. It was scary, but I knew I might never get an opportunity like this again, so I decided to take the leap.
What are some of your key learning experiences during exchange?
I learnt to be more independent and adaptable. Living in a foreign country makes you realise how many things you take for granted at home.
Food was one example. In Singapore, getting a meal is so convenient, but eating out in the Netherlands was much more expensive. I ended up cooking almost every day and learnt to make the most of my groceries.
I also learnt how to cycle. I actually didn’t know how to before the exchange and cycling alongside so many people and vehicles was terrifying at first. I almost gave up, but I really wanted to embrace Dutch culture. Eventually, I got the hang of it, and cycling became such a big part of my daily life.
Exchange also taught me that conflicting emotions can exist at the same time. I could be excited but anxious, happy but homesick, and ready to go home yet not want to leave. I learnt that life can be full of contradictions, and that we can grow through them.
What are some of your fondest memories?
I have many and some of my favourite memories were the simplest ones.
One was a night bike ride with my unit mates early in the semester. I was still quite nervous about cycling, but it turned into such a beautiful night. The sky was clear, we could see the stars, and we cycled past fields and buildings with the wind in our faces, chatting and laughing along the way. My unit mates even made sure someone always cycled behind me to keep me safe.
Another was our final dinner together. We cooked a huge meal and had a Secret Santa exchange. One of my friends gave me an album by a singer we had bonded over and wrote me a letter in Chinese — even though he’s Italian-Thai! He had spent ages translating what he wanted to say and copying out the characters, which really touched me. It was bittersweet knowing it was our last night together, but I tried to stay present and appreciate how many memories we had created in just a few months.
What did you learn from interacting with students from different cultures?
I learnt that cultural differences aren’t something to be intimidated by. Even if we grew up in completely different environments, there are still so many ways to connect.
My unit mates were really open and curious about one another’s cultures. We loved exchanging stories about life back home. They were shocked when I told them Singapore is hot all year round, while I was equally shocked that some of them used to travel up to two hours by car just to get to school.
Those little conversations helped me understand what their lives were like back home and get to know them beyond just being my unit mates. My biggest takeaway was to approach people with openness, kindness and genuine curiosity. Our differences can give us more to talk about.
Any tips for NUS students interested in going on exchange?
My biggest tip is to live in the present and experience exchange on your own terms. There’s no single “ideal” exchange. Some people want to travel every weekend, while others care more about their classes, friendships, or simply experiencing everyday life in their host country. You don’t have to follow what everyone else is doing.
Think about what would make exchange meaningful to you. It’s such a unique experience, so make it your own and try to be fully present while you’re there.

title: Building a healthier NUS, one habit at a time
author: National University of Singapore
summary: Designed to help NUS employees build lasting habits to support their health, NUS Health is the latest in a slew of initiatives to ensure employees lead happy, healthy lives. The programme is built around three key pillars: optimising sleep, reducing sedentary time and increasing physical activity.NUS Health follows the year-long NUS1000 and NUS ...
text:
Building a healthier NUS, one habit at a time
New initiatives aim to help NUS staff build healthier lives and stronger connections
Designed to help NUS employees build lasting habits to support their health, NUS Health is the latest in a slew of initiatives to ensure employees lead happy, healthy lives. The programme is built around three key pillars: optimising sleep, reducing sedentary time and increasing physical activity.
NUS Health follows the year-long NUS1000 and NUS 1000 Staff Edition studies conducted by the Centre for Sleep and Cognition at the NUS Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine (NUS Medicine). The studies found that undergraduate freshmen and staff are more sedentary and less physically active than participants in the SG70 Towards Healthy Longevity study, who are above 70 years old. This is a concern due to the national uptick in chronic conditions such as hypertension and type 2 diabetes, which are linked to modifiable lifestyle factors such as insufficient sleep and prolonged inactivity.
Turning data into healthy habits
Led by Professor Michael Chee, Assistant Professor June Lo and Assistant Professor Jocelyn Chew from NUS Medicine, NUS Health comprises a multidisciplinary team that includes members from NUS Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health, NUS Health and Wellbeing, and NUS Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences. Drawing on different areas of expertise, the team will harness insights from the study to devise the right solutions. Among participants, substituting 30 minutes of physical inactivity with sleep or moderately vigorous physical activity was associated with significantly lower body mass index (BMI) and arterial stiffness, which are measures of vascular ageing.
“Many health programmes like to highlight panels of biomarkers and AI-driven advice,” noted Prof Chee. “While these tools are valuable, their effectiveness ultimately depends on tracking markers that are functionally meaningful and actionable, and providing guidance that is scientifically sound, practical and sustainable.”
NUS Health builds on years of research into sleep patterns, behavioural change and physical activity. It also draws from real-world experience with wearable health devices.
“Our goal is not simply to generate research, but to translate the best available science into meaningful improvements in everyday health for our staff,” he said.
How NUS Health works
From August to October 2026, NUS Health will recruit 2,000 staff members for a study that will run for 15 to 16 months across three phases.
In the first phase, participants will be fitted with an Oura Ring to track sleep patterns and daily physical activity, with daily stress and mental wellbeing ratings collected via smartphone. They will also undergo functional tests and provide information about their existing health values and habits.
In the second phase, participants will receive personalised prompts and goals set against the baseline data that has been collected. Those who hit their health goals will receive tickets for a monthly ballot to win cash prizes.
“The cumulative effect of modest sustainable choices may seem unremarkable in the moment, yet over years and decades they become profoundly meaningful,” explained Prof Chee.
In the final phase, participants will continue wearing their health trackers and attend regular screenings to assess habit retention. These assessments will evaluate the impact on their health markers, wellbeing and physical performance, demonstrating the intrinsic rewards of investing in health.
Focus on wellbeing at NUS
NUS Health is just one of many initiatives that support the mental, social and physical wellbeing of the NUS community. The NUS Health and Wellbeing (HWB) unit regularly shares educational posts on social media, spanning topics on mental wellness, emotional literacy and managing grief. NUS HWB also set up the Peer Staff Supporters (PSS) network, now in its fifth year, which trains peer volunteers to help fellow colleagues who may be going through a rough patch. According to the annual HWB Wellbeing Survey, staff who had been trained as PSS reported significantly higher levels of resilience, compassion and wellbeing at work than their non-PSS colleagues.
In addition to emotional support, NUS HWB is encouraging personal growth among staff. In partnership with the NUS School of Continuing and Lifelong Education, they are launching The Happiness Ripple in October 2026, a five-week masterclass aimed at helping participants grow and live well through understanding themselves better, strengthening relationships and building optimism. The programme, which takes place for three hours every week, is also open to members of the public, offering an opportunity for staff to learn alongside friends and loved ones.
Together, these initiatives show NUS’ commitment to empowering staff to build healthier, more fulfilling lives.

title: NUS Enterprise rebrands as NUSX at inaugural A5X summit
author: National University of Singapore
summary: NUS Enterprise becomes NUSX, unveiling new initiatives in research commercialisation and global venture building at the inaugural A5X summit.
text:
NUS Enterprise evolves into NUSX, expanding global pathways for deep tech ventures
Opening a new chapter in a 25-year journey, NUSX convened A5X, Asia’s first global innovation and venture summit, which also featured the Singapore Defense Tech Hackathon to advance innovation and venture creation.
NUS Enterprise celebrated its 25th anniversary with a new identity: NUSX, where breakthroughs become advantage.
The integrated venture-building and research commercialisation platform aims to connect research, talent, industry, capital and global markets to turn discoveries into scalable ventures.
Its rebrand was unveiled on 24 September 2026 at the inaugural A5X, Asia's first global innovation and venture summit, which brought together investors, founders, researchers and policymakers. Also hosting the inaugural Singapore Defense Tech Hackathon (SDTH), the event was held at the NUS i³ building from 24 to 27 September.
The next decade, all in one room
In his welcome remarks, NUS President Professor Tan Eng Chye reflected on 25 years of NUS Enterprise — from nurturing entrepreneurial talent through NUS Overseas Colleges (NOC), to building start-up communities such as B71 (formerly BLOCK71) and, more recently, a network of global outposts.
Looking ahead, he said, “We want NUS to be a place where students, faculty and researchers dare to dream and are willing to try. Where the path from discovery to impact is clear. Where founders can find the people, capital and markets they need.”
Referencing the event’s theme, Guest-of-Honour Mr Tan Kiat How, Senior Minister of State, Ministry of Digital Development and Information, said that “the next decade is in this room”, highlighting A5X’s value in facilitating connections, which eventually translate to capability and impact. As AI makes intelligence more capable, accessible and abundant, Singapore's opportunity lies in being the bridge between intelligence and impact.
“We cannot compete with the largest economies on scale. Our opportunity is to become exceptionally good at connecting these strengths and turning new ideas into real-world impact,” he said.
Universities have an important role in making these connections and shortening the journey from discovery to application, enterprise and global scale. “A great university should not only produce knowledge. It should help knowledge travel, from the lab into products, from products into enterprises, and from enterprises into society,” he added.
A new name for a bigger ambition
NUS Enterprise’s rebrand as NUSX is part of its evolution into a global, integrated venture-building platform. Its work spans four innovation tracks: “Logic” (AI and software), “Pulse” (healthcare and biotech), “Matter” (physical sciences, materials and semiconductors) and “Resilience” (dual-use technologies).
Through 2035, NUSX aims to create at least one NUS venture; generate more than US$100 million (S$127.9 million) in annual revenue or create 1,000 jobs; US$1 billion in financial returns from NUS ventures; and build ventures that collectively improve the lives of one billion people.
“As the global race to commercialise deep tech accelerates, breakthrough research is only the starting point. The real challenge is translation,” said Dr Tan Sian Wee, NUS Senior Vice President (Innovation and Enterprise).
One initiative addressing that challenge is Nova, an AI-powered engine for research commercialisation jointly developed by NUSX and development partner Zima Labs.
Within minutes, Nova can analyse a granted patent, assess its licensing potential against live market evidence, rank potential licensees and draft tailored proposals, while flagging the patent's limitations. The platform draws on more than 20,000 NUS patents and invention disclosures, 9,000 research projects and 11,000 inventors.
By connecting these with external intelligence on companies, investors and industry needs, Nova can also surface licensing, co-development and partnership opportunities, as well as potential investors and team members.
Building bridges between Singapore and the world
Plans are in the works to expand NUSX’s global outpost network beyond Silicon Valley — it has since established a second outpost in Munich, with a third planned for Shanghai in the fourth quarter of 2026.
At A5X, NUSX also announced a new partnership with start-up incubator UnternehmerTUM spanning reciprocal outposts, investment and talent development, focusing initially on biotech, AI and semiconductors.
NUS is also in advanced discussions with a Munich-based venture capital firm closely affiliated with UnternehmerTUM to join the S$150 million NUS Venture Capital (VC) Programme as its fifth partner. Under the programme, NUS students will gain new opportunities to intern with the firm's portfolio companies and join UnternehmerTUM's venture creation programmes — building on NOC Munich, which has connected nearly 120 NUS students and more than 90 TUM students since 2017.
“Deep tech ventures need more than one home market to grow — they need access to research, capital and industry partners across continents,” said Professor Dr Helmut Schönenberger, Co-Founder and CEO of UnternehmerTUM and Vice President, Entrepreneurship, TUM.
From research to real-world impact
Beyond the new initiatives, a common thread running through the A5X Conference was how technological breakthroughs can be translated into enduring impact.
At the opening keynote dialogue, moderated by Dr Tan, three panellists with experience across academia, industry and venture building discussed how research, talent and capital can come together to drive national innovation.
The flagship event also honoured the researchers and ventures translating ideas into impact. The NUS Innovation and Venture Creation Awards recognised eight NUS faculty members and researchers, while Professor David Silver from Duke-NUS Medical School received the President's Venture Creation Chair Professor Award for research that could lead to new treatments for Type 2 diabetes.
At the Innovation Showcase, more than 40 NUS-affiliated ventures and teams presented emerging technologies across NUSX's four innovation tracks. They included Lightsage, which is helping developer-tool companies improve how their products are discovered and used by AI coding agents, and Ecovolt, whose AI-native system helps organisations monitor and optimise energy use across buildings. Lightsage and Ecovolt have been both supported through NOC and B71.
Strengthening defence innovation
The “Resilience” track took centre stage at the inaugural SDTH from 25 to 27 September, which brought together about 300 engineers, operators and founders to develop working solutions for real-world defence and security needs.
Co-organised by NUSX, the European Defense Tech Hub and TUM Venture Labs, the hackathon comprised two challenge tracks: a two-day main challenge on site and a three-month extended challenge prior to the event. These culminated in a Pitch & Demo Showcase on 27 September.
Team NeuroMech topped the two-day main challenge, finishing first among 39 teams with a brain-computer interface designed to give operators a new way to control unmanned systems. Meanwhile, Team MAELSTROM finished first among 22 teams in the three-month extended challenge with a micro-missile system designed to intercept enemy drone swarms, coordinated through a networked command system.
Both challenges also featured the "Lord of the Rings" Prize, which recognised teams that combined their technologies into a larger, integrated capability. The two-day prize went to Acoustics, DomeCommand and AEGIS, while the three-month prize went to SwarmBreakers and Sentinel.
For some teams, the hackathon could mark the beginning of a longer venture journey. Up to three promising teams will be selected for NUS Defence Venture Lab’s (DVL) six-month incubation programme, receiving cash and in-kind support worth S$100,000, technical and venture mentorship, and access to testbeds in Singapore and Europe.
“The prizes are only the start. Through the NUS Defence Venture Lab, we will help the most promising teams become companies,” said Professor Gary Ang, Professor of Practice for Defence Innovation and Applications, NUS, and founder of DVL.
By NUSX

title: NUS CTPCLC: 15 years of community leadership
author: National University of Singapore
summary: CTPCLC marks 15 years of nurturing community-minded leaders at NUS, with students, alumni and partners reflecting on its impact and next chapter.
text:
From students to changemakers: 15 years of nurturing community leaders at CTPCLC
Having shaped generations of NUS students into community-minded leaders, the Chua Thian Poh Community Leadership Centre reflects on its impact as it seeks new ways for learning and engaging in community development.
Strong communities do not happen by chance. For 15 years, this belief has underpinned the work of the Chua Thian Poh Community Leadership Programme, which began in 2011 and expanded into the Chua Thian Poh Community Leadership Centre (CTPCLC) in 2017.
Marking the Programme’s 15th anniversary on 19 September 2026, students, alumni, community partners and supporters came together to reflect on a journey that has taken students beyond learning about communities to learning and working with them.
Returning as Guest-of-Honour after having graced the Programme’s inaugural symposium in 2013, Mr Chan Chun Sing, Coordinating Minister for Public Services and Minister for Defence, highlighted the importance of cultivating Singapore’s social capital — the "invisible glue" that brings people together and motivates them to contribute beyond their individual obligations for the greater good.
Building this social capital requires deliberate effort and leadership, he said, and successive generations of young people have an important part to play.
“We want the young people of every generation to be actively involved in this, to have the agency to take responsibility, to take charge of building this,” said Mr Chan.
Learning to work with communities
That emphasis on agency has been part of the Programme’s philosophy from the beginning, following its establishment with the support of philanthropist and Ho Bee Land Founder Dr Chua Thian Poh.
In 2017, Dr Chua extended his support, enabling the Programme to scale and evolve into the Chua Thian Poh Community Leadership Centre.
Reflecting on the Centre's origins, founding director Professor Albert Teo recalled that it was deliberately conceived as more than another service-learning platform. Instead, students would learn community development principles while undertaking applied research on community issues — addressing a gap faced by social service organisations that wanted to better understand the communities they worked with but often lacked the bandwidth to conduct such research themselves.
The aim was not only to equip students with knowledge and skills, but also to change how they approached community work.
"Changemakers cannot and do not empower communities. Changemakers can only create the right conditions for communities to empower themselves," said Prof Teo, who is now Dean of the School of Management at Tung Wah College in Hong Kong.
This thinking informed the Centre's emphasis on Asset-Based Community Development, which encourages students to recognise and harness the assets, resources and strengths that already exist within communities, alongside understanding their needs and aspirations.
Today, CTPCLC offers a Minor and a Certificate in Community Development and Leadership, with close to 300 students enrolled in its courses each semester. To date, 67 NUS graduates have completed the Minor and another 311 NUS graduates have completed the Certificate. Under the Minor programme, students can work on a year-long research project by partnering with social service organisations.
Putting learning to work in communities
For CTPCLC Director Associate Professor Chng Huang Hoon, however, the goal extends beyond the curriculum.
“In some ways, it is an introduction to community development,” she said. “It doesn't matter what workspace you go into. It’s the mindset that you are bringing into that workspace — to be community-minded, to be people-centric.”
Such a mindset is developed through opportunities for students to work on real issues alongside community partners.
Year 3 Nursing student Miao Yu and Year 4 Geography student Seah Jie Hui, for example, partnered with the Foundation of Rotary Clubs Singapore Family Service Centre (FRCS FSC) in 2025 and 2026 to examine how it could better support individuals and families affected by alcohol use.
The pair interviewed community practitioners, including medical social workers and social service agency staff, and gathered survey responses from healthcare and social service organisations in the Western region of Singapore.
For Jie Hui, the experience changed his understanding of what research could achieve.
“One of the FRCS FSC staff told me that what we did wasn’t just research. It was advocacy. And that stunned me,” he recalled. “I realised that this work really impacts people, and it might impact even more people if it is scaled up.”
For Miao Yu, the lessons have carried directly into her nursing training. During clinical attachments, she now pays closer attention to patients’ social connections and the support available to them after discharge, bringing a community lens to clinical care.
“I will further explore the needs of the community in the future and bring it back to my own major… to support people in the community when they are hospitalised and even give back to the community and the people around me,” she said.
A community mindset beyond graduation
These experiences stay with students long after they leave NUS.
At an alumni panel held as part of the anniversary celebration, CTPCLC graduates reflected on how the perspectives they developed as students continue to shape their careers and community involvement.
Ms Cheong Ming Fang, a 2021 graduate and now Senior Manager at philanthropic organisation The Majurity Trust, said her CTPCLC experience continues to inform how she approaches her work with donors, non-profits, grassroots groups, social enterprises and charities.
“It has informed the way I think,” said Ms Cheong, who also teaches part-time at the NUS Department of Social Work.
For Ms Adriana Rasip, who was from the 2016 cohort, an applied research project changed the way she viewed the communities she works with. She learnt to see communities “not as passive recipients of help or assistance, but as active agents of their own change”.
Today, Ms Rasip is an Assistant Director at Singapore Children’s Society and the Co-Founder and Board Chair of Empowered Families Initiative, which works with less-resourced families through grants, savings matching and peer-support collectives.
Her reflection echoes the philosophy Prof Teo described from the Programme’s earliest years: sustainable community development starts not by assuming that change must be delivered to communities, but by recognising their strengths and enabling people to play an active role in shaping the changes that affect their lives.
This spirit of community finds expression in a mural created to commemorate the anniversary.
Led by three CTPCLC students Tan Kia Shuang (Year 3, Geography), Yeow Zong Wei (Year 4, Environmental Studies) and Yap Yu En (Life Sciences ’26), and designed and painted together with students, staff and alumni, the mural depicts people coming together around a familiar Singapore playground.
“We decided on a playground, a quintessential community space in Singapore, because it's where we learn and build connections,” said Zong Wei. “It embodies a shared vision of a harmonious and inclusive society.”
New pathways in learning community leadership
As it enters its next chapter, CTPCLC is looking to create more avenues for students to learn about and participate in community development.
The Centre will be offering a new course entitled “Building communities for collective impact” in January 2028 under the newly launched Master of Science (Social Impact & Nonprofit Leadership) Programme hosted by NUS School of Continuing and Lifelong Education.
From 2027, CTPCLC also plans to introduce an internship as an alternative to the research project, giving students another pathway to apply their learning with social organisations.
For Assoc Prof Chng, however, the measure of CTPCLC’s impact will ultimately remain with the people who pass through its programmes — and what they subsequently contribute to the communities around them.
“For us, success is defined by how well our students and alumni show up in the community and the work they do as community builders,” she said.
“We want to keep on trying to expand that, to have more and more graduates going into the community space, so that they can become changemakers and leaders in the field.”
This story is part two of a two-part series about the Chua Thian Poh Community Leadership Centre at NUS, as it celebrates the 15th anniversary of its programme this year. Read part one, “From knowing to doing: NUS academics and students drive impact through community research”, here.

title: NUS College students turn ideas into impact.
author: National University of Singapore
summary: NUS College students turn ideas into lasting impact through the Impact Experience programme, co-creating solutions with communities across Asia.
text:
Chance for change: How NUS College students turn ideas into lasting impact
From supporting communities in Singapore and Southeast Asia to creating solutions that can carry on, NUS College students are learning what it takes for their ideas to change lives through its two-year Impact Experience programme
What if a student project wasn’t seen as something merely for experience or grades, but a real chance to change lives?
For NUS College (NUSC) students, the answer to these questions came through the experiences they have gained from the College’s flagship Impact Experience programme (IEx). Embodying its philosophy of ‘breaking open the classroom’, IEx allows students to go beyond lectures and books to learn from the communities and environment around the world.
“The projects that have emerged from IEx remind us that, in a world where technology is helping us move faster and generate solutions more quickly, meaningful change often takes time,” said Professor Simon Chesterman, Dean of NUSC.
“Students need time to build relationships, test ideas and stay engaged over a longer period for their work to grow and continue with the communities and students that come after them. This is what ‘Resonance’ means to us — seeing the work continue to have meaning and impact for years to come.”
At NUSC’s second Impact Festival, themed ‘Resonance’, on 16 September 2026, 57 projects were put on display, offering a glimpse into what students had learnt from putting their ideas to the test and how to turn them into lasting impact.
The Festival also featured a specially curated Creative Showcase, which brought the students’ work to life through illustrations and performances, on top of two Conferences, where representatives from seven projects shared about their communities and causes, as well as their experience working alongside NUSC students to drive change for good.
One key takeaway from the presentations was the importance of forming meaningful connections to offer appropriate solutions. However, the students faced various challenges, from experiencing failures and language barriers to figuring out how to deliver lasting impact.
Overcoming language barriers
For students who took their projects overseas, building connections meant navigating communication challenges. “The language barrier is the highest wall that we have to break through,” said Ms Arum Kartika, one of the co-founders of Karasa, an Indonesian ground-up initiative that engages local youths through art.
Ms Kartika and her husband started Karasa in 2019 as they worried for the youths in their Bandung neighbourhood, located next to Southeast Asia’s largest textile factory. In their area, air, water and soil quality are poor and crime rates are high.
Karasa, which means “to be felt” in Sundanese, gives at-risk local youths an outlet for constructive pursuits. “We want to make a space for them so that they can do something good for their neighbourhood,” explained Ms Kartika.
IEx students worked with the youngsters to revitalise the neighbourhood by turning walls along alleyways into vibrant murals. At another wall, participants used bottle caps salvaged from a nearby river to create a head-turning whale.
Although the two groups of youths spoke different languages, the two-year IEx programme gave the students room to gradually pick up the basics of Bahasa Indonesia and, over time, engage more meaningfully with their Indonesian peers.
But communication was only the first step. At another non-governmental organisation (NGO) Yayasan Juang Laut Lestari (JARI), students learned that meaningful engagement also meant being able to co-develop solutions with a community, rather than simply bringing solutions to it.
In Gili Balu, a marine tourism area in the Alas Strait off West Sumbawa, Indonesia, students worked with the Poto Tano community and JARI to redesign four ecotour programmes. The aim was to ensure that as tourism grows, its benefits remain with the local community, including fisherfolk, women and youth.
“NUSC students sit and discuss together with the local community to try to find solutions,” said Ms Hani Nusantari, Program Manager of JARI. “They don’t just create a project, but help the local community find what’s best for them.”
Language wasn’t the only barrier. Students also had to adapt to an unfamiliar environment, but the IEx programme structure gave the students time to immerse in the culture and gradually pick up the basics of Bahasa Indonesia.
“By the end of our trip, we actually learnt quite a few words and managed to have conversations,” said Zhou Ze Hao, a second-year Computer Science major, who visited Alas Strait with his project team for their recce in the initial stages of the project in April 2026.
“It’s really a very enriching experience. I learnt a lot from the community there,” said Ethan Divyanathan, one of Ze Hao’s project mates, a second-year Mechanical Engineering major. “They have a lot of different kinds of knowledge that you can never pick up from sitting around the classroom.”
Navigating community dynamics
In the Lisu village of Doi Lan in Chiang Rai, Thailand, IEx students encountered a community that is far more complex than it first appeared.
“People see the village as culturally homogeneous. Instead, there are conflicts, disagreements and contestations,” said Ms Amema “Mimi” Saeju, founder of the Lisu Cultural Heritage Centre in Chiang Mai, which seeks to preserve Lisu culture by promoting the traditional art of Lisu handicrafts.
Residents have different social and economic backgrounds, from farmers to lawyers, government officials and businesspeople. These differences can lead to competing priorities, including over Ms Saeju’s efforts to preserve Lisu culture.
For students supporting her work, understanding these dynamics is an important part of the project. Ms Saeju noted that students can be seen as aligned with the community partner they work with, which can affect how other residents respond to them.
“The students would be viewed as an extension of the [community] partner,” she said. “The students are not neutral.”
IEx’s two-year project timeline gives students more time to understand these different perspectives, build relationships and adapt their projects to the community context.
“It takes time for the community to figure out what you’re doing,” said Ms Saeju, adding that it took more than 10 years for members of her community to understand and appreciate her own preservation work.
Her advice to students: “Don’t expect immediate results.”
Building lasting impact
But building relationships and understanding a community are only part of the challenge. For the students, the bigger question is whether the work can continue after they leave.
That, to them, is the real test of success.
NUSC class of 2026 alumni, Andrew Roy Toh and Naomi Ang, first joined Bamboo Bootcamp in 2023, an NGO based in Davao, Philippines that trains local workers in bamboo construction, building livelihoods while promoting native bamboo as a viable alternative to concrete.
From the get-go, the students had to rethink what it meant to make an impact. Rather than create a solution that depended on their repeated involvement, they realised that lasting impact meant ensuring that the community could continue the projects sustainably.
“One of the targets we had was to make ourselves obsolete from the community,” Andrew said. “After we finish our project, they must be able to stand on their own two feet, pick it up and carry it on even without our presence.”
That meant co-creating projects with the community rather than delivering a templated solution.
“The best thing that we can do as visitors is to listen to the community,” said Naomi, adding that it was a better approach to let the community decide on what works for them.
Over four trips, the team put this into practice by testing and refining a bamboo workshop for children based on feedback from local teachers. They eventually condensed it into a two-day programme and trained the teachers to run it independently.
“The beautiful thing is the consistent influx of NUS students,” said Mr Jed Michael de Guzman, Chief Operating Officer of Bamboo Bootcamp. “The community now recognises when there’s a new batch of NUS students coming and there’s anticipation. They are excited to co-work with them,” he added.
The idea of continuity is already playing out in Gili Balu. The marine conservation and responsible ecotourism project which began in August 2024 has since been handed to a new cohort of NUSC students, who are continuing to co-develop the ecotours with the community as new needs and challenges emerge.
Nuryanee Anisah, a final-year Business Administration major who was a pioneer on the project, said: “One of my biggest takeaways was that sustainability is not just about protecting the environment but also understanding the people whose lives and livelihoods are connected to it. Some of my most meaningful memories were the simplest ones — sitting with the fisherfolk at night, sharing music and stories, and learning about their lives beyond what we could ever learn in a classroom.”

title: NUS launches S$50M National Centre for Engineering Biology to accelerate AI-guided sustainable biomanufacturing
author: National University of Singapore
summary: The National Centre for Engineering Biology (NCEB), hosted at NUS, was officially launched today together with its new research facility. Mr Desmond Lee, Minister for Education and Minister-in-Charge of Social Services Integration, graced the occasion as Guest of Honour. The national-level centre will build foundational knowledge and technologie...
text:
NUS launches S$50M National Centre for Engineering Biology to accelerate AI-guided sustainable biomanufacturing
The Centre brings together AI, automation, shared data platforms and pilot-scale bioprocessing to advance predictive biological design for manufacturing specialty chemicals.
The National Centre for Engineering Biology (NCEB), hosted at NUS, was officially launched today together with its new research facility. Mr Desmond Lee, Minister for Education and Minister-in-Charge of Social Services Integration, graced the occasion as Guest of Honour. The national-level centre will build foundational knowledge and technologies in engineering biology for the sustainable biomanufacturing of specialty chemicals, an important class of high-value products and materials.
Established in partnership with Nanyang Technological University, Singapore Institute of Technology, Temasek Polytechnic, Nanyang Polytechnic, and the Agency for Science, Technology and Research, NCEB enables new research discoveries, drives technological advancement and develops the talent needed to design and engineer living systems predictively. This whole-of-nation platform strongly positions Singapore in the field internationally. Supported by the National Research Foundation (NRF) under the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2025 (RIE2025) plan, the Centre was established through the NRF Mid-sized Grant of close to S$50 million awarded over seven years from 2023.
“NCEB builds on engineering biology capabilities developed over more than a decade, anchored by initiatives such as the NUS Synthetic Biology for Clinical and Technological Innovation (SynCTI) and the Singapore Consortium for Synthetic Biology (SINERGY), and reinforced by strong industry partnerships and interdisciplinary expertise across science, engineering, medicine and computing,” said Professor Matthew Chang, who leads NCEB as Executive Director. He is also the Director of NUS SynCTI and SINERGY, and holds an appointment in the Department of Biochemistry at the NUS Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine.
“Through NCEB, we will bring these strengths together, working closely with academic, government and industry partners to create an impactful shared research ecosystem. Our goal is to enable more sustainable ways of making products that society depends on, using renewable feedstocks and cleaner manufacturing processes,” Prof Chang added.
NCEB aims to move engineering biology from largely empirical approaches towards predictive biological design where the relationship between genetic composition and cell function can be understood and modelled to engineer cells that perform reliably. Its work is organised around three research thrusts: machine learning for predictive biodesign, engineering biology for specialty chemical production, and advanced biofoundry capabilities.
Boosting capabilities for predictive design, testing and scaling up
A key research outcome for NCEB is to establish design rules and models that allow researchers to predict how engineered biological systems will behave before they are built. This addresses a central challenge in synthetic biology: living systems are powerful, but difficult to design because they are dynamic and adaptive.
To support this, NCEB is developing shared data foundations and automated experimental platforms that generate large, standardised datasets. These datasets allow results from different laboratories to be compared, combined and used to train AI models.
NCEB’s flagship project, led by NUS, focuses on AI-guided Engineering Biology for Sustainable Specialty Chemicals. Specialty chemicals are a diverse class of high-value molecules, including biosurfactants, specialty lipids, flavour and fragrance compounds, bioactive compounds, and building blocks for advanced materials. Many are difficult to make by conventional chemistry and rely on energy-intensive, fossil-derived processes.
The project aims to engineer microbes and enzymes that convert renewable feedstocks into specialty chemicals using predictively designed biological systems. Its first targets are functional fatty acids, an important class of specialty chemicals used across multiple industrial sectors.
The approach is AI-guided throughout. AI-synthetic biology platforms developed at NCEB propose improved enzyme and pathway designs, which the Advanced BioFoundry – a highly automated research facility at NUS – builds and tests in large numbers rather than one at a time. Results are captured using common data standards and fed back into the models, so each experimental cycle improves the next round of design.
Another highlight of NCEB is the Bioprocessing Innovation Platform (BIP) established in partnership with the Singapore Institute of Technology. The BIP addresses the challenge of translating scientific breakthroughs in the laboratory into industrial-scale production, through pilot-scale fermentation and downstream processing capability. The platform houses an integrated fermentation and downstream bioprocessing system supporting process optimisation, scale-up studies and technology demonstration.
NCEB has also developed a digital backbone comprising the AI-Augmented Synthetic Biology Database (SynBioDB), a platform for standardising biological and experimental data; the Synthetic Biology AI Designer (SynDe), an AI platform for biological design; and Enzyme Function Initiative Tools@NCEB (EFI@NCEB), a secure enzyme informatics platform. Please refer to the Annexe for more information on these digital platforms.
Closing the loop between AI design and the laboratory
NCEB’s new facility at NUS is laid out to follow the Design–Build–Test–Learn cycle, with four connected zones: a computational and data zone where AI models propose new designs and learn from the results; a main laboratory for hands-on experimental work; the Advanced BioFoundry where designs are built and tested automatically; and a bioproduction area where the best performers are grown and assessed. This “one floor, one workflow” layout places computational and experimental researchers side by side, shortening the feedback loop between AI prediction and laboratory result — one of the strongest determinants of how quickly the Centre improves.
At the heart of the facility is the Advanced BioFoundry, the experimental engine of the Centre’s Design–Build–Test–Learn cycle, where AI-proposed designs are turned into engineered cells and tested at a scale that manual laboratory work cannot reach.
Key features of NCEB’s new facility include:
- Automated build and test: robotic liquid handlers, an automated colony picker, automated incubators and microplate readers run as a single workflow, so large numbers of biological designs are built and screened in parallel rather than one at a time;
- Ultra-high-throughput screening: single cells are encapsulated in tiny droplets, each acting as a miniature reaction vessel, and sorted by performance to narrow very large populations down to the best producers in a fraction of the time that conventional screening requires;
- High-throughput analytics: liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry systems, together with high-throughput mass spectrometry workflows, measure what each engineered cell actually produces across thousands of samples;
- Integrated bioproduction: laboratory-scale bioreactors and an integrated fermentation and downstream bioprocessing system confirm that promising designs hold up under production conditions, and prepare them for scaleup at the Bioprocessing Innovation Platform; and
- Computing and data: dedicated computing infrastructure hosts the Centre’s AI design models and shared data platforms, capturing results from every experiment in a common format so they can be used across partner laboratories.
A national centre bringing together leading talent
As a distributed national centre, more than 150 researchers, students and professional staff contribute to the Centre’s work across partner institutions, with recruitment ongoing for about 50 more positions. These include principal investigators, postdoctoral researchers and graduate students, as well as technical, engineering, laboratory support and centre management staff.
The Centre will also provide research opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students.
Strengthening Singapore’s leadership in engineering biology
NCEB’s current goals include bringing the Advanced BioFoundry and BIP into routine use, delivering milestones for its specialty chemicals flagship project, extending the AI-ready synthetic biology data platform SynBioDB to partners and industry collaborators, and growing its industry and international partnerships.
Over the longer term, NCEB aims to establish a fully operational AI-enabled Design–Build–Test–Learn platform, demonstrate scalable production of high-value specialty chemicals from renewable feedstocks, build a federated national data ecosystem, contribute to international standards, and train the next generation of engineering biology talent.
Through these efforts, NCEB will provide Singapore with an end-to-end engineering biology capability — from AI-guided design and automated experimentation to pilot-scale production — supporting cleaner manufacturing, industry translation and the future bioeconomy.
Singapore Engineering Biology Week
The launch of NCEB marks the start of the inaugural Singapore Engineering Biology Week, organised by the Centre. Held from 5 to 8 October 2026, this national-level event will bring together about 300 researchers, innovators, students and industry partners from Singapore and around the world. The programme will cover topics in engineering biology including research, translation, industry and talent. Singapore Engineering Biology Week will be held annually going forward.

author: National University of Singapore

text:
Learning to ask a new question
Working between statistics and geometry has changed how Assoc Prof Yao Zhigang thinks about where research questions come from, and how students learn to find their own.
When I began working on manifold fitting, a recurring question was not whether the method would work, but whether it counted as statistics at all. To many, statistical work meant estimating parameters within a given model, while estimating geometry itself belonged elsewhere. Yet statistics has long reached beyond parameter estimation. A question that looks natural from one discipline can look unfamiliar from another, and before making progress I first had to argue that it was worth asking.
That experience shifted my priorities. I grew less concerned with finding the right disciplinary label and more concerned with what would go unexplained if the question were left unasked. In a recent commentary in The Straits Times, I argued that recovering geometric structure could help us interrogate medical AI. Here I want to describe how that question took shape, because how research questions form matters as much as how they are answered.
When geometry becomes the question
In analysing complex data, geometry usually plays a supporting role: it helps us organise observations, reduce dimensions or separate groups. The question that came to drive my work inverts that role. What if geometric structure is itself something we should recover from the data — geometry as signal rather than scaffolding? Manifold fitting, which seeks to recover a lower-dimensional structure from noisy observations in high-dimensional space, gives this idea a concrete statistical form.
This changes what counts as an answer. A method can classify observations accurately without recovering the structure we set out to understand. So the test is no longer only whether a method works, but whether the task captures what we actually want to know.
Before a project has a name
This conviction shapes how I work with students. On Saturdays, those who wish to join meet with me for open-ended conversations about problems we find important. We ask why a problem deserves attention and whether any part of it is ready to be explored. An idea need not arrive with a method or a clear route to a solution, and I share in that uncertainty. Some problems lie beyond what I currently know how to tackle yet still seem worth thinking about. My own experience has made me wary of forcing a familiar formulation too early.
Applications keep these conversations grounded. An observation a method cannot explain may expose a weakness in the method or reveal something important about the phenomenon, sometimes changing the question itself. Many ideas never become projects; some lose their appeal after further reading, others stay out of reach. But there is a quieter form of progress worth valuing: when a vague concern sharpens into a question precise enough to show where to begin. The aim is for students to find questions they have their own reasons to pursue, including ones that lead beyond where I first pointed.
Staying with a question
Talk of using AI to generate research questions tends to skip the harder part. Finding a question is one thing and deciding it is worth staying with is another. That judgment rarely arrives all at once. It develops through reading, discussion and attempts that expose what one has misunderstood. A question can remain worth pursuing even when no route to an answer is visible and, equally, familiarity can supply good reasons to let it go.
When near-term results looked unlikely, I was sometimes advised to move on. It was genuinely hard to tell whether slow progress signalled a flawed direction or simply how much I still had to understand; the absence of quick results settled nothing. As I prepare to speak on “Geometry as Signal” in Germany this winter, I keep returning to the question that started this work, and to how much my understanding of it has changed.
That is what I bring to our Saturday conversations. Where an unfamiliar question will lead is often impossible to see in advance. Learning not to dismiss it too quickly, and learning when it is worth staying with, is a part of research I am still navigating myself.
Yao Zhigang is an Associate Professor in the Department of Statistics and Data Science at the National University of Singapore’s Faculty of Science, with a joint appointment in the Department of Mathematics

title: NUS brings health technology from the lab to the community
author: National University of Singapore
summary: From contactless health screening to cognitive training and eye care, NUS researchers are testing technologies to support healthier, longer lives
text:
NUS researchers take healthcare innovation beyond the lab and into the community
From contactless health screening to cognitive training and eye care, NUS researchers working with the Health District @ Queenstown (HD@QT) are exploring how technology can support healthier, longer lives
Could a quick facial scan help flag the risk of high blood pressure? Could games based on everyday activities support cognitive health among older adults? And could people at risk of glaucoma have aspects of their eye health monitored closer to home?
These are among the questions being explored through the Health District @ Queenstown (HD@QT), where NUS researchers work with residents and partners to develop and test health and social solutions with communities in real-world settings. The aim is not simply to create new tools, but to understand how technology can make preventive health and care more accessible and relevant to everyday life.
Smart screening
One project will soon bring contactless health screening into the Queenstown community. Led by Dr Yoann Sapanel, Head of Health Innovation at the Institute for Digital Medicine (WisDM), Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine (NUS Medicine), the study will explore whether a wellness kiosk could provide a convenient way to engage people in their health and identify those who may not know they are at risk of hypertension. The kiosk uses remote photoplethysmography (rPPG), a contactless technology that uses a standard camera to detect subtle changes in facial colour caused by blood flow with each heartbeat. These changes, which are invisible to the human eye, can be used to estimate vital signs.
The issue is significant. About one in three Singapore residents aged 18 to 74 has hypertension, according to the National Population Health Survey cited by the project team. Of these, more than half were unaware they had the condition.
From 11 November 2026, residents visiting HD@QT's Come 4Tea Lah! community hub will be able to participate in the study, which is conducted in collaboration with Singapore health technology company Nervotec. Participants will undergo a facial scan at the kiosk and answer a few questions. The technology will subsequently be trialled at Happy Village @ Mei Ling.
For Dr Sapanel, testing the technology in Queenstown is crucial to understanding whether it can work beyond controlled research environments.
“Running this pilot in Queenstown, in a real-world environment rather than a lab, lets us test whether the kiosk meets a clinical need and something residents themselves would actually want help with, which is very much in line with our co-creation approach,” he said.
Importantly, the study is not intended to replace clinical assessment. Researchers will examine how residents respond to the technology, including whether they are comfortable using it, what makes them trust the results and whether those receiving a higher-risk reading subsequently consult a doctor.
Living longer, living better
Other NUS researchers are exploring how technology can support health as people live longer.
At National Engineers Day 2026, Dr Sapanel joined Associate Professor Bina Rai and Dr Rubin Yong from HD@QT's Technology and Innovation team to share their work in preventive health, cognitive health and eye care.
Together with her team, Assoc Prof Rai, from the Department of Biomedical Engineering, College of Design and Engineering at NUS, has developed a digital cognitive training platform that uses games inspired by familiar activities such as gardening to engage older adults. The platform adjusts the level of challenge according to individual performance, enabling more personalised cognitive training.
Dr Yong, a Research Fellow at the NUS Centre for Innovation and Precision Eye Health (INVISION), is working on another aspect of healthy ageing. The FourSight project explores community-based monitoring for people at risk of glaucoma, with the aim of making routine eye monitoring more accessible while connecting it with existing healthcare services.
While the technologies differ, the researchers share a common approach: taking innovation beyond the laboratory and designing it around the people expected to use it. Through HD@QT, researchers can pilot ideas in community settings, gather feedback from residents, and work with healthcare and industry partners to understand what it takes for promising technologies to work in everyday life.
As Singapore's population lives longer, such approaches could open new ways to support health and independence — not only when people enter the healthcare system, but also in the communities where they live.
Find out more about Health District @ Queenstown.

title: NUS Geography: Rethinking education for a changing world
author: National University of Singapore
summary: NUS Geography, ranked among the world’s best, equips students to tackle climate change, AI and global challenges through cutting-edge education and research.
text:
NUS Geography offers a front-row seat to a world reshaped by climate change, AI and rapid urban transformation
Ranked 1st in the 2026 ShanghaiRanking Global Ranking of Academic Subjects and 4th in the 2026 QS World University Rankings by Subject, NUS Geography is expanding its teaching and research to address emerging global challenges.
As the challenges of climate change, urbanisation, migration, health and the rise of new technologies become increasingly complex, the study of geography is taking on renewed relevance — helping us understand how our world is changing and how we can respond.
Few are better placed to understand these changes than the Department of Geography at the NUS Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences (NUS Geography), where researchers and students have a front-row seat to the forces reshaping our world.
Research that informs policy in Singapore and shapes debates worldwide has put NUS Geography among the global leaders in the discipline: first in the 2026 ShanghaiRanking’s Global Ranking of Academic Subjects, for the second consecutive year, and fourth in the 2026 QS World University Rankings by Subject.
The results come as the Department continues to evolve both what and how it teaches and the research questions it tackles.
Over the years, the Department has refreshed its curriculum, embraced new technologies and forged connections with other disciplines, while its researchers continue to expand the boundaries of geographic inquiry to address emerging challenges.
“Modern geography sits at the intersection of people, places and the environment, helping us understand not only how the world is changing, but also how these changes affect the way we live, work and shape our communities,” said Professor David Taylor, Head of the Department of Geography.
“The result is a geography education and research that is no longer confined to understanding the world as it is but also helps students explore how it might be shaped in future and how we might best respond in anticipation.
Changing geographies for a changing world
Today, studying geography broadens not just students’ perspectives on global issues, but also their career paths.
Alongside a Geography major, students will have the option to pursue a new Second Major in Environmental Science for Sustainability from January 2027, complementing their geographical understanding of people, places and environments with scientific perspectives on environmental systems, sustainability and change.
Technology is also changing how geography is studied. New interdisciplinary courses launched under the NUS College of Humanities and Sciences cover topics such as clean and just energy (which considers both the environmental and social dimensions of a low-carbon energy transition), earth studies, and the motivations behind environmental decisions.
The Geospatial Intelligence Cross-Disciplinary Programme (GIX), introduced in 2026, is the first bachelor’s degree of its kind in Asia. Offered in collaboration with the School of Computing, the programme allows a pioneer batch of 28 students to explore new frontiers in the field, including geospatial data, computing and artificial intelligence (GeoAI). This enables them to better understand and respond to issues ranging from climate change and smart city design to urban planning and business planning.
At the same time, the Department’s graduate programmes have also expanded into areas like climate change and planetary health where geographical perspectives are increasingly important.
Building on the Master of Science (MSc) in Applied GIS launched in 2015, and the MSc in Climate Change and Sustainability in 2024, the upcoming Master of Social Sciences in Planetary Health and Wellbeing postgraduate programme will explore the connections between human health, wellbeing and the environments in which people live. It is slated for introduction in 2027.
All the Department’s taught Master’s graduate programmes are stackable, offering flexibility to students to take a graduate certificate before building towards a graduate diploma and full Master’s degree incrementally.
Breaking research frontiers
Outside the classroom, research at NUS Geography is tackling complex challenges that have wide-ranging implications for Singapore, from climate issues such as urban heat, rising sea levels and carbon governance; to ageing and migration; and even how changes in finance, money and markets have uneven impacts within communities and across space.
Professor Elaine Ho, for example, has led numerous research projects on ageing and social networks in Singapore. They have contributed significantly to policymaking and infrastructure planning, ensuring that older Singaporeans have opportunities to remain physically mobile and socially connected as the country moves into a super-aged society.
Elsewhere, Dr Remi Luo is leading a project funded by the National Parks Board to monitor Singapore’s green spaces over the long term to generate insights that inform climate-resilient urban planning.
Meanwhile, Professor Matthias Roth, a prominent researcher in urban climatology, is collaborating with the National Environment Agency on research to improve forecasting of weather and climate conditions so that tropical cities such as Singapore can better prepare for extreme weather, reduce risks and strengthen climate resilience.
As new frontiers emerge, Geography will continue to ask new questions about the places we inhabit, even as they extend into areas such as outer space and virtual worlds.
For the next generation of geographers — researchers, faculty and students alike — this means engaging with a discipline that is constantly uncovering new questions, new connections and new possibilities, and in doing so matching the skillset of its graduates with the ever-changing requirements of society.

title: Oxford researchers to help make electronics more sustainable
summary: Professor Lucia Corsini, Department of Engineering Science, University of Oxford, will lead research and training activities within a new £1.4m UK-wide network aiming to make the electronics materials sector more sustainable and strengthen the UK’s supply of critical minerals.
text:
23 Oct 2026
Oxford researchers to help make electronics more sustainable
Professor Lucia Corsini will lead research and training activities within a new £1.4m UK-wide network aiming to make the electronics materials sector more sustainable and strengthen the UK’s supply of critical minerals.
The University of Oxford is partnering in the newly launched Responsible and Resilient Electronic and Electromagnetic (RaRE) Materials Network Plus, led by the University of Glasgow and bringing together more than 50 partners from industry, universities and government.
The network is one of four networks and nine partnerships connecting research and industry which will share in £12.8m in new funding from UKRI’s National Material Innovation Programme, announced this week. The network aims to strengthen the UK’s electronics industry by improving the way researchers share knowledge and work together across areas such as semiconductors, wireless communications and electronic systems – bringing materials researchers closer to the people who design and manufacture electronic devices.
The UK’s electronics and technology sector supports around 100,000 jobs and contributes £100 billion a year to the economy, according to the network’s launch news release. However, disruptions to global supply chains can affect industries including telecommunications, defence, energy and car manufacturing.
Combining Oxford’s work on sustainable design and researcher development, the network will help build the knowledge, skills and partnerships needed to make the UK’s electronics industry more resilient and reduce its reliance on newly mined materials.
Professor Lucia Corsini from the Department of Engineering Science will lead two key activities: the Design for Circularity and Sustainability Challenge Driven Theme, and the Career Development and Training pathway.
Designing electronics for a more sustainable future
Electronic devices rely on critical raw materials, which can be difficult to source and recover. Growing demand and disruption to global supply chains make it increasingly important to use these materials wisely and reduce waste.
The Design for Circularity and Sustainability theme, co-led by Professor Corsini and Professor Jeff Kettle (University of Glasgow), will explore how electronic products can be designed to make them easier to repair, reuse and recycle. Keeping materials in use for longer could reduce the need to extract new resources.
Choices made when a product is first designed can affect how easily it can be repaired or recycled later. The team will bring together expertise in materials, product design, manufacturing and environmental assessment to help make sustainability a priority from the start.
“Materials innovation is a key lever for achieving a circular economy in electronics. The University of Oxford is thrilled to join the RaRE Network Plus, bringing expertise in circular economy design, circular business models and sustainability assessment, and building on existing initiatives on circular electronics.”
Professor Lucia Corsini
The team will explore how technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) and digital twins – computer-based models of real-world products or systems – can help researchers understand how materials and products might perform over time. They will also use life-cycle assessment, a way of examining a product’s environmental impact throughout its life, to help identify more sustainable choices.
Planned activities include online seminars, annual events bringing together researchers and industry, and a platform to connect businesses with researchers who can help solve design challenges. Funding will also support projects exploring sustainable materials and ways to reduce environmental impacts.
The aim is to build lasting partnerships between universities, industry and policymakers, helping turn research into practical ways to make electronics more sustainable.
Supporting the next generation of researchers
Professor Corsini will also co-lead the network’s Career Development and Training pathway alongside academics from the University of Glasgow, which aims to help early-career researchers build the skills, experience and connections they need to develop their careers and put their research into practice.
Activities will include an annual forum for early-career researchers and research schools developed with the network’s specialist groups. A dedicated programme will help researchers with backgrounds in materials science learn more about electronics, encouraging people from different fields to work together.
Researchers will also have opportunities to gain experience supervising students through funded research internships. Professional organisations including the IEEE, IET, Royal Society of Chemistry and Institute of Physics will support activities to connect researchers and help them develop their careers.
The UK Electronics Skills Foundation will help coordinate activities and links with industry, drawing on its connections with more than 700 scholars involved in semiconductor-related programmes.

title: Oxford researcher leads new thermofluids–AI programme for smarter AIDC cooling
summary: Dr Muting Hao, Associate Member of Faculty in Engineering Science and Career Development Research Fellow at St John’s College, developed the research direction and is leading the resulting programme at the Oxford Thermofluids Institute -- the only Engineering team in the current Oxford–Cambridge–Imperial QRT Labs cohort.
text:
22 Oct 2026
Oxford researcher leads new thermofluids–AI programme for smarter AIDC cooling
The QRT Labs-support programme aims to develop real-time thermofluid -AI algorithm, which will enable real-time prediction, smarter control, and more energy-efficient data-centre cooling.
Dr Muting Hao, Associate Member of Faculty in Engineering Science and Career Development Research Fellow at St John’s College, developed the research direction and is leading the resulting programme at the Oxford Thermofluids Institute - the only Engineering team in the current Oxford–Cambridge–Imperial QRT Labs cohort.
As AI use grows, data centres need more effective ways to keep their powerful computers cool. The amount of heat generated can change rapidly as computing demands fluctuate, making it difficult for conventional computer models to predict cooling needs quickly enough or support fast operational decisions. More responsive modelling and cooling strategies could therefore play an important role in reducing energy use while maintaining reliability and enabling higher-density AI computing.
To address this challenge, Dr Hao is combining engineering models with AI to predict how heat moves through complex systems and help engineers make faster decisions. DPhil student Jierui Li has been awarded an Oxford × QRT Scholarship, to undertake a project within this programme (representing around £200,000 of support).
Supported by the Scholarship, Jierui Li will investigate how AI can help dynamic thermofluid modelling in different thermofluid systems, for example how AI can help cooling systems respond to changing computing demands. The aim is to reduce wasted energy on cooling while keeping data-centre equipment at safe operating temperatures. The research could help strengthen the UK's AI infrastructure by advancing more energy-efficient and reliable liquid-cooling technologies for next-generation data centres.
Dr Hao’s research team at the Oxford Thermofluids Institute develops computational methods for complex, dynamic thermofluid systems. Building on computational fluid dynamics, conjugate heat transfer and reduced-order modelling, her research combines physical modelling with AI and machine learning to support rapid prediction, optimisation and engineering decision-making. Applications span AI data-centre cooling, dynamic energy systems and aerospace propulsion.
The programme forms part of the wider QRT Labs network spanning Oxford, Cambridge and Imperial College London, bringing together researchers working across AI, mathematics, computing and quantitative science. Dr Hao’s team represents the only Engineering team in the current cross-university cohort, with Jierui as its only Engineering DPhil student. This gives the work a distinctive role in bringing physical engineering problems into the wider mathematical and computational AI research community. Dr Hao said:
“I am delighted that QRT’s support recognises the potential of bringing AI and dynamic thermofluid research together, and to see this new research direction taking shape. Our aim is not simply to make engineering models faster, but to do so without losing the physical understanding that makes their predictions trustworthy. In the modern By combining machine learning with governing physics, we hope to develop computational tools that can ultimately support real-time engineering decisions.
I am particularly pleased that this programme brings thermofluid engineering into the wider QRT Labs community and creates new opportunities for interaction across engineering, mathematics and computer science.”
Jierui will undertake his DPhil under the supervision of Dr Muting Hao and Professor Luca di Mare, whose expertise includes computational fluid dynamics . The scholarship also connects the project with researchers across Oxford, Cambridge and Imperial, as well as researchers and technologists at QRT.
Jierui says, “I am delighted to have been awarded the Oxford × QRT Scholarship, and I am deeply grateful to QRT, the Department of Engineering Science and my supervisor, Dr Muting Hao, for their generous support in making this possible. I am excited to be starting my DPhil at Oxford and really looking forward to the years of research ahead”.
