title: Abdallah Hasaballa named overall winner of the ARCHER2 Image Competition 2026
summary: Research Associate Abdallah Hasaballa has been named the overall winner of the ARCHER2 Image Competition 2026 for his striking visualisation of the hidden fibre architecture of the human heart.
text:
Abdallah Hasaballa named overall winner of the ARCHER2 Image Competition 2026
Posted: 21st October 2026
Research Associate Abdallah Hasaballa has been named the overall winner of the ARCHER2 Image Competition 2026 for his striking visualisation of the hidden fibre architecture of the human heart.
His image, ‘Blueprint of a Beat: The Heart’s Hidden Fibre Architecture’, was selected as both the winner of its category and the overall competition winner.
The winning image reveals the intricate structure that helps the heart beat efficiently. It presents a healthy control heart in two complementary ways: one half shows the three-dimensional geometry of the ventricles, while the other reveals the orientation of the cardiac muscle fibres that enable the heart to contract and pump blood.
These fibres follow a highly organised pattern, gradually rotating across the heart wall. Their orientation changes from approximately +60 degrees at the inner surface, represented in dark blue, to around −60 degrees at the outer surface, shown in dark red. This smooth transition in fibre direction is fundamental to the coordinated contraction and twisting motion that allows the heart to pump blood effectively.
Using large-scale computer simulations on ARCHER2, researchers can visualise this complex architecture in remarkable detail. These computational models provide a foundation for investigating how the heart functions in health and how its structure and behaviour may change in disease.
The work showcased in the image forms part of research being undertaken through the joint UKRI/EU SMASH-HCM project, which is developing hybrid digital twin solutions to support the stratification, management and clinical guidance of patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM).
Alongside the winning image, an additional entry connected with the project was also featured in the ARCHER2 competition. Both visualisations were generated using computational resources made available through the parallel SMASH-HPC Award, a UKRI Access Award for High Performance Computing facilities secured this year on ARCHER2.
ARCHER2 is the UK’s largest national supercomputing service, providing researchers with access to large-scale computing resources for computationally intensive research. Alfonso Bueno-Orovio is Principal Investigator of the SMASH-HPC Award.
The recognition highlights both the scientific work taking place within SMASH-HCM and the power of advanced computational modelling and visualisation to reveal complex aspects of cardiac structure and disease.
The SMASH-HCM project brings together expertise across disciplines to develop new approaches for understanding hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, with the aim of improving how patients are stratified and managed through personalised, digitally enabled solutions.
Find out more
View the full ARCHER2 Winners Gallery to see the entries from the 2026 competition: https://www.archer2.ac.uk/about/gallery/2026-image-comp/
More information about the SMASH-HCM project is available at www.smash-hcm.eu.

title: Oxford Robotics Institute and Autodiscovery partner in European Space Agency-funded project on multi-robot scouting
summary: The project will develop and field-trial solutions for multi-cooperative robot systems for real-time exploration, mapping and inspection of critical infrastructure
text:
21 Oct 2026
Oxford Robotics Institute and Autodiscovery partner in European Space Agency-funded project on multi-robot scouting
The project will develop and field-trial solutions for multi-cooperative robot systems for real-time exploration, mapping and inspection of critical infrastructure
In the Threat Monitoring Networked Team (TMNT) project, the Articulated Robotic Group (ARG) and Dynamic Robot Systems Group (DRS) of the Oxford Robotics Institute (ORI), University of Oxford, will partner with Autodiscovery, a system integrator for mobile robots, to develop a team of robots to support exploration, mapping and visualisation for a range of applications from security surveillance to lunar exploration.
The project, which is funded by a €1.8 million grant from the European Space Agency (ESA), aims to develop a cooperative team of four quadruped robots and a support drone, while leveraging 5G/6G inter-robotic communications to enable real-time, autonomous data sharing to support tasks such as multimodal object detection, manipulation, visualisation and mapping.
Teams of robots – multiple robot systems that act cooperatively – are used in numerous applications to improve the speed and coverage for tasks like mapping, search or surveillance. Having multiple robots working collaboratively also offers greater resilience in case of challenging situations or in instances of redundancy due to technical problems. However, core challenges remain in collaborative mapping, planning, and sharing AI in fleets of robots in the field, which requires novel development.
To ensure the technology developments are in line with real-world needs, the project aims to validate and verify the multi-robot system through a comprehensive set of field trials across a range of application areas, including critical infrastructure. This includes security-related site mapping and surveillance at university campuses, data centres and factories, as well as at the ESA LUNA facility for space exploration and planetary scouting.
Prof Ioannis Havoutis, Principal Investigator of ARG, will lead the project. The project will see ORI contribute their expertise in robotic software, with Prof. Havoutis leading the AI-stack development and Prof. Maurice Fallon leading software support for SLAM. Autodiscovery, who have expertise in building bespoke robotic systems and proof-of-concept deployment, will lead on the hardware development and field trials. Prof Havoutis said:
"Robot teams that can scout, map and share information in real time have huge potential not just for security applications, but for space exploration, disaster response and industrial inspection too. This project lets us push cooperative robotics out of the lab and into genuinely demanding field conditions, working with a partner who understands how to turn that research into deployable hardware. We're excited to see what a four-robot team with next-generation connectivity can achieve."
Aron Kisdi Managing Director of Autodiscovery said: “Mobile robotics is at a turning point where we are moving beyond lab demonstrations and pushing to industrial scale deployment. Connectivity is a critically important part of this transition. We are seeing growing customer demand for robots helping with security and safety of industrial sites and this project enables us to bring the highest quality products to our customers and to prepare for the future with scalable connectivity and robots working in close collaboration with people and each other.”

title: Oxford engineering researchers win Royal Academy of Engineering Fellowship
summary: Among this year’s awardees is Dr Emma Edwards, who will investigate how the design of floating offshore wind platforms could make renewable energy cheaper and more efficient.
text:
19 Oct 2026
Oxford engineering researchers win Royal Academy of Engineering Fellowship
Dr Emma Edwards and Bradley Mee have been awarded Royal Academy of Engineering fellowships to advance research in sustainable offshore wind energy and next-generation wireless communications.
The Royal Academy of Engineering has awarded Research Fellowships to outstanding early-career researchers to help them establish independent research programmes and become future leaders in engineering. The fellowships provide funding for ambitious, five-year research programmes, giving recipients the freedom to advance fundamental research in their fields. Funded by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, the scheme supports engineering innovation with the potential to address major societal challenges and strengthen the UK’s research and innovation capability.
Among this year’s awardees is Dr Emma Edwards, who will investigate how the design of floating offshore wind platforms could make renewable energy cheaper and more efficient.
Around 80% of the UK’s offshore wind resources lie in waters too deep for conventional fixed-bottom foundations. Floating turbines could unlock these resources, but their platforms currently cost around four times as much as fixed-bottom foundations. Reducing these costs will be essential if floating wind is to expand at the scale needed to support the UK’s net-zero ambitions.
Dr Edwards’ research will examine how the shape and arrangement of floating structures influence their interaction with waves. By optimising these interactions, she aims to develop platforms that use less material, experience lower structural loads and deliver greater energy output.
“Floating wind is central to the UK’s Net-Zero strategy,” says Dr Edwards. “This fellowship will answer the question: how can floating wind platforms be optimised to deliver high power at low cost?”
One promising approach involves multi-body platforms, in which auxiliary structures help stabilise the main turbine platform by damping its movement in waves. These additional structures could also function as wave energy converters, capturing energy from the sea and helping to diversify electricity generation.
The project will combine theoretical and numerical modelling to identify optimal geometries, followed by assessments of practical constraints, including structural survivability and manufacturability. Working with industry partners, Dr Edwards aims to develop one or two viable designs that reduce platform mass while increasing energy yield, with a pathway towards prototyping.
The research could help address one of the key barriers to scaling up floating offshore wind: the cost of the structures needed to support turbines in deep water. Dr Edwards will also develop tools that can be shared openly and help train the next generation of engineers specialising in offshore renewable energy.
“What excites me most about this award is the opportunity to tackle a research challenge that brings together my previous expertise while addressing a problem I am deeply passionate about: making offshore renewable energy more viable and affordable,” she says.
The fellowship will support Dr Edwards’ ambition to establish a leading research programme in offshore renewable energy hydrodynamics. Alongside her research, she plans to expand her public engagement activities and encourage more people from under-represented groups to pursue careers in engineering. Dr Edwards has previously written about the engineering challenges of floating wind platforms in The Conversation: Six innovative ways to float skyscraper-sized wind turbines.
Alongside her, Bradley Mee, our DPhil alumnus has been awarded a Royal Academy of Engineering UK Intelligence Community Postdoctoral Research Fellowship to develop transparent metasurfaces that could improve indoor wireless network coverage for future 6G communications.
As wireless networks move towards higher frequencies to support faster data transmission, signals can be more easily weakened by obstacles such as windows and walls, resulting in poor indoor coverage. Bradley’s research aims to address this challenge using transparent metasurfaces that can shape wireless signals as they pass through glass, without requiring additional visible infrastructure. This could be particularly valuable in secure, sensitive or listed buildings, where conventional communications equipment may be unsuitable.
During the two-year fellowship, Bradley will investigate optically transparent, electrically conductive materials that can be incorporated into existing glazing, alongside techniques to improve the coverage of wireless signals inside buildings. The project aims to produce a prototype metasurface suitable for integration into standard double-glazed windows. By improving how wireless signals travel into indoor spaces, the technology could help future networks make more efficient use of the electromagnetic spectrum, reducing the need for additional infrastructure or increased transmission power.

title: Oxford × QRT Labs welcomes first DPhil cohort
summary: The University of Oxford has welcomed the first cohort of DPhil students to Oxford × QRT Labs, part of a long-term research initiative between Qube Research & Technologies (QRT) and the universities of Oxford, Cambridge and Imperial College London.
text:
16 Oct 2026
Oxford × QRT Labs welcomes first DPhil cohort
The University of Oxford has welcomed the first cohort of DPhil students to Oxford × QRT Labs, part of a long-term research initiative between Qube Research & Technologies (QRT) and the universities of Oxford, Cambridge and Imperial College London.
Four DPhil students make up Oxford × QRT Labs’ first cohort, with one researcher based in Engineering Science and the others in the Mathematical Institute, the Department of Statistics, and the Department of Computer Science.
The launch also marks the appointment of Professor Blanka Horvath as Director of Oxford × QRT Labs.
Oxford × QRT Labs forms part of a wider research network bringing together early-career researchers, academics and QRT’s research and technology community. The initiative is designed to support fundamental research while creating opportunities for researchers to exchange ideas across disciplines and institutions and to engage with industry and the wider scientific and technological community.
Across Oxford, Cambridge and Imperial, the first QRT Labs cohort comprises 13 early-career researchers working across mathematics, statistics, computer science and engineering. Their research spans areas including AI and its mathematical foundations, intelligent systems, decision-making under uncertainty, scientific and high-performance computing, optimisation, and advanced mathematical and statistical modelling.
Professor Blanka Horvath, Director of Oxford × QRT Labs, says, 'It is a privilege to lead Oxford × QRT Labs at the beginning of this ambitious partnership. Oxford’s particular strength lies in the depth of expertise across mathematics, statistics, computer science and engineering. My ambition is to make this more than a collection of individual research projects: to build a genuinely connected community in which doctoral and postdoctoral researchers can pursue fundamental questions, exchange ideas across disciplinary boundaries, and benefit from sustained engagement with QRT’s researchers. I am especially delighted to welcome our first four DPhil students and look forward to building the Lab with them".
The first cohort forms part of QRT’s longer-term commitment to supporting early-career research. Across the three partner universities, the initiative is expected to support more than 70 doctoral students and postdoctoral researchers/research fellows. Researchers will also have opportunities to connect across the wider QRT Labs network through seminars, events and an annual conference, encouraging exchange between disciplines, institutions and QRT’s research community.
The first cohort and the developing QRT Labs community were celebrated at a launch event at QRT’s headquarters in London on 12 October, bringing together researchers, academics and university representatives from Oxford, Cambridge and Imperial.

title: Why some metals stay tough in extreme cold?
summary:
New study reveals metal alloys that unexpectedly resist extreme cold, staying tough at -253°C
.
text:
15 Oct 2026
Why some metals stay tough in extreme cold?
Researchers including Professor Dong Liu, uncover how certain alloys resist cracking at temperatures as low as −196°C
New study reveals metal alloys that unexpectedly resist extreme cold, staying tough at -253°C An international team led by the University of Oxford, University of California, Berkeley, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory has uncovered a novel microscopic mechanism that allows two metal alloys to remain remarkably damage-tolerant at just 20 kelvin, or -253°C. The findings, published today in Nature, point to new principles for designing materials for cryogenic environments.
Most metals become stronger when they are cooled, but some pay a price. The class of metals called body-centred cubic metals (such as iron, tungsten and chromium) have a particular atomic structure which can make them increasingly brittle as temperatures fall. At extremely low temperatures, a crack that might normally be absorbed by the metal bending or deforming can instead cause it to fracture. The Engin-X beamline, seen as a room-sized array of scientific equipment on metal rigs, in a large warehouse-like building.
The new study discovered that two experimental niobium-titanium-based alloys can avoid this problem even at just 20 kelvin, or -253°C. The metals remained remarkably resistant to cracking, with no measurable transition to brittle behaviour at the lowest temperature tested. The researchers found that this is due to the alloys effectively switching how they deform as they enter the deep freeze.
Normally, bending and deformation of body-centred cubic metals relies heavily on the movement of line-like defects in their crystal structure known as dislocations. At low temperatures, these become increasingly difficult to move, restricting the material's ability to deform around a crack and making a fracture more likely.
In the alloys studied, however, a different process takes over. The researchers observed nanoscale ‘twinning’, in which small regions of the crystal reorganise into mirror-image orientations, coupled with a local transformation of the crystal structure. When these newly formed structures reach the boundaries between neighbouring crystals, they create concentrated points of stress that trigger new defects in the metal. These defects then allow the material to keep deforming rather than cracking.
The process is a little like a road network responding to frozen, blocked roads by opening new routes. As the conventional routes for deformation become increasingly difficult to use, the formation of twins creates new sites from which the defects needed for deformation can emerge. This helps the metal to absorb the forces building up around a crack, rather than breaking.
The discovery could provide scientists with a new strategy for designing metals capable of operating in exceptionally cold environments, including for energy, transport and aerospace sectors. Portrait of Dong Liu, a young woman of Asian descent with dark hair and glasses. Oxford corresponding author Professor Dong Liu said:
“What surprised us is that these alloys remain remarkably damage tolerant even at 20 kelvin. By uncovering how twinning and phase transformation work together to generate plasticity before conventional dislocation motion, we identified a new pathway for designing structural body-centred cubic metals that can operate in extreme cryogenic environments. This class of materials will be extremely useful for components experiencing extreme hot and cold temperatures in one application.”
Lead author Dr David Cook (University of California, Berkeley at the time of the study, now University of Cambridge) said: "Our results suggest we should change how we think about what governs the transition to brittleness for these metals. Traditionally, the focus was on how readily existing dislocations can move through a metal but now it appears that the ability to create new dislocations at interfaces may also be critical. Using these insights, we may be able to design underlying microstructural conditions that allow a material to create its own routes to remain ductile at extreme temperatures.”
To find out how the alloys behaved in such extreme cold, the researchers used the Engin-X instrument at the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source in Oxfordshire. They cooled samples to around -253°C using gaseous helium while a testing machine pulled them from either end, precisely measuring how much force they could withstand and how far they stretched before breaking.
The team then used powerful electron microscopes to examine the tested metal at extremely small scales, allowing them to see the tiny structural changes that had taken place around cracks and inside the material. They also used atom-probe analysis to map the distribution of individual elements, alongside computer modelling to understand how the different mechanisms worked together to prevent brittle failure.
The paper ‘Competing mechanisms toughen bcc binary and medium-entropy alloys at 20 K’ has been published in Nature.
The study involved researchers from the University of California, Berkeley; Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory; the University of Oxford; the University of Bristol; the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source, Science and Technology Facilities Council; the University of California, Irvine; Pacific Northwest National Laboratory; Texas A&M University; and Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. For more information about this story or republishing this content, please contact news.office@admin.ox.ac.uk

title: Dr Mishal Patel appointed Visiting Professor of Practice in AI and Digital Innovation
summary: The department is delighted to announce that Dr Mishal Patel has been appointed Visiting Professor of Practice in AI and Digital Innovation.
text:
Dr Mishal Patel appointed Visiting Professor of Practice in AI and Digital Innovation
Posted: 14th October 2026
The department is delighted to announce that Dr Mishal Patel has been appointed Visiting Professor of Practice in AI and Digital Innovation.
Dr Patel will bring his experience and expertise to the department’s academic community, contributing to our teaching, research and engagement at a time of rapid development in artificial intelligence and digital technologies.
Dr Patel is a leader in the application of artificial intelligence and machine learning to drug discovery and development. His career has spanned medicinal chemistry, life sciences and technology, with a particular focus on how advanced computational approaches can help accelerate biopharmaceutical research and support the development of new therapies for patients.
He is currently Global Vice President of AI & Digital Innovation and UK Research & Early Development Site Head at Novo Nordisk, where he leads work using AI and machine learning to transform approaches to drug discovery and development.
Dr Patel began his career as a researcher and medicinal chemist and has worked across organisations including the Institute of Cancer Research and AstraZeneca. His experience across different stages of the research and development process has shaped his interest in bringing together computational science, drug discovery and organisational innovation to address complex challenges in healthcare.
His appointment as Visiting Professor of Practice will provide opportunities to share this expertise with the department’s students and researchers and to contribute to teaching and research at the intersection of computer science and healthcare innovation.
We are delighted to welcome Mishal to our department as Visiting Professor of Practice. His appointment gives us a great opportunity to strengthen the scientific alliance between Oxford and Novo Nordisk, particularly in AI and computer science.

title: Oxford and Terumo launch six-year partnership to advance organ perfusion technologies
summary: Global healthcare company Terumo Corporation will provide over $9m USD of financial support, access to proprietary technology and world-leading expertise in medical device development to support a major Oxford research programme exploring advances in transplantation and future patient-connected therapeutic technologies.
text:
14 Oct 2026
Oxford and Terumo launch six-year partnership to advance organ perfusion technologies
The collaboration will combine Oxford’s research expertise with Terumo’s medical technology capabilities to develop new applications for organ perfusion in transplantation and patient care
Global healthcare company Terumo Corporation will provide over $9m USD of financial support, access to proprietary technology and world-leading expertise in medical device development to support a major Oxford research programme exploring advances in transplantation and future patient-connected therapeutic technologies.
The University of Oxford and Terumo Corporation have established a six-year strategic research collaboration to advance organ perfusion technologies and explore new applications in transplantation and patient-connected therapies.
The Terumo-Oxford Collaborative Research Programme brings together researchers from Oxford’s Medical Sciences and Mathematical, Physical and Life Sciences Divisions with Terumo’s expertise in medical technology, engineering and global healthcare deployment.
The collaboration, which will be hosted at the IBME, builds on the scientific relationship that contributed to OrganOx, the IBME-developed Oxford University spin-out co-founded by transplant surgeon Prof Peter Friend and biomedical engineer and former Director of Oxford’s Institute of Biomedical Engineering, Prof Constantin Coussios, and acquired by Terumo in 2025.
The programme aims to expand the use of organ perfusion technologies beyond their established role in transplantation and explore how they might support new approaches to treatment development and delivery.
Professor Constantin Coussios, Pro-Vice-Chancellor for Innovation at the University of Oxford and Co-ordinating Director of the Terumo-Oxford programme, said: “OrganOx demonstrated what can happen when world-class research, engineering and clinical expertise come together around a major healthcare challenge.
This new collaboration allows us to build on that foundation and explore entirely new possibilities for organ perfusion technologies. Our ambition is to investigate how these technologies can support transplantation and future therapeutic applications, with the goal of improving outcomes for patients.”
Hikaru Samejima, Chief Executive Officer, Terumo said: “For more than a century, Terumo has pursued its mission of contributing to society through healthcare. This new partnership with the University of Oxford brings together world-class research and global healthcare expertise with a shared purpose: creating new value for patients. We are excited by the opportunities ahead and look forward to supporting research that can help shape the future of healthcare and improve patient lives around the world.”
Professor Irene Tracey, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Oxford, said: “Oxford’s excellence in research is matched by our ambition to translate discovery into innovations that can change lives. OrganOx is a powerful example of that journey: born from pioneering Oxford research, developed through a successful University spinout, and now being scaled by Terumo to transform organ transplantation and patient outcomes around the world.
“Our partnership with Terumo builds on that success, bringing together Oxford’s world-leading research with Terumo’s deep industry expertise and global reach. By giving our researchers access to the knowledge and experience needed to translate new discoveries into practical applications, this collaboration will help create the next generation of life-changing technologies for transplantation and patient care. This is an exciting next chapter in Oxford’s relationship with Terumo, and I look forward to seeing the discoveries and innovations that this partnership will make possible.”
The programme will operate across Oxford’s Institute of Biomedical Engineering in the Department of Engineering Science and the Nuffield Department of Surgical Sciences, bringing together engineering and clinical expertise.

title: Engineering DPhil student wins prize at Podium Institute Conference
summary: Engineering DPhil student wins prize at Podium Institute Conference on Sports Medicine & Technology 2026
text:
12 Oct 2026
Engineering DPhil student wins prize at Podium Institute Conference
Phoebe Cheung won Best Student Presentation 3rd prize for ‘Foot Loading Adaptations During Walking in an Achilles Tendon Rehabilitation Boot’
The awards, given at the Podium Institute Conference on Sports Medicine and Technology in September, recognise contributions from students, early-career researchers within 10 years of PhD completion, and newcomers presenting technology or medicine research in a sports context for the first time. There was an impressive standard of work on display, spanning concussion, biomechanics, protective equipment and human performance, showcasing the innovation and interdisciplinary collaboration driving the future of sports medicine and technology.
Phoebe Cheung is a Rhodes Scholar and DPhil in Engineering Science student, working under the supervision of Professor Amy Zavatsky, and Dr Julie Stebbins and Professor David Keene (NDORMS). Her research currently focuses on patient monitoring during Achilles tendon rupture rehabilitation. Prior coming to Oxford, Phoebe graduated in 2023 from the University of British Columbia (UBC) with a Bachelor of Applied Science in Mechanical Engineering. She continued to be involved with research at the UBC Micro-Electromechanical Systems Lab after graduation by assisting in the development of novel technology in the soft robotics field. She also worked as a mechanical manufacturing engineer at Kardium, a medical device company developing novel technology for the treatment of atrial fibrillation.
"It was great to hear about the work being done to advance our knowledge of sports performance and injury prevention at this conference. I am grateful for the opportunity to present my work, as understanding the biomechanics of rehabilitation can improve clinical care for athletes returning to sport after injury".
Phoebe Cheung
The Podium Institute Conference on Sports Medicine and Technology explores how emerging science and technology can improve athlete health and performance across all levels of competition. Director Professor Constantin Coussios OBE FREng FMedSci welcomed participants from around the world to the Life and Mind Building, University of Oxford, for two days of inspiring discussion, discovery and cross-disciplinary collaboration.
“This year’s conference was another great meeting. It was very inspiring to see the collective momentum of the diverse range of Podium student projects and to appreciate the impact their research will have on sports. I really enjoyed hearing from clinical experts and leaders in other research fields that have turned to sports to make it safer.”
Professor Johannes Weickenmeier, The Podium Institute
The conference programme explored four major themes: musculoskeletal health, brain health, cardiovascular health, and mental health, sleep and cognition, opening with a plenary keynote from Rugby Football Union’s Dr Karen Jones, who reflected on her experience in elite rugby and discussed how sport is developing a more integrated approach to athlete health and performance.

title: Exploring pathways to more resilient energy systems
summary: Oxford Energy Day, hosted by the Oxford Energy Network and the ZERO  Institute on 17 September at the Mathematical Institute, explored pathways to more resilient energy systems
text:
07 Oct 2026
Exploring pathways to more resilient energy systems
Oxford Engineers contributed to the 2026 Oxford Energy Day, hosted by the Oxford Energy Network and the ZERO Institute on 17 September at the Mathematical Institute
Under the theme Towards resilient energy systems: research, policy and practice, the event brought together researchers, industry leaders, policymakers and civil society representatives to examine how resilience can be strengthened across energy systems. Discussions focused on the growing importance of resilience in the face of fossil fuel price volatility, rapid socio-technical change, and increasing dependence on electricity across critical infrastructure sectors.
The Oxford Energy Day provides a unique forum for collaboration across disciplines and sectors. Networking opportunities remain one of the event's most valued features, enabling participants to share ideas, establish new partnerships, and develop innovative approaches to the challenges facing the energy transition.
The event was opened by Vice-Chancellor Professor Irene Tracey, who highlighted the University's longstanding contribution to energy research and innovation. She also paid tribute to Professor Malcolm McCulloch, a pioneering engineer, outstanding educator, and internationally recognised leader in sustainable energy systems. Professor McCulloch, who passed away earlier this year, played a transformative role in advancing the University's commitment to the energy transition and continues to inspire colleagues and students across the sector.
Throughout the day, speakers from academia, industry and government shared perspectives on the future of energy resilience, covering topics ranging from advances in individual technologies to whole-system modelling and socio-political analysis. Resilience was explored as the capacity of energy systems to anticipate, withstand, recover from and adapt to disruptions.
The programme featured keynote presentations, cutting-edge research talks, and a research poster competition for postgraduate students and early career researchers from Oxford and other universities. The posters showcased innovative research spanning energy technologies, advanced materials and systems, alongside policy, economic and social science perspectives.
Engineering researchers involved in the day included Deborah Greaves, Statutory Professor of Civil Engineering, who gave a keynote on offshore renewable energy, and Dr Jesus Lizana, who leads research on Zero-Carbon Heating and Cooling at the ZERO Institute, who contributed to a session on resilience & technologies, economics, and energy security. Professor Paul Shearing, Statutory Professor in Sustainable Energy Engineering and Director of the ZERO Institute, led a panel discussion, with panellists including Professor of Informatics David Wallom and Associate Professor Dr Phil Grünewald.
"Achieving a resilient, net-zero energy future will depend on combining technological innovation with effective policy, governance and public engagement. Oxford Energy Day showcases the breadth of expertise across the University and beyond, while creating the connections that help translate research into real-world impact. It was inspiring to see such a strong commitment to collaboration across the energy community."
Professor Paul Shearing
Key themes across the day included technologies that enhance resilience, such as battery storage, advanced materials and renewable energy generation; the economic foundations of resilient energy systems, including market design, innovation and business opportunities; and the links between resilience and energy security through electrification, demand reduction, diversification of energy sources and the evolving role of fossil fuels. The afternoon programme was divided into two parallel streams. The first focused on scientific and technical perspectives, covering resilience technologies, economics and energy security. The second explored social science dimensions, including organising for resilience and examining resilience through the lens of social equity and public value. Additional discussions considered how resilience can be supported through effective governance, data sharing and policymaking, while also examining broader societal questions around who benefits from resilience measures and how resilience can be delivered equitably.

title: Women in Sustainable Aviation presented at WISE Conference
summary: Dr Ashley van Bruygom and Dr Alicia Torres Gomez from the University of Oxford presented their Women in Sustainable Aviation initiative at the WISE Conference 2026 in London, where their poster was selected for a special viewing and discussion with Her Royal Highness The Princess Royal.
text:
05 Oct 2026
Women in Sustainable Aviation presented at WISE Conference
Dr Ashley van Bruygom and Dr Alicia Torres Gomez's initiative was selected for a special viewing and discussion with Her Royal Highness The Princess Royal at the WISE Conference recently in London
The Women in Sustainable Aviation initiative was presented at the WISE Conference 2026 by Dr Ashley van Bruygom (Loughborough University) and Dr Alicia Torres Gomez (University of Oxford). Their poster was among those selected to be viewed and discussed with Her Royal Highness The Princess Royal, Princess Anne, giving Ashley and Alicia the opportunity to introduce the initiative and talk about the role of women in the transition towards more sustainable aviation.
The initiative is being developed as part of the EPSRC Programme Grant, Making Hydrogen Work in Zero Carbon Jet Engines, and aims to bring together women working across sustainable aviation, from engineering and scientific research to industry and policy.
The WISE Conference, held at IET London: Savoy Place on 28 September, brought together people from across science, technology, engineering and mathematics to discuss gender equity in STEM. This year's programme focused on active allyship, young professionals and collaboration across sectors.
For Ashley and Alicia, the conference was also an opportunity to share their work within the Programme Grant and to discuss how the technical challenges involved in developing hydrogen-powered aviation can go hand in hand with supporting a more diverse and inclusive research community. Aviation's transition towards lower-carbon technologies draws on expertise from many different areas, including propulsion, hydrogen and cryogenic fuels, aircraft design, infrastructure, operations and policy.
Women in Sustainable Aviation was developed to bring some of those communities together and to create stronger connections between women working in the field. Through this initiative, Ashley and Alicia hope to make their own contribution to supporting women pursuing careers in aviation, while also drawing attention to the opportunities for women to take part in emerging areas of sustainable aviation research.
The selection of the poster for discussion with The Princess Royal gave the team an opportunity to explain why they felt such a network would be useful and what they hope to achieve through the Women in Sustainable Aviation event to be held in Oxford this December. It also connected with one of the main themes of this year's WISE Conference: moving beyond discussions of gender equity towards practical action.
Dr van Bruygom says, “It was a real privilege to present our plans at WISE and to have the opportunity to discuss the poster with The Princess Royal. Sustainable aviation is a huge engineering challenge, and we want to make sure that women working across the field are part of that conversation.”
“One of the things I enjoyed most about the WISE conference was meeting people who are trying to make practical changes in their own organisations and fields. There is still work to do to ensure women can enter, stay and progress in STEM careers, and networks like this can be one useful part of that.”

Professor David Gavaghan appointed next President of Reuben College

title: IBME student wins Best Poster Award at Computing in Cardiology (CinC) 2026
summary: MRes student Adrian McIntosh has won the prestigious Computing in Cardiology (CinC) Gary and Bill Sanders Poster Award for research supervised by Professor Abhirup Banerjee.
text:
01 Oct 2026
IBME student wins Best Poster Award at Computing in Cardiology (CinC) 2026
MRes student Adrian McIntosh has won the prestigious Computing in Cardiology (CinC) Gary and Bill Sanders Poster Award for research supervised by Professor Abhirup Banerjee.
The “Gary and Bill Sanders Poster Award” is presented at the annual Computing in Cardiology (CinC) conference, which is focused on applications of computing in clinical cardiology and cardiovascular physiology. The award was established to recognise, celebrate, and promote excellence in poster presentations. At this year’s CinC conference, held from 20th to 23rd September, the Gary and Bill Sanders Poster award was awarded to Oxford MRes student Adrian McIntosh from the Institute of Biomedical Engineering’s MultiMeDIA Lab supervised by Prof Abhirup Banerjee.
Adrian’s work, titled “End-to-End ECG Digitisation with Soft Segmentation and BiLSTM Signal Reconstruction”, presented an end-to-end system for the digitisation of paper electrocardiographs (ECGs). As the most widely used modality for cardiovascular diagnosis, there have been many developments in automating their analysis, but most ECGs remain available only in paper form, not in the digital format required for deployment of these automated methods.
The team, also including Dr Mojtaba Lashgari from IBME’s MultiMeDIA Lab and Longa Maimbo from University of Cape Town, collaborated with clinicians to develop a method to convert paper ECG signals into their time-series form using a deep learning framework. During the poster presentation, Adrian demonstrated the method through a mobile application that captures photos of paper ECGs, and using the framework the team developed, digitally flattens the paper, automatically extracting the associated high resolution digital signals. The presentation received enthusiastic feedback from several clinicians attending the conference.
This award marks the third consecutive year that the MultiMeDIA Lab has won a presentation award at CinC. Adrian, who led the project, said:
“I am very grateful for the opportunity to receive this award, the team behind the paper and the MultiMeDIA Lab who supported us throughout.”
The MultiMeDIA lab delivered a total of three posters and one oral presentation at CinC this year, including poster presentations from previous award winners Thalia Seale and Dr Alexander Sharp. Thalia’s poster analysed the motion of the heart muscle using tagged magnetic resonance imaging to understand differences between healthy individuals and those suffering with myocardial infarction. Alex’s poster presented a statistical framework for reconstructing dense conduction velocity maps of the left atrium from sparse clinical measurements. Charlotte Richardson, 4th year undergraduate student at the lab, was selected for oral presentation for her work presenting a multi-modal deep learning framework to classify myocardial infarction. This presentation was delivered by the paper’s second author Thalia Seale. Further details on these presentations can be found on the MultiMeDIA Lab’s website.
Professor Banerjee commented on the event:
“I am extremely honoured to see the continuous appreciation of the MultiMeDIA Lab in the CinC Family. What Thalia (CinC 2024 Best Poster Award) and Alex (CinC 2025 Young Investigator Award) started, Adrian and others are taking them forward! Already feeling excited for the next year…”

title: In the AI Era, Entrepreneurship Educators Seek to Challenge and Motivate Student Founders
summary: Stanford’s Steve Blank, Riitta Katila, and Perry Klebahn encourage educators around the globe to rethink course structure and experiment with new ways to teach the art of innovation
text:
In the AI Era, Entrepreneurship Educators Seek to Challenge and Motivate Student Founders
In the AI age, entrepreneurship educators are having a startup experience, Stanford adjunct professor Perry Klebahn told an international group of educators at an Oct. 13 webinar hosted by the Stanford Technology Ventures Program (STVP).
Like any startup experience, it’s full of uncertainty and chaos.
Klebahn joined Steve Blank, an adjunct professor in the Department of Management Science & Engineering (MS&E), and Riitta Katila, the W. M. Keck Sr. Professor of Management Science and STVP Faculty Director, to discuss how they integrate AI tools as they teach, motivate, and evaluate entrepreneurship students.
“We are going to innovate and change and come out far stronger for that,” said Klebahn, who is director of executive education at the Stanford d.school. “The magic still has to happen. You still have to churn through it. I think you can do it with these tools – I don’t think they need to be excluded.”
With the venture creation processes changing rapidly, the Stanford instructors wanted “to give our colleagues around the world a glimpse of what we are observing here and how the curriculum is really evolving and adapting in real time,” said MS&E Professor and STVP Faculty Director Saikat Chaudhuri, who moderated the panel.
Observations in Stanford’s Startup Courses
In Klebahn and Blank’s courses, AI is reshaping how students begin their startups.
In Klebahn’s LaunchPad (DESIGN 399), student founders launch a company in a quarter. Klebahn previously looked for applicants with a tendency to build. But with AI tools making prototyping dramatically easier, the area of focus has shifted.
Now, founders get stuck refining prototypes instead of “the problem validation and the problem-finding that entrepreneurs naturally did by, frankly, completely missing and then having to go back and toil and work pretty hard to build something,” Klebahn said.
Blank has seen a similar pattern in Lean LaunchPad (ENGR 245), where student teams test startup ideas with customers. For years, Blank’s students started with customer interviews and a minimum viable product. This year, every team already had a digital twin or demo ready.
“We had to pry what they thought was a finished product out of their hands and get them to actually spend time trying to deeply understand customer problems and needs,” he said.
Blank’s teaching team decided to “rejigger the entire class,” which Blank documented on his blog. Now, students dive into customer discovery and must work with a design partner. Instead of an MVP, they refer to their IUP: “initial untested product.”
Embracing the Human Connection
The challenges presented by AI aren’t limited to entrepreneurs in the classroom.
Katila co-authored a forthcoming paper in Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal examining how early-stage entrepreneurs around the world are adapting to AI. She found that “expertise is being decoupled from the production, the struggle, the suffering of creating something.”
Educators need to motivate students to think about the reasoning behind their work, she said. “How do we get our students to become experts in a world where everything is – everywhere, all at once – at your fingertips?”
The panelists emphasized the importance of integrating human connection alongside AI tools.
Blank expects his students to use AI to accelerate getting products to customers.
“I think it will be a while before AI is buying from AI,” he said. “As long as human beings are involved, then it’s people who have the problems.”
At a recent meeting with Stanford first-year students, Katila was intrigued to learn their appreciation for small-group discussions. She suggested bringing in more course assistants for conversations.
Klebahn has been studying critique techniques and looking for ways to teach self-awareness and discernment. This is additionally challenging because more students are now working solo rather than in teams.
“If you want to work alone, that’s amazing,” he said. “I still want to land that there is enormous value to being vulnerable and showing this to other people.”
A group of alumni who guest-taught LaunchPad recently had the students switch projects with each other.
“I could see the lights go on for so many students: ‘Oh I never thought of all these decisions I’ve made that now somebody else is exposing by working on my stuff,’” Klebahn said.
Practical Advice for Educators
Blank urged entrepreneurship educators to understand that everything they taught last year is now obsolete.
It helps to go back to first principles, he said: Figure out what you truly want students to learn and consider how to use AI to prepare them for the world – “not the world that we wish they lived in, but the world that they’re going to live in.”
Katila and Klebahn said educators should see teaching in the time of AI as an exciting opportunity, and Klebahn encouraged them to be transparent about the need to experiment.
“You’re going to live a lifetime with these tools, and you’re at an unbelievable point to be involved with smart co-founders and founders in the classroom and good professors, and we are asking these questions together,” he envisioned telling students. “It’s a fabulous experience to learn about this.”

title: ‘Digital twins’ of immune system in pregnancy identify drugs to prevent early labor, Stanford Medicine-led study finds
summary: Stanford Medicine researchers built an AI-enabled model of immune system changes in pregnancy, allowing them to test medications to avert premature birth.
text:
Researchers have identified two common drugs that may, when given together during pregnancy, prevent premature births.
The finding is the fruit of a new, Stanford Medicine-led, artificial intelligence-powered technique for screening drugs to prevent early labor. It uses a comprehensive atlas of the immune system, which the researchers built to be accurate at a cell-by-cell level, to create “digital twins” of the immune systems of individual pregnant women for virtual drug testing.
The study, which published online Oct. 21 in Science Advances, builds on two decades of Stanford Medicine research on how the maternal immune system shifts during pregnancy. When the immune clock of pregnancy runs too quickly, preterm labor can result. Being born prematurely, meaning three or more weeks before the due date, carries a host of risks for the baby. Prematurity is now the leading cause of death in children under age 5 worldwide.
After screening several possible treatments with the digital twin system, the researchers identified one drug combination that promises to markedly lower the risk of early labor. It shows so much potential for averting preterm birth that researchers are starting a clinical trial in real patients.
“We’re on the brink of having a real impact for the treatment of preterm birth, a global health problem that affects 10% of pregnancies worldwide,” said senior study author Brice Gaudilliere, MD, PhD, professor of anesthesiology, perioperative and pain medicine. It’s been decades since there was a new pharmacological intervention for preventing preterm birth, he noted.
The winning drug combination was aspirin and lansoprazole. Low-dose aspirin alone has a modest ability to prevent premature birth, prior research has shown. Lansoprazole is sometimes prescribed in pregnancy to treat acid reflux.
“In the digital twin system, these two drugs in combination had a large effect on the delay of labor, 15 times higher than aspirin alone,” Gaudilliere said.
Modeling how the immune clock ticks
Although the triggers of labor in humans are still not fully explained, Stanford Medicine research has demonstrated that immune signals play a key role in readying the mother’s body for labor.
Early in pregnancy, the mother’s immune system adjusts to tolerate the immunologically different fetus. Late in pregnancy, a series of immune changes — including a switch toward pro-inflammatory signals — help prepare the body for labor. When the immune clock of pregnancy runs too fast, with pro-inflammatory signals activated too soon, early labor can result.
The new digital twin system, called SIMCO (simulated immune modeling of clinical outcomes), uses AI and machine-learning techniques to integrate into its model an enormous amount of data on how all the body’s immune cells behave during pregnancy.
To create the model, the researchers first collected blood samples from pregnant women, then exposed immune cells from these samples to many different drugs.
“We measured responses from a quarter of a billion cells, training the algorithm on a massive single-cell dataset,” Gaudilliere said.
Such a deep foundation of real biological knowledge is a key element of building a working digital twin that realistically mimics an individual’s biology.
“A digital twin has the prerequisite that you understand a biological system very well,” said co-lead author Jakob Einhaus, MD, a postdoctoral scholar at Stanford Medicine. “The digital twin represents the complexity and connections in the immune system.”
Einhaus shares lead authorship of the study with graduate students Peter Neidlinger and Olivier Fondeur, and with Masaki Sato, MD, PhD, who was a postdoctoral scholar at Stanford Medicine when the research was conducted and is now at the National Center for Child Health and Development in Tokyo.
Once they had constructed the cell-response model, the researchers integrated longitudinal data from 63 pregnancies, linked to information about the patients’ clinical outcomes, to help the model understand which patterns of cell behavior match which clinical states and to train the model to understand patient-to-patient variability.
The final algorithm has both the ability to predict how individual immune cells will respond to various drugs, and — with a bit of starting knowledge about a specific patient, such as that obtained from a small blood sample — what this means clinically for the patient. For example, do findings from the digital twin predict that a certain medication will make her immune clock of pregnancy run faster or slower?
“You’re making the prediction for one individual based on knowledge of millions of single cells from dozens of patients,” Einhaus said.
Common medications may delay delivery
After validating that SIMCO accurately forecasts time to labor — by comparing its predictions with what happened in the pregnancies of the patients in their dataset — the scientists used the digital twin system to evaluate nine possible drug regimens to see whether they would likely speed up or slow down the immune clock of pregnancy. The drugs were chosen based on a drug-repurposing pipeline — developed by a group led by study coauthor Marina Sirota, PhD, a professor of pediatrics at the University of California, San Francisco — because they were already known to be safe for pregnancy.
The researchers evaluated multiple copies of each digital twin, comparing what would happen to the immune system in treated versus untreated scenarios for each individual, with each drug.
The research team was surprised by how strongly the model predicted that the aspirin-lansoprazole combination would delay labor.
“Our findings suggest that salicylic acid [aspirin] and lansoprazole act synergistically … this synergy may enhance their immunomodulatory effect,” the investigators write in their paper.
The study also found that taking folic acid — a B vitamin already recommended in pregnancy to reduce the risk of spinal cord defects in the fetus — can delay immunological progression toward labor.
“We’re giving folic acid for spina bifida prevention, but maybe, unknowingly, we’re also helping the maternal immune system adapt to pregnancy,” Einhaus said. “We didn’t know it had such profound immunomodulatory properties.”
The digital twin model gave the researchers information about which specific immune signals were predicted to change with each of the medications, details that could help contribute to further understanding premature labor’s exact mechanics.
For instance, for the aspirin-plus-lansoprazole combination, immune processes that help pregnancy continue are enhanced, whereas those involved in triggering labor are inhibited, Gaudilliere said. “So it all makes sense biologically. That was super exciting.”
The model lets researchers test many possible drugs and drug combinations before exposing any patients, offering an ethical way to narrow down possible therapies for early labor without risking real pregnancies.
Because the model captures variation among patients, it could also show that not all individuals respond to each drug equally well. Being able to predict likely responders and non-responders would be a valuable addition to planning clinical trials, the research team said: By restricting clinical trial enrollment to likely responders to any drug being tested, researchers could get clear answers about a drug’s effectiveness from smaller trials.
The researchers tested the drug combination of aspirin plus lansoprazole in an animal model of an inflammatory state in pregnancy, demonstrating that the combination delays the onset of labor in that context. They subsequently obtained approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to try the combination in a human clinical trial.
“We’re going in a short time from discovery work — done the Stanford way, using technology, AI and really understanding the mechanism of a disease process — all the way to identifying a potentially impactful new treatment and testing in patients,” Gaudilliere said.
Researchers from UC San Diego and the AP-HP Sorbonne University Hospital Group in Paris also contributed to the study.
This work was supported by the Stanford Maternal and Child Health Research Institute, the March of Dimes Prematurity Research Center at Stanford, the March of Dimes Prematurity Research Center at UCSF, the Center for Human Systems Immunology at Stanford, the Charles and Mary Robertson Foundation, the National Institute of Health (grants P01HD106414, K99HD115829 and 1K99HD105016), and a Society for Reproductive Investigation Bayer Discovery/Innovation grant.

title: Antony Jameson, longtime Stanford engineering professor who transformed aircraft design through computation, dies at 91
summary: Jameson helped establish computational fluid dynamics as a practical engineering discipline, then developed mathematical methods that allowed computers not only to analyze aircraft but to improve their designs.
text:
Antony Jameson, longtime Stanford engineering professor who transformed aircraft design through computation, dies at 91
Antony “Tony” Jameson, professor emeritus of aeronautics and astronautics at Stanford University, died on June 11, 2026. He was 91.
Across a groundbreaking career spanning more than six decades, Jameson developed mathematical methods and computer programs that helped transform aircraft design. His work made it possible not only to calculate how air would move around a proposed airplane shape but also to use those calculations to improve the airplane’s performance.
“Many of the techniques, the methods, the theories that he came up with have been used by every single airplane company in the world,” said Juan Alonso, the Vance D. and Arlene C. Coffman Professor and the James and Anna Marie Spilker Chair of the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics, who was Jameson’s doctoral student and later his colleague. “They most certainly have influenced the design of all the airplanes that you and I fly in.”
Jameson’s fascination with what Alonso called the “magic” of flight animated his work. Alonso described Jameson as soft-spoken and without pretension, with a “childlike enthusiasm about technical matters.” He wrote code beside students and filled lecture notes with sketches of airplanes, birds, and improbable hybrids of the two.
Before bringing that curiosity to Stanford as a researcher and mentor, Jameson followed a circuitous path through engineering, economics, and applied mathematics, eventually turning to aircraft design.
From mathematics to aircraft
Born on Nov. 20, 1934, in Gillingham, Kent, England, Jameson spent part of his childhood in India, where his father served as a British Army officer. He earned a bachelor’s degree with first-class honors from the University of Cambridge in 1958 and a PhD in magnetohydrodynamics – the study of how electrically conducting fluids behave in magnetic fields – in 1963.
After a postdoctoral fellowship at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, he worked briefly as an economist for the British Trades Union Congress, then returned to engineering as chief mathematician for Hawker Siddeley Dynamics’ missile division.
Jameson moved to the United States in 1966 to join Grumman Aerospace’s aerodynamics section. His first work there applied automatic control theory to aircraft stability systems. In 1970, he turned to predicting airflow near the speed of sound after existing numerical methods proved inadequate.
Working at Grumman on an IBM 1130 punched-card computer, he wrote FLO1, which calculated airflow past a two-dimensional airfoil, and SYN1, which worked backward from a desired pressure distribution to determine an airfoil shape. Those were the first in his FLO and SYN series of computer programs, which grew to model wings and complete aircraft, establishing computational fluid dynamics as a practical engineering discipline.
Jameson joined the Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences at New York University in 1972, then moved to Princeton University in 1980. He and his collaborators steadily expanded what computers could model. By 1976, their FLO22 program could calculate transonic airflow around a swept wing. In 1985, their AIRPLANE program, running on a Cray-1 supercomputer, calculated the inviscid flow around a complete aircraft – a milestone in modern computational aerodynamics.
He joined Stanford’s Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics as the Thomas V. Jones Professor of Engineering in 1997. Over the next 21 years, he extended his foundational work into increasingly realistic methods for computational aircraft design.
Turning analysis into design
During his Stanford years, Jameson concentrated his research on aerodynamic optimization. Conventional computational fluid dynamics predicted how air would flow around a proposed wing; his methods allowed engineers to use those calculations to reshape the wing to reduce drag, maintain lift, or meet other performance goals.
A wing’s shape can involve thousands of variables, and testing each possible adjustment separately would require thousands of costly simulations. Jameson’s adjoint method analyzed them together, showing how the changes would affect drag, lift, or another goal at roughly the cost of one extra simulation. That made it practical to optimize a shape with thousands of variables instead of testing each alteration at a time.
The adjoint approach predated Jameson’s arrival at Stanford. But his early Stanford-era studies used the power of parallel computing to extend it to optimize full aircraft configurations – including wings, fuselages, engine nacelles, and pylons – under multiple operating conditions and constraints.
Jameson and his Stanford collaborators then extended the approach to simulations that accounted for air’s viscosity. In a 2004 paper, his group applied it to the wings, flaps, and slats used during takeoff and landing, where air moves through narrow gaps between surfaces. Other studies coupled aerodynamic and structural calculations, allowing researchers to alter a wing’s overall planform while accounting for its weight, flexibility, and performance in several flight conditions.
Later at Stanford, Jameson pursued high-order methods, which represented airflow more precisely within each section of a computational grid. Because the calculations demanded enormous computing power, he was early to using graphics processing units (GPUs) to perform many calculations at once, accelerating the work.
A 2018 study with Jacob Crabill (PhD ’18) and Freddie Witherden combined these methods with overlapping grids and GPU-oriented algorithms to simulate airflow over a spinning golf ball, tracking its rotation and the flow around individual dimples. The example demonstrated that the methods could handle moving, complex surfaces under realistic conditions.
Throughout his career, Jameson remained a hands-on programmer, testing new methods on his own computer. Sanjiva Lele, the Edward C. Wells Professor in the School of Engineering and a professor of mechanical engineering and of aeronautics and astronautics at Stanford, said Jameson often recognized computing trends early. “Tony could see where the field was going to go, and that’s what he would work on,” Lele said.
At Stanford, Jameson created an advanced computational fluid dynamics course sequence that taught the methods he used in his research. Students trained in it went on to university posts and careers in aerospace and software companies, Alonso said. Most spring quarters, he also organized Stanford’s Case Studies in Aerospace Design seminar series, where leading designers explained how landmark aircraft were developed.
Jameson also contributed to Stanford’s Center for Integrated Turbulence Simulations, established in 1997 as part of the Department of Energy’s Accelerated Strategic Computing Initiative. Over the program’s decade-long run, the center helped expand simulations from relatively modest systems to hundreds of thousands of processors and entire jet engines, Alonso said. Jameson’s 2022 book, Computational Aerodynamics, distilled the mathematical and practical knowledge he had developed and taught over his decades at Stanford.
Jameson became emeritus in 2018 and joined Texas A&M University as a professor of aerospace engineering and ocean engineering, where he continued researching and teaching into his 90s. At a Stanford symposium honoring his 90th birthday, “Tony was attending and asking questions, as usual,” Lele said. “He was sharp.”
About a month before Jameson’s death, Alonso visited with him at Texas A&M. “I had lunch with him and chatted about research,” Alonso said. “I think he enjoyed what he did so much that he still wanted to spend time doing it at age 91.”
Over his career, Jameson authored or co-authored more than 500 scientific papers. His honors included the Daniel Guggenheim Medal, the Elmer A. Sperry Award, the Royal Aeronautical Society Gold Medal, and election as a fellow of the Royal Society and a foreign member of the National Academy of Engineering. The U.S. Association for Computational Mechanics awarded him the John von Neumann Medal, and he was an Honorary Fellow of the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics.
Outside the lab, Jameson was athletic. He would play squash with Alonso and students on Sunday mornings and watch soccer and football games. He read voraciously about economics and world affairs. He was also a gifted storyteller whose wide-ranging conversations could move easily from aircraft to exchange rates, inflation, and international trade.
Jameson is survived by his wife, Charlotte Ansted-Jameson; five children; and multiple grandchildren.

title: Sergiu Pasca elected to the National Academy of Medicine
summary: The professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences joins the prestigious medical association.
text:
The National Academy of Medicine has elected Sergiu Pasca, MD, the Kenneth T. Norris, Jr. Professor II of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, to its membership — one of the highest honors in medicine.
Pasca, who is also the Bonnie Uytengsu and Family Director of the Stanford Brain Organogenesis Program, was chosen “for seminal contributions to the development and study of brain organoids and assembloids that have provided a new understanding of human brain development and plasticity as well as brain dysfunction in disorders such as autism and schizophrenia,” according to the academy.
“I am incredibly honored to be elected to the National Academy of Medicine,” Pasca said. “This recognition reflects the work of many talented trainees and wonderful collaborators with whom I have had the privilege of working. This is an especially exciting time for human stem cell neuroscience, as new approaches are allowing us to study the human brain in ways that were simply not possible before. These advances are opening new opportunities to understand human brain development and disease, and, importantly, to develop therapeutics for devastating neurological and psychiatric disorders.”
Pasca is among the 90 regular members and 10 international members elected this year to the academy, which provides independent, scientifically informed analyses and recommendations on health and biomedical sciences to policymakers, business leaders and the public. Members elected to the academy have demonstrated outstanding professional achievement and commitment to service.
Each year, the academy chooses new members from a list of nominees, basing the selection on publications and research grants that show high levels of accomplishment.
“I am grateful to Stanford for providing an environment where ambitious ideas can be pursued, and particularly excited about the progress we are making toward translating some of these discoveries into the clinic,” Pasca said.
Pasca is a member of Bio-X, the Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute and the Maternal and Child Health Research Institute; he is also a faculty fellow at Sarafan ChEM-H and a senior fellow (by courtesy) at the Hoover Institution.

title: The future of social hierarchies
summary: A professor who studies workplace hierarchies and human well-being says that collaboration is key to healthy work environments.
text:
The future of social hierarchies
Nir Halevy, an expert on organizational behavior, first grew interested in social hierarchies as a basketball fan.
He now studies what makes for healthy workplaces. Organizational hierarchies can be beneficial, but can turn toxic. When people have power without status – control but little respect – conflict often follows. Halevy says that collaboration, not competition, is key to employee well-being. “If you care about freedom, seek cooperative environments. They will liberate you,” Halevy tells listeners – and host Russ Altman – on this episode of Stanford Engineering’s The Future of Everything podcast.
