title: New genetic study reveals surprising origin of Native Hawaiians
summary: The first settlers of Hawaii were the most capable sailors of their time, crossing 7,000 kilometers of open ocean to reach their new home.
text:
Europe was deep in the Middle Ages when halfway around the world, on the remote, windswept shores of tiny Easter Island, a group of skilled seafarers prepared for a long voyage. They stocked their double-hulled catamarans with taro, sweet potato and bananas — food for many weeks at sea, but also, they hoped, to plant on a distant land they would make their new home.
There is no written record of their journey, but Stanford Medicine researchers and collaborators analyzing the genomes of modern-day Polynesians have discovered indelible genetic evidence that ancient sailors from this region did settle a faraway land. To the researcher’s surprise, their new home was Hawaii, some 7,000 kilometers away, among the most distant Polynesian islands from Easter Island.
The findings are reported in a study published Oct. 8 in Science.
“What we uncover in this paper is where the native people of Hawaii had come from,” said Alexander Ioannidis, PhD, assistant professor of genetics and of biomedical data science, and co-senior author of the study. “Hawaii is the only Polynesian island in the Northern Hemisphere, so it’s a long way from everything.”
The other co-senior author is Keolu Fox, PhD, an associate professor of anthropology at the University of California, San Diego, and a Native Hawaiian.
Polynesia consists of more than 1,000 islands spread over an area of the Pacific Ocean roughly equivalent to the areas of North and South America combined. Tropical, lush Hawaii is about as far away from temperate Easter Island in the far south Pacific as San Francisco is from Lima, Peru.
But the new findings do more than help reconstruct the settlement of Polynesia and add to evidence of an ancient ultravoyaging culture — they also identify genetic bottlenecks that have profound implications for precision medicine and disease risks among modern Polynesians.
Founder effects
These genetic bottlenecks are known as founder effects when they result from a small portion of a population separating and founding a new population. This narrowing of the gene pool can amplify the frequency of otherwise rare genetic variants, sometimes linked to disease. Founder effects have been well studied in groups of European descent like the Amish, the Ashkenazi Jews and the Finns, resulting in standard screenings for certain genetic conditions in these groups.
The new study reveals that an even stronger founder effect has been overlooked among Native Hawaiians.
“What we discovered is in the Eastern Polynesians, such as Native Hawaiians, the founder effects are more than an order of magnitude, so more than 10 times, larger than what we have in the populations of European descent we’ve studied so well,” Ioannidis said.
That’s because Native Hawaiians sit at the end of a long sequence of genetic bottlenecks as their ancestors sent off small groups, perhaps only a few hundred individuals at a time, to settle new islands over the course of a few centuries.
An earlier genetic study by the researchers had traced the settlement of Polynesia from Samoa to Fiji and Tonga, then gradually eastward to the Cook Islands, the Society Islands (including Tahiti), Mangareva and ultimately Easter Island around the year 1210. But the longest journey was still to come.
“We thought Easter Island was the end when we were first doing that study, but now it looks like it was part of this path to Hawaii, which is really incredible,” Ioannidis said. “By the time you’ve gotten all the way to Hawaii, you’re at the end of a series of founder effects, so it’s really intense.”
Encoded genealogy
The researchers made their latest discovery by analyzing the genomes of over 1,000 individuals throughout Polynesia.
“People on the islands today have encoded in their genomes essentially the genealogy of all of their ancestors,” Ioannidis said.
They focused on genome segments of Polynesian ancestry, removing more recent additions of European and Asian ancestry, for example. They compared the length of chromosomal segments, known as identity-by-descent segments, shared among people from different islands. The longer the shared segments between two people, the more recently they shared a common ancestor.
They found that Hawaiians share the most Polynesian ancestry with people on Easter Island, followed by people on Mangareva, an island nearly 3,000 kilometers west of Easter Island. Though no one had connected these distant dots previously, it makes sense that an ultravoyaging culture capable of reaching Easter Island from Mangareva would be the one to then settle Hawaii, Ioannidis said. (An earlier study by the researchers found that members of the same ultravoyaging population also reached South America and came in contact with Native Americans.)
The team also conducted a more detailed genomic analysis of people from Tahiti, the island for which they had the most genomes. By comparing identity-by-descent segments within the population, they could estimate the size and date of the founding generation — a group of approximately 800 people who arrived on the island about 34 generations ago, around the year 1070. (The population estimate is of a single generation of reproductive age and doesn’t include children and elders they may have brought along.)
“Archaeologists and others have long wondered how many people founded these islands. That’s not something that you can determine definitively from archaeology, but we can determine it from genetics,” Ioannidis said.
The genomic analysis also reconstructed the rapid population growth on Tahiti after the initial settlement and a significant population crash in the 1700s following European colonial contact.
“This is a population that should be getting research resources and attention from geneticists even more urgently.”
—Alexander Ioannidis
The researchers are working on similar reconstructions for Easter Island and Hawaii, which will require more genomes.
Clinical urgency
But more pressing is the need for large-scale genomic studies to identify clinically relevant variants that may be unusually prevalent among Polynesians.
The researchers analyzed three variants that recently have been linked to autosomal recessive conditions (requiring two copies of the gene) among Eastern Polynesians: ADAMTSL4, which can cause dislocated lens in the eyes; PDE6B, which can cause progressive vision loss; and FAN1, which can lead to kidney failure.
These variants are exceedingly rare among the global population and hardly present in international genome databases, but they are carried by 2% to 3% of the Eastern Polynesians studied. That level meets standard thresholds for genetic screening recommendations.
“We should be doing more sequencing and trying to characterize more of these conditions among Native Hawaiians,” said Ioannidis, noting that the Native Hawaiian population is nearly twice the size of the Amish population, yet still lacks genetic testing guidelines. “We don’t have recommendations for genetic testing, and there’s no reimbursement from insurance because these are conditions we don’t even know about.”
“This is a population that should be getting research resources and attention from geneticists even more urgently.”
Researchers from the University of California, Santa Cruz; Variant Bio; Direction de la Santé de Polynésie Française in Tahiti; Hôpital Saint-Philibert in France; the University of Chile; the National Polytechnic Institute in Mexico; and the University of Alabama at Birmingham contributed to the study.
The study received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grants T32HG012344, U01HG007417 and U01HG007419).

title: Gut microbes across continents trace ancient human migration
summary: A study of the microbiome of groups in Africa and South America indicates that diverse gut microbes joined us as we migrated out of Africa — a diversity that is lost among industrialized peoples.
text:
As waves of humans left Africa tens of thousands of years ago, eventually populating the entire planet, they were joined on their world-conquering ride by the trillions of microorganisms that compose the gut microbiome. These bacteria, viruses and fungi in our intestines play essential roles in enabling our bodies to function properly, from digesting fibrous food to making vitamins and training our immune systems.
The microbiome has emerged as a focus of intense study due to evidence that lifestyle impacts its composition, which in turn can affect health. People living in industrialized countries show a profound loss of microbiome diversity compared with people living non-industrialized lifestyles. People in industrialized countries suffer from autoimmune diseases, Type 2 diabetes, obesity and other chronic conditions that are rare among non-industrialized groups, raising the important but still unresolved question of whether microbiome loss contributes to these diseases.
A new study published Oct. 7 in Nature and led by Stanford University researchers has attempted to answer the question of whether homo sapiens hosted a characteristic and diverse microbiome going back millennia. Gaining insight into which, if any, long-term residents of the microbiome co-evolved with humans could point to ways to investigate how the loss of microbial diversity through industrialization impacts human biology.
For their study, the researchers conducted the first-ever deep comparison of the microbiomes of the Hadza in Tanzania — one of the world’s few remaining hunter-gatherer groups — and the Tsimane, indigenous forager-horticulturalists living in the Bolivian Amazon whose lifestyles have had comparatively limited exposure to industrialization. Although the ancestral human populations that gave rise to the two groups became geographically separated tens of thousands of years ago, the Hadza and Tsimane share over 1,200 bacterial species, nearly 90% of which were identified in the highly diverse Tsimane microbiomes. Most of those species — about 60% — are rare or completely absent in industrialized populations’ microbiomes.
Using several complementary population genetics analysis techniques, the researchers estimated when microbial strains separated. For many species, those estimates correspond to the time frame of major prehistoric human migrations out of Africa and into the Americas. The ultimate takeaway: Many microbial lineages in these contemporary populations have deep evolutionary roots extending back through ancient human migrations.
“Our study establishes that the hundreds of bacterial species that are rare or missing in industrialized microbiomes were ancient companions of ours as we migrated around the globe, likely passed from generation to generation for millennia,” said Justin Sonnenburg, PhD, a professor of microbiology and immunology, the Alex and Susie Algard Endowed Professor, and the study’s senior author. “This long-term association has implications for how such recent biodiversity loss in our microbiome may impact our biology and thus our health.”
Deep genomic analysis
For the study, the researchers used deep metagenomic sequencing, a method that characterizes the microbes present in a sample by reading out all the letters of the building blocks of DNA present. Millions of small sequences of DNA are generated with overlapping stretches of letters indicating where the small sequences match up into longer sequences. Those long sequences are then compared with databases of microbial genomes to identify the detected organism.
The Tsimane Health and Life History Project team, who are collaborators on the study, had obtained voluntary stool samples from the Tsimane. Sonnenburg and colleagues previously completed a metagenomic sequencing on Hadza samples — reported in a 2023 Cell study — showing, among other findings, that the average Hadza individual has about 750 species in their microbiome, while the average Californian has a mere 250. For the new study, the Stanford University researchers did the first deep sequencing of the Tsimane samples, which had previously been sequenced only at low resolution (in the 2020 Nature Communications study).
The sequencing efforts enabled the researchers to build a comprehensive census of the microbes in the respective microbiomes, including hard-to-capture, low-abundance species. Overall, the sampled Tsimane individuals hosted about 1,400 different species; they shared a total of 1,231 of these species (about 90%) with the Hadza, according to the new analysis.
“We were really surprised to see that the vast majority of the species in the Tsimane’s microbiome correspond with the Hadza’s,” Sonnenburg said.
Different lifestyles, similar results
Some of that surprise stems from the considerably different diets between the two groups. The Hadza hunt meat from mammals including impala and porcupine, along with birds and fish, and forage for fruits and vegetables including tubers and berries. The Tsimane instead grow much of their food and consume high levels of fiber through plantains, rice, manioc root and corn, along with lean meat from fish, peccary and other forest animals.
Additionally, the two groups have been separated for tens of thousands of years. Despite this geographic and lifestyle separation, the two microbiomes showed a high level of overlap at the species level.
“That made us wonder if there really is a core set of bacterial and other species that traveled with the ancestors of the Tsimane as they migrated around the globe,” said Benjamin Good, PhD, the study’s senior co-author and an assistant professor of applied physics who specializes in investigating evolutionary dynamics and population genetics of the human gut microbiome.
“Could these bugs have been in continual interaction with us since long before the ancestors of today’s Hadza and Tsimane became geographically separated?” Sonnenburg asked. “To answer that, we turned to Ben’s team, and what they found blew our minds.”
- Addiction
An interwoven biology goes way back
Unpacking the evolutionary history of a microbiome overall has proven daunting given complexities posed by how quickly microbes evolve and the changes a given person’s microbiome can undergo from season to season, or based on other aspects of food availability.
Good’s group sought to get around these issues. Bacteria complicate evolutionary reconstruction because they not only inherit DNA from their direct ancestors as they clone themselves to reproduce, but also frequently exchange DNA with other strains in a process known as horizontal gene transfer. The researchers therefore looked for several independent genomic signatures to distinguish deep shared ancestry from more recent microbial exchange. Looking at mutation rates in vertically inherited DNA also helped estimate when species diverged from a common ancestor because mutations accumulate at a steady pace, like ticks of a clock.
That analysis squarely indicated that many of the shared bacterial species between the non-industrialized groups’ microbiomes have evolutionary histories that trace back over thousands of years. These detailed analyses of genetic isolation of strains produced time estimates consistent with the major human migrations. “We see evidence that these bacteria were present in the ancestors of both the Tsimane and the Hadza, and therefore presumably the ancestors of all of us,” Good said.
The researchers said the findings highlight an important hypothesis: If humans interacted with many of these organisms for tens of thousands of years, what happens when industrialization eliminates a large portion of them over just a few generations? Previous work in the field links changes in microbiomes to many disease states. Dramatic changes to our resident microbial populations — attributed to antibiotic exposure; low-fiber, high-fat and -sugar diets of processed food; highly sanitized living conditions; and other factors — could be incompatible with the biology encoded in our human genomes. The biological consequences of this recent biodiversity loss is an important target for future study.
The Stanford University researchers plan to continue investigating the history of our microbiome and its links to health and well-being.
“If these microbes hosted by the Hadza and Tsimane really are part of our evolutionary biology, then those of us in industrialized countries are missing a huge part of what our human genome has potentially adapted to over a vast time period,” Sonnenburg said. “We’re interested in more fully exploring these long-standing relationships between humans and our gut microbes.”
Researchers from the University of Colorado; the University of California, Santa Barbara; the University of Washington; Wake Forest University School of Medicine; Arizona State University; Chapman University; Toulouse School of Economics; Universidad Mayor San Simeon; Veterans Affairs Palo Alto Health System; and Chan Zuckerberg Biohub contributed to the study.
This study was funded by Open Philanthropy, a Stanford Bio-X Bowes Fellowship, the National Institutes of Health/National Institute on Aging (grants R01-AG054442 and R35- GM146949), the National Science Foundation, the Wenner-Gren Foundation, the Thomas C. and Joan M. Merigan Endowment at Stanford University, and the French National Research Agency under the Investments for the Future (Investissements d’Avenir) program.

title: Patrick Hsu receives early career prize for rewriting and redesigning genomes
summary: Pathology professor Patrick Hsu’s $250,000 prize will accelerate the development of new gene-editing tools and artificial intelligence models that can identify disease-causing mutations.
text:
Patrick Hsu, PhD, assistant professor of pathology, has been named a laureate of the 2026 Blavatnik National Award for Young Scientists in life sciences by the Blavatnik Family Foundation and The New York Academy of Sciences.
Hsu is being recognized for his work developing a new class of tools for rewriting the genetic code and the largest machine learning model of genomes. The annual awards, given to U.S.-based researchers aged 42 and younger, support scientists early in their careers.
“Biologists have spent a century learning to read biological information, but with AI, it’s now possible to design a DNA sequence and predict what it will do before writing it into living cells for lab testing,” said Hsu, who is also a co-founder and core investigator at the Arc Institute, a nonprofit research organization in Palo Alto, California, that combines artificial intelligence and biology to understand the causes of complex diseases. “This recognition belongs to a lot of people in my lab and across the field.”
Hsu has spent his career looking for the next generation of programmable molecular systems. He was an early pioneer of CRISPR-Cas9, a precise gene editing tool, as a graduate student at Harvard University and the Broad Institute.
In 2024, Hsu and colleagues announced the discovery of a new kind of RNA-guided enzyme they called bridge recombinases. Where a CRISPR enzyme is guided to a single site and makes a cut, a bridge recombinase is guided to two sites by a self-encoded bridge RNA, the first known example of a bispecific guide RNA that recognizes the target sequence to be changed and the donor sequence to be installed. The bridge recombinase then holds both together while it joins them.
“This award is a testament to Patrick’s curiosity and ambition working at the cutting edge of genetics and artificial intelligence,” said Lloyd Minor, MD, the Carl and Elizabeth Naumann Dean of the School of Medicine and vice president for medical affairs at Stanford University. “He leads by example, seeking to understand human biology at its most fundamental level, and exhibits the hallmarks of an explorer and scientist whose discoveries could one day lead to curing or eliminating genetic disorders and diseases.”
Because both binding sites of the bridge RNA are programmable, bridge recombinases can swap in, cut out or flip stretches of DNA on much larger scales than what is possible with CRISPR.
“Rather than changing individual mutations or single genes with CRISPR, bridge recombinases can rearrange entire regions of DNA,” Hsu said. “Patients with the same genetic disorder often have very different mutations located in different parts of the disease-associated gene. Because bridge editing can replace the whole genomic region, it no longer depends on fixing each variant separately.”
If bridge recombinases can install a genetic sequence, Hsu’s machine learning work helps determine what to install. Evo 2, a genome foundation model he and collaborators published this year, can flag which mutations in a stretch of DNA are likely to cause disease, including in the noncoding regions that other methods overlook, and it does so without being trained for that specific task. Evo 2 can also work in the other direction, generating new functional sequences rather than just evaluating existing ones.
The unrestricted $250,000 award will support Hsu’s efforts to discover and improve molecular tools for rewriting DNA. Better genome language models will guide where those tools go, and better tools will make the sequences those models design possible to build.
“The overall long-term impact of our work is taking biology from what has historically been a primarily guess-and-check, experimental discipline into a predictive, model-guided, engineering discipline,” Hsu said. “We’re tremendously excited to take on this design problem.”
